items.model_answer:
If Russia had modernized earlier and more thoroughly—roughly in the mid-to-late 19th century rather than only partially before 1914—the likely result would have been a more stable, wealthier, and militarily effective Russian state, with a reduced chance of the 1917 revolutions occurring in the form they did.

The key issue is that Imperial Russia did modernize, but unevenly. The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 was a major reform, yet it left many peasants burdened by redemption payments and land hunger. Industrialization accelerated under Sergei Witte in the 1890s, but it was late, state-driven, and concentrated in a few urban centers. Political modernization lagged even further: the autocracy resisted meaningful constitutional government, and the Duma created after 1905 remained weak. This created a dangerous imbalance: Russia developed factories, railways, educated professionals, and mass politics without developing institutions capable of peacefully absorbing social conflict.

A more thorough modernization would probably have required several things: genuine land reform, broad education, a professional and less corrupt bureaucracy, stronger local government, industrial expansion earlier in the century, and some form of constitutional monarchy or representative politics. If these had taken root by, say, the 1870s or 1880s, Russia might have resembled a more conservative version of Germany or Japan: authoritarian in some respects, but administratively capable, industrializing fast, and better able to mobilize society.

Domestically, this would likely have reduced revolutionary pressures. A peasantry with more secure landownership and fewer crushing obligations would have been less explosive. A larger middle class and more representative institutions might have given liberals, professionals, workers, and national minorities legal channels for political participation. Revolutionary socialism would still have existed, but it might have remained marginal rather than becoming a mass alternative after state collapse.

Economically, earlier modernization could have made Russia one of the dominant industrial powers by the early 20th century. Russia had enormous resources, a large population, and strategic depth. With better railways, literacy, agricultural productivity, banking, and industrial capacity, it could have narrowed the gap with Germany and Britain. A more productive agricultural sector would also have freed labor for industry without creating the same level of rural misery.

Militarily, the consequences could have been dramatic. Russia’s defeats in the Crimean War and Russo-Japanese War exposed weaknesses in logistics, command, technology, and administration. Earlier modernization might have prevented or softened those humiliations. In World War I, a more modern Russia would have been better supplied, better led, and better able to coordinate transport and production. That does not guarantee victory, but it makes the catastrophic breakdown of 1915–1917 less likely.

The biggest geopolitical effect might have been on Europe before and during World War I. A stronger Russia could have deterred Germany and Austria-Hungary, possibly making a general European war less likely. Alternatively, it could have made Germany feel encircled earlier and act more aggressively sooner. If World War I still occurred, a modernized Russia might have stayed in the war, making a German victory in the east impossible and perhaps shortening the conflict. Without the collapse of the Russian monarchy and the Bolshevik seizure of power, there may have been no Soviet Union, no Russian Civil War in its historical form, and no global communist movement centered on Moscow.

However, modernization would not have solved every problem. Russia’s size, ethnic diversity, autocratic traditions, and social inequalities were major obstacles. Nationalist tensions in Poland, Finland, Ukraine, the Caucasus, and Central Asia would still have posed challenges. Rapid industrialization could still have produced labor unrest. A constitutional Russia might have faced instability similar to other multiethnic empires.

The most plausible counterfactual outcome is not a liberal democratic Russia overnight, but a stronger constitutional or semi-constitutional empire: more like Imperial Germany or Meiji Japan than like Britain or France. Such a Russia would probably have avoided the extreme rupture of 1917 and might have become the dominant land power in Eurasia. The 20th century would likely have been less shaped by Bolshevism, Soviet totalitarianism, and the Cold War, though it might still have been marked by great-power rivalry, nationalism, and authoritarian politics.

items.question: What If Britain and France made peace in 1811?
human_answers: I definitely agree that the conflict in Spain would continue, and that some form of renewed conflict in Europe down the line is inevitable, but I don’t think Napoleon wouldn’t try to conclude a peace with Britain, so long as it was on terms favourable to him. Now, whether that is possible is a rather different question. The Whigs at least had no interest in continuing to fund the peninsular war regardless, but in negotiations, they are likely to push for a restoration of Portugal and Hannover, and for France to at least withdraw from direct control of the rest of the Hanseatic cities and the Netherlands. It’s quite a lot for Napoleon to be willing to give up, though could possibly be paired with his longstanding designs on Sicily and a British withdrawal from Malta, as well as the return of occupied Dutch and French colonies. Regardless, I don’t think the British could get everything they want.

No mention has been made of the Continental System. I presume it is abolished as part of the peace treaty. And Britain's blockade is lifted. Anything less makes peace a non starter. Predictions from here: Overall peace is going to be short lived. Every one will be watching France waiting for a propitious moment to reduce the almost total hegemony France has. Nap will maintain a large military to enforce his hegemony. I don't know that this is sustainable. Spain will remain a bleeding ulcer. The Spanish people will continue to resist. Nap's best chance at lasting peace is to pull out and return a Bourbon to power. Remaining in a constant state of this kind of war drains resources, but brings no benefits. The best he can hope for (remaining in the conflict) is an uneasy truce where Joseph is somewhat accepted/propped up, while a low level of guerilla warfare continues. The entire Spanish colonial sphere is lost even faster than OTL. Cuba/puerto rico might remain attached, but I doubt it. I don't know whether Britain has destroyed Spain's infrastructure yet, but if not, Spain could actually emerge from the conflict in better shape without Britain's help than with it. Portugal might be able to hold out behind the line of T, as their soldiers have been trained up to a better level than before 1807, but as the British had supplied the top chain of command, they'll be left rudderless. I think their fate lies in how much stomach Nap has for continuing his Iberian adventure. It would be interesting to see what results if Nap simply walks away. OTL, the British acted as a regency while the Braganza court remained in Brazil. Joao did not want to return. Pedro was too young. Portugal is likely to be chaos. Should France manage to take control, Portugal itself may end up in better shape, but the entirety of the colonial sphere attaches to Brazil. I don't think the return of French colonies does much for France. Haiti is finished as a rich colony. Martinique and Guadeloupe, where Britain ironically enforced the status quo maintaining the slave system after capturing the islands, might still hold value. When the Nap Wars resume, Britain faces a hard choice - join in and try to reset the balance of power, or stay on the sidelines and have the European dynamic dictated to them. If they join in, they're quickly going to regret dropping out in the first place. They had France on the ropes in Portugal/Spain, and now they'll have to start all over again. Who knows what has become of Wellington.

The default of the Revolution certainly left its mark, but Napoleon was also ideologically opposed to debt, in part because of fiscal conservatism (there was a hyperinflation crisis during the Revolution), but also because it would have meant making himself dependent on the financial market, and he feared that the banker would try to exert political pressure on him. But I don't think he necessarily tried to raise a large amount of debt from the public market, he preferred to use a sinking fund controlled by one of his appointees for that. For the reparation, he had ways to force the issue, like sending his army in and making the host pay for its quartering. This was the way he was making his puppets, like the Kingdom of Italy, contribute, and alongside their allied contingent, it saved him as much money as the reparations brought him. For Prussia specifically, they were raising a large debt to pay the reparation, with Napoleon himself being one of their creditors, so they probably intended to pay. But you also have to take into account that Napoleon did not hesitate too much to raise taxes (he essentially brought back every indirect tax of the Ancien Régime) or defer payment, after the Restoration, the Bourbons had to pay the equivalent of one year of fiscal revenues in unpaid expenses.
items.original_question: What if Britain and France made peace in 1811? In 1810 King George III suffered a mental breakdown, and in early 1811, his son the Prince of Wales, later to reign as King George IV, was installed as regent by Parliament. The Prince Regent was widely expected to dismiss Spencer Percival’s government, and appoint Lord Grenville as Prime Minister, but was dissuaded from this course by his mother. Unlike the Tories, Grenville and the Whigs were sceptical of the conflict with France, particularly the expense of maintaining Wellington’s army in the Peninsula War, and had they taken power in 1811, whilst Wellesley’s army was holed up behind the lines of Torres Vedras, attempts at negotiating a peace with France are not an unrealistic prospect. Negotiations in 1807 touted an exchange of Sicily for Hannover, and Britain would retain the Cape Colony and Malta, whilst returning other Dutch and French colonial possessions, though these ultimately broke down over Sicily. Talks in 1808 even saw Napoleon offer to concede both Hannover and Portugal, though there is some question of how serious both sides were in this later negotiation. Both of these were also viewed by the Tory governments as a chance for a respite alike to Amiens, rather than to conclude the conflict. The Whigs, less intractable towards the idea of a French dominated Europe would be willing to pursue a long term peace. In addition to questions over Portugal, Hannover and the colonies though, France had by this point annexed the Netherlands and the Hanseatic cities, both of which are likely to be sticking points for British negotiators (although these annexations were in part to enforce the continental system). What terms could realistically be feasibly agreed by both sides at this time? With the end of the war with Britain in 1811, Napoleon’s invasion of Russia appears unlikely to my mind, though relations between the two emperors would undoubtedly continue to deteriorate. The peace would also presumably be unpopular domestically in Britain, where support for the war remained high. Austria, Prussia and Sweden all additionally had cause to want revenge against France and Napoleon, and so it seems unlikely that this peace would be entirely conclusive, and some form of renewed conflict seems eventually likely, even if it only comes with Bonaparte’s death. The aftermath of Amiens however suggests that this might well come sooner. There is however also the question of whether France could afford to maintain their precarious financial situation, and in particular continue to field their army without the subsides of allies, the reparations of former enemies and loot. It seems unlikely France can afford to demobilise in the face of their European rivals, so would this possibly prompt further campaigns? Perhaps against Russia regardless or the Ottomans?
items.model_answer:
If Britain and France made peace in 1811, the most likely result would be the survival of Napoleon’s empire for much longer, not a permanent end to Anglo-French rivalry.

A plausible peace in 1811 would have looked like a second Treaty of Amiens: Britain would recognize, at least temporarily, French dominance over much of continental Europe, while France would accept British naval and colonial superiority. Britain would probably keep many of its overseas gains and its command of the seas; Napoleon would keep his satellite kingdoms and influence over the Netherlands, Italy, western Germany, and perhaps Spain. Neither side would truly trust the other, but both had reasons to pause: Britain was under financial and military strain, and Napoleon’s Continental System was damaging Europe and worsening his conflict with Russia.

The biggest immediate change would be in the Peninsular War. Without British money, supplies, and Wellington’s army in Portugal and Spain, resistance to French rule in Iberia would be much weaker. Spanish guerrilla warfare would probably continue, but it would be far harder to sustain. Napoleon might have been able either to consolidate Joseph Bonaparte’s rule in Spain or negotiate some compromise that left France dominant there. Portugal, dependent on Britain, would be especially vulnerable unless its independence were guaranteed in the peace terms.

The second major change is that Napoleon might not invade Russia in 1812. The breakdown between France and Russia was closely tied to the Continental System, which tried to close Europe to British trade. If Britain and France made peace, the need for that system would diminish. Russia would have less reason to defy Napoleon economically, and Napoleon would have less reason to coerce Russia. Without the Russian campaign, there would likely be no catastrophic destruction of the Grande Armée, no Sixth Coalition victory in 1813–14, no first abdication, and no Waterloo.

That means the Napoleonic order could have become semi-permanent. France would dominate western and central Europe; Austria and Prussia would remain weakened and cautious; Russia would remain powerful but more isolated; Britain would concentrate on empire, finance, and maritime trade. The map of Europe after 1815 would be entirely different because there would be no Congress of Vienna settlement as we know it. German and Italian unification might still happen later, but under very different pressures, possibly with stronger French influence.

There would also be wider effects. The War of 1812 between Britain and the United States would be less likely, because many of the maritime issues driving it came from the Anglo-French war. Latin American independence might proceed differently too: the crisis of the Spanish monarchy had already begun, but if French control in Spain stabilized and Britain was no longer fighting France, Spanish American revolutions might receive less favorable external conditions.

Still, such a peace would probably be unstable. Britain had long feared any single power controlling the Low Countries, Antwerp, and the Channel coast. Napoleon, for his part, was unlikely to accept a world in which Britain dominated the seas and overseas commerce indefinitely. A truce might last several years, perhaps even a decade, especially if trade revived and neither side wanted renewed war. But the underlying conflict—French continental hegemony versus British maritime and commercial supremacy—would remain.

So the direct answer is: peace in 1811 would probably have prevented Napoleon’s disastrous Russian campaign, prolonged the French Empire, weakened Iberian resistance, and avoided the 1813–15 collapse of Napoleonic France. But it would more likely have postponed the final struggle between Britain and France than ended it permanently.

In this TL, during the reign of Möngke Khan, the Mongol Empire invaded Europe again instead of attacking the Abbasid Caliphate. Assume that, starting with the Kingdom of Hungary, they continue pushing westward into the Holy Roman Empire, France, and beyond Western Europe for as long as they keep winning. What I’m curious about is this: 1. What kind of POD would be needed for this to be possible? 2. To what extent would this actually be feasible? - Could the Mongol Empire conquer Western Europe as well, just as it did in Eastern Europe? - Or, unlike in Eastern Europe, would it struggle in Western Europe? 3. items.model_answer:
If the Mongol Empire had directed its main western effort into Western Europe rather than the Levant, the most likely result would have been a devastating but incomplete conquest: large parts of Central Europe could have been ravaged or made tributary, but a durable Mongol conquest of all Western Europe would have been difficult.

In open battle, mid-thirteenth-century European armies were badly suited to fight the Mongols. The battles of Legnica and Mohi in 1241 showed that Polish, German, Hungarian, and knightly forces could be outmaneuvered and destroyed by Mongol cavalry, feigned retreats, coordinated columns, and superior operational mobility. If the Mongols had continued west with full imperial backing, Hungary, Poland, Bohemia, Austria, and parts of Germany would likely have suffered enormous destruction. Some rulers might have submitted and paid tribute rather than risk annihilation.

But Western Europe was not an ideal conquest zone for the Mongols. The farther west they went, the more they faced forests, mountains, rivers, dense towns, stone castles, and less suitable pasture for their horses. France, northern Italy, the Alps, the Low Countries, Iberia, and Britain posed different logistical problems from the Eurasian steppe. The Mongols could defeat field armies and besiege cities, especially with Chinese and Persian siege engineers, but holding hundreds of fortified towns and castles would have required garrisons, supply lines, and political administration on a scale that reduced their greatest advantage: mobility.

So the likely outcome is that Central Europe would have become a devastated frontier or tribute zone, while Western Europe proper—France, England, Iberia, and perhaps much of Italy—would probably not have been fully absorbed into the empire. The Mongols might have reached the Rhine, northern Italy, or even raided into France, but permanent rule west of the Danube and the German plains would have been much harder.

Politically, the invasion could have transformed Europe. The papacy would probably have declared a crusade against the Mongols. Rivalries between France, England, the Holy Roman Empire, and Italian states might have weakened resistance at first, but fear of Mongol conquest could also have encouraged greater military coordination. European monarchies might have centralized faster, raising taxes and building stronger armies to respond to the crisis. Castles, walled towns, crossbowmen, infantry formations, and eventually gunpowder weapons might have gained importance sooner.

The Levant and the Islamic world would also have changed. If Mongol attention shifted away from Syria and Palestine, the Mamluks of Egypt would have faced less pressure and might have remained the dominant military power in the eastern Mediterranean. The Crusader states might have survived a little longer as buffer states, but without Mongol pressure on the Muslims, they would still have been vulnerable to the Mamluks. If the counterfactual also means no Mongol assault on Baghdad and the wider Middle East, then Islamic political and intellectual history would be altered even more dramatically.

The biggest limiting factor would still have been Mongol politics. The empire’s campaigns often depended on the death or election of Great Khans, and internal rivalries repeatedly redirected armies. Even a successful invasion of Western Europe might have stalled once succession disputes began. In that sense, the Mongols could probably have shattered Western European armies and forced tribute from some regions, but turning Paris, London, Rome, or Toledo into stable parts of a Mongol imperial system is much less likely.

items.question: What If Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop?
human_answers: I can easily see Quebec not wanting to be part of either France, or USA. So they'll opt for independence. France never really wanted it back, so they won't get into their own American Revolution. Even if they did, it is the cost that will impact the French Revolution. The cost will add to French woes. This notion that France will rise up in revolution because Quebec wants independence is erroneous. France wanted regime/gov't change, which is not at all what Quebec wants (independence). France will add Quebec to the list of grievances. That does NOT make Quebec the birthplace of this alt FR. There were various causes of the ARW. One of them was putting Ohio under Canadian jurisdiction. Plus the French and Indian War was fought over the Ohio Valley, and led to a lot of the grievances leading to ARW. It is difficult to ascertain how the French in Canada felt, as they lived in a quasi-medieval subsistence economy. Although not under full-blown feudalism, their society was paternalistic, hierarchical, and agrarian. The Church and the seigneurs (many of the seigneuries were owned by religious orders) were the pillars of authority. This is crucial in explaining the lack of widespread revolutionary fervour. However, in the late eighteenth century, there remained a cultural and sentimental connection to France, particularly to the Ancien Régime and the monarchy. After the executions of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, masses were said for them, and the French press in Quebec noted this. They were mourning the grandson of their last French sovereign, not celebrating the secular republic that executed him. In December 1778, from Boston, French Admiral d’Estaing called on the Canadiens to rise and rejoin their motherland, but this was difficult as Canada was where most British forces were stationed. It is unclear whether they wished to return to France, but the Continental Congress felt uneasy about the French returning to North America. Because the Canadiens were largely illiterate (literacy was still below 40% in 1850), it is difficult to say whether they were politically sophisticated, as the colony had been largely marginal and lacked a large merchant class under French rule. Education was not widespread and was largely controlled by seminaries or convents. It was even less politically sophisticated than the Spanish colonies in the Americas. My guess is that independence would have been the least likely of options, unless the Bishop of Quebec assumed the role of head of government.

Then the place will find a way to get out of American control ASAP. Mismatched expectations and all that because of a fundamental misreading by the Continental Army/Congress of the situation, particularly WRT the Quebec Act. The French never wanted to retain Canada après la Conquête because the sugar colonies in the Caribbean were far more valuable, plus lots of bad blood between the Canadiens and Versailles about which direction their part of New France should go. You'd basically be accelerating the French Revolution's TL but with a Canadien cause - and this time the British would come off as the good guys by allying with the habitants, whether or not it takes it back under its wing or accepts it as an independent country but under the British sphere of influence. And it finds a way to get out of the US ASAP, particularly if the initial military occupation goes as OTL and they basically alienated everyone. More probable than getting annexed by the US. Considering Quebec in this case would be a direct cause for the French Revolution ITTL, that's easy to remark on. While still predominantly Francophone (albeit with Canadian French given the same recognition as, say, Brazilian Portuguese), society and culture would take a more, say, Argentine or Uruguayan-like direction but w/ its own quirks (including probably far more indigenous influence) and probably different relationships among groups that would be relatively more egalitarian and opposed to reinstating the colonial relationship. Considering the British would still be next door viz. Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, as well as the HBC doing its thing, British influence would remain strong and that would include the cultural sphere, too.

It depends on how the Americans treat the Canadiens, and how they handle the Iroquois. If the Americans can't keep the Iroquois mostly neutral, and if they prevent them from trading with the Canadiens, then Quebec will want want to leave in a hurry. If the Americans could be deft in the administration of Quebec, better in battle, luckier with allied victories, and more skillful in peace negotiation I think there is a good chance that the Canadiens would want to be in a confederacy, or a customs union with a mutual defense pact. The centralizing reforms of the Constitution would likely have been opposed by the Canadiens as antifederalism, which brings me to the next point, though it is possible they could remain in the union if it transitions from Articles of Confederation to Constitution. While the Canadiens would most likely have forbade slavery, that doesn't mean they would have been abolitionists in the vein of the northeastern Calvinists and Quakers. While they could have been like the 1840s and 1850s Free Soilers, their antifederalism and relative lack of industrialization might have moved them into common cause with Southern states. The Canadiens also could have been aligned with the "Westerners" in looking for federally funded internal developments to help with their access to Atlantic ports, and their access to settling Upper Canada and Indiana/Illinois Territory. Being so close to Nova Scotia and Newfoundland the Canadiens could also be interested in a strong navy. So perhaps an American Quebec could be allied with someone like Calhoun. As for the issue of Loyalist Migration, their emigration would likely have been reduced if they didn't have British Upper Canada as a destination. Many of the Loyalists would have resigned themselves to life in the new government. There still would have been Loyalist emigration from both America and Lower Canada, and there would still be a movement of Loyalists to Upper Canada and other territories despite them being no longer British Empire owned. So those populations would have thrown a new political impulse into the country later especially after the Constitution is ratified.

I'd assume a French route with independence after the French revolution. Maybe some nobility or rich flee to Quebec during the revolution. I'd think US keeps what it would get otl plus Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward island. Ontario might go to the U.S. While Newfoundland and Labrador goes to Quebec. The American loyalists could be moved into western Canada to try to colonize Western Canada. England might be more harsh in dealing with the Oregon territory. You could see a war over it with Quebec siding with a side. Should U.S. Win they might get British Columbia in the treaty. Quebec might get islands in Nunavut. Russia in this timeline would probably favor selling Alaska to England. With more northern territory. I can see the South looking for more Mexican territory. There's a possibility the slave and free state addition could continue on longer. This causes a delay of the civil war potentially.

Meanwhile, Carleton received reinforcements and made a counter offensive that drove the Americans back to Fort Ticonderoga. For context, what if the Americans captured Quebec? Say Montgomery captured Govenor Guy Carleton and the Americans managed to catch Quebec City by surprise. In my previous thread about the fate of Quebec (Roughly around Lower Canada; Upper Canada is a whole other can of worms), there were four possibilities I gave, but we're going to talk about three: A) French route- The Americans offer Quebec back to France for support in their war, meaning France regains Quebec by the end of the war B) American route- The Americans annex Quebec, making Quebec part of the USA. C) Independent route- The Americans make Quebec into a sister republic, making Quebec independent by the end of the war. (There's no British route since that OTL) Now, I want to focus on one particular aspect of the fate of Quebec: Culture. If Quebec wasn't under the British/TTL Canada, what would culture be like for the French Canadians. Depending on the route we take, how would culture, society, art, cuisine, fashion, etc, develop for the French Canadians? In the French route, how would Quebec be affected by the French Revolution? In the American route, how would Quebec develop under the USA? In the Independent route, how would Quebec develop stuck between the British and Americans while having access to the St Lawrence?
items.model_answer:
If the Americans captured Quebec in 1775 and then actually held it through the Revolution, Quebec would probably develop as a French-Catholic region inside the United States rather than as the core of a future British Canada. Its culture would remain recognizably French for a long time, but its institutions and political identity would become much more American and republican than they did historically.

The first key point is that conquest alone would not automatically anglicize Quebec. In 1775 the population of the St. Lawrence valley was overwhelmingly French-speaking and Catholic. American soldiers and politicians could occupy Quebec City and Montreal, but they could not easily replace the parish system, the clergy, French family life, local notables, or the rural seigneurial society overnight. To keep the province loyal, the Continental Congress would probably have had to tolerate Catholic worship, French language use, and much of French civil law, even if many New England Protestants disliked “popery” and the Quebec Act.

So in the short term, Quebec would likely remain a French-Catholic society with American political overlays. Parish life would continue. The Catholic Church would still be central to education, marriage, charity, and local identity. French would remain the language of the countryside and probably of local courts and administration in many areas. But Quebec would no longer develop under a British imperial framework that protected French civil law and Catholic rights as a way of securing loyalty to the Crown. Instead, its protections would depend on American constitutional politics.

That would change Quebec’s development in several ways.

Politically, Quebec would likely be organized as a U.S. territory and eventually perhaps as one or more states. Its inhabitants would become part of republican politics: elected assemblies, state constitutions, town meetings or county governments, and party competition. The old seigneurial elite would probably lose influence faster than it did historically. Seigneurial land tenure might be abolished earlier under pressure from American ideas of freehold property and equal citizenship. Quebec society would become less formally hierarchical and more market-oriented.

Religiously, Catholicism would survive, but the Catholic Church would probably be weaker as a public institution than it became in historical Quebec. In British Quebec and later Lower Canada, the Church eventually became a major guardian of French-Canadian identity, especially after the failed rebellions of 1837–38 and during the conservative nationalist period of the 19th century. In an American Quebec, church establishment would be impossible under republican norms. Catholic schools and parishes would remain important, but the Church would face stronger competition from secular public institutions, Protestant missionary activity, and American political culture. The result would likely be a still-Catholic but somewhat less clerically dominated society.

Linguistically, French would persist, but under heavier pressure. Because Quebec’s French-speaking population was large and compact, it would not simply disappear like some smaller immigrant languages in the United States. Rural Quebec would remain French-speaking for generations. But Montreal, Quebec City, and frontier regions would attract more English-speaking settlers from New England and New York. Commerce, higher courts, federal politics, and interstate trade would favor English. Over time, Quebec might become officially or practically bilingual, with French strongest in rural parishes and English dominant in business and federal life.

The closest comparison might be Louisiana, but Quebec would probably retain French more successfully than Louisiana because its French-speaking population was larger, older, more rural, and more geographically concentrated. A U.S. Quebec might resemble a much larger, more politically powerful Franco-American region: culturally French and Catholic at home, but increasingly bilingual and American in public life.

Montreal would likely develop differently as well. Instead of becoming the commercial metropolis of British North America, it would be integrated into the economy of the northeastern United States. Its merchants would trade south and west through New York, New England, the Hudson River system, the Great Lakes, and later American canals and railroads. It might become a major bilingual American city, perhaps something like a French-English version of New Orleans, Boston, and Buffalo combined. English-speaking merchants would be influential, but French workers, artisans, and neighborhoods would remain central.

National identity would be very different. Historically, French Canadians in Quebec defined themselves partly against British rule and later against English Canada. In this counterfactual world, they would define themselves within the United States. Their identity might become “French American,” “Canadien American,” or “Québécois American” rather than French Canadian in the historical sense. They might become a distinctive voting bloc in American politics, defending Catholic rights, French-language schooling, local autonomy, and civil-law traditions.

There would probably be recurring cultural conflict. Protestant Americans might distrust Catholic Quebec; French Catholics might fear assimilation; English settlers might demand common-law courts and English schools; French communities might demand bilingual government and protection for parish education. These conflicts could resemble American disputes over Catholics, immigrants, language schooling, and states’ rights, but with a much older and more territorially rooted French population.

One major consequence is that Quebec would likely modernize earlier in some respects. Its land system, political institutions, and economy would be pulled into the American market sooner. The conservative rural-clerical order that dominated historical Quebec in the 19th and early 20th centuries might be less powerful. There might be no exact equivalent of the historical “Quiet Revolution,” because Quebec would already have been exposed longer to American secularism, electoral politics, capitalism, and public education. French culture would still survive, but it would be less insulated.

So the likely outcome is not an English-speaking Quebec, nor simply the same Quebec under a different flag. It would be a hybrid: a French-Catholic, bilingual, republican society inside the United States. French language and Catholic culture would remain deeply rooted, especially in the St. Lawrence valley, but American political institutions, English-language commerce, religious disestablishment, and migration from the surrounding states would gradually make Quebec more secular, more bilingual, less clerically controlled, and more economically integrated with the northeastern United States.

items.original_question: Administration of British colonies in North America if the USA would have never existed? I have seen several maps of North America in alternate history scenarios where the 13 colonies lost in 1775/1776. IF England would have won, how would they have administered their colonies in North America afterwards in the late 18th, the 19th, and the 20th century? Would they have administered their colonies separately (Pensilvania, Massachusetts, Newfoundland, Quebec, "Canada?", Florida, Louisiana, Oregon etc.) or would they have united them sooner or later in a big north american british dominion? Also, would they have eventually taken oregon/nootka? what about louisiana and alaska from france and russia respectively? PS: Yes I know there are a lot of "What if the US lost the war of 1776..." threads here but this is mostly about the administration of these colonies
items.model_answer:
If the United States had never come into existence, the former British colonies in North America would most likely have remained part of the British Empire and evolved into something resembling a larger version of Canada rather than being administered indefinitely as tightly controlled possessions from London.

In the short term, each colony would probably have continued to be governed separately under the Crown. A royal governor, appointed by Britain, would represent imperial authority, while local elected assemblies would handle taxation, local laws, roads, courts, and internal administration. London—through bodies such as the Board of Trade and later the Colonial Office—would oversee imperial trade policy, defense, foreign relations, westward expansion, and relations with Indigenous nations.

Over time, Britain would likely have reorganized the colonies into larger provinces or federations. The northern colonies, the Atlantic colonies, the southern plantation colonies, Quebec, and later western territories might have been grouped into a broader “British North America.” This federation could have developed along lines similar to the Dominion of Canada: self-governing in domestic affairs, loyal to the British Crown, and tied to Britain for diplomacy and defense until gradually gaining fuller autonomy.

Important policy differences would likely have followed. Slavery, for example, would probably have been abolished throughout these colonies when Britain abolished slavery in most of its empire in 1833, rather than surviving until a civil war. Westward expansion might have been more regulated by imperial treaties and land policies, though not necessarily benign for Indigenous peoples. Trade would have remained more closely tied to the British imperial economy, at least until the 19th century brought freer trade.

So the most plausible answer is: British North America would probably have been administered through a combination of imperial oversight and local colonial self-government, eventually becoming one or more self-governing dominions within the British Empire/Commonwealth rather than forming an independent United States.

items.question: What If the Southern Ming had survived?
human_answers: I foresee a successful Chinese expedition to retake the North within a decade or two. Sichuan was perhaps ironically where the most effective anti-Qing forces were based in OTL. Remnants of Zhang Xianzhong and Li Zicheng’s forces continued fighting there for decades until well into Kangxi’s reign IOTL. The site saw repeated struggles between different forces for many decades. It’s actually the reason for the significant decline in the population of Sichuan IOTL, not Zhang Xianzhong’s Sichuan massacre. Population wise, the Qing Dynasty would have difficulty regrowing the population of the north due to lack of food. The North has always been a basket case since the end of the Northern Song Dynasty. During the Ming Dynasty, Southern China had at least two times the population of the North. And that is before the collapse of the Ming Dynasty Which saw massive fighting. You see plenty of areas throughout Northern China eating rice as staples today, but the truth was that this is evidence for how much northerners have come to rely on Southern grain. Rice does not grow in the North, and has to be imported from the South. Before the Sui-Tang Dynasties when the Grand Canal was not built, Northern diet was based on wheat. Still is to a lesser extent today. After this period, they became increasingly reliant on Southern crops until from the Ming Dynasty onwards, they became entirely reliant on it. Northern Qing can’t just regrow when they don’t even have the rice to feed the people. As time goes on, even by the 17th century, warfare is gonna increasingly dependant upon firearms, meaning population,technology and economy is gonna become decisive in eventual Southern victory. Individual prowess of the troops that the Manchus relied heavily on will become less relevant,especially as the Qing simply does not have Manchu population to supply large armies to both stamp out rebellions or to fight the Southern dynasty. The Manchus iotl exploited a critical window before that was gonna be a problem to conquer the South.

This is what I have in mind: 1. In OTL, as I understand it, by this point the Ming dynasty’s North China had been devastated, the population had grown unevenly, and the state had come to depend heavily on Jiangnan’s grain resources. In that situation, if the Qing were to occupy only North China while the Ming retained control of Jiangnan, the Qing would likely suffer from serious food shortages. Under such conditions, I think it is highly likely that the Qing would resort to massacres in North China similar to the Yangzhou massacre seen in OTL. However, in the end, the Qing might later face the problem of overpopulation once again. Personally, when it comes to the Malthusian trap, I think the Northern Qing would suffer from it more severely than the Southern Ming. What do you think? 2. In OTL, the Dzungars were destroyed by Qing expeditions. However, in this timeline, the Dzungars would likely expand their power significantly across Mongolia and Tibet. Unlike in OTL, the Qing would probably remain largely on the defensive. As a result, the Dzungars would not be destroyed and would likely enjoy a substantial imperial existence until they were eventually conquered by the Russian Empire. Russia, too, would likely push into Manchuria more frequently and more deeply than it did in OTL. The Qing would have a much harder time containing them and would probably have to request military assistance from Joseon more often than in OTL . It is even possible that, unlike the Treaty of Nerchinsk, Russia might succeed in extracting territorial gains much deeper inside the region. And here is the next question. In your view, assuming that the Southern Ming and the Northern Qing both survived until the mid-18th century, which state do you think would collapse first? And in what ways do you think each polity would face its respective crises? First of all, in OTL, the course of the Yellow River changed in the 1850s. This could also have significant effects on China.

Why do you say they will sinicise faster? By contrast, I think they’d sinicise even slower, as they can’t hope to match the southern Ming in chineseness and so would have to rely on other pillars of legitimacy to prop up their rule, perhaps leaning further into Tibetan Buddhism. Edit- looking more into how Tibetan Buddhism had spread so deeply into Mongol society in the late 16th century, people seem to say that the Qing need to appeal to Taoist and Confucian ideologies meant they could not be called a primarily Buddhist state. Ittl, I think the Qing would lean much more heavily into buddhist kingship, and this might also make their policy towards Han people less racist- there would be a way for Han people to politically abandon the Confucian-Taoist kingship embodied by the Ming, by adopting Tibetan Buddhism, which would make them part of the ruling group without becoming Manchu. Why do you say it didn’t happen in India? As an aside, there was a mid 17th century equivalent to the treaty of Westphalia in Central Asia, the Great Code of 1640, by which various Oirat and Mongol clans agreed to act as a collective body to uphold general peace and a universal legal code, while upholding the sovereignty of the individual tribes. Otl, it became irrelevant once the Qing got rid of any form of Mongol sovereignty by defeating the Dzunghars and winning the Khalkha Mongols to their cause, but in a world where the Qing aren’t so powerful, the “Holy Mongol Empire” likely maintains its constitutional structure for longer. Instead of a Dzunghar khanate, we’d therefore talk Ming China allying with the Western Yuan Dynasty to hold back the Qing, and perhaps the federal Yuan would be more successful than the Dzunghar were otl in their wars against the Kazakhs/the Khanates of Bukhara. Or perhaps, the Qing end up functioning as the Austria analogue- personally controlling by far the most land and people, but still unable to strip away the autonomy of the various Mongol and oirat ulus’, who regularly meet and would all revolt against imperial overreach.
items.original_question: If the Southern Ming had survived? Thread 'Perpetual Brightness: Surviving Southern Ming' Apr 12, 2006 Once, the Confucian school outside Quanzhou had bustled with students and scholars. Some of China’s greatest administrators had come from there, and in its day the school had been a center of learning. But since the famines, and the Manchu invasion, the school had grown quiet. The buildings were dilapidated, with peeling paint and rotten timber. There was only one man there, in the dark of night, standing by a fire. The man watched as the flames cast a red glow over the temple, as it consumed the robes of a scholar. An Empire was collapsing outside its walls, but inside the silence was... Faeelin Replies: 168 Forum: Alternate History Discussion: Before 1900 In OTL, after an empire collapsed in China, there were many cases where it was not completely destroyed and replaced by another empire, but instead split into northern and southern regimes. Even before the Qing dynasty, the Jurchen states themselves formed a northern empire, while the Southern Song continued to exist in the south. In the 17th century, the Ming dynasty, like the Song before it, also established the Southern Ming. However, it ultimately fell after only twenty years. Was there no way for the Southern Ming to survive? The problems of the Southern Ming, as I see them, are as follows. 1. In the case of the Southern Song, all other imperial claimants were captured by the Jurchens, and as a result, a person low in the line of succession became the only remaining claimant. This, paradoxically, allowed him to secure a certain degree of legitimacy and take power. By contrast, the Southern Ming began in a situation where the legitimate imperial princes had largely been captured from the outset, while there were still too many lower-ranking imperial relatives remaining. This excess of potential claimants triggered disputes over the imperial succession. 2. In the case of the Jin dynasty, it had not yet fully subdued the Western Xia or the Mongols. In particular, the Mongols were later unified by Genghis Khan, who went on to establish the most powerful nomadic empire in history. At the time, the Goryeo dynasty was nominally a tributary state of the Jin, but it had not been decisively subdued through war. The Jin lacked the capacity to invade Goryeo and had no choice but to settle for maintaining relatively moderate relations. In other words, the Jin dynasty could not devote all of its national strength to the conquest of the Southern Song. By contrast, the Qing dynasty had already conquered the Chahar Mongols and had invaded the capital of the Joseon dynasty, forcing it into clear submission. Although the Dzungars and Russia would later enter the Chinese arena, this occurred only after the game had effectively already been decided. 3. The Southern Song was able to survive thanks to outstanding generals such as Yue Fei and Han Shizhong, who successfully defeated the Jurchen armies. By contrast, on the eve of the Ming dynasty’s collapse, Wu Sangui’s forces—virtually the only remaining elite army—defected outright to the Qing side. As a result, the Southern Ming was forced to struggle on with inadequate military strength, trapped in a situation where incompetent warlords fought among themselves in constant internal conflict. Taking these factors into account, I think that for the Southern Ming to have survived for a long time, things would have had to be different from the very beginning. “Before the fall of Beijing, the Chongzhen Emperor decides to transfer the capital to Nanjing. Abandoning Beijing, he withdraws south, and Wu Sangui’s army joins the emperor’s entourage and moves to Nanjing as well.” In effect, this would mean that the Chongzhen Emperor is “ceding North China to the Jurchens,” but even so, the southern regions would be far more securely preserved. However, he did not do so. The reasons lie here. In short, he was an “indecisive and irresolute emperor,” and as a result, instead of taking responsibility for such a momentous decision, he merely kept postponing it. What I am curious about is this: 1. If the Chongzhen Emperor were to decide on relocating the capital, what kind of POD (point of divergence) would need to occur? 2. If the Southern Ming had survived at least until the 19th century, how would East Asian history from the 17th to the 19th centuries have changed? Assuming the Southern Ming succeeded in repelling the initial Qing offensives, who would be in the more advantageous position thereafter? If the Southern Ming were to endure, how would Western powers in the 19th century approach China?
items.model_answer:
If the Southern Ming had survived, China would probably have developed as a divided empire for a significant period rather than being quickly unified under the Qing.

The most plausible version is not a full Ming restoration over all China, but a durable Southern Ming state based in the lower Yangtze, Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi, Yunnan, or some combination of these regions. The Qing would likely have controlled North China, Manchuria, and perhaps much of the central plain, while the Southern Ming held the richer maritime and commercial south. This would have resembled earlier periods of Chinese division, such as Northern and Southern dynasties or Song-Jin coexistence.

A surviving Southern Ming would have changed several major things.

First, the Qing conquest would have been much less complete. The Manchus succeeded historically because Ming loyalist resistance was fragmented, regional commanders defected, and Southern Ming courts were plagued by factionalism and weak legitimacy. If the Southern Ming had avoided those failures, the Qing would have faced a long-term rival with access to wealthy tax bases, seaborne trade, and anti-Manchu legitimacy. The Qing might still have remained powerful, but it would not have been the uncontested dynasty of China.

Second, Chinese politics would likely have become more militarized and regional. A Southern Ming state would have depended heavily on generals, naval forces, merchant elites, and local gentry. To survive, it would have needed stronger fiscal and military institutions than the late Ming possessed. That could have produced reform, but it could also have entrenched warlord-like military governors and court factionalism. Survival would not automatically mean stability.

Third, maritime China would probably have become more important. Southern Ming loyalists historically had strong links to coastal resistance, including Zheng Chenggong/Koxinga and his network. A lasting Southern Ming might have relied on sea trade, overseas Chinese merchants, Taiwan, Japan, Southeast Asia, and perhaps selective dealings with Europeans. This could have made southern China more outward-looking than Qing China was in the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Taiwan might have become a core Ming loyalist base rather than being incorporated into the Qing Empire in 1683.

Fourth, relations with Europeans would have been different. The Southern Ming, needing money, weapons, and naval power, might have been more willing to bargain with the Portuguese, Dutch, Spanish, or later the English. That does not mean China would have been “colonized” earlier; a surviving Southern Ming could have played Europeans against one another. But foreign trade, firearms procurement, and missionary diplomacy would likely have mattered more.

Fifth, the cultural meaning of “China” might have changed. Historically, the Qing eventually presented themselves as legitimate Chinese emperors while also ruling a multiethnic empire including Manchuria, Mongolia, Tibet, Xinjiang, and Taiwan. If a Ming state survived in the south, it would have continued to claim Han Chinese dynastic legitimacy against a Manchu northern dynasty. This could have sharpened ethnic and cultural distinctions between “Ming/Chinese” and “Qing/Manchu,” making later Chinese nationalism more explicitly anti-Manchu and southern-centered.

Sixth, the Qing Empire might have been smaller. Without full control over China’s southern wealth, the Qing may have had fewer resources for the great eighteenth-century expansions into Mongolia, Tibet, and Xinjiang. Alternatively, the Qing might have focused even more on Inner Asia while leaving the south contested. In that case, East Asia might have contained two large Sinosphere states: a northern Manchu-Qing empire and a southern Ming Chinese kingdom.

The long-term outcome would depend on whether the Southern Ming could reform. If it remained like the late Ming—fiscally weak, faction-ridden, and dependent on unreliable commanders—it might survive only a few decades before collapsing. If it created a stable tax system, disciplined army, and effective naval-commercial policy, it could have endured for centuries, perhaps like the Southern Song did against northern conquest dynasties.

So the best answer is: a surviving Southern Ming would most likely have produced a divided early modern China, with a Manchu Qing north and a Ming loyalist south. The south would probably have been more maritime, commercially connected, and anti-Manchu in identity, while the Qing would have been less able to claim full Chinese legitimacy. This would have reshaped China’s territorial expansion, foreign relations, and later nationalism, but it would not necessarily have made China stronger; it could just as easily have meant prolonged war, fiscal strain, and political fragmentation.

human_answers: As far as the political landscape is concerned, I think the Federalists are routed as per OTL. The Virginian dynasty probably crumbles and Monroe probably stays put as Secretary of State instead of seeking the presidency. If the Battle of New Orleans doeant take place Jackson's path to power is much longer and more arduous, if he even seeks the office at all. I would consider OTL to be a tie, and I think spin city can depict it as such at the time. I've seen threads arguing it was a USAmerican victory because Britain wasn't able to conquer them. What does winning look like? Typically, it means taking something from the loser. Since USA never gained anything during the war, there's nothing they can be forced to give back. So, it would have to be something they held prior (or had claim to). Retaking control of any of the lost colonies is largely devoid of reality. Border adjustments in Maine/Vermont/New York are on the table. Making the old Northwest part of Canada, perhaps as a Native Reserve, is a possibility. Would Britain keep New Orleans if they had taken it prior to truce and/or the rest of Louisiana? Give it back to Spain? Trade it for full control of the NW, if they haven't secured control of that already? Realistically, how much could Britain gain? But, I think OP wants to discuss political ramifications if the war ends with there being zero doubt which side won. There could be a major territorial concession which is bound to completely change the USA even if it rebounds spectacularly (such as loss of New Orleans/Louisiana), in which case political ramifications are a secondary concern. Or, territorial concessions are more limited, leaving things a bit more recognizable. A lot of things left unsettled by the ARW, are going to be settled in Britain's favor. Trade agreements may emerge also favoring Britain. Depending on the severity of the peace, politics will also be severely affected far beyond a 'USA lost, unequivocally, but otherwise everything is the same' . So, yeah, we need to know the scope of the peace. The OP needs to be fleshed out more.
items.original_question: What if the British won the 1812 War? How would this influence the US political landscape? My opinion is: 1840 Democratic (Jacksonian, pro-States´ Rights) Whig (Anti-Jacksonian, pro-States´ Rights) Federalist (Anti-Jacksonian, anti-States´ Rights)
items.model_answer:
If Britain had clearly won the War of 1812, the most likely result would not have been the reconquest of the United States. Britain did not have the political interest or practical ability to permanently occupy the U.S.; it was focused mainly on defeating Napoleon and protecting Canada. A “British victory” would more likely have meant forcing the United States to accept harsher peace terms than the real Treaty of Ghent, which restored the prewar status quo.

The biggest likely change would have been in the Old Northwest, around present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, and Wisconsin. Britain had supported Native confederacies led by figures such as Tecumseh, and a strong British victory might have produced an independent Native buffer state between the U.S. and Canada. That would have slowed or complicated American westward expansion and could have preserved Native political power in the Great Lakes region for longer.

Canada would also have emerged stronger and more secure. A British victory would have confirmed that the United States could not conquer Canada, likely strengthening Canadian loyalty to Britain and accelerating the development of a distinct Canadian identity. Anti-American feeling in Canada might have been even stronger than it became historically.

In the United States, defeat would have seriously damaged the Democratic-Republican Party leadership of James Madison and possibly revived the Federalists, at least temporarily. The postwar surge of American nationalism—the “Era of Good Feelings”—would probably have been weaker or might not have happened. The U.S. Army and Navy would still likely have been reformed, but under the pressure of humiliation rather than celebrated survival.

American expansion into the South and West might also have been slower. If Britain had captured and held New Orleans, even temporarily, it could have threatened U.S. access to the Mississippi River. That would have been a major blow to western farmers and to the growth of the cotton economy. Still, Britain probably would not have kept New Orleans permanently unless it was willing to risk another long conflict.

Slavery would probably not have ended as a direct result. Britain opposed the Atlantic slave trade by then, but it was unlikely to impose abolition on the United States in a peace settlement. However, if U.S. expansion into the Deep South and Southwest had slowed, the spread of plantation slavery might have been delayed or altered.

Overall, a British victory would likely have meant a weaker, more cautious United States; a safer British Canada; stronger Native resistance in the Great Lakes; and slower American expansion. But it probably would not have meant the end of American independence. The most plausible outcome is not a restored British America, but a United States whose rise as a continental power was delayed and made more uncertain.

items.question: What If the English Armada of 1589 had succeeded in destroying Spain's remaining Atlantic fleet and triggering a Portuguese revolt?
human_answers: Actually, I think one could argue the opposite: that it's magically deterministic to assume that, in some unspecified way, this crisis will send the whole country into a downward spiral that will lead to its implosion. I mean, once you go over the list of changes, there isn't too much difference: yes, the Spanish Navy has been severely damaged; yes, Portugal has become independent; yes, Spain has lost all its possessions in Europe that are outside the Iberian Peninsula... but really the only significant difference from OTL is that Portugal became independent earlier, the burden that the Netherlands represented is now "someone else's problem," the remaining Spanish Navy is much smaller, and now Portugal has very serious reasons to hate England for keeping the Azores "because we can." The American Empire remains intact, it is doubtful that the English will be more successful in appropriating anything than in OTL, and they are possibly too busy antagonizing someone else once they see that the possibility of another Invincible Armada is not going to happen in the near future. OTL Spain recovered from that, even if 200 years later they declined for other reasons, but this alone should not condemn them to failure.

Spanish resilience at the time was incredible, considering how Philip II expended so many resources on fronts that ultimately yielded no tangible gains beyond preserving his honor (which was the sole reason he remained in the Flanders War). Even if England were to seize the Azores, I do not believe this would satisfy the Portuguese nobility and bourgeoisie—the main factions Antonio, Prior of Crato, would need in order to legitimize his rule. Furthermore, if Spain was able to rebuild a second fleet within two or three years—not as large as the first, but still significant—we must not forget that while the English might capture a treasure fleet, they could not always be expected to capture all of them. If there was one defining trait of Spanish admirals regarding their treasure fleets, it was their elusiveness. Even so, a Spain under Philip II, burdened by numerous problems, could compel Philip III to reconsider his policies and explore the possibility of a genuine peace with the Dutch Republic—something that could ultimately benefit Spain in the long run.

While I agree the OP is going way too far and too fast, I'd say 1589 had the potential to screw Spain over far worse than it did in OTL. I'd say your best POD is probably for Antonio to die on the way to the Iberian Peninsula, but too late for the fleet to turn back. To get out of that pickle, Drake and Norris opt to just try to do as much damage to Spain's fleet and resources as they can. In that they proved far more successful than in OTL, even temporarily occupying some of the Azores and capturing the treasure fleet. Spain has even more money problems than in OTL. The rebuilding of the Spanish fleet is an even bigger task than in OTL, and the Royal Navy does start to gain a reputation for invincibility. In France, Henri III's OTL assassin made his attempt when the Royalists celebrated the English successes, and the butterflies ensured Henri III survived ITTL. Henri III retakes Paris, and the wheel starts to come off the Catholic League significantly earlier than OTL, especially since the retaking of the capital is quickly followed by Henri of Navarre also winning the ITTL version of the battle of Arques. Spain is stuck providing far more resources to sustain the elements of the Catholic League than it had to in OTL until significantly later, when it has less resources available in the first place. And all over the Western World, the Habsburgs' enemies are taking heart... Colapse might be too strong a word but the ruin of Philip II's continental ambitions would probably come earlier, and cost more to Spain in the long run, than in OTL.
items.original_question: What if Spanish "collapse" in 1589 One of the most famous failures in modern European history, the 1588 Spanish Armada destroyed a big part of the Spanish naval forces, and was a major humiliation for Philip II. Yet England, one year later, completely blew its chance to fully wreck the Spanish by launching the ill-fated English Armada, which sought three main objectives: 1) Destroy the remaining Atlantic fleet of Spain 2) Incite a rebellion in Portugal against Philip II 3) Seize the Azores and turn it into a permanent English possession It failed in all of these objectives. Yet, the POD is not a minor or major decision, it is simple: somehow England succeeds. The remaining fleet of Spain that survived the 1588 Armada is destroyed in a series of naval battles, a landing is made in Portugal and António Prior of Crato is installed King of Portugal, starting a Portuguese Restoration War 50 years before OTL, and finally England manages to seize the Azores from Philip II's forces. Say that the Spanish naval forces are completely obliterated by the English; Portugal gains independence from Spain in 1590 with heavy English backing; the Azores (through negotiation with Portugal) become a English territory. What would happen with England, Spain, Portugal and the rest of Europe? How might the colonization of the New World be altered by a successful English Armada? Let's not get into details on **how** this happens, but assuming that it just does happen
items.model_answer:
If the English Armada of 1589 had destroyed Spain’s remaining Atlantic fleet and successfully triggered a Portuguese revolt, the result would likely have been a major strategic disaster for Philip II and a turning point in the Anglo-Spanish War, though not necessarily an immediate collapse of Spanish power.

The most immediate effect would have been naval. Spain was still recovering from the failed Armada of 1588, and the destruction of its remaining Atlantic fleet would have left it badly exposed in the eastern Atlantic. Spain would have struggled to escort treasure fleets, defend Iberian ports, protect communications with the Americas, and maintain pressure on England and the Dutch Republic. English and Dutch privateering would probably have intensified, with much greater success against Spanish shipping.

A Portuguese revolt would have been even more serious. Portugal had been joined to the Spanish crown in 1580, but loyalty to Philip II was not universal. If English forces had helped install or at least rally support around Dom António, Prior of Crato, Portugal might have broken away from the Iberian Union decades before its actual restoration in 1640. That would have deprived Spain of Portuguese ports, sailors, ships, and imperial resources. Lisbon, the Azores, Madeira, and perhaps parts of the Portuguese Atlantic network would have become either hostile to Spain or contested.

The Azores would have been especially important. Control or friendly access there would have given England a forward base astride the routes of Spanish and Portuguese treasure fleets. Even if England did not directly conquer the islands, a pro-English Portugal could have allowed English fleets to operate far more effectively in the Atlantic. Spain’s American silver shipments would have become more vulnerable, creating fiscal strain for a monarchy already financing wars in the Netherlands, France, and the Mediterranean.

The Dutch Revolt would probably have benefited greatly. Spain’s ability to send money and troops to the Army of Flanders depended on Atlantic resources and maritime security. A weakened Spain, deprived of Portuguese support and under heavier attack at sea, would have found it harder to sustain the war in the Low Countries. The Dutch Republic might have secured its independence sooner or on more favorable terms.

For England, success in 1589 would have transformed the war. Instead of being remembered as a costly failure, the Drake-Norris expedition would have become the offensive counterpart to the defeat of the Spanish Armada. Elizabeth I’s government would have gained prestige, and England might have emerged earlier as a serious Atlantic naval power. English privateering, colonial ventures, and attempts to penetrate Iberian overseas trade would likely have expanded in the 1590s.

But there are limits to the counterfactual. Spain remained a vast composite monarchy with deep resources, experienced administrators, and access to American silver. Even after a catastrophic defeat, Philip II could have rebuilt fleets, as Spain historically did after 1588. A Portuguese revolt would not automatically have succeeded nationwide; many Portuguese elites had accommodated Spanish rule, and English troops were not necessarily popular liberators. If English forces overreached, looted, or failed to supply themselves, the revolt could still have collapsed.

So the most plausible outcome is not the immediate fall of the Spanish Empire, but a sharp weakening of Spanish Atlantic dominance. Portugal might have regained independence much earlier, England and the Dutch would have gained major strategic advantages, and Spain’s ability to project power into northern Europe would have been reduced. The balance of power in the Atlantic would likely have shifted earlier away from Iberian supremacy and toward English and Dutch maritime expansion.

items.question: What If Britain pursued a more hostile stance against the American Colonies following the Boston Tea Party, going on the offensive in 1774?
human_answers: This is why it might have been shortsighted for the British Empire to put so much investment in achieving the total conquest and liquidation of the French Colonial position in the Ohio Country and Canada in the 1754-1763 timeframe, to disproportionate benefit of their Colonial 'Fortunate Sons'. While for Britain, it had the side benefit of defeating French forces, which feels nice, and drawing French fleets out for fights they would lose, and capturing some value from the fur trade, Britain particularly "got over its skis" in providing all this support for the Colonies *without* first compelling the Colonies, then under some fears for their frontier populations, to revise their Charters to accept the principle and practice of taxation by the Westminster Parliament, as a regular, reliable contribution to common defense of the empire, its frontiers, and its trade-based prosperity. Instead, by 1763, Britain brought home French North America like Christmas toys and puppies on its own schilling (though Colonial Assemblies chipped in some from their allowance, but often got reimbursed). But then, late 1763 turned out to be a cold, cold, bitter post-Christmas January hangover, when London Parliament started to tell the Colonies, "now start paying tax for all your presents........oh and by the way, sorry, can't let you play with the new Christmas puppy (settle the new lands in the Ohio, west of the Alleghenies), because it turns out the puppy bites and scratches and we can't afford to keep going to the clinic." ---The Americans certainly were not going to react well to the new message of 'fun's over, time to pay up'. While Britain and the American colonies had certain minimum legal rights, even for tenant farmers (still far less than for small freeholders though) I certainly do not think the three protections you mentioned were observed universally, neither in Britain nor even in all the Colonies, in the 1700s pre and post independence. Making this assertion might be a bit of falling for and repeating English/British self-congratulatory propaganda. Evictions were a fact of life in the English-speaking world in the 1700s and all other centuries. The 1700s were known for the enclosure of common lands [yes, that by itself is not eviction but can lead to starvation-inducing poverty even if one is in a cottage, but it can also lead to failure to meet rent obligations and consequent eviction] and consequent driving of English peasants from the countryside to create an ever increasing town and urban laboring population for industry. White tenants on southern landholdings in the Colonies could be subject to evictions as could tenants in Hudson Valley patroonships. Yes, I'm thinking this is descriptive of the Scandinavian situation until after 1800, or nearly that late, which made it, legally speaking more like serfdom systems East of the Elbe than like tenancy systems in Britain or Western Europe. Serfs lacking really any rights of appeal or any rights at all, whereas tenants in England, parts of France, and I would think the Low Countries and Switzerland would have some rights of appeal, even though their landlords would have superior rights through the 1600s and 1700s.

If the British objective was to set off a full-scale war in every colony right off the bat in which they would lose that is exactly what they should do. The British had no means to do what you're suggesting. The incident that set off the fighting was the British trying to disarm the colonists. In the first year of the war the British lost control in all 13 Colonies. Britian had to spend a year mobilizing an army 1/3 of which were German mercenaries for the invasion of the New York. After winning a number of tactical victories they were unable to bring a single colony back under their control. At no time were they ever able to bring even 10% of the population under occupation. After 1777 all they could hold were coastal enclaves, although there was fratricidal warfare in Georgia & South Carolina. They could hold no territory without the Presence of British or Hessian regulars. Loyalist forces were weak everywhere. The coastal enclaves they held became shells eventually with most of the people leaving, and little trade with the interior. What had brought about the war were British policies to control American trade to force them to trade only with England. That alienated the merchant class. Planters had to sell into a closed market were the buyers set the price, and controlled credit terms. That alienated the planter class. They tried to strangle early industrialization so the colonies could only sell raw materials, and buy English finished goods. That alienated the rising manufacturing class. They blocked westward expansion beyond the Proclamation Line. That alienated the landed class. The overall effect was to squeeze specie out of the colonies creating a growing barter system which alienated everyone. Closing courts, and assemblies, and finally trying to disarm the militia left the colonies with the choice of ether abject surrender or rebellion. It wasn't easy but the British Crown went from being very popular in 1765 to every colony taking up arms against them in 1775.

There are tons of things they could do. They could dissolve the militias and ban the Americans from owning weapons. They could introduce an actual tax to fund a permanent military presence - the Americans paid no land rent, only tarriffs. They could abolished the American right to elect judges and sheriffs, instead appointing crown loyalists by decree. They could have given soldiers immunity from local prosecution and law enforcement, instead tasking their commanding officers (who would of course do pretty much nothing) with upholding the law for their soldiers. They could have created an American trading company owned by the crown and banned Americans from any imports and exports except through this company and cracked down on smuggling. The facts are that the Americans enjoyed the most liberal and democratic system in the world at the time of their revolt. They wanted something even more democratic and liberal. But to most people at the time, especially colonial subjects, they would seem like spoiled toddlers throwing a tantrum. Swedish peasants paid roughly 30-40% of the value of an average harvest in land rent at this time. Icelanders could only trade with the very corrupt royal Danish tradign company, which paid aroudn 5% of the value of their wool and forced the Icelanders to buy moldy flour in return. Austrian and Prussian peasants were banned from owning arms, and their courts were handled by government-appointed bailiffs, unless nobility had the right to neck and hand (to be police, prosecutor, judge and executioner all in one, Judge Dredd style) on their estate.

This is a quote from Wikipedia, as of January 20th, 2026: "With the ascension of peace in 1763 the army was dramatically reduced to a peacetime home establishment of just over 11,000 men, with a further 9,750 for the Irish establishment and 10,000 for the colonies. Curtis, Ph.D. www.americanrevolution.org "The English establishment comprised 25,871 infantry organized into 46 regiments and 20 independent companies; 4,151 cavalry organized into 16 regiments; and 2,256 artillerymen organized into one regiment of 4 battalions."
