"An examination of the location of the British army in 1775 reveals the fact that while small detachments of it were to be found in many distant quarters of the globe, the bulk of it was distributed unequally among three different countries. There were roughly speaking 15,000 men in England, 12,000 in Ireland, and 8,000 in America. The remaining 10,000 were distributed among the West Indies, Africa, Minorca, Gibraltar, and Scotland." Each regiment had a listed strength of 477 men. The British concentrated four of these, or just under 2,000 men, in Boston in 1773 to close the port and essentially establish martial law in Massachusetts. This was achieved by moving them New York City, where these regiments had been stationed. The other 6,000 to 8,000 men to cover Canada, Fort Ticonderoga, the forts around the Great Lakes, Florida, Jamaica, and the West Indies. After abandoning Boston, in 1776 the British increased the size of their army from roughly 45,000 to 60,000 troops, mainly be recruiting in Germany. Out of these, they were able to concentrate about 40,000 to take New York, including troops that had been sent to and which failed to take Charleston. Another 10,000 or so chased the Americans out of Canada. Peak strength of the Briitsh army during the American War of Independence was around 80,000. Note that the British were expecting a rematch with France during this time. In fact, Amherst, the commander of the British army, pointed out that the British simply didn't have the strength to garrison the thirteen colonies and advised against trying to reconquer them. The point is that in 1773, the British had the strength to do a show of force in Boston only. And since 90% of the disturbances were coming from New England, the calculation had to be that this would be sufficient. It was only in New England where the situation was turning violent, and it was only after the formation of the Continental Army, and armed clashes between British and American troops, that they declared all thirteen colonies to be in rebellion and started expanding the army. And they really had to wait for the situation to turn that bad to be able to do that.

People in general don't see stuff like that in objective terms. What people see is that suddenly the government made it more expensive or difficult for them to conduct the usual business of life (which was the effect of all the legislation regarding the colonies from 1763 on) and of course they will complain about it, regardless of how good they have it on a cosmic scale. You might as well tell workers in a first world country that they shouldn't go on strike because slavery is still practiced in certain places. That's a very bad idea, because, you know, there are still hostile natives in the borders . In order to not to lose the territory to them, they'd have to station a permanent army all over the border, and that most likely would end up being more expensive than just let the settlers take care of their own defense. And that's not even going into the possibility of slave rebellions in the places where slavery is still legal...
items.original_question: What if Britain pursued a more hostile stance against the American Colonies following the Boston Tea Party, going on the offensive in 1774? As the title suggests, I've been trying to figure out what an earlier beginning to the American Revolutionary War might entail. As to how this happens specifically, military action was advocated as soon as news of the tea party reached London by some hard-line MPs such as Germain OTL. Some thoughts: - This happens before the Continental Congress even assembles, so everything might happen much more hastily. There probably is much less wrangling over things like sending an olive branch to the King and instead a more decisive stance taken on independence. - With the states forced to pick sides immediately, I think it's highly likely that Georgia remains decidedly loyalist, which has very interesting implications for the US post-independence Other than that, my knowledge on the American Revolutionary War is very much limited and it'd be great to have some input on this scenario. Cheers!
items.model_answer:
If Britain had gone on the offensive against the American colonies in 1774 after the Boston Tea Party, the most likely result would have been an earlier and more intense revolutionary war, not a quick restoration of imperial control.

Britain could have gained some short-term advantages. In 1774 the colonial resistance was still politically divided, the Continental Congress had only just begun to coordinate opposition, and many Americans still hoped for reconciliation with the Crown. A decisive British move—arresting radical leaders such as Samuel Adams and John Hancock, seizing militia arms, imposing martial law in Massachusetts, occupying key ports, and using the navy to blockade rebellious towns—might have disrupted Patriot organization before it fully matured. If carried out swiftly and intelligently, it could have delayed the outbreak of open rebellion or weakened Massachusetts as the center of resistance.

But the deeper strategic problem for Britain would have remained: it could punish coastal cities, but it could not easily control the countryside. The colonies were large, decentralized, and full of local political networks, militias, committees of correspondence, and town meetings. Even if Boston were firmly occupied, resistance would likely shift inland and spread through New England. British troops in 1774 were also limited in number, and any offensive campaign would require long supply lines across the Atlantic.

A harsher British response would probably have radicalized colonial opinion faster. In the real timeline, many colonists still framed their protests as a defense of English liberties, not a demand for independence. If Britain had moved from coercive legislation to open military repression in 1774, moderates would have found it harder to argue that Parliament and the Crown could be trusted. The First Continental Congress might have transformed sooner from a protest body into a wartime coordinating authority. Colonies that were hesitant about Massachusetts could have seen the offensive as proof that their own rights were next.

The political effect would likely have been especially damaging for Britain. Arrested colonial leaders might have become martyrs. Loyalists might have been more reluctant to openly support Britain if Patriot anger intensified around them. Southern and middle colonies, despite their differences from New England, might have joined resistance earlier out of fear that imperial force would eventually be used against them too.

So the counterfactual turns on how successful the first British strikes were. If Britain had quickly seized arms, detained leaders, and prevented Massachusetts from mobilizing, it might have postponed the Revolution and strengthened loyalist confidence. But if the offensive produced civilian casualties, town burnings, or broad arrests, it would almost certainly have unified colonial resistance earlier than in reality.

Overall, a more hostile British offensive in 1774 would probably have accelerated the break between Britain and the colonies. Britain might have won tactical victories around Boston and other ports, but it would have made reconciliation far less likely and pushed the colonies toward armed rebellion—and possibly independence—sooner.

items.question: What If not Russia, which country could have become the Soviet Union?
human_answers: Also, with or without overseas colonies, Communist France / Germany would be in a relatively poor position to defend themselves, as their territory is relatively small, so they can't trade space for time, or evacuate their industry far behind the frontlines (the way Russia did), and most of their core industrial and agricultural are close to borders or to coasts. They also would also be outnumbered by their combined enemies (eg. Communist France having to fight an anti-communist coalition of Britain, Germany and other countries), while the USSR actually outnumbered the Axis in WWII (and always had more reserves). Communist France would be very vulnerable to an Anglo-German invasion, with the British blockading the country and possibly landing in Brittany, Normandy, Picardy and/or Nord-Pas-de-Calais, and the Germans invading from the east (possibly with Italians and Spaniards also attacking, and those attacks could probably be contained thanks to the Alps and Pyrenees, but would divert men away from the main fronts). Communist Germany would essentially be in the same position as OTL WWI Germany, stuck between the Anglo-French and Russians. Now, a Franco-German communist union already has more potential. In addition, if France and Germany become a communist state together, there's a strong possibility that other nations will join them. Belgium and Netherlands are quite likely give their position, and also Italy, Spain and Portugal, due to their economical conditions and political instability.

Leading up to WW1, moat of the communist parties of the great powers were following the line of the second international, and therefore we're unable to seize power, the exception being of course the Russians. Had lines equivalent to those of Lenin prospered in the communist parties of other great powers, it is likely that any number of them could have had a successful communist revolution during or immediately after WW1. Germany is the most obvious candidate, as they had a big revolution irl even though it failed. Italy is another candidate, and to a lesser extent France. However, any of these countries would have issues with surviving alone under siege socialism as the Russians did. It was assumed at the time that a revolutionary state could only survive with the export of the revolution, lest it be surrounded and defeated by hostile imperialist powers. Stalin proved this wrong, Russia did benefit from it's unique geography in this sense. Could greater German industrial power make a German Soviet Republic defensible? I'd argue yes. Whilst Russian geography helped defensible, it was the economic boom, industrialisation, and enthusiasm of the people that helped it survive imperialist intervention. History ahs shown how enthusiastic armies fighting for a cause can and do defeat foreign powers. France is far more vulnerable to attack than Russia, and yet the French revolutionary wars showed how successful a mobiles french populace could be against the powers of the day. Whilst Germany does not have all the strategic depth and resources of Russia, could Britain France and Russia really afford fulls cake invasions just after WW1? They would run the risk of Revolution spreading among their own tired soldiers. AS for exporting revolution, depending on timing, an established communist Germany could be in a good position to support revolutions in Hungary and Finland , to give a couple of examples.

I think the stickiest element here is the combo of ideology and great/superpower status necessary to mimic the Soviets. If all that was needed was a large and relatively undeveloped country, China or India are easy picks. The problem is ideology. China only went communist in OTL because of the Soviets. No Soviets, no communist China (or India). These places could hypothetically adopt some other far-left socialist ideology, but it probably wouldn't be identifiably Marxist. Meanwhile, if all that was needed was ideology, many other European countries could conceivably fulfill the role. But if, say, France and France alone went communist, they would be considered threatening, but their industry was already decently developed and central planning isn't exactly good at innovating. Their threat level would not be able to rise much compared to the Soviets who had the wiggle room of being able to look at more developed countries and copy their homework. The Soviets also had a massive pool of labor and natural resources that France would lack. A France that probably lost its colonies and has a lagging industry is a middling concern, ultimately. Ditto with Germany. What's really needed, IMO, for another communist entity to arise to pose a similar threat to the Soviets is a multinational revolution in places where Marxism had decent traction. This means multiple Western European countries experiencing revolution and then deciding to cooperate heavily. Alternatively, a multinational coalition of revolutionary socialist states in South America (which must include Brazil since it has the largest population) could potentially adopt a similar role to the Soviets, although they'd be working with both a somewhat smaller population than the Soviets and a less developed industry than Western Europe. As an outside bet, maybe a revolutionary Spain somehow inspires its former colonies to follow suit and they join hands? Wouldn't need Brazil if you could pick up most of Hispanic America.

I do agree to some extent. Germany and France, though geopolitically disadvantaged, both demonstrated explosive potential for modernization. France, during the Napoleonic Wars, nearly conquered Europe by maximizing the advantages of advanced military doctrines, exceptional leadership, and the power of the nation-state. It’s interesting to think, though, how things might have unfolded if Napoleon had pursued democratic ideals rather than imperial ambitions. What if, instead of installing his relatives as kings, he had focused on exporting republicanism to other nations? Germany also revived after its defeat in World War I, almost conquering Europe by defeating France in just six weeks. However, their ideology, which was not universal but rather intended for domestic consumption, was deeply flawed in terms of fairness and equality. However, there is an issue with the immediate post-World War I period. It was the time when Germany's political system was most vulnerable, yet it was also the period when Germany faced the greatest risk of invasion. If the Kiel mutiny had led to a communist regime in Germany, the Entente Powers would likely have continued the war, eventually attempting to capture Berlin. Indeed, the Soviet Union only became one of the dominant global powers after World War II. Before that, it primarily focused on spreading communism in its neighboring countries.

I think Tsarist Russia was the only country able to become a truly 'marxist' superpower. And even they immediately morphed into a 'Marxist-Leninist' and eventually 'Stalinist' one-party state. If for some reason the Russian Revolution never happened, failed, or never became 'Marxist', Marxism as we know it would remain a political philosophy rather than an ideology, although it would be embraced by various socialist or workers-right parties in the various European parliamentary systems. The closest to a 'soviet-style' communist state I can think of would be Mao's China in the 1940's/1950's where due to it effectively still being run by the last remaining pre-WWII era warlord, China would still be. One-party state with the one party adhering to Chinese-style communism. Before that, any country where the Socialist/communist parties gain a majority in the democratic parliament would be the 'communist' world leader, be it Labour Britain, France, Weimar Germany or even a USA with a pro-labour pro-social(ist) president.
items.original_question: If not Russia, which country could have become the Soviet Union? In OTL, the Soviet Union was essentially the leader of communism, the state that embodied and exported the ideology. In France, after the birth of the “first republic in Europe,” the country faced massive wars against the old Western monarchies. As a result, although Napoleon, an extraordinary hero, almost succeeded in conquering Europe, France ultimately fell. Soviet Russia also faced a similar crisis. After the October Revolution, the first communist state was born, and the great powers, much like the monarchies a century before, sought to destroy Soviet Russia. However, unlike France, Soviet Russia survived the Russian Civil War. Afterward, the Soviet Union was no longer simply "Communist State A." They developed the potential of the land that was Russia. They transformed the underdeveloped economy of the Russian Empire into one of growth. Using that newfound capability, they exported revolution to various countries around the world. From Eastern Europe to Asia, the surrounding countries of Russia were all affected by communism. Furthermore, after 1945, they became a superpower alongside the United States, exporting revolution globally. Let’s consider a historical counterfactual. After Alexander II, the imperial succession changed. Unlike in OTL, Tsarevich Nicholas survived, and instead of the reactionary Alexander III, he ascended the throne. This alternate Nicholas II continued the reforms initiated by Alexander II, complementing, improving, and strengthening them. Unlike in OTL, Russia underwent a different trajectory. The Russian Empire was preserved, and Soviet Russia never came into being. In this scenario, which country could have replaced the Soviet Union? Which nation would need to become communist in order to "survive against surrounding capitalist powers" and "become a great power capable of exporting revolution?" Sometimes, in alternate history works (especially in game mods by Paradox Interactive), there are many timelines where a socialist revolution occurs in a country other than Russia. However, in my view, it’s questionable how many countries could do what the Soviet Union did. France? Germany? They have many geopolitical enemies. Even if they were to become communist after World War I, could they, like the Soviet Union, export revolution worldwide and become a superpower? It seems more likely that they would struggle just to survive. Britain, the United States? In OTL, Marx argued that a sufficiently developed capitalist system was necessary for a communist revolution to occur, with Britain being his example. Britain was also the world’s leading superpower at the time. However, a communist revolution did not occur in Britain. Because capitalism was so advanced, ironically, the entrenched privileges of the system were also too strong. British socialists who advocated for a revolutionary overthrow of the system did not have the power to challenge the entrenched elites, while others accepted the system and sought reforms within it. Ultimately, the conditions I believe are necessary for a "Soviet candidate" are as follows: 1. Geopolitically, it must be easy to defend. The country should be able to secure its borders and have a strategic position that allows for long-term survival and expansion. 2. It must have the potential to become a great power. The country needs the necessary resources, population, and industrial capacity to rise as a major global player. 3. Capitalism cannot be overly developed, and the elites must be driven toward 'system overthrow' rather than 'system compliance.' There must be enough dissatisfaction with the existing system to foster a desire for revolution, not merely reforms within the system. These are the core elements for a country to replicate the role of the Soviet Union. Where, besides Russia, could there be a land or country that fits these conditions? As a side note, it doesn’t necessarily have to be pure communism in this alternative Soviet ideology. It could be something like Maoism, syndicalism, or a unique form of socialism tailored to the needs of that country.
items.model_answer:
If Russia had not been the core of the Soviet Union, the most plausible alternative would have been Ukraine—but only in a limited, counterfactual sense.

The USSR was not just “Russia under another name”; it was a union of Soviet republics formed after the Russian Revolution and civil war. But Russia was overwhelmingly the central piece: it had the largest population, territory, army, administrative institutions, and the Bolshevik leadership centered in Petrograd/Moscow. Without Russia, a Soviet Union on the historical scale probably would not have existed.

If one had to name another country that could have served as the nucleus, Ukraine is the strongest candidate because it was populous, economically important, agriculturally rich, industrialized in the east, and became one of the founding Soviet republics. A Ukraine-centered socialist federation might have emerged if Bolshevik power had collapsed in Russia but survived in Ukraine.

However, it likely would have been much smaller and weaker than the actual USSR. Belarus or the Transcaucasian republics were too small to replace Russia’s role. Germany is another theoretical possibility if its post–World War I communist revolution had succeeded, but that would have produced a different communist state or federation, not the Soviet Union as we know it.

So the careful answer is: probably no country could truly have replaced Russia; but if forced to choose, Ukraine was the most plausible alternative core.

If the Alans had formed a lasting kingdom in Europe after the collapse of Roman authority in the West, the main result would likely have been another “barbarian successor state” alongside the Visigothic, Frankish, Burgundian, Vandal, and Ostrogothic kingdoms—but with a distinctive Iranian steppe character.

The Alans were an Iranian-speaking nomadic or semi-nomadic people originally from the Pontic-Caspian steppe. In the early 5th century, groups of Alans crossed the Rhine with Vandals and Suebi, entered Gaul and Iberia, and briefly held territory in parts of Spain before being absorbed by the Vandals or other powers. Historically, they did not maintain an independent European kingdom for long. A lasting Alan kingdom would therefore require one of two things: either a stronger Alan military-political leadership in Gaul or Iberia, or a successful settlement under Roman or post-Roman patronage that gave them land, legitimacy, and time to consolidate.

The most likely location would have been western Gaul or northern/central Iberia. In Gaul, an Alan kingdom might have emerged as a federate state under late Roman authority, similar to the Visigoths in Aquitaine. In Iberia, it might have survived if the Alans had not been crushed by the Visigoths in the 410s and had instead consolidated territory before the Vandals moved into North Africa. Either way, the kingdom would probably have become increasingly Romanized over time, adopting Latin administration, Christianity, Roman law, and local aristocratic customs.

Its distinctive contribution would have been military. The Alans were famous cavalry fighters, especially heavy cavalry. A stable Alan kingdom could have accelerated the development of mounted aristocratic warfare in western Europe. This does not mean medieval knighthood would have been “Alan,” but an Alan-ruled state might have strengthened the prestige of cavalry elites earlier and more visibly, especially in Gaul or Spain. Some historians already connect Sarmatian and Alan traditions loosely with later European cavalry culture; a lasting kingdom would have made that influence more concrete.

Linguistically, the result would depend on how numerous the Alans were. They were probably too few to replace Latin or emerging Romance languages across a large region. More likely, their Iranian language would have survived for a few centuries as an elite or regional language, leaving place names, personal names, military terms, and noble family traditions. Over time, unless reinforced by further migration from the steppe, an Alan kingdom in Gaul or Spain would probably have shifted to a Romance language, as the Franks, Visigoths, and Burgundians largely shifted culturally toward Latin-Christian norms.

Religiously, they would likely have become Christian, but the denomination matters. If they followed the pattern of many Germanic successor kingdoms, they might initially have adopted Arian Christianity, creating tension with the Catholic Roman population. If they converted early to Nicene Catholicism, as the Franks did under Clovis, they would have gained stronger support from bishops and Roman landowners. A Catholic Alan kingdom could have become a serious rival to the Franks or Visigoths; an Arian one would have faced more internal resistance.

Politically, a lasting Alan kingdom could have changed the balance of power in early medieval Europe. If located in Gaul, it might have blocked or slowed Frankish expansion toward the Loire and Aquitaine. The Frankish kingdom might have remained more northern and Germanic for longer, while southern Gaul developed under Alan-Roman rule. If located in Iberia, it could have prevented Visigothic dominance of the peninsula, producing a three-way balance among Alans, Suebi, and Visigoths, or later altering the conditions under which Islamic armies entered Iberia in the 8th century.

A durable Alan state might also have maintained stronger cultural links between western Europe and the steppe world. Because the Alans were related to peoples of the Iranian steppe and to the later Ossetians of the Caucasus, their survival in Europe could have left a visible Iranian-speaking Christian kingdom in the West. That would have made Europe’s ethnic and linguistic map more diverse, with an Indo-Iranian element embedded among Romance, Germanic, Celtic, and Slavic peoples.

In the long run, however, the most plausible outcome is not a permanently “steppe” Europe, but an Alan dynasty ruling a largely Roman provincial population. Like the Franks in Gaul or the Visigoths in Spain, the Alans would probably have been absorbed culturally while preserving a political name and aristocratic identity. A medieval “Kingdom of Alania” in Gaul or Iberia might have resembled a hybrid state: Roman in law and religion, Romance-speaking in the countryside, but with an Alan military nobility and origin myth.

So the careful answer is: a lasting Alan kingdom would probably not have transformed all of European history, but it could have significantly reshaped the post-Roman West. It might have checked Frankish or Visigothic expansion, strengthened cavalry-based aristocratic culture, preserved Iranian names and traditions in western Europe, and created a distinctive Christian Alan-Roman kingdom whose legacy would resemble that of the Franks or Visigoths—except with roots in the Iranian steppe rather than the Germanic world.

items.original_question: What if Partition of the Austrian Netherlands in the 18th Century? Hi, everyone. This is my second post sharing some lesser-known yet fascinating PoDs in European history. I stumbled upon a historical academic journal written by Frederik Dhondt, a history professor from the Ghent University in Belgium titled " So Great a Revolution’: Charles Townshend and the Partition of the Austrian Netherlands, September 1725 " (2012, Journal of Low Countries Studies). According to the article, Charles Townshend, the British Northern Secretary (equivalent to the Foreign Minister) and his predecessor James Stanhope (†. 1721) had proposed a partition of the Austrian Netherlands. The plan would see Austria surrendering its holdings in the Low Countries. The article summarised three possibilities. Some background before moving on. In the Nine Years' Year and the War of the Spanish Succession, Austria had allied with the Dutch Republic and Great Britain (or England-Scotland before 1707) to counter French ambitions in the Low Countries and the Rhineland. Towards the end of the Spanish Succession War, Britain became weary of increasing Austrian power. In 1716, it allied with France. The Austro-Spanish alliance confirmed by the Treaty of Vienna rang alarm bells in London. Not only did it reconcile the enmity between Emperor Charles XI and King Philip V, the combined power of Spain and Austria threatened the established balance of power. There were even talks to marry Maria Theresa to Don Carlos (future Charles III). Prime Minister Walpole and Townshend, therefore, desired to weaken the power of Austria. These plans were never made public, Townshend only discussed them with the ambassador in Paris, Horace Walpole. On page 56, Townshend suggested the partition plan could be implemented if the marriage between Maria Theresa and Don Carlos took place. James Stanhope first suggested that the Duke of Lorraine could receive Austria Netherlands. Alternatively, Stanhope suggested awarding it either to the Elector of Cologne or the Elector of Trier. The Electorate would be secularised. Townshend outright dismissed these ridiculous ideas, and offered his own solution. The Dutch will annex some territories including Antwerp. Ypres, Bruges, and Ostend would fall under joint Dutch-British control while the inland and southern portions of the Austrian Netherlands will go to France. What will be the geopolitical and diplomatic consequences of one of these plans was realised? Although I personally doubt the likelihood of this happening, nevertheless the ramifications will be interesting. You can access the article here through your university: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1179/0309656411Z.0000000002 .

If the Austrian Netherlands—roughly modern Belgium and Luxembourg—had been partitioned in the eighteenth century, the most likely result would have been a stronger France, a more anxious Dutch Republic, and a very different “Belgian question” in nineteenth-century Europe.

The Austrian Netherlands were an awkward Habsburg possession. They were rich, urbanized, Catholic, and strategically important, but they were geographically detached from Austria’s main lands. Vienna often viewed them less as a core territory than as a bargaining chip. So a partition was plausible, especially if tied to a broader diplomatic exchange: Austria might have surrendered the Netherlands in return for Bavaria, Italian concessions, or recognition of gains elsewhere.

The most plausible partition would have given France some or all of Flanders, Hainaut, Artois-adjacent districts, Namur, or Luxembourg, while the Dutch Republic might have received a fortified southern buffer or control over parts of Brabant and the Scheldt region. But that division would have been difficult. The Dutch wanted security against France, not necessarily millions of Catholic southern subjects or the reopening of Antwerp as a rival to Amsterdam. France, meanwhile, would have wanted precisely the territories that made the Dutch feel unsafe.

If France gained a large share, the balance of power would shift sharply. French control of the Scheldt, Antwerp, or the Meuse approaches would alarm Britain and the Dutch. Antwerp in particular was seen by Britain as a potential naval and commercial threat. A France already entrenched in Belgium before the Revolution would have been strategically stronger, but also more isolated diplomatically. Britain, the Dutch, Austria, and possibly Prussia would have had greater incentive to contain France earlier.

For Austria, partition would probably have simplified imperial policy. Vienna would no longer need to defend a distant, exposed province. Joseph II’s later conflicts with the Belgian estates—the reforms that helped provoke the Brabant Revolution of 1789—would never occur in the same form. Austria might focus more heavily on Bavaria, Italy, Hungary, and the Balkans. If compensated well, Austria could actually emerge more coherent strategically, even if it lost a wealthy province.

For the inhabitants of the Austrian Netherlands, the consequences would depend on who ruled them. Regions annexed by France would likely face earlier administrative centralization, legal integration, and cultural Frenchification. Catholic institutions might initially be respected under the monarchy, but during the French Revolution they would face confiscation and secularization earlier and more thoroughly. Areas absorbed by the Dutch Republic would create serious religious and political tension, because a Protestant-led republic would be ruling a large Catholic population. This could produce unrest similar to, or earlier than, the later Belgian revolt against the United Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1830.

The French Revolution would also unfold differently. Historically, revolutionary France invaded and annexed the Austrian Netherlands in the 1790s, turning Belgium into a major battlefield. If France already possessed much of the region, one of the Revolution’s early strategic goals would disappear. But the conflict might not be avoided. Instead, the war could focus sooner on the Dutch Republic, the Rhineland, or British fears of French dominance of the Low Countries. France’s northern frontier would be stronger, but the coalition against it might form faster.

In the long run, there might be no independent Belgium in 1830. The southern Low Countries would already have been divided between France, the Netherlands, and perhaps another power. Flemish and Walloon political development would diverge. Walloon and western Flemish areas under France might become more fully integrated into the French state. Dutch-held Brabant or Limburg might become a troubled Catholic frontier, possibly leading to later autonomy movements or foreign intervention.

The biggest geopolitical consequence is that the Low Countries would cease to function as a single buffer zone. Historically, Belgium became important because Britain and other powers did not want France to control the Channel-facing ports. A partition giving France Antwerp or the Belgian coast would make Britain much more hostile to France. A partition denying France those areas would leave France dissatisfied. Either way, the settlement would be unstable.

So, a partition of the Austrian Netherlands in the eighteenth century would probably not produce a quiet or permanent solution. It would remove Austria from the Low Countries but intensify rivalry between France, Britain, and the Dutch. It might prevent the later creation of Belgium, but it would replace the Belgian question with an earlier and possibly more dangerous struggle over Antwerp, the Scheldt, and the security of northwestern Europe.

EPISODE THREE​ German Pact ​ ​ A sudden storm breaking out across Europe had created a massive shockwave. Austria, still struggling to recover from the economic and military wounds of the War of the Second Coalition, was deeply displeased by France’s abrupt rekindling of hostilities. Emperor Francis II had been expecting a long period of peace, one he intended to devote to revitalizing Germany. Unfortunately, history had once again disappointed him. His federalist ambitions had not yet completely faded, but this meant confronting French republicanism earlier than anticipated. Moreover, following the referendum held on 18 February 1803 and the subsequent election, the country transitioned into what was called a presidential system. As a result, Fourier—who came to power and was a prominent representative of socialist thought—began spreading his ideas more widely across Europe. This signified a gradual shift of the German peoples toward republicanism. Although the Kingdom of Prussia and the Habsburg Monarchy did not hold each other in high regard, they shared a common enemy: France and republicanism. Approximately one week had passed since the outbreak of the Franco-Spanish War. French armies advanced rapidly, exploiting the dire condition of the Spanish forces to seize Catalonia and push toward Eastern Aragon. The Basque region had also fallen. Emperor Francis convened his cabinet, and they debated at length what course of action should be taken. Johann Amadeus Franz, the Minister of Finance of the era, was firmly opposed to breaking the peace with France, as any potential war would further devastate Austria’s already fragile economy. József Alvinczi, the Chief of the General Staff, argued that this war represented an opportunity to eliminate both France and the spread of republican ideas on the European continent. He maintained that, as demonstrated in the previous conflict, the Austrian army was not in as poor a condition as believed and demanded that an open ultimatum be issued to France. However, the Emperor had a different plan in mind. Although there was no certainty it would succeed, he deemed it worth attempting. For this reason, he decided to send a delegate to the Kingdom of Prussia, carrying a note requesting a private meeting with the King. The delegation set out on 15 March 1803. Meanwhile, across Europe, no clear decision had yet emerged from the British Isles. Prime Minister Henry Addington had no desire to see Spain under French control, but he also believed that the British Army was not yet prepared. After lengthy discussions with other statesmen, he sent an envoy to the Kingdom of Portugal to further expand the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance and present several proposals. In the meantime, the delegation sent by Austria to Prussia returned two weeks later. The Emperor’s proposal to the King of Prussia was to intervene in the Franco-Spanish War by forming a German coalition. The Prussian King, eager to enhance his prestige among the German states, responded favorably and announced his acceptance. Thus, the German Pact was formed. Both sides began final preparations for their already mobilized armies, and within approximately two weeks, everything was ready. A note bearing the personal signatures of both the Emperor and the King was delivered to the French delegates by a joint Austro-Prussian mission. The note demanded that France sever its alliance with the United States, withdraw from Spain, and agree to certain trade arrangements. French President Charles Fourier tore the original document to pieces in parliament. This act provided the Habsburg Monarchy and the Kingdom of Prussia with sufficient legitimacy to launch a military intervention against France. Emperor Francis II was deeply uneasy about Russia’s ambiguous stance. He neither wanted Russia to emerge excessively strong nor excessively weak. Poland could be the first step, and the Russian flag might one day fly over Hungary or the borders of the Holy Roman Empire. Taking such a risk seemed irrational. Therefore, depending on the course of the war, he considered enticing Russia into joining their side by offering the Balkan territories of the already weakened Ottoman Empire—despite his preference for preserving the balance of power in the Balkans and Eastern Europe. The French threat, however, took precedence. Although the United States did not yet pose a direct threat to Europe, it continued to threaten the colonial powers in the Americas. While it had not yet entered the conflict, such an involvement was not impossible. On the other hand, the Emperor foresaw that the French government’s aggressive and overly idealistic actions would ultimately lead to its downfall. By initiating this war, France had effectively shot itself in the foot, and these events would pave the way for a rise in anti-French sentiment throughout Europe.

If Napoleon could not return to France in 1799, the most likely result is that the Coup of 18 Brumaire would either fail, be delayed, or be carried out by someone else with a weaker outcome. France would probably not get the Napoleonic Consulate in the form we know, and Europe’s history would change dramatically.

In real history, Napoleon’s return from Egypt came at the perfect moment. France’s Directory government was unpopular, corrupt, financially weak, and politically unstable. France was also under pressure from the Second Coalition, though the military situation was beginning to improve. Emmanuel-Joseph Sieyès and other political figures wanted a coup to replace the Directory with a stronger executive system, but they needed a popular general to give the coup military legitimacy. Napoleon was ideal: famous, ambitious, politically flexible, and seen by many French people as a national savior.

If Napoleon remained stuck in Egypt, died, was captured by the British, or simply arrived too late, Sieyès would have had to choose another general. The most likely candidate would have been Jean Victor Moreau, a respected and successful French commander. However, Moreau lacked Napoleon’s political boldness and charisma. He was a capable soldier but not the same kind of revolutionary political operator. A coup might still have happened, because the Directory was weak and many elites wanted constitutional change, but the resulting regime would probably have been more civilian and less personalist than Napoleon’s Consulate.

France might still have defeated the Second Coalition. Napoleon was not the only talented French general. Moreau, Masséna, Brune, and others were capable commanders. In fact, in 1799–1800, French recovery depended on several generals, not only Napoleon. Without Napoleon’s later Italian campaign and victory at Marengo in 1800, the war could have lasted longer, but Austria and Russia were already divided in their goals. The Second Coalition might still have collapsed eventually, though perhaps with a less spectacular French victory and less favorable peace terms.

The biggest change would come after 1800. Without Napoleon as First Consul, France probably would not become a military empire so quickly. There might be no Napoleonic Code in its famous form, no coronation as emperor in 1804, no sale of Louisiana under the same circumstances, no massive restructuring of Germany through the Confederation of the Rhine, no invasion of Spain, and no disastrous invasion of Russia in 1812. France might remain a powerful republic or semi-authoritarian military state, but not necessarily a Europe-dominating empire.

The revolutionary wars would likely continue in some form, because the conflict between revolutionary France and the monarchies of Europe did not depend solely on Napoleon. But the wars would probably be less centered on one man’s ambition. France’s borders might remain expanded to the Rhine and into parts of Italy or the Low Countries, but it would be less likely to impose a continent-wide imperial order.

For Egypt, Napoleon’s absence from France would likely mean the French expedition collapses even more clearly. The British controlled the sea, and the French army in Egypt was isolated. In real history, the army surrendered in 1801 after Napoleon had already abandoned it. If Napoleon stayed, he might attempt to rule Egypt longer, but without naval support and supplies, his position would remain extremely weak. He could be killed, captured, or forced to surrender. His legend would be very different: instead of becoming ruler of France, he might be remembered as a brilliant general whose Egyptian adventure ended in failure.

So the most plausible outcome is this: France still undergoes political change after the Directory, possibly through a coup led by Sieyès and another general, but without Napoleon it does not become the Napoleonic Empire. France remains a major revolutionary military power, but Europe probably avoids the specific chain of Napoleonic Wars that reshaped the continent between 1803 and 1815. The French Revolution’s influence would still spread, but less through Napoleon’s personal empire and more through gradual military, legal, and ideological pressure.

items.question: What If the Greek 'Great Plan' had succeeded and the Greek War of Independence had triggered an early collapse of the Ottoman Empire?
human_answers: A more decisive Ottoman defeat against Greece can give birth to the "Megali Idea" before 1844. In such a scenario, a larger independent Greek state can invited Louis-Philippe d’Orléans to become its king, before 1830 of course. This arrangement can be supported by both France and its Bourbon king, who might want to sideline a troublesome cousin, and by the United Kingdom. For the British, the presence of a Great European power south of the Straits, one aligned with neither Austria nor Russia can further divide the continental great powers and serve British strategic interests. With France satisfied in Greece and Austria compensated with territories along the Adriatic coast, Britain can focus on securing Egypt for itself. Even if the Suez Canal is not even a dream, control of Egypt is already strategically valuable for strengthening connections with India. By 1829, railway projects are already under consideration, making overland transit increasingly plausible and reinforcing Egypt’s geopolitical importance. And if its happen after 1830, Louis-Philippe has enough sons (6 minus one who died in 1828) to send one to Greece.

Considering their interest is not even religious (GB: Protestant, France: Catholic, Russia: Orthodox) and that really none of these Great Powers saw the Greek War of Independence with positive eyes (to them it was no different than the revolutions in Spain, Portugal and Naples; which, btw, they sent huge armies to crush). There was later a British change, but even the Metternich, Alexander and so on weren't super happy about it. Remember: at this point, the memory of Napoleon is far fresher than that of the Ottoman invasions into the Balkans, so the concern, far above Islam, is revolutionary sentiment. What I do see happening is them deliberating and taking too long to make a decision that the situation ends up devolving on its own (it took them like 3 years to agree to send an invasion to Spain). Then again, the French were sympathetic to Muhammad Ali while the British aided Ali Pasha plenty of times (through Maitland, specifically). They will always prefer a rotting corpse of the Ottoman empire maintaining power over the ambitious and reformist Albanian Pashas in power, this is why they went out of their way to put them out IRL, but when shit hits the fan, they have to re-examine their approach of course.

Agreed that the Great Powers, including even Russia under Alexander, don't want a full Ottoman collapse. That's not the same as saying they would intervene to stop it. It's hard to conceive of a situation in which Great Britain, France, or Russia would go to war to suppress Christian rebels fighting against the Sultan, particularly after the various atrocities committed at Chios and other places. There were also similar atrocities committed by the Greeks against Muslims, but this did not register in the European consciousness of the time and would not be a factor. It's also not a given that any intervention would be successful at stopping chaos and preserving the Empire, even if it did somehow occur. This would be a formidable job if the situation became so extreme that the Ottomans asked for such support. More likely the intervention would be directed towards managing the collapse and achieving a partition either formally or in terms of spheres of influence.
items.original_question: What if 'Great Plan' more or fully successful - Greek War of Independence causes early Ottoman collapse? There have been many threads about the Greek War of Independence here, but one what if I haven't seen anyone talk about might be one of the most crazy ones. Mark Mazower states the following in his book on the Greek War of Indepdendence: Of course, aside from the revolt in the Peloponnese, none of these plans ever came close to succeeding. These plans were modified or abandoned entirely when the focus of the revolt shifted from the Peloponnese to the Danubian Principalities. There was a letter sent to cause terror in Constantinople, but the letter never made it and plans were changing so often that no action was taken. Now this seems like an insane scheme which would be insanely hard to pull off, even if all the circumstances were right, but let's hypothetically ask, what if some, or all of them did? Would this cause the Ottoman Empire to collapse entirely, or enter a prolonged period of unrest? A torching of the fleet, coordinated with the assassination of Mahmud II, coupled with all the other issues the empire was facing in the early 1820's seem like they would be a complete headache, who would even be Sultan had this happened, considering Abdulmecid wasn't even born yet and Mahmud II had no sons? Edit: Turns out Mahmud II had a single surviving son by this point, Abdulhamid. But he died in 1825 IOTL, which, if it still happens, might actually make things even worse if the revolt didn't fizzle out by then.
items.model_answer:
If the Greek “Great Plan” had succeeded and the Greek War of Independence had set off an early collapse of the Ottoman Empire in the 1820s, the result would probably not have been a restored Greek-Byzantine empire ruling the eastern Mediterranean. It would more likely have produced an early partition of Ottoman lands under heavy Great Power supervision, with Greece becoming larger and more important than it did historically, but not dominant enough to inherit the empire.

The immediate consequence would have been a much wider Balkan revolt. Serbia, the Danubian Principalities, Bulgaria, parts of Albania, Epirus, Macedonia, Thrace, and the Aegean islands might all have been pulled into rebellion or occupation. Russia would almost certainly have intervened, claiming to protect Orthodox Christians and to secure influence over the Straits. Britain and Austria would have opposed any outcome that gave Russia control of Constantinople or the Bosporus. France might have supported a limited Greek expansion but would also have wanted influence in the eastern Mediterranean. So the “Greek victory” would quickly have become an international crisis over who would replace Ottoman authority.

Greece itself would probably have emerged much larger than the small kingdom created in 1832. It might have gained the Peloponnese, central Greece, many Aegean islands, Thessaly, Epirus, and possibly parts of Macedonia and western Anatolia with large Greek populations. Constantinople would have been the central prize, but it is unlikely the Great Powers would simply have allowed it to become the capital of a new Greek empire. More plausibly, the city and the Straits would have become an internationalized zone, a Russian-protected enclave, or a carefully balanced neutral territory.

The Balkans would have become independent or semi-independent much earlier. Serbia would likely have become a recognized state decades before it did historically. Bulgaria might have emerged earlier as an autonomous Orthodox principality, though its borders would have been fiercely disputed with Greece and Serbia. The Romanian principalities would probably have slipped out of Ottoman suzerainty under Russian or Austrian influence. Albania and Bosnia would have been especially unstable, because large Muslim populations there would have resisted Christian nationalist states and because Austria would have feared unrest spreading into its own Balkan possessions.

In the Arab provinces, Ottoman collapse would have empowered local rulers rather than Greece. Egypt under Muhammad Ali would likely have become fully independent and might have expanded into Syria, Palestine, or Arabia. North Africa would have fallen more quickly under European influence, especially French and British. Iraq and the Levant might have fragmented into local dynasties, Egyptian possessions, or early European protectorates. The Ottoman Empire’s collapse would thus have accelerated European imperial competition in the Middle East by several decades.

For Greece, success would have been both a triumph and a burden. A much larger Greek state would have contained many non-Greek populations: Turks, Albanians, Slavs, Vlachs, Jews, Armenians, and others. That would have made state-building difficult and could have produced earlier ethnic expulsions, massacres, and population exchanges. The real nineteenth-century Balkan conflicts over Macedonia, Thrace, and Anatolia would not disappear; they would simply arrive earlier and under different borders.

The wider European balance of power would also change dramatically. The “Eastern Question” would erupt in the 1820s rather than dominating diplomacy later in the century. A version of the Crimean War might happen earlier, as Britain, France, and Austria tried to prevent Russia from becoming the chief heir to Ottoman power. Without a surviving Ottoman Empire, there would be no Tanzimat reforms, no late Ottoman constitutionalism, no Young Turk movement in the same form, and probably no Ottoman entry into World War I. The First World War itself, if it still occurred, would have had a very different eastern Mediterranean and Middle Eastern map.

So the likely outcome is an earlier de-Ottomanized Balkans and eastern Mediterranean: a larger Greece, earlier Serbian/Bulgarian/Romanian independence, an independent or expansionist Egypt, intensified Russian-Austrian-British rivalry, and much earlier nationalist violence over mixed populations. The Greek cause would have won far more than it did historically, but the collapse of the Ottoman Empire would have created a power vacuum too large for Greece alone to fill.

items.question: What If the French become one of the largest communities in the US
human_answers: Hordes of Catholics, even if not all that devout, descending on the US will cause some tension. On the flip side, though, France is one of the civilized nations, and they're seen as more desirable shade of white. Timing matters, too. Napoleonic era, when immigration is still low, is a whole lot different than the final decades of the 19th century, when millions is a drop in the bucket. Location matters, too. Are the French hordes joining into the crowded East, where they likely assimilate? Or are they carving out a big chunk of the midwest/west as largely French? Reason for the diaspora might matter. If we mess with the Napoleonic era, especially if we butterfly it (not killing off a generation or two of males would be a good start in having excess population to export), the state of the world could affect the state of the USA (maybe even the size if no Mex-Am War/Texas). With such a generic What if, we can only talk in generics. If we stipulate a recognizable world, more or less the same, except a massive French diaspora for some reason that hasn't caused OTL to derail.... I would guess the French would be like any other large group. There'll be tension, but everyone will adapt. It's an age of racism, and French are in the top class, so I suspect they'll have an easier time of it. (caveat edit: In no way am I saying French are better than any other nation, but reality is that skin color mattered. My understanding is that not all whites were considered equal)

I would assume rather than staying in the east, the French would largely settle in former Louisiana- centring probably on New Orleans. Texas and Florida as well are likely spots for French settlement. Of the 13 colonies, I would guess it’s the southern ones which would be most amenable to French settlement- though how that affects racial dynamics in the south, and how that affects potential north south tensions is difficult to say. It’s difficult as well to say what the economic impact of French settlement would be- I’d say as a community they’d probably be more educated and thus better off than the Irish or Italians, perhaps more comparable to German or Swedish immigrants. Perhaps the planter class ends up going fully bilingual. Depending on how the 19th century goes you could end up with an Alt-confederacy that stays independent because it has so many French speakers and Catholics that the north simply isn’t interested in reintegrating them.
items.original_question: What if the French become one of the largest communities in the US Let’s suppose that millions of French flocked to the US in the 19th century for one reason or another—for example, because harsher Napoleonic Wars and a more severe Congress of Vienna plunged France into a deep economic crisis, while the Irish and Italians would be less numerous in the US, for example because the Irish Great Famine never happened and the Italian peninsula unified and modernized earlier. No PoD before 1780. How would the French be treated in the US? Would they face xenophobia and form a distinct community like the Irish and Italians, or would they be assimilated among the WASPs within one or two generations like the Germans did IOTL? French culture was admired, but I’m not sure that the arrival of millions of French people (with a Latin culture and Catholic religion) would be particularly well received.
items.model_answer:
If the French became one of the largest communities in the United States, the effects would likely be cultural, economic, political, and linguistic, but the scale would depend on whether this happened through new immigration from France, growth of French-speaking communities, or more Americans identifying with French ancestry.

Culturally, French influence in the U.S. would become much more visible. French food, fashion, film, literature, design, and holiday traditions would likely have a stronger presence in major cities and in regions where French communities settled. Cities might develop larger French neighborhoods, French-language schools, cultural centers, media outlets, restaurants, and festivals. French could become a more commonly taught and spoken language, especially in areas with large French populations.

Economically, a large French community could deepen ties between the U.S. and France. There might be more French investment in American industries such as aerospace, luxury goods, wine, energy, technology, pharmaceuticals, and transportation. More French entrepreneurs, researchers, and skilled workers could contribute to U.S. innovation and business. At the same time, if the growth came from rapid mass migration, there could be short-term pressures on housing, schools, public services, and labor markets in the areas where newcomers concentrated.

Politically, French Americans could become a more influential voting bloc. Politicians might pay more attention to issues important to them, such as immigration policy, bilingual education, U.S.-France relations, European affairs, climate policy, labor protections, and cultural exchange. If the community were large enough and geographically concentrated, it could affect local elections and possibly national politics.

Socially, the French would likely integrate into American society while also reshaping parts of it. The U.S. has historically absorbed large immigrant communities—Irish, German, Italian, Jewish, Mexican, Chinese, Indian, and others—who influenced American identity over time. A large French community would probably follow a similar pattern: first maintaining strong cultural institutions, then gradually blending into broader American life while preserving some distinct traditions.

In foreign policy, U.S.-France relations might become even closer. France is already a major American ally, but a large French-descended or French-born population in the U.S. could increase public interest in European politics, NATO, trade with the European Union, and cooperation on global issues. However, it could also create political debates if French and American policy preferences diverged.

Overall, the U.S. would likely become more visibly Francophone and more culturally connected to France, while France would gain a stronger social and political link to American life. The change would not necessarily transform the U.S. completely, but it would add a major new layer to American multicultural identity.

items.question: Independent Naples: What If Catherine of Aragon marries Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505?
human_answers: I wouldn't say that Philip is foolish, simply naive, since it is impossible for him to imagine that Ferdinand II and Catherine are plotting against him, to shape Joanna and especially the little Charles into a figure totally different from his own ( so that he may become the perfect archetype of a Christian Monarch ), but in any case I am certain that Queen Isabella would never do anything wrong in compromising her nephew's chances of inheriting his father's possessions ( Burgundy and Austria ) or preventing him from aspiring to the imperial throne, after all doing this risks it compromise to the international prestige of his family ( the Trastamaras ) let's say that the Catholic Monarchs only want to make sure that the future King of Castile and Aragon is not too accommodating to French wishes, it is realistic to think that Charles was initially educated at his mother's court, and then, when he was sure he could face a sea voyage, he was transferred to his grandfather Maximilian

Oh, please… the POD is interesting but the development is full of things that are blatantly false. OTL Isabella and Ferdinand were the ones that wanted Catalina’s remarriage to the future Henry VIII, and insisted that her marriage with Arthur was not consummated. Henry VII OTL was bullied in accepting the engagement of his second son to Catalina as he believed she was too old for his son. He would have zero troubles in giving back the half of her dowry he had already received (for all that getting back her dowry meant that Catherine had no right to any English money or lands) and send Catherine back at home as he had no use for her. Catalina’s aunt, the Dowager Queen of Naples would first try to marry her own daughter to the new Ferdinand III of Naples, as Giovanna was still in her mid-20s (or she would expect to see another match arranged for her daughter before agreeing to support Catalina as future Queen of Naples. Sea journeys at the time were extremely dangerous (I don’t remember if Catalina got lucky, but both Joanna and Margaret got close to die in their respective wedding journeys) reason for which Philip used his friendship with the French King for securing a land passage into France for going to receive the investitures. Eleanor and Charles at the time were too little for making safely the long journey, for not talking about baby Isabella, and Philip would never agree to bring them in Castile in any case. And if she had been so inclined Catalina, being the youngest of her sisters, could very well be allowed to take the veil. In 1502 Juana had three children and Maria one and both were likely to have soon more…

The year 1502 starts very rough for Catalina of Aragon. She and her husband, Arthur , Prince of Wales had both fallen ill at the end of March and when she recovered, she discovered that her husband had died. She could not believe it. She was a widow after only five months of marriage. She knew that she was not pregnant, as her marriage was unconsummated. One month after she was made a widow, Catalina was moved to Durham House in London and was visited by King Henry VII and his wife, Queen Elizabeth of York. Catalina told them that she had bled already and there was no hope for an heir from their late son, so his younger brother, Prince Henry, Duke of York, was officially declared as the heir. When the news to Catalina's parents, King Fernando II of Aragon and Queen Isabella I of Castile, they were disappointed that the alliance seemed to have fallen through and that their daughter was widowed at only sixteen years old. This began a struggle over Catalina. Queen Isabella was adamant that her youngest child be returned to her, since there was not a hope of an English grandchild to seal the alliance with Spain and England. King Henry VII, however, did not want to lose her or her dowry. He offered to marry her to his younger son and she could still be Queen of England one day. Queen Isabella made up her mind and told her husband that she wanted their daughter to be returned home. King Ferdinand sent an ambassador to tell King Henry that the Princess would be returned to Spain, either with her entourage or by force. When King Henry VII heard this, he was furious, but also terrified. He needed this alliance with Spain and he did not want to let his daughter-in-law go. Finally, an agreement was finally reached. The Infanta would return to her parents and half her dowry would be returned with her and she would retain her status of Dowager Princess of Wales and would still receive her marriage jointure for the remainder of her life. Her English attendants, like Margaret Pole, would remain in England. When she was told Princess Catalina had a mix of grief and relief. She was happy to return home to her parents, especially since her older sister, Juana, who was now Princess of Asturias, was back home as well. On August 1, 1502, Princess Catalina and her entourage arrived at Dover, preparing to board the ship that will cross the sea once again. Prince Henry, the young Prince of Wales accompanied her, just like he escorted her down the aisle to marry his late older brother. The eleven year old, who was talkative and social, was unusually quiet through the journey. Princess Catalina gave him a little kiss on his forehead and told him that she will never forget him or her time in England and she knew that one day, he will be the greatest King that England ever had, before she boarded the ship. Thankfully, this journey was much easier than her original one taking her to England. She and her entourage arrived in Laredo on the 15th of August. Princess Catalina found herself smiling, as she saw the familiar Castilian villages and knew she was home. However, she then was wondering what would happen to her and her future. Due to the deaths of her older brother, sister and nephew, she knew that taking holy vows was not an option, as he parents only had three surviving daughters. Would she just remain a spinster? Would she be married off again to a foreign Kingdom, even France?
