items.original_question: Independent Naples: What if Catherine of Aragon marries Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505? Hey all! This question has been on my mind a little too. What if instead of the long seven years in England in virtual poverty, Catherine of Aragon returns to her parents in the summer of 1502 and they arrange a marriage for the young King of Naples, which is still an independent Kingdom in this timeline? In this timeline, Henry VIII will instead marry Eleanor of Austria instead.
items.model_answer:
If Catherine of Aragon married Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, in 1505, the most plausible result is not a fully sovereign Naples immediately, but a semi-independent Aragonese client kingdom built around a compromise between conquest and legitimacy.

Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, was the heir of the displaced Neapolitan Aragonese line. Catherine was the daughter of Ferdinand the Catholic, who had just taken Naples from the French and did not want either France or the old Neapolitan dynasty to recover it independently. A marriage between Catherine and the Duke would have been a neat dynastic solution: the conquered kingdom could be presented not simply as a Spanish possession, but as restored to its native Aragonese house under the protection of Catherine’s father.

In that scenario, Ferdinand the Catholic might install the couple in Naples as king and queen, or more likely as nominal rulers under strong Aragonese supervision. Naples would have its own court, its own dynasty, and greater local legitimacy than under a Spanish viceroy, but its foreign policy and defense would remain tied to Aragon and Sicily. In practice it would resemble a protected kingdom, not a modern independent state.

The main benefit would be stability. The Neapolitan nobility had reasons to resent direct Spanish rule, while the Duke of Calabria possessed a strong hereditary claim. Catherine’s marriage would reconcile the old Neapolitan line with the new Spanish conquerors. It would also make French claims harder to present as liberation, because Naples would appear to have a legitimate native ruler backed by Aragon.

The major danger would come after Ferdinand the Catholic’s death in 1516. In real history, Naples passed into the wider Habsburg-Spanish inheritance of Charles V. In this counterfactual, Catherine and the Duke could argue that Naples was theirs by dynastic settlement. Charles V, Catherine’s nephew, would face a choice: absorb Naples into the Habsburg monarchy by pressure, or recognize it as an allied cadet kingdom. Given his huge commitments in Germany, Spain, the Low Countries, and against France, he might accept a loyal independent Naples if it remained anti-French and pro-Habsburg.

France would almost certainly challenge the arrangement. Francis I would still want influence in Italy, and Naples remained one of the great prizes of the Italian Wars. So an independent Naples could survive only if backed by Spain, the Empire, the papacy, or some combination of them. Without that backing, France or the Habsburgs would eventually swallow it. With backing, Naples becomes a buffer state: formally independent, but strategically dependent.

The English consequences are enormous. Catherine would leave England and never marry Henry VIII. That means no Princess Mary by Catherine, no “Great Matter” over annulment from Catherine, and likely no Henrician break with Rome in the same form. Henry VIII would marry someone else, probably a French, Habsburg, or another Iberian princess. England might still experience religious reform, but the specific chain that produced the English Reformation, Mary I, and Elizabeth I would be radically altered or absent.

For Italy, an independent Naples weakens direct Spanish domination. Spain would still be powerful in Sicily, Sardinia, and later Milanese politics, but without direct possession of Naples its hold over southern Italy and the central Mediterranean is less absolute. The papacy, Venice, France, and the Empire would all have more room to maneuver. The Italian Wars would continue, but the balance would be less clearly tilted toward a Spanish-Habsburg Italy.

So the most likely outcome is this: Catherine becomes queen or consort-ruler of a restored Aragonese Naples; the Duke of Calabria gains legitimacy and a throne; Naples becomes a semi-independent but Spanish-aligned kingdom; England avoids the Catherine-Henry marriage and therefore the classic annulment crisis; and Habsburg control of Italy becomes less direct. True Neapolitan independence is possible, but only as protected independence within the anti-French Aragonese-Habsburg system.

items.question: What If Curb Global Warming after 1980
human_answers: India has only recently emerged as one of the world’s chief polluters; some two decades ago, Russia and Japan had a bigger mark, and in 1980 Canada was the bigger polluter. Depending on how decarbonized the economies of the First World are by 2000, India’s subsequent economic growth could be magnitudes cleaner than it was OTL. China you have a better point about, though first, their massive economic rise in the three decades after Mao’s death or so is pretty contingent, and second, they still only caught up to the already carbon stagnant EU in 2002. Imagine if the US was still comparable, as they were OTL until the mid 1980’s; now imagine, as China is getting ready to join the WTO in the late 90’s and early 2000’s, the west is also pushing a world climate treaty that (among other things) pushed these three major blocs (the US, Europe, and China) to curb their emissions going into the future. Even if India still sees their emissions rise, wouldn’t the fact that by far the largest producers are simultaneously cutting emissions lead to net reduction?

Well, is the point of your question, can we limit temperature rise by today , or in perpetuity? If the former, then greater adoption of nuclear energy in the West is probably a good enough answer; by the time Chinese and Indian energy use spikes, the resultant temperature spike won't come until after today. Maybe. But that seems like the wrong question, I interpret it as how to prevent such a spike from EVER occurring, rather than just occurring 10 years late. And for that, there's a big challenge. How do developing countries get off the ground? Hydrocarbons are great for that. If the big emitters of the 60s all switched to nuclear, that's fantastic--but China and India can't afford to START with nuclear, nobody can, which means a huge amount of hydrocarbons being burned when they start heavily industrializing. As a solution, perhaps their rise as industrial powers can be delayed a few decades? If they started industrializing in 2025 instead, they might use shale gas or solar, which are now the cheapest sources of power. But the production of those isn't domestic to China, which is a huge part of their use of coal--they don't have to import it. Tentatively, maybe the Soviet Union needs to have greater economic development and a softer landing when it falls? If they can be an industrial exporter while powered off domestic nuclear and natural gas, and remain so in the 1990s, then Chinese growth will be very different, and overall emissions will be lower. Cars and planes are obvious problems. I would also posit beef as a problem--methane is significantly more powerful than carbon in greenhouse effect, and is estimated as responsible for 20 to 30 percent of human-origin warming. Sixty percent of methane emissions are estimated as human-caused, with a big one being agriculture, and beef is responsible for a LOT of agriculture. So a poorer world, that eats less meat, would have lower methane emissions. So too would a world with fewer wetlands, so perhaps a little more paving of swamps would be good from the perspective of this question. Just thoughts. I'll be back for more, probably.

No, because they're already too anti-nuclear. The R&D and thus cost curves on silicon-based solar cell production, and on improved battery capacity, are both pushed pretty hard historically by electronics industry spinoffs. It's hard to see any sort of policy pushes for renewables accelerating those more than marginally, and dramatic acceleration is what you need to make them cost-viable decades ahead of schedule. On the other hand, nuclear was deliberately hobbled by US policy in the 1970s. People like to blame 1979's Three Mile Island, but (for a couple examples) the AEC to NRC switchover was passed by Congress and signed by Ford in 1974, while Carter's anti-reprocessing moratorium was in 1977. If you instead have the US adopt its own version of France's Messmer Plan in 1974 (which is tricky, because Messmer was able to simply ignore anti-nuclear sentiments due to government and economy structure in ways the US government couldn't), you get nuclear power economies of scale driven by the joint US-French demand that make it a more-attractive alternative throughout the rest of the industrialized world. Imagine Thatcher's government nuclearizing Britain in part to undercut the coal unions, for example. Then, if US electricity is something like 75% nuclear in 1990 (like France in 1990, instead of the historical 20%), with the UK fast-following? Now you have the necessary condition (it not hobbling the US) for international trade treaties and the like based on carbon emissions, after a decade of greenhouse effect publicity (since the 1979 NAS report), with the first IPCC report coming out. (Yes, sure, butterflies will scramble the details, but "coal is bad" science, if anything, will be better-funded if the US is transitioning from coal.) If Japan has (as is likely) lagged the US/France/UK in adoption of nuclear, this will be a particularly easy sell, since everybody in the West in 1990 is looking for an excuse to be protectionist against "Japan, Inc." And with that set up, you have the trick for going forward. If China (etc.) has to avoid coal power to export to Western markets, China either will figure out how to avoid coal, or it won't develop because it won't have markets to sell into.

I can give you two, PODs, One being no 3 Mile Island and the other being no John Sununu. So the real easy way to cut down on CO2 emissions is to cut down on coal use, and both PODs give easy ways to do just that. After the banning of CFCs in the late 80s, momentum existed for much harder caps on carbon than were discussed later. In particular, serious curtailment of coal as an energy source in the developed world was mooted. However, this momentum was handicapped with a lack of US Presidential support, with Bush Sr being advised against supporting these efforts by his Chief of Staff, John Sununu. Remove Sununu, and US support for carbon caps become more likely earlier. In addition with no 3MI incident, nuclear technology in the west could become less taboo, giving a viable alternative to coal fired power earlier. I could see a scenario where industry, much like CFCs, sees the financial opportunities in replacing coal with a nuclear/gas mix, and does not get in the way of any cuts to carbon emissions. A good book on the subject in your timeframe is Loosing Earth, by Nathanial Rich, which goes into detail about the drive to curtail emissions in the late 80s. would highly recommend giving it a read.
items.original_question:
AHC: Curb Global Warming after 1980

So you know how Global Surface Temperatures have increased 1.3°C over pre-industrial levels at present, and how a big part of the current Climate Movement is trying to limit further change as much as possible, 1.5°C being the best known* goal? Well, as recently as circa 1980, GST above PIL was only about 0.3°C, and had been hovering just below those levels for decades since the aftermath of WWII; in other words, a full degrees celsius of global warming only happened in the past 45 years alone. This is actually pretty astonishing when you realize how much of a turning point circa 1980 was to global carbon emissions -- both the biggest producers world-wide at the time, the US and Europe, initially saw their emissions peak, with Europe remaining controlled even as the US reversed course after a few years; Japan and Canada have a similar "false peaks" around the same time as the US; the USSR, of course, collapse circa 1990 and saw their emissions collapse thereafter, never to recover; and China was about to undergo a massive economic expansion that would see them become the world's largest emitters. So what I want to determine here is -- what is the latest PoD for avoiding this massive escalation of climate change, or of making it as small as possible? Could a PoD in the late 1970's (eg a continuation of Carter's energy policies in the US) have done the trick? If avoiding a full degrees celsius of warming wasn't seriously avertable by, say, 1975, how early do we need to go? 1960? The aftermath of WWII? In the event we can come to a consensus on the latest possible PoD and what would do the trick, we might also discuss how those changes to said countries' energy polices and to the global economy as a whole would have changed things overall. Thanks. *I'm really trying to avoid getting sidetracked in this discussion for the thread, so for anyone wanting to weigh in on whether its still feasible or how big of a deal missing that goal is, please take that to one of the Chat discussions -- much thanks!
items.model_answer:
If the world had seriously curbed global warming after 1980, the present would likely be noticeably safer, cleaner, and less politically strained by climate impacts, though not climate-free.

By 1980, scientists already understood that rising carbon dioxide from fossil fuels would warm the planet. If governments had acted then—through carbon pricing, efficiency standards, rapid renewable and nuclear deployment, protection of forests, and limits on coal and oil dependence—global emissions could have peaked in the 1980s or 1990s instead of continuing to rise for decades.

The biggest difference would be temperature. Earth had already warmed somewhat by 1980, so warming would not have stopped entirely. But instead of today’s roughly 1.2°C or more of warming above preindustrial levels, the world might have been closer to perhaps 0.6–0.9°C, depending on how aggressive the policies were. That difference sounds small, but it would mean fewer deadly heat waves, less severe drought in many regions, lower wildfire risk, reduced coral reef loss, slower Arctic ice decline, and less stress on crops and water systems.

Sea-level rise would still have continued because oceans and ice sheets respond slowly, but it would likely be lower today and much lower in the long run. Many coastal cities would still face risks, but the urgency and cost of adaptation would be less severe.

Economically, an early transition would probably have been cheaper than today’s delayed one. Industries would have had decades to adjust gradually. Renewable energy, batteries, electric transport, and efficiency technologies would likely have matured earlier. Air pollution deaths from coal and oil combustion would also have been substantially lower. However, fossil-fuel-producing regions and companies would have faced earlier disruption, and there would have been major political fights over jobs, energy prices, and development rights.

Geopolitically, the world might be less dependent on oil and gas exporters, altering the power of petrostates and possibly reducing some resource-driven tensions. Developing countries would have needed financial and technological support to grow without following the same high-carbon path as the industrialized world. If wealthy countries had provided that support, global inequality around climate responsibility might be less bitter today.

The most important consequence is that climate change would feel less like an emergency. Adaptation would still be necessary, and some damage would still occur, but many of the worst projected risks for the twenty-first century would be less likely. In short, curbing global warming after 1980 would not have prevented all climate change, but it could have avoided a large share of today’s danger and made the remaining problem far easier to manage.
