Three major factors were at play in the Russo-British diplomatic relations at the turn of the century. 1. Generational change at the Foreign Office, with the rise of more eurocentric and anti-German key decisionmakers. 2. The failed French attempts to form an anti-British coalition during Second Boer War. This more or less forced Britain to come to terms with France, or accept the fact that von Holstein had been right, and that by merely waiting Germany could indeed ultimately dictate terms for her new treaties with Britain. 3. The Eastern Question and the Boxer war were drawing new powers in to the old Great Game in Asia, and Britain had to react to the rising power of Japan and their genuine attempts to strike a bargain with expansionist Russia that had just occupied northern Manchuria and was viewing the Korean peninsula as the logical next target. Combined with the determined naval buildup of Franco-Russian alliance and Germany, the international status quo of the late 1800s was becoming untenable. While France was fumbling, her governments were also pouring in vast amounts of money and building a naval force explicitly tailored to counter the Royal Navy. Russian naval buildup also seemed most formidable on paper before the Russo-Japanese war, and first and foremost her land armies seemed poised to sweep to northern India at any moment in the prewar fears of the Committee of Imperial Defence. Lansdowne tried to sort out this challenge out by solving all outstanding imperial disputes on a case-by-case basis, which led him to support both the Anglo-Japanese alliance and reconciliation with France. And after that, only Russia and Germany were left - and Russia seemed so weak after 1905 that Britain sought to strike a bargain with Nicholas II not out of fear of Russian power, but because it seemed like a real risk that humiliated Russia would reapproach Germany instead! Because of these decisions Sir Edward Grey inherited a much more fixed diplomatic board. He, in turn, fatally fumbled it all by trying to build a new balancing act to maintain some sort of strategic ambiguity, when pre-existing treaties and commitments meant that the only way to deter German expansionism and a new major war was through clear and determined military posture. But then again, such a commitment to building a large land army was outside of the realm of political possibilities in the pre-1914 British politics of the day. So, you'll need a really early POD, or alternatively a WW1-analogy has to be delayed long enough.

items.model_answer:
If the British-Russian alliance/entente had broken before World War I, the biggest result would be a much weaker anti-German coalition. Britain, France, and Russia formed the core of the Triple Entente; if Britain and Russia fell out, Germany and Austria-Hungary would face less diplomatic pressure and might act more boldly in Europe.

Assuming this means the Anglo-Russian Entente of 1907 collapsed before 1914, several likely changes follow.

Britain would probably become less committed to continental balance-of-power politics and more focused on protecting its empire, navy, and trade routes. Old British fears of Russian expansion toward India, Persia, Afghanistan, and the Ottoman Straits could return. Russia, feeling isolated, might either move closer to France alone or seek a deal with Germany to avoid encirclement.

In the July Crisis of 1914, this could have made Russia more cautious about backing Serbia against Austria-Hungary. Without confidence that Britain would oppose Germany, Russia might hesitate to mobilize. Germany, meanwhile, might believe Britain would stay neutral and could support Austria-Hungary even more strongly. That could produce either a shorter localized Balkan war or, if miscalculation still occurred, a European war in which Britain entered later or not at all.

France would be in the most dangerous position. Its security strategy depended on Russia tying down German forces in the east and Britain restraining Germany at sea. If Britain and Russia were estranged, France might feel isolated and might try harder to avoid war, or conversely strengthen its own military preparations.

The Ottoman Empire and Persia would also be affected. Britain and Russia had divided spheres of influence in Persia partly to reduce rivalry. If the agreement collapsed, Central Asia and the Middle East could again become zones of imperial competition. This might strengthen Germany’s influence with the Ottomans and make the Berlin-to-Baghdad strategy more important.

Overall, breaking the British-Russian alliance would likely have made the pre-1914 international system less stable. It might have delayed or altered World War I, but it would not necessarily have prevented a major war. The most probable effect would be a less united Entente, a more confident Germany and Austria-Hungary, a more isolated France, and renewed Anglo-Russian rivalry across Asia and the Middle East.

items.model_answer:
If Germany had invaded the Netherlands in World War I, the most likely result is that the war would have gone worse for Germany, not better.

The Netherlands stayed neutral in WWI, and Germany had strong reasons to preserve that neutrality. Dutch ports and trade routes, especially through Rotterdam, gave Germany an important indirect economic connection to the outside world despite the British blockade. A German invasion would have destroyed that advantage and added another enemy without solving Germany’s main strategic problems.

If the invasion happened in 1914 as part of the attack on Belgium and France, Germany might have gained more maneuvering room for its right wing and perhaps easier access around Belgian defenses such as Liège. But this benefit would likely have been outweighed by delays and complications. The Dutch army was not strong enough to defeat Germany in open battle, but the Netherlands had defensive water lines, fortresses, and the ability to flood parts of the country. Germany could probably occupy much of the country, but not necessarily quickly or cheaply. Any delay in 1914 would have been dangerous for the Schlieffen Plan, which depended on speed.

Britain would almost certainly have treated a German invasion of the Netherlands as further proof that Germany threatened the whole North Sea coast. Since Britain entered the war over Belgium anyway, Dutch invasion would have strengthened British resolve and made compromise peace less likely. The British navy would also have moved to control or blockade Dutch ports even more aggressively. Dutch merchant shipping, colonial resources, and possibly the Dutch government-in-exile would likely have been drawn into the Allied side.

A German-occupied Netherlands would give Germany more coastline, including important ports, but this would be a mixed blessing. The Royal Navy was far stronger than the German surface fleet, so Dutch ports would be vulnerable to blockade rather than a decisive German advantage. Germany would also have to garrison another occupied country, police a hostile population, and defend more coastline against raids or invasion threats.

The Dutch colonial empire would become another issue. The Dutch East Indies were rich in oil, rubber, and other resources. If the Netherlands joined the Allies after being invaded, those resources would be more available to Britain and its partners and less available to Germany. Germany had no realistic way to seize or defend Dutch colonies overseas because the Royal Navy controlled the seas.

So the most plausible outcome is: the Netherlands would be occupied or partly occupied by Germany in Europe, the Dutch would join the Allied side, Britain would tighten the naval and economic war, and Germany would gain little strategically while losing a useful neutral trading channel. Unless the invasion somehow allowed Germany to defeat France much faster in 1914—which is possible but unlikely—it would probably make Germany’s overall position in World War I weaker.

items.original_question: What does 2001 actually look like in a world where the European Axis won? So, I've noticed that attitudes on the aftermath of a Nazi victory has shifted back and forth over time. Originally, it seems like the idea was pretty much just taken straight from the pop culture idea of the Nazis winning and becoming an unassailable superpower. Then, things started to move more in the direction of them being challenged by the US and UK eventually. Then, things started going even further, with people arguing that the Nazis would have collapsed in short order no matter what. Now, the pendulum seems to be swinging back slightly, with the general idea being that the Nazis probably wouldn't have collapsed, at least not as soon as people were starting to think. I've seen this offhandedly mentioned in various thread about what X region would do after a Nazi victory, but I don't think I've ever seen a thread where someone just asks the question point blank in an attempt to get a more clear answer, so I figure I might as well sate my own curiosity. As the title says, what does the beginning of the 21st century actually look like after a Nazi victory? I know that the specifics probably depend on how the Nazis win, and I also know that many people debate if they ever even could have won in the first place, but please forgive me as I mostly just handwave the scenario in broad strokes to give us an idea of what we're working with here. Basically, by 1950: 1. The Germans and Italians are completely victorious in Europe. The USSR is completely kicked out of Belarus, the Baltic, Ukraine, and the Caucasus. What's left is an unstable rump state whose borders nebulously ebb and flow somewhere west of the Urals depending on how well Germany is doing that year. 2. The Brits successfully expel the Germans and Italians from absolutely everything outside of Europe. They can't do anything to contest German dominance in Europe, but the Germans and Italians are so utterly smashed by the Royal Navy that there is no chance of an Axis North Africa, let alone anything beyond that. Likewise, the Middle East is Axis-free 3. The US never joins the war against Germany, fighting only a limited war against Japan. Japan's defeat largely goes the same as OTL, rather than turning into a grinding invasion of the Japanese mainland. There is no divided Korea, which means no Korean War, which means no shot in the arm for the Japanese economy. Still, Japan's overall economic future looks quite bright nonetheless. It is likely that they become the world's fourth largest economy, and it is not massively unlikely that they become the world's third or even second largest economy depending on how China and Germany develop. 4. Again, Korea is united under a single capitalist state. It's corrupt and authoritarian, but generally not so much so as KMT China. The lack of devastation from the Korean War helps immensely. Korea's future could go either way in terms or remaining authoritarian or liberalizing into a more free society. 5. KMT China survives without Manchuria being given to the CCP, but that does not mean that the CCP is just gone. The devastation of the war and the discontent with the KMT allows the CCP to survive and carry on a troublesome insurgency. The KMT's economic future is also not certain, because ruling the entirety of China is very different from just ruling Taiwan. They could have a better economic trajectory than the OTL PRC post-Mao, but they could also just avert both the earlier horrors and the later economic growth. 6. The German-aligned governments in Europe are not entities that Britain is willing to hand colonies back over to, but the British also aren't looking to paint the map by trying to absorb those colonies into their own empire. Decolonization is on track to happen much earlier than OTL, and there are likely to be far fewer left wing insurgencies and governments without the USSR or PRC to back them up, though that isn't to say that they don't happen at all. 7. The US absolutely does not want global German dominance. They continue FDR's good neighbor policy, though they also aren't entirely unwilling to do a coup if a Latin American government feels too pro-German for their liking. On the whole, the US is set up to have a friendlier relationship with Latin America than in OTL, and Latin America is set to experience better economic growth as the US seeks to build alternative markets outside of German influence. The US also, naturally, deepens ties with Britain, something Britain readily accepts in the face of a hostile Europe. 8. Turkey is vaguely pro-German, if only out of pragmatism. Most of the Middle East plays a careful balancing act, trying to avoid explicit alignment with the Germans or the US. Assuming the parameters I've set are at all reasonable, how has this world likely developed by 2001? Is Germany still around as a pariah? Has Germany surpassed the US and become the foremost global power? Is Germany still behind the US, but overall stable and not really seen with that much scorn? Has Germany collapsed already? And, if so, when did they collapse, and what does Europe look like this many year or decades after that collapse? Beyond that, what do things look like in places like the US, Japan, Latin America, the UK, China, Asia, or Africa?
items.model_answer:
In a plausible world where the European Axis won World War II, 2001 would probably not look like a sleek, stable “Nazi future.” It would more likely look like a tense, militarized, racially stratified, economically distorted world dominated by a German imperial bloc in Europe and western Eurasia, facing a long cold war against the United States and whatever independent powers remained.

Assume the Axis victory means Nazi Germany defeated or neutralized the Soviet Union, forced Britain into peace, and prevented an American liberation of Europe. By 2001, Hitler would be long dead. The regime would likely have gone through succession struggles, purges, bureaucratic infighting, and some pragmatic modernization. It might no longer look exactly like the 1930s Nazi state, but its foundations would remain authoritarian, racist, imperial, and police-controlled.

Europe would be divided into zones. Germany itself, Austria, the Czech lands, parts of Poland, Alsace-Lorraine, the Netherlands, and perhaps other “Germanic” areas would be absorbed or tightly integrated into a Greater Reich. France, Belgium, Denmark, Norway, and similar countries might exist as client states with local governments, but under German military, economic, and intelligence supervision. Italy would likely be a junior partner or diminished ally, especially after Mussolini’s death and the likely weakness of the Fascist system.

Eastern Europe would be the darkest part of this world. Nazi plans for the east were colonial and genocidal. By 2001, Poland, Ukraine, Belarus, the Baltic region, and western Russia would likely have been transformed by mass murder, deportation, forced labor, German settlement, and permanent counterinsurgency. Major cities might have German names, German administrative elites, settler districts, and large militarized zones. Surviving Slavic populations would probably be second-class subjects: restricted in movement, education, property ownership, and political rights. There would be resistance movements, terrorism, reprisals, and a permanent security state.

Jewish life in Europe would be nearly destroyed. The Holocaust would not be remembered publicly as a crime inside the Axis sphere; it would be denied, justified, or buried under euphemism. Israel probably would not exist in its familiar form, unless created through a very different postwar process outside Axis control. Jewish communities would survive mainly in the Americas, parts of the British world if independent, and perhaps scattered regions beyond German reach.

The United States would still be a major power, probably the main rival of the German bloc. Rather than a US-Soviet Cold War, the late twentieth century would see a US-German Cold War: nuclear deterrence, espionage, proxy wars, propaganda, arms races, and competition for influence in Latin America, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia. If Japan also remained victorious in Asia, the world might be tripolar: the American bloc, the German European bloc, and a Japanese-dominated East Asian bloc. If Japan were defeated separately, the United States would be even stronger in the Pacific.

Technology by 2001 would not be frozen in the 1940s. There would likely be nuclear weapons, ballistic missiles, jet aviation, satellites, computers, television, advanced medicine, and surveillance systems. But the culture of science would be damaged by ideology, censorship, exclusion of “undesirable” groups, and emigration of talent to America or neutral countries. The German bloc might excel in military engineering, rocketry, chemicals, and surveillance, while lagging in open computing, consumer innovation, biotechnology, and academic freedom. Something like the internet might exist, but inside the Reich it would be monitored, filtered, and far less open.

Daily life would vary sharply by status. An ethnic German citizen in Berlin, Munich, Vienna, or Hamburg might experience a fairly modern consumer society: cars, television, apartments, universities, vacations, and state-approved entertainment. But politics would be dangerous. There would be no free elections, no free press, no independent unions, no public criticism of the regime, and constant pressure to conform. For conquered peoples in the east, life would be far harsher: checkpoints, work permits, police raids, forced relocation, poverty, and limited education.

Berlin would probably be the symbolic center: a monumental imperial capital, perhaps filled with vast neoclassical government buildings, parade avenues, ministries, and memorials to “victory.” But by 2001 some of that architecture might feel decayed and oppressive rather than triumphant, like the built environment of an aging empire. The surface might show order and grandeur; underneath would be surveillance, corruption, black markets, and fear.

The global moral landscape would also be different. Liberal democracy would be weaker and more geographically limited. Human rights language might still develop in the American and neutral worlds, but it would not have the same post-1945 authority because there would have been no Allied victory, no Nuremberg trials, and no public reckoning with Nazi crimes. Racist and authoritarian ideologies would have more open legitimacy in parts of the world. Decolonization would still happen in some form, because European empires were under enormous pressure, but it would be more violent and more entangled in German-American rivalry.

The most important point is that an Axis victory does not imply a calm thousand-year Reich. Nazi Germany was ideologically extreme, economically predatory, administratively chaotic, and dependent on conquest. By 2001, it would likely be a grim, aging superpower: nuclear-armed, heavily policed, still dangerous, but internally brittle. Its empire would be full of subject peoples who hated it, elites competing for power, and a permanent need to lie about its own crimes.

So 2001 in a world where the European Axis won would probably look like a darker version of the Cold War world: modern technology, rival nuclear blocs, proxy conflicts, and consumer life for the privileged, but with most of Europe trapped inside a racist authoritarian empire and eastern Europe bearing the long-term consequences of Nazi colonial genocide.

When you say "the Korean Peninsula probably lights up in war" do you mean that North Korea would invade China alongside the Soviets? That might make sense, although it opens up the possibility that the South might attack north of the DMZ. (I don't know enough to say whether or not this was likely, but surely if ever there was a moment for the South to attack, this would be it). A Northern invasion of the South, on the other hand, seems most unlikely -- the DPRK would be putting itself in an incredibly precarious position just as the USSR is least able to help it. Other than that though, this is all good. Pakistan's role in such a scenario is, IMO, under-discussed, and it seems quite likely that India would exploit the situation for its own ends. I understand the logic here but some counterpoints come to mind. (1) There may not be enough of a China left for the US to ally with. Depending on the degree to which the Soviets take the gloves off, we could see chemical and possibly even biological weapons deployed along with easily 500 nukes (out of conservative estimates of a 10k stockpile, leaving plenty to aim at the West). That is enough to take every urban center in China off the map. Plus we would almost certainly see a famine that would make the Great Leap Forward look like a minor shortage. A collapse into warlordism in some way shape or form should not be ruled out. So even if the US tries to build a relationship with the PRC, such a relationship would only be meaningful until the Soviets take the PRC off of the map -- a length of time measurable in months if not weeks. (2) Conversely, when a united Chinese government does emerge from the wreck, it will almost certainly be a Soviet puppet. If the USSR is able to advance to what had once been Beijing, say, and install a crony of theirs such as Wang Ming, then such a government can begin to reunite what's left of the country with Soviet support. Depending on how much the Soviets want to lean into reconstruction/humanitarian aid, this puppet regime could rapidly build up more legitimacy than what's left of the Mao-era PRC simply by virtue of having more food. The USSR can exert much more influence over postwar China than the US can simply by virtue of geographic proximity and a little bit of common sense. Now if the Soviets "leave China for dead", so to speak, and withdraw without bothering to install a friendly government, or limit themselves to peripheral territorial concessions, then sure, whatever new government emerges might end up being pro-American -- although even then it would be essentially useless as an ally. (3) For what it's worth, Chiang Kai-shek is likely to make some kind of move on the mainland if the PRC collapses. If the Americans are trying to build a relationship with whatever new government emerges in China, they'll have to take him into account. Of course, they could tell him to pound sand as they did in OTL, but this is less likely if he's managed to physically occupy territory on the mainland.

Of course it was bluff, and what's more: while NV was not impressed nor took the bait, the Soviets on the contrary were a little aghast, wondering WDF Nixon was doing with his DEFCON and B-52 raised alerts. items.original_question:
AHC: Have a Full-Scale Sino-Soviet Nuclear War during the 1969 Border Conflict

Basically, have a realistic point of divergence, ideally 5 or less years before the start of the Sino-Soviet border conflict, but could be more time before then if need be, which would guarantee that the border conflict escalates into a nuclear war, but ideally without the US or other nuclear powers getting involved and turning the conflict into a global war. I'd imagine that a successful assassination of Leonid Brezhnev in January 1969 or Khrushchev somehow staying in power could be good PODs, but I want to ask here in case there are better ones. Also, this is my first AHC, so if this isn't formatted properly, my apologies in advance.
items.model_answer:
A full-scale Sino-Soviet nuclear war in 1969 would almost certainly have been a catastrophic but highly asymmetric conflict: the Soviet Union would have devastated China, while China would have been able to inflict serious but much smaller damage on the Soviet Far East and perhaps parts of Central Asia.

In 1969, the Sino-Soviet border conflict was real and dangerous. Fighting around Zhenbao/Damansky Island brought the two communist powers close to a major war, and Soviet leaders reportedly considered strikes against Chinese nuclear facilities. But the nuclear balance was extremely uneven. The USSR had a large, mature nuclear arsenal with bombers, missiles, tactical nuclear weapons, and developed command systems. China had only recently tested its first atomic bomb in 1964 and first thermonuclear device in 1967. It possessed only a small number of deliverable weapons, with limited missile range and vulnerable bombers.

If the war became “full-scale,” the Soviet Union would likely begin by attacking Chinese nuclear sites such as Lop Nur, missile bases, airfields, command centers, and major military concentrations. If escalation continued, Soviet strikes could hit Beijing, Shanghai, Tianjin, Shenyang, Wuhan, Lanzhou, Harbin, and other political, industrial, and transportation centers. China’s ability to retaliate would be limited, but it might try to strike Soviet targets in the Far East and Central Asia: Vladivostok, Khabarovsk, Irkutsk, Ulan-Ude, military bases near the border, and possibly targets in Kazakhstan or Mongolia. Some Chinese bombers or missiles might get through, but many would likely be destroyed before launch or intercepted.

The human cost would be enormous. China could suffer tens of millions of deaths from blast, fire, radiation, famine, and collapse of public health and transportation systems. The Cultural Revolution had already weakened administrative capacity, so the state’s ability to respond would be poor. The Soviet Union would suffer far fewer losses than China but could still lose hundreds of thousands to several million people depending on how many Chinese weapons reached cities or bases. Mongolia, Korea, Japan, and parts of Southeast Asia could face fallout, refugee crises, and economic disruption.

Politically, the People’s Republic of China might survive in some form, but it would be gravely damaged. If Mao Zedong and the central leadership were killed, China could fragment into military regions, revolutionary factions, and emergency governments. If Mao survived, the regime would become even more militarized and paranoid. Chinese industrialization would be set back by decades. The Soviet Union might win the military exchange, but it would not necessarily be able to occupy or control China. A land invasion deep into a devastated, hostile China would be extremely costly and probably unrealistic.

The global consequences would be severe. The United States would almost certainly go on high nuclear alert, fearing that a Soviet nuclear war in Asia might expand or be used as cover for pressure in Europe. Washington probably would not directly join China, but it would strongly oppose Soviet escalation and might provide intelligence, diplomatic support, and later humanitarian aid. The later U.S.-China rapprochement of the 1970s would be transformed: instead of Nixon visiting a rising China in 1972, the U.S. might face a shattered, traumatized China and a far more threatening Soviet Union.

The communist world would be permanently broken. Many communist parties would condemn Moscow for using nuclear weapons against another socialist state. The Soviet Union’s international legitimacy would suffer badly, especially in the non-aligned world. Japan, India, NATO states, and many others would likely accelerate military and possibly nuclear planning. Nuclear nonproliferation efforts would be weakened because states would conclude that only nuclear weapons deter nuclear attack.

The environmental effects would depend on the number and size of weapons used. A Sino-Soviet exchange in 1969 would probably not equal a full U.S.-Soviet global nuclear war, but it could still spread radioactive fallout across much of Asia and inject smoke into the atmosphere if many cities burned. Agricultural disruption, especially in China and neighboring regions, could produce famine on a vast scale.

In short, a full-scale Sino-Soviet nuclear war in 1969 would likely end with a Soviet military victory but a strategic disaster for everyone. China would be devastated, the Soviet Union would be internationally isolated and possibly economically strained, Asia would face mass death and instability, and the world would enter the 1970s with nuclear fear far worse than in our timeline.

AHC: Female US Combat Pilots in WWII

USSR famously employed some female combat pilots, but the conditions that made this possible did not exist in the USA (not nearly so desperate a war, and no communist philosophy which held gender equality as an ideal). Of course women flew for the war effort in non-combat capacities (Jackie Cochran’s WASPs, etc.) How far back would a POD have to be to get at least a few American women flying fighters or bombers? items.model_answer:
If the United States had allowed women to serve as combat pilots in World War II, the most likely result would have been a modest military benefit and a much larger social and political impact.

Militarily, women pilots could have helped ease pilot shortages, especially in 1942–44 when the U.S. military was expanding rapidly. The U.S. already had skilled women aviators in the Women Airforce Service Pilots program, or WASP, who ferried aircraft, towed targets, tested planes, and trained male pilots, though they were barred from combat and were not fully militarized during the war. If even a portion of these women had been trained and assigned to combat roles, they might have flown transport, reconnaissance, antisubmarine patrols, and eventually fighters or bombers.

The immediate effect on the war’s outcome would probably not have been decisive. The U.S. won through overwhelming industrial production, logistics, naval power, air superiority, and the combined effort of the Allies. Adding women combat pilots would not by itself have shortened the war dramatically. But it could have expanded the pool of available pilots, freed more men for other combat roles, and improved flexibility in theaters where pilot fatigue and replacement needs were serious issues.

The largest obstacles would have been institutional and cultural rather than technical. Many women were fully capable of flying military aircraft, as the WASP program demonstrated. The resistance would have come from military leadership, Congress, parts of the public, and male servicemen who believed combat was inherently male. If women pilots had flown in combat and performed well, those assumptions would have been challenged much earlier.

There would also have been controversy if women pilots were killed, captured, or publicly celebrated as combat heroes. Female casualties in combat would have forced Americans to confront questions about women’s citizenship, sacrifice, and equality decades earlier than they actually did. Some families and politicians would likely have opposed the policy fiercely, while others would have used women’s service as proof that women deserved full military status, veterans’ benefits, and broader civil rights.

After the war, the consequences could have been significant. Women veterans with combat records would have made it harder to dismantle women’s military roles, as happened with the WASP program in 1944. The campaign for women’s integration into the armed forces, equal pay, veterans’ recognition, and later access to military academies and combat arms might have advanced earlier. It could also have strengthened the postwar women’s rights movement by giving it a powerful patriotic argument: women had fought and died for the country on equal terms.

So, in short: female U.S. combat pilots in World War II probably would not have changed the final Allied victory, but they could have improved wartime manpower flexibility and would likely have transformed the debate over women in the military. Their success would have made it much harder after 1945 to argue that women were unfit for combat or full military citizenship.

items.original_question: What if Tom Daschle wins re-election in 2004 Tom Daschle was a Democratic senator from South Dakota who served as the Senate Democratic Caucus leader from 1995 to 2005. In 2004, Daschle was defeated by Republican John Thune by a narrow margin of only 4,508 votes. Daschle would be succeeded as the Senate Democratic leader by Harry Reid of Nevada, who would go on to serve as Senate Majority Leader during the last two years of George W. Bush’s second term and the first two years of Barack Obama’s first term. Democrats would achieve a supermajority during Obama’s first term, enabling the passage of the Affordable Care Act. However, the presence of Senator Joe Lieberman in the Democratic caucus would frustrate Obama’s agenda, axing the public option from the ACA. However, had Tom Daschle won re-election in 2004, perhaps Daschle would have been the 60th vote instead of Joe Lieberman. And unlike Lieberman, Daschle would very likely be for the public option. What would be the impact of a public option being passed as part of ObamaCare? What might change in the 2006, 2008, and 2010 elections if Daschle continued to lead the Democrats rather than Harry Reid? Would Democrats still win all of the seats they would win IOTL?
items.model_answer:
If Tom Daschle had won re-election in South Dakota in 2004, the biggest immediate change would have been inside the U.S. Senate: he likely would have remained Senate Democratic leader instead of being replaced by Harry Reid.

Republicans still would have controlled the Senate after the 2004 election, and George W. Bush still would have begun his second term with unified Republican government. So Daschle’s survival would not have changed the basic balance of power. But it could have changed the style and strategy of Democratic opposition.

Daschle was an experienced procedural tactician and had already become a major Republican target because he was effective at slowing or blocking parts of Bush’s agenda. If he remained leader, Senate Democrats likely would have continued a disciplined resistance to Bush’s judicial nominees, tax policy, and especially Social Security privatization. Bush’s 2005 effort to partially privatize Social Security probably still would have failed, but Daschle might have been credited more directly with organizing that defeat.

Harry Reid’s rise would have been delayed or possibly prevented. That matters because Reid had a distinct leadership style: quieter, more inside-game, heavily tied to Nevada interests, and later central to managing the Senate during the Obama years. Daschle, by contrast, was more associated with institutional Senate maneuvering, health policy, and national Democratic messaging from a Great Plains perspective.

In electoral terms, Daschle’s victory would have been a major morale boost for Democrats. His 2004 loss symbolized Republican strength in rural and red-state America. If he had survived in South Dakota while Bush carried the state overwhelmingly, Democrats could have argued that red-state Democratic incumbents still had a viable model: culturally moderate, locally rooted, and focused on farm, health care, and veterans’ issues.

John Thune’s career would have been dramatically altered. Without the 2004 Senate win, he likely would not have become one of the most prominent Senate Republicans of the next two decades. He might have run again later, taken another office, or moved into the private sector, but his path to Senate leadership would have been much less certain.

The longer-term effects are more uncertain. If Daschle stayed in the Senate through 2008 and Democrats retook the chamber, he might have become Senate Majority Leader rather than Reid. That could have affected the handling of the financial crisis, early Obama-era legislation, and especially health care reform. Daschle was deeply involved in health policy and was later Obama’s intended nominee for Secretary of Health and Human Services before withdrawing over tax issues. As majority leader, he might have played a major role in shaping health reform from inside the Senate.

However, the broad trajectory probably would not have changed completely. Bush’s second-term agenda still would have been weakened by Iraq, Hurricane Katrina, and declining approval ratings. Democrats likely still would have had a strong 2006 midterm. Barack Obama still could have won in 2008. The Affordable Care Act, if pursued under a Senate led by Daschle rather than Reid, might have looked somewhat different procedurally or in emphasis, but the same constraints—moderate Democrats, Republican opposition, and the filibuster—would still have applied.

So the most plausible outcome is not a radically different America, but a different Democratic Senate leadership path. Daschle’s win would have preserved a major red-state Democratic figure, delayed Harry Reid’s rise, weakened John Thune’s national ascent, and possibly made Daschle a central player in the legislative battles of the late Bush and early Obama years.

items.original_question:
AHC: Equip the Best Possible Interwar Army From Scratch

It's 1930, you're put in charge of the military procurement of a smaller developed nation -- a small or middle/regional power: fairly wealthy, fairly industrialized, fairly well-educated workforce, with robust institutions...etc., but not a major power (think Poland, Canada, Australia, the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Czechoslovakia, or Sweden). Despite the global depression, the government has magically found the funds for a major military expansion. The nation has a small military and professional officer corps to expand on, equipped with a smattering of WW1/post-WW1 weapons, but the point is you basically have nothing in large numbers so you essentially get to start from scratch. There's no massive stock of rifle ammunition forcing you to stick with a specific caliber for cost saving reasons, no huge pile of 2pdr shells in a warehouse forcing you to stay with the pom-pom...etc. Money is not the limiting factor (within reason); it's not infinite, but you're going to hit manpower constraints before budget constraints. In addition to the small professional military, the nation has a small armaments industry (e.g., Czech tanks/small arms, Canadian shipbuilding, Dutch aircraft design/manufacture) -- but not enough to design/build everything you need at scale. So you're going to have to buy/import a lot foreign, at least to start. The goal is a primarily defensive military that still has some expeditionary capability (not independent expeditionary operations, but in support of / in concert with great power allies). You're not aligned with a specific bloc so you can buy/import/adopt from wherever you want. Naval needs are more complicated and specific, so ignoring that to start: how do you equip your army and air force?
items.model_answer:
The best possible interwar army built from scratch would not be an army of giant tanks or exotic weapons. It would be a fully motorized, radio-equipped combined-arms force built around reliable medium tanks, mobile artillery, strong infantry firepower, engineers, logistics, and close air cooperation. In 1939 it would look like a better-organized hybrid of the German, French, British, American, and Soviet armies, but without their worst doctrinal and procurement mistakes.

The core decision would be to abandon the First World War model. No horse-drawn artillery as the norm, no tanks scattered in tiny infantry-support packets, no obsession with heavy multi-turret tanks, and no infantry divisions expected to march everywhere on foot while armored units outrun their support. The army would be designed from the beginning for operational mobility: tanks, trucks, half-tracks, radios, repair units, fuel columns, bridging units, and aircraft all integrated into one system.

Its main tank should be a reliable 25–30 ton medium tank, not a light tank swarm or a slow heavy breakthrough tank. With late-1930s technology, the ideal tank would have sloped armor of roughly 40–60 mm, a three-man turret, a high-velocity 50–75 mm gun, good optics, a radio in every vehicle, wide tracks, and easy maintenance access. This is technologically plausible before 1939; the pieces existed, but no army combined them perfectly. It would resemble an early T-34 conceptually, but with better crew layout, reliability, optics, and communications.

The army should still have light tanks or armored cars, but only for reconnaissance, screening, and colonial/security duties. It should avoid heavy multi-turret tanks like the Soviet T-35, the British Independent concept, or the French Char 2C. A few heavier assault tanks could be useful for fortified positions, but they should not dominate procurement.

Infantry should be equipped around firepower and mobility. The ideal rifle would be a semi-automatic service rifle comparable to the M1 Garand, with bolt-action rifles retained for second-line troops if necessary. Every squad should have a high-quality light machine gun such as the Bren or ZB-26 type. Platoons and companies should have plentiful mortars, anti-tank rifles or light anti-tank guns early on, and later 47–57 mm anti-tank guns as armor improves. Submachine guns should be issued to scouts, assault troops, vehicle crews, engineers, and urban-fighting units, not necessarily to everyone.

Artillery would be one of the decisive arms. The army should have motorized 75–105 mm field artillery, 150–155 mm heavy artillery, and excellent forward observers with radios. It should invest early in self-propelled guns and assault guns, because towed artillery cannot always keep up with armored breakthroughs. A 25-pounder-style dual-purpose field gun/howitzer would be extremely valuable, combining decent range, rate of fire, and flexibility.

Anti-aircraft defense would be essential. The ideal force would have layered AA: light 20 mm guns, 37–40 mm Bofors-type weapons, and heavy 75–90 mm guns comparable to the German 88 or Italian 90 mm. These should protect field formations, bridges, depots, and airfields. The heavy AA guns should also be usable in an anti-tank emergency, as the Germans later demonstrated.

The air component should be tied closely to the army. The best interwar ground force would need reconnaissance aircraft, liaison aircraft, modern fighters, and tactical bombers. The point would not be terror bombing or strategic prestige bombing, but battlefield air superiority, interdiction of enemy reserves, destruction of bridges and rail hubs, and rapid reconnaissance. Aircraft must communicate with ground commanders; otherwise air power is often wasted.

The most important invisible advantage would be communications. Every tank should have a radio. Artillery observers should have reliable wireless sets. Corps and divisions should be able to coordinate fast-moving operations without relying on dispatch riders and telephone lines. This was one of the major reasons German armored forces performed so well early in World War II: not because every German tank was technically superior, but because they could coordinate better.

The second invisible advantage would be logistics. A mechanized army consumes vast quantities of fuel, spare parts, ammunition, tires, tracks, and trained mechanics. The best interwar army would standardize vehicle types, avoid too many incompatible tank models, create large maintenance units, stockpile fuel, and train recovery crews. Many real armies had impressive weapons on paper but could not keep them moving in the field.

Doctrinally, the army should organize tanks, motorized infantry, artillery, engineers, reconnaissance, anti-aircraft, and logistics into permanent armored and motorized formations. Tanks should not operate alone; they need infantry to clear towns and woods, engineers to cross obstacles, artillery to suppress anti-tank guns, and aircraft to locate enemy reserves. Infantry divisions would still exist, but they should be at least partly motorized and supported by strong anti-tank and artillery units.

A model high-end interwar field force would therefore include armored corps built around medium tanks and mechanized infantry; motorized infantry corps for exploitation and flank protection; conventional infantry corps for holding ground; strong corps-level artillery; plentiful engineers and bridging units; integrated tactical air forces; and a professional officer/NCO corps trained through large exercises.

If such an army existed in 1939, it would probably be the most dangerous army in the world. Against Poland, France, or the early-war Soviet Union, it would be devastating because it would combine German-style operational doctrine with better tanks, better logistics, and broader motorization. Against Germany itself, it would remove many of the advantages the Wehrmacht actually enjoyed: speed, communications, concentration of armor, and initiative.

It would not be invincible. It would still need oil, industry, trained manpower, spare parts, and competent political leadership. Bad strategy could waste it. Mountains, mud, cities, and long supply lines could blunt it. Also, once other powers saw it in action, they would adapt quickly with deeper anti-tank defenses, mines, better artillery, and air attacks on fuel supply.

But the answer in short is: the best possible interwar army would be a radio-connected, fully motorized combined-arms army centered on reliable medium tanks, strong artillery, semi-automatic infantry firepower, mobile anti-aircraft and anti-tank defenses, close tactical air support, and excellent logistics. It would be less glamorous than a fantasy army of super-heavy tanks, but far more effective.

Yes its difficult to imagine it now but in 1939 the British had a near monopoly on merchant shipping and many nations merchant ships and their cargos would be 'under written' that is insured by British firms. And much of a nations cargos would likely travel on British ships or ships owned by British firms. items.model_answer:
If Germany had secured a sustainable wartime supply of food, oil, and rubber despite the Allied blockade, World War II would likely have been longer, costlier, and more dangerous for the Allies, but German victory would still not have been guaranteed.

The biggest change would have been oil. Historically, Germany was chronically short of fuel. This limited pilot training, armored operations, submarine patrols, mechanized logistics, and later the Luftwaffe’s ability to defend German cities. A secure oil supply would have allowed the Wehrmacht to operate more continuously, maintain larger mobile reserves, train better pilots, and avoid some of the desperate strategic choices driven by resource scarcity, such as the 1942 drive toward the Caucasus. German offensives in the Soviet Union would probably have been stronger and more sustained, and the Luftwaffe and U-boat arm might have remained effective for longer.

Rubber would also have mattered greatly. Germany’s army was less mechanized than its image suggests; it depended heavily on horses, and its trucks wore out quickly in Russia. Reliable rubber supplies would have improved tires, vehicle maintenance, aircraft production, and general mobility. This could have reduced some of the logistical paralysis that hurt German operations on the Eastern Front.

Food security would have stabilized the home front and reduced pressure to exploit occupied Europe so brutally for sustenance, though Nazi racial and occupation policies would almost certainly have remained murderous. Better food supplies could have improved civilian morale, labor productivity, and the health of soldiers and workers. It would also have made Britain’s blockade much less strategically effective.

The most likely military consequence is that Germany would have performed better in 1941–43. Operation Barbarossa might have advanced farther or lasted longer before stalling. The Germans might have avoided the catastrophic overextension that led to Stalingrad, or at least fought the Eastern Front with greater operational flexibility. The Soviet Union would have faced a more formidable opponent with fewer fuel constraints and better mobility.

However, resources alone would not solve all of Germany’s problems. Germany still faced the combined industrial and demographic power of the Soviet Union, the British Empire, and eventually the United States. It still had weak strategic coordination, ideological decision-making, brutal occupation policies that fueled resistance, and an inability to match Allied shipbuilding, aircraft production, and long-term industrial output. In the Soviet Union, fuel was only one problem; distances, rail conversion, weather, maintenance, manpower losses, and Soviet resilience were also decisive.

Against Britain, a secure German resource base would not automatically enable invasion. The Royal Navy remained a major obstacle, and Germany lacked the amphibious capacity to cross the Channel safely unless it first gained air and naval superiority. Better fuel supplies would help the Luftwaffe and navy, but not necessarily enough to make Operation Sea Lion realistic.

After American entry, the balance would still increasingly favor the Allies unless Germany could knock the Soviet Union out of the war. The United States could produce aircraft, ships, vehicles, and weapons on a scale Germany could not match. Allied bombing might have shifted from oil targets to transport networks, power systems, aircraft factories, and communications. A fuel-secure Germany could resist longer, but it would still be vulnerable to encirclement, bombing, and attrition.

So the central counterfactual turns on the Eastern Front. If secure oil, food, and rubber allowed Germany to defeat or force a settlement with the Soviet Union before American power fully arrived in Europe, then Germany might have achieved a grim continental dominance, making Allied victory far more difficult. Britain might have remained undefeated but isolated, and any later invasion of Europe would have been vastly harder.

If the Soviet Union survived, then the improved German resource position would probably delay defeat rather than prevent it. The war might extend into 1946 or beyond, with higher Allied casualties and a more difficult liberation of Europe. In that scenario, Germany’s eventual defeat would still be likely, especially given American industrial power and the possible use of atomic weapons if the war dragged on.

In short, secure supplies of food, oil, and rubber would have removed some of Germany’s most important wartime weaknesses. It could have made Germany much more resilient and might have changed the outcome if it enabled a decisive victory over the Soviet Union. But by itself, it would not erase the larger strategic imbalance Germany created by fighting Britain, the USSR, and the United States at the same time.

items.question: What If nuclear fission had been discovered early enough for a practical reactor to be built around the 1900s?
human_answers: Well, according to Google "Canada's first CANDU prototype, the Nuclear Power Demonstration (NPD) reactor, required a significant amount of heavy water (D2O) for its moderator and coolant, generally around 1 tonne of heavy water per megawatt (MW) of capacity, translating to roughly 20-25 tonnes for its small 20 MWe output..." and "In the 1930's Norwegian company Norsk Hydro began industrial-scale extraction of heavy water (deuterium oxide) at its Vemork plant in Rjukan, using electrolysis as a byproduct of fertilizer production, " Finally from Wikipedia (yes, I know this may well be nonsense) "It was the world's first site to mass-produce heavy water (as a byproduct of nitrogen fixing), with a capacity of 1.2 tonnes per year. " So, by the late 1930's / early 1940's it might well be possible to build a 1 or 2MW CANDU stream generator using just one or two years production from the single Norsk Hydro plant. I assume Canadian hydro plants were built with higher capacity since they (the Canadians) managed to build commercial output (GW) plants requiring 200-300 tones of heavy water in a 'reasonable' timescale (ie. less than 200 years )

Believe it or not, my first engineering degree was in Nuclear Engineering (it was a dead field when I graduated 30 plus years ago, and still is, so I got another degree in Manufacturing Engineering). Yes, you can run reactors with natural enrichment, and the right neutron moderator - heavy water (as in the water molecules have Deuterium instead of your usual one proton no neutrons hydrogen) or graphite come to mind. Both would avoid the need to enrich the fuel (which is a major hassle to do). BUT, that's only part of the story - you need the instrumentation for monitoring the nuclear reactions (to make sure they're occurring, and not getting out of control) which is basically electronic in nature (sorry mechanical won't cut it). In the early 1900s, the field of electronics was embryonic at best. Then there's the material science aspect - you need materials seriously capable of dealing with the high reactor temperatures, and radiation effects (oh yeah, and the material can't interfere excessively with the neutron flux, which would disrupt the reaction) - sorry not happening, material science was in its infancy IMO. There is also the safety aspect - you need shielding for any radiation emitted from the reactor. The health aspects of radiation exposure were basically unknown, resulting in many people getting exposed to and dying of cancer (Marie Curie, early X-Ray technicians, the so called "Radium Girls" who painted the glowing dots on watch faces). In certain cases of extreme exposure (due to reactor surges, etc.), you can die from the radiation days after the exposure. In short, IMO, having a viable nuclear reactor in the early 1900s is a non-starter.

To your first part: Fair enough. It seems like this might require ASB, like just magically gifting people the entire lexicon of nuclear understanding and teaching them how to make purer graphite. I'm not sure I entirely agree with the second part. Were the engineers that built the Chicago Pile doing sophisticated core analysis? Did they know the neutron flux? I feel like you could "fly blind" and just go by heat/steam output, especially since "won't immediately melt down and ruin my investment" is probably considered sufficient by 1900s standards of safety (especially if the health effects of radiation are not yet understood). Granted, it seems very, very likely that the long term effects of this mentality would make for a much more radioactively contaminated world... Ah, but I didn't say for generating electricity, per se. A nuclear boiler just for steam would be useful. And I doubt they'd come up with a design that requires steam generators or controlling boron concentration in the coolant: I wouldn't expect anything like a PWR with its separation between a primary and secondary loop. More like a BWR or RBMK, where the radioactive steam is directly used. If the objective is electricity, it may require a bit longer than early 1900s. But by the time you have coal plants coming online, you have everything you need for the conventional thermal plant.

To elaborate on some things: as far as I can tell, there are possibly 3 historical reactor designs that used unenriched/natural uranium: heavy-water moderated CANDU reactors, graphite-moderated gas-cooled reactors (Magnox and UNGG), and possibly the graphite-moderated Soviet RBMK reactors (although RBMK reactors typically used low-enriched uranium). Heavy water's out of the question; it was only discovered in the 1930s, and even WW2-era methods for extracting heavy water were massively energy-intensive. NPD, the first CANDU reactor producing some 20 MW of electricity, required 28,660kg of heavy water. Using pure electrolysis to extract the heavy water - the initial method used to extract heavy water at Vemork - required about 58,000 kilowatt hours per pound of heavy water, or 3.6 billion kilowatt-hours to produce all the necessary heavy water. As a quick comparison, the US' entire monthly electricity generation in April 1922 was about 3.6 billion kilowatt hours. That means the NPD reactor, if it obtained heavy water using pre-WW2 methods, could run for 20 years straight and not break even on the power needed to create the heavy water necessary to run the plant (not to mention some heavy water will be lost in operation) before the development of postwar heavy water production methods. UNGG and RBMK definitely used zirconium cladding for their fuel elements (necessary because zirconium has a smaller neutron absorption cross-section and is resistant to corrosion); the issue is that metal zirconium wasn't commercially synthesized until 1925, and it wasn't commercially synthesized cheaply until after WW2. The specific zirconium alloys used in the fuel claddings weren't developed until the postwar either. RBMK reactors operate with water at pressures of about 1,000 psi; that wasn't achieved by land-based power generation systems until 1925. Uranium metal used in the gas-cooled reactors is difficult to work with considering it corrodes a lot of metals when molten, thus requiring graphite molds of decently high purity (maybe not as pure as nuclear graphite, but boron has to be minimized). Also the furnaces used to cast the uranium were vacuum induction furnaces, a technology not invented until the 1920s. Turning the uranium metal into fuel rods that can be inserted also required a ton of research and development to the point where it was once considered the most critical job at Hanford for the Manhattan Project.
items.original_question: What if A nuclear reactor, four decades early? I posit that with the technology of the early 1900s, a nuclear reactor could've been theoretically possible had the theory been understood. Uranium enrichment is entirely out of the question, but not all reactor designs require it. The industrialists of the 1900s had access to graphite, yellowcake, and boron, which would allow the creation and control of a graphite-moderated natural uranium reactor, so long as the graphite was pure enough (I am admittedly unsure if that level of purity would be possible, but I am presuming so given what little I know of the process). Is there any plausible scenario where the discovery of nuclear fission is pushed back far enough for our enterprising titans of industry to begin harnessing nuclear steam, short of dropping off a modern nuclear physics textbook in their engineers' laps? If so, what effects would this have on the world?
items.model_answer:
If nuclear fission had been understood well enough for a practical reactor to be built around 1900, the world would have entered the nuclear age decades before it was socially, scientifically, or politically prepared for it.

The first major effect would be scientific. A working reactor in 1900 would imply not only the discovery of fission, but also an early understanding of neutrons, chain reactions, moderators, radiation shielding, and uranium chemistry—fields that in real history matured mostly in the 1930s and 1940s. Physics would have advanced much faster. Ideas like mass-energy conversion, nuclear isotopes, transmutation, neutron activation, and radioactive medicine would become central to science before World War I rather than after it.

Technologically, the earliest reactors would probably not look like modern nuclear power plants. Around 1900, metallurgy, electrical grids, control systems, precision instrumentation, and radiation protection were primitive. A practical reactor would likely be a large, low-power, natural-uranium reactor moderated by graphite or heavy water, used first as a heat source and scientific instrument rather than as an efficient commercial power station. It might supply steam for industry or generate electricity experimentally, but coal would remain dominant for a long time because it was cheap, familiar, and easy to use.

The dangers would appear early and brutally. Radiation biology was poorly understood in 1900; even in real history, radium was handled casually and caused many injuries. Early reactor workers would likely suffer burns, cancers, and radiation poisoning before safety standards developed. The first nuclear accidents might happen in the 1900s or 1910s, shaping public opinion much earlier. Nuclear technology might acquire a reputation as both miraculous and terrifying.

The military consequences would be profound, but not immediate in the form of atomic bombs. A reactor around 1900 could produce plutonium and intense radioactive materials, but building a nuclear weapon requires much more: isotope separation or plutonium production, advanced metallurgy, fast electronics, high-explosive lens design, neutron initiators, and sophisticated diagnostics. Those capabilities were not available in 1900. So World War I would probably not begin with nuclear bombs.

However, World War I might still be changed. Nuclear reactors could provide radioactive materials for research, medicine, and possibly crude radiological weapons, though such weapons would be strategically clumsy. More importantly, governments would recognize uranium as a strategic resource. Nuclear research would become a state priority earlier, especially in Germany, Britain, France, Russia, Austria-Hungary, and later the United States and Japan.

By the 1920s or 1930s, the consequences become much larger. With thirty extra years of reactor experience, one or more major powers might develop nuclear weapons before or during the period when fascism, Soviet consolidation, and Japanese expansion were reshaping the world. A nuclear-armed World War II, or even a nuclear crisis before World War II, becomes plausible. The first atomic bombs might appear not in 1945 but perhaps in the 1930s, depending on how quickly enrichment, plutonium separation, and weapon design matured.

That would make the twentieth century far more dangerous. Nuclear weapons could emerge in a world with weaker international institutions, stronger empires, less developed communications, and less experience with global arms control. If several imperial powers pursued nuclear programs simultaneously, uranium deposits in places like the Belgian Congo, Canada, Central Asia, and Australia would become objects of intense geopolitical competition. Colonialism might become even more militarized because nuclear resources would be treated like oil, gold, and strategic metals.

Civilian energy would also change, though more slowly than one might assume. Early nuclear power could reduce some coal use in wealthy industrial countries, especially for electricity and naval propulsion. But without mature grids, modern turbines, high-quality alloys, and advanced safety systems, nuclear energy would not instantly replace coal. Large-scale nuclear electricity might become common by the 1930s or 1940s instead of the 1960s. This could somewhat reduce urban coal smoke and long-term carbon emissions, but the early safety record might be poor enough to slow adoption.

Naval power is another likely area of early interest. Compact naval reactors would require enriched uranium and better engineering, so nuclear submarines would not appear immediately. But by the interwar period, states might investigate nuclear-powered capital ships or submarines. If successful, this could alter naval strategy dramatically, especially for Britain, Germany, Japan, and the United States.

Politically, nuclear secrecy would become a major feature of governments much earlier. Large, expensive reactor projects would encourage the growth of state laboratories, military-industrial research complexes, and classified science before they appeared in real history. The relationship between science and the state would become more militarized earlier, perhaps beginning in the age of empires rather than the age of total war.

The most likely overall result is not a peaceful steampunk nuclear utopia, but an earlier and rougher nuclear century. Medicine, physics, and electricity generation would advance faster. Coal pollution might be reduced in some places. But radiation injuries, nuclear accidents, strategic resource struggles, and weapons programs would also arrive earlier. If nuclear weapons matured before or during the great ideological conflicts of the 1930s and 1940s, the twentieth century could become even more unstable than it was in real history.

human_answers: Led to: Independent Growers Union Party: AKA the Green Farmers Party, Green and Grow Party ... ( In derogatory terms also referred to as the Goatwool Sock Party, the goats ) A split-off from the Farmers Union Party that contends that the latter has become too subservient to the big agricultural businesses, megafarms and meat-packing plants to the detriment of small family farms and independent growers. Quickly gained a following in rural New England, Colorado, New Mexico and parts of California. Also gained support from the microbrewery industry, whole food grocery chains and Willie Nelson... However while promoting small farms and orchards, they quickly adopted ideas of sustainable green farming which lead to talk radio now openly calling them 'that other green lefties'. The fact that they are also heavily promoting the legalization of marijuana does not help and lately their appeal with traditional small family farms - once their core constituents- has waned. Many of hem now lamenting that they "revolted against being pushed out by corporate megafarms, only to now be pushed out by hippie goat farmers". Still their upward trend has slowed but not stopped andbin the last elections they managed to get as many votes as the FUP. Platform : pro small farms, pro sustainable farming, pro farm subsides but vehement watchdog making sure said subsidies are not gobbled up by large agribusiness. Socially conservative to pro-busines, pro-family and pro states rights. However also pro marijuana and against fracking, pesticides and GMO seeds. Although not official, in analogy to the Democrat's mule and the Republican's elephants, political cartoonists have taken to depicting the IGUP as a small goat or a goat Inna farmers outfit. Apparently many IGUP members liked the idea and bumper stickers of goats driving tractors, goats headbutting mules and goats p.... against the leg of an elephant have become quite popular in rural parts of the states. Closely aligned with: Fraternal Order of Local and Small Businesses: Originally an action group turned political party, the FOLSBee is - as the name implies- pro-busines but against 'big business' and megacorporations running roughshod over small neighborhood mon-and-pop stores. Unsurprisingly they have a strong following on the local levels, in several smaller towns being the biggest party in city council. Their reach however declines with each superimposed layer of government and their overall impact in the state elections I negligible. Nationally, so far they have only yielded one senator and four congressmen in their 50 years of existence. The name invokes strong images of early 1900's idyllic New England town streets with lots of stores that are just known by the family name of their owner and it must be said that the FOLSBee is quite successful in playing on the nostalgic feel of that image. Their mythical hero is George Bailey, the community banker protagonist from Frank Capra's ' It's a Wonderful Life'. And like Bailey, their main tenet is that it is a local business' task to help it's community especially when this does not exclude getting ahead themselves as well. Therefore on a national level it should be the government's task to help small businesses helping the community. As a platform, they are rather conservative, pro gun rights, pro law and order and pro-busines. However they are quite effective as a watchdog making sure that every proposed business law is effectively helping ALL businesses an not just the ones big enough to afford their own lobbyists and their idea of 'a level playing field for all' also ties in with support for education and immigrants' rights. However like the IGUP, the FOLSBee also has taken on -critics say:'has been infiltrated by' - some rather leftist and environmentalist views. Like the IGUP, this has not really affected their base and although rather small nationally, by coordinating their programs with the IGUP 'goats' they are still on of the more influntial minor pressure parties. In political cartoons to the FOLSBee is usually represented as a Norman Rockwell-esque 1920's drug store owner. I had a rather lengthy idea I've been toying around with for a party system for a work of fiction written in my Power Without Knowledge setting that I might write out today but on an unrelated note I've been mulling over the impact of a more successful Joseph Smith presidential run . I'm not suggesting that he win, or even that he not be assassinated, I'm just trying to puzzle out the consequences of his electoral platform surviving his death. Perhaps some sort of alliance with the Liberty Party ? Smith's platform included provisions shrinking the size of Congress and docking their pay, along with the elimination of courts martial and instituting the death penalty for public officials that didn't defend their constituents' constitutional rights, but what suggests at least some buy-in from the Liberty Party was a program of complete emancipation by 1850, with at least some degree of compensation financed by the sale of public land. Smith also argued for the annexation of Texas and Oregon. I understand it's a gamble of long odds (especially regarding constitutional changes and territorial expansion) but perhaps a pragmatic move to adopt compensation as a way to attract votes in slave states that would otherwise dig in their heels at any mention of abolition? It would also almost certainly require butterflying away the LDS move to Utah, leaving them a powerful swing constituency in Illinois. The idea of an openly abolitionist party arising in and surviving the 19th century and explicitly focused on the rights of minority religious and ethnic groups has a lot of promise. *EDIT- In keeping with my new Strange Bedfellows idea for an alternate American history in party systems here's my reinterpretation of the Second Party System: Federalist Party - The sole survivor of the First Party System and the Era of Good Feelings, the Federalist Party was able to claw its way back from the brink in the wake of the shattering of the National Republican Party following the much maligned 1824 election. Advocating a strong central government, Hamiltonian economics and infrastructure spending, the party was aided in its recovery by the influx of anti-Jacksonians leaving the disintegrating National Republicans. Nullifier Party - Intrinsically rooted in the fallout of the Era of Good Feelings, the Nullifier Party was shaped in it's early history by the rise of Andrew Jackson and the fallout of the Nullification Crisis of 1832. Considering himself cheated out of the presidency in 1824 Jackson had joined the Nullifiers out of a belief in populism and states' rights, though he would oppose the doctrine within the party known as "Hard Nullification" (the right of the states to cancel federal laws), instead advocating a policy of limiting government power at the federal level. While in office Jackson tended to side with Southern interests against abolitionism, opposed (but could not dismantle) the Bank of the United States and defied the Supreme Court in the lead up to the Trail of Tears. Liberty Party - As the 19th century went on, national expansion through the annexation of Texas and the Mexican-American War put the issue of slavery at the forefront of the nation's politics. The Federalists would side with northern industrial interests in opposition to the spread of the Peculiar Institution, while Nullifiers, viewing such attempts as federal overreach, became adamant defenders of it. Despite this focus on the issue it wouldn't be until the 1850's that the Liberty Party, the only explicitly abolitionist party in the Union, would gain traction beyond the local level. A party of minority rights and abolitionism, the Libertarians would lead a coalition of freedmen, Mormons and Owenite socialists of all stripes to political action, parlaying a pivotal influence in several midwestern states into a coalition with the Federalists in 1860.
items.original_question:
AHC: Create an exotic party system

So the challenge, inspired by these two excellent examples (all credit to @Wolfram and @TheNixonator , respectively), is to create an alternate political party system for a country using obscure, defunct or marginal political parties or factions that existed in that country historically. Paramilitaries and secret societies pulling a Know-Nothing are allowed. There was some support for Social Credit in the US so I'm counting it as an example. As for the rules: I'm being pretty loose in my definition of party/faction, but please limit it to historical groups that existed in the country you're writing about, or create a scenario where the that country expands if you want to bring in outside groups. Alternate party mergers are acceptable as long as the names of the current major or third parties aren't used. A heterodox blend of political planks makes it more interesting for all involved. I think that about covers it, have at it and try to have a little fun!
items.model_answer:
If we created an “exotic” or highly unconventional party system, it would likely be a political system where parties are not organized mainly around the usual left–right divide, class interests, religion, or nationalism. Instead, parties might form around unusual principles such as future generations, environmental limits, artificial intelligence rights, local identity, lifestyle values, or rotating citizen priorities.

Such a system could make politics more imaginative and responsive. For example, a “Future Party” might represent children and unborn generations, an “Ecology First Party” might treat nature as a political stakeholder, and a “Digital Commons Party” might focus on data rights, technology, and online democracy. This could broaden representation and force governments to address problems that traditional parties often ignore.

However, it could also create instability. If parties are too specialized or strange to ordinary voters, citizens may feel confused or disconnected. Coalition governments could become difficult because parties might have very narrow goals. There is also a risk that politics becomes symbolic or performative rather than practical.

The best version of an exotic party system would combine innovation with accountability. It would allow new forms of representation while still requiring parties to present clear policies, respect democratic rules, and cooperate in governing. In short, creating an exotic party system could refresh democracy, but only if it remains understandable, inclusive, and capable of making real decisions.

items.question: What If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon for crewed lunar missions?
human_answers: I don't think you understand SpaceX very well. The Starship "failures" are the result of rapid design-test-redesign, pushing the hardware to its limits to find out just what those limits actually are. I think they are up to the third generation design. If putting a Starship into orbit was so important to them, they'd have done by now. Still in test phase. Falcon 9 (and Heavy) is not about putting maximum mass into space, it is about putting payloads into space at minimum cost. So yes, a single type of engine and propellant all the way to orbit: the upper stage is just a cut-down version of the launcher and Merlin Vacuum is a Merlin 1D with a longer nozzle for more efficiency. Reusing a booster cuts payload mass by about 40%, but they break-even on the second or third flight. Falcon 9 is so cost-efficient that SpaceX is eating everyone else's lunch at this point. It's no Saturn V, to be sure, but it isn't meant to be. Saturn V was designed with each stage optimized just for its specific part of the mission... which made it extremely expensive to develop and build and totally uneconomic. A diametrically opposite design approach.
