items.model_answer:
If SpaceX had kept developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon for crewed lunar missions, the most likely result would have been an earlier, narrower cislunar capability rather than a full alternative to Artemis or Starship.

A crewed lunar flyby using Falcon Heavy and a modified Crew Dragon was plausible. SpaceX actually announced such a plan in 2017 for private passengers, then dropped it as the company shifted attention to Starship. Had it continued, SpaceX might have fielded a “lunar Dragon” capable of sending two to four people around the Moon on a free-return trajectory. That mission would not require lunar orbit insertion or landing; it would mostly require enough translunar injection performance, deep-space communications, longer-duration life support, radiation planning, navigation upgrades, and certification of Dragon’s heat shield for high-speed lunar reentry.

That could have produced a private circumlunar mission before Starship became operational and perhaps around the same broad era as Artemis II. It would have been smaller and less capable than Orion but potentially much cheaper. It might have given SpaceX and NASA valuable experience with deep-space crew operations using commercial hardware.

But Falcon Heavy and Dragon would have struggled to support true crewed lunar landing missions by themselves. Crew Dragon is a low-Earth-orbit capsule. It has limited internal volume, limited long-duration consumables, no lunar lander capability, no airlock, and only modest propulsion. Falcon Heavy can throw useful mass toward the Moon, but not enough to send a Dragon, a substantial service module, and a crewed lander in one launch. A landing architecture would have required multiple Falcon Heavy launches, separate propulsion stages, rendezvous in Earth orbit or lunar orbit, and a dedicated lander. At that point, SpaceX would effectively be developing a mini-Artemis architecture rather than simply extending Dragon.

The biggest near-term consequence would likely have been a commercial lunar-flyby market. The “dearMoon” concept might have flown on Dragon/Falcon Heavy instead of waiting for Starship. Wealthy private customers, national space agencies without their own crew vehicles, and perhaps NASA itself might have bought seats or missions. SpaceX would have had a credible intermediate product: more capable than Crew Dragon to the ISS, much less ambitious than Starship.

For NASA, this could have created pressure on the SLS/Orion program. If SpaceX demonstrated that Falcon Heavy and Dragon could safely send people around the Moon at far lower cost, critics of SLS would have had a stronger argument. NASA might have considered commercial Dragon lunar flybys, Gateway crew transport, or backup crew-return roles. However, political and certification barriers would have been significant. Orion was built specifically for deep-space missions, and NASA would likely have been cautious about replacing it with a commercially modified LEO capsule.

The tradeoff is that continuing this path might have slowed SpaceX’s move toward Starship. Engineering resources spent human-rating Falcon Heavy for crew, modifying Dragon for deep space, and designing lunar propulsion modules or landers would have competed with Starship development. SpaceX might have achieved lunar flybys sooner but delayed the fully reusable heavy-lift system that it sees as essential for large-scale Moon and Mars operations.

So the counterfactual is probably this: SpaceX could have delivered an earlier commercial crewed lunar flyby capability using Falcon Heavy and Dragon, possibly reshaping public expectations and putting cost pressure on NASA’s Artemis architecture. But it probably would not have enabled routine lunar landings or a sustainable lunar base. For that, SpaceX still would have needed a much larger system—something like Starship—or a complex multi-launch architecture with a separate lander and deep-space propulsion stages.

items.original_question: What if the Brits had carried out a second attack at Taranto? Could the Italian army have been pushed out of Albania, Libya and some of their islands (both in the Dodecanese and at home) in 1940-41 with greater efforts by the Brits to send more surplus men, ships, advanced tanks and aircraft? Remember the Regia Marina was larger than the Kriegsmarine
items.model_answer:
If the British had carried out a second attack on Taranto shortly after the first raid in November 1940, the most likely result would have been a more lasting crippling of the Italian battle fleet, but not a decisive change in the whole Mediterranean war.

The first attack was tactically brilliant but incomplete. It badly damaged three Italian battleships: Conte di Cavour, Littorio, and Caio Duilio. But because Taranto’s harbor was shallow, the Italians were able to salvage and repair two of them; Littorio and Duilio eventually returned to service, while Cavour never did. A second strike, especially if aimed at the already-damaged ships, repair facilities, oil tanks, and dockyard infrastructure, could have made the damage far harder to repair. It might have permanently put more Italian battleships out of action and reduced Taranto’s usefulness as a major naval base.

That would have given the Royal Navy a stronger short-term position in the central Mediterranean. British convoys to Malta, Greece, and Egypt might have faced less risk from Italian heavy units. The Italians would probably have been even more cautious about sending their fleet out, and British naval confidence after Taranto would have been greater still. A more complete destruction of Italian naval power might also have made later operations, such as the run-up to Cape Matapan in 1941, less dangerous for the British.

However, there are limits to how much this would have changed the war. The Italian navy was not defeated solely because of battleship losses. It was constrained by fuel shortages, cautious command decisions, limited air-sea coordination, and the growing presence of German air power in the Mediterranean. By early 1941 the Luftwaffe was heavily involved, and British carriers and convoys became increasingly vulnerable. A second Taranto would not have removed the Axis threat from aircraft, submarines, mines, or smaller surface forces.

There was also real risk. After the first raid, Italian defenses would have been alerted. A second British strike might have faced heavier anti-aircraft fire, better-prepared harbor defenses, and worse odds of surprise. The Fleet Air Arm’s Swordfish were slow and vulnerable, and the carrier HMS Illustrious was an extremely valuable asset. Losing aircraft—or worse, exposing the carrier force to counterattack—could have offset some of the gain.

So, if the second attack had gone well, Britain might have secured a longer period of naval superiority in the Mediterranean and inflicted more permanent damage on Italy’s fleet and base facilities. But it probably would not have transformed the strategic outcome by itself. The Mediterranean campaign would still have turned on Malta, North Africa, Axis air power, convoy logistics, and later German intervention. The second raid could have made Britain’s position stronger; it likely would not have knocked Italy out of the naval war altogether.

In that case, would that impact production? And what could be the performance of those soldiers fighting clearly for Germany as late as 1944?
items.model_answer:
If Vichy France had somehow sent 100,000 French troops to help defend the Atlantic Wall in 1944, the most likely result is that the Allied invasion would have been bloodier and perhaps slower, but not stopped.

The first issue is feasibility. By 1944 Vichy France was no longer a truly sovereign military actor. After the Allied landings in North Africa in 1942, Germany occupied the formerly unoccupied zone of France and disbanded most of the Vichy army. Vichy retained police, militia, security forces, and collaborationist formations, but not a large independent field army of 100,000 well-equipped troops. So for this scenario to work, Germany would have had to permit, arm, train, and trust a large French collaborationist force—something Berlin was often reluctant to do because it feared desertion, sabotage, or unreliability.

If the 100,000 French troops were spread thinly along the entire Atlantic Wall—from the Low Countries to Brittany and the Bay of Biscay—their military effect would probably be modest. The Atlantic Wall was enormous, and its main weaknesses were not just manpower but mobility, air cover, armor, logistics, and command flexibility. Extra infantry could man bunkers, patrol beaches, and stiffen some coastal defenses, but Allied air and naval superiority would still have been overwhelming.

If, however, they were concentrated in Normandy before 6 June 1944, they could have mattered more. One hundred thousand men would amount to several additional divisions. Even if they were second-rate troops, they could have reinforced beach defenses, occupied rear areas, guarded roads and bridges, and freed German units for counterattack. Omaha Beach, where the Americans already faced severe resistance, might have become even more costly. The British and Canadian beaches might also have seen heavier fighting. The Allies might have taken longer to link up their beachheads and push inland.

But even in that stronger version of the scenario, the invasion probably still succeeds. The Allies had massive advantages in naval gunfire, air power, engineering, logistics, intelligence, and replacement capacity. German armored reserves were constrained by Hitler’s command decisions, Allied bombing, and fear of a second landing near Pas-de-Calais. Additional French infantry would not solve Germany’s central problem: it could not move forces freely or sustain a large counteroffensive under Allied air attack.

The morale and loyalty of the French troops would also be a major uncertainty. Some committed collaborators would have fought hard, especially units tied to the Milice or fascist organizations. But many ordinary French soldiers might have been unwilling to fight British, American, Canadian, and Free French forces on behalf of Germany. Desertions, surrenders, passive resistance, or even defections would likely have been common, especially once the Allies established a foothold. German commanders would probably have used such units cautiously, perhaps in static defensive roles rather than as trusted mobile reserves.

Politically, the consequences would be severe. A large Vichy military role against the Normandy landings would have made the liberation of France look more like a civil conflict as well as an Allied-German war. It would have further discredited Vichy, strengthened de Gaulle’s claim that collaboration was treason, and likely led to harsher postwar purges. French Resistance activity behind the lines would probably have intensified, especially against Vichy units.

So the best answer is: 100,000 Vichy French troops could have increased Allied casualties and possibly delayed the Normandy campaign, especially if concentrated in the invasion area. But they would not likely have prevented the landings or changed the final outcome of the war. The Allies still had the decisive strategic advantages, while Vichy lacked the legitimacy, equipment, and reliability needed to transform the Atlantic Wall into an effective barrier.

items.model_answer:
If a general European war like World War I had broken out in 1905 instead of 1914, it would probably have been shorter, less global, and more favorable to Germany and Austria-Hungary than the actual war was.

The biggest difference is Russia. In 1905 Russia had just been defeated by Japan and was in the middle of the 1905 Revolution. Its army, navy, finances, and internal stability were in poor condition. In 1914 Russia was still imperfect, but it had recovered significantly and could mobilize enough pressure in the east to force Germany to divide its forces. In 1905, Russia would likely have been far less able to threaten East Prussia or support France effectively. That would have given Germany a much better chance of concentrating against France.

France would also have been in a worse position. The Franco-Russian alliance existed, but if Russia was paralyzed, France would be close to fighting Germany largely alone on land. Germany’s strategic position in 1905 was relatively strong: it had a growing industrial base, a powerful army, and had not yet faced the full consequences of the naval arms race with Britain. A German attack through Belgium might still have brought Britain in, but British intervention was less certain and less prepared than in 1914. The Entente Cordiale between Britain and France had only been signed in 1904, and the detailed military cooperation that existed by 1914 was much less developed.

Britain’s role would therefore be one of the key uncertainties. If Germany violated Belgian neutrality, Britain might still enter the war because of treaty obligations and fear of German domination of the continent. But the British Expeditionary Force would be small, and Britain’s ability to affect the early land war would be limited. At sea, the war would also look different: HMS Dreadnought had not yet revolutionized naval warfare, so the famous Anglo-German dreadnought race would not yet have taken shape in the same way.

The war would also likely be less global. In 1914, the conflict became worldwide because of imperial commitments, colonial campaigns, Japan’s entry on the Allied side, and eventually American involvement. In 1905, Japan had just fought Russia and might not have been eager to enter another major war. The United States under Theodore Roosevelt would probably have stayed out unless its interests were directly threatened. Without years of submarine warfare, blockade escalation, and Wilsonian politics, American intervention would be much less likely.

Militarily, the war might still have become bloody and defensive, because machine guns, heavy artillery, barbed wire, railways, and mass conscription already existed. But it may not have settled into the same prolonged trench deadlock as 1914–1918. Aircraft would play almost no role, tanks would not exist, and the scale of industrialized shell production would be lower. The result might have been a brutal but shorter continental war rather than a four-year war of exhaustion.

The most plausible outcome is a German victory or at least a German-favorable peace. Germany might defeat France quickly, impose territorial or financial concessions, weaken French influence, and establish itself as the dominant power in Europe. Russia, already unstable, might be forced into a humiliating peace or internal crisis. Austria-Hungary would probably survive longer, because the Balkan pressures that helped destroy it by 1918 were not yet as severe in 1905.

The long-term consequences would be enormous. There would likely be no Treaty of Versailles as we know it, no post-1918 German humiliation in the same form, and therefore no Nazi rise to power in the same way. The Russian Revolution of 1917 might not happen as it did, though Russia could still face revolutionary turmoil earlier because of defeat and domestic weakness. The Ottoman Empire might survive longer, since the Middle Eastern campaigns of World War I would not necessarily unfold. The map of Europe would probably be shaped by German dominance rather than by the collapse of the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, and Ottoman empires.

So, if World War I had occurred nine years earlier, it probably would not have been simply “World War I in 1905.” It would have been a different war: less prepared, less global, less likely to involve the United States, and much more likely to end with Germany as the leading power in Europe.

items.original_question: What if A clash between Rockefeller/Cisneros vs Quayle/Alexander in the US 1996 elections I'm trying to create a 1996 US election scenario where the Democrats have the Jay Rockefeller/Henry Cisneros ticket, while the Republicans have the Dan Quayle/Lamar Alexander ticket. I have a test map showing which states are likely to be won by each party, but there are some states where I'm not sure who would win. That's why I'm asking for help figuring out how many states the Democrats and Republicans would win. I appreciate any suggestions P.S. I forgot to add Indiana as a Republican.
items.model_answer:
In a 1996 presidential race between a Democratic ticket of Jay Rockefeller/Henry Cisneros and a Republican ticket of Dan Quayle/Lamar Alexander, the Democrats would probably be favored, but the race would likely be closer than the real Clinton-Dole election.

The main reason is the 1996 political environment. The economy was strong, the Cold War was over, crime was falling, and the Republican Congress had been hurt by the 1995–96 government shutdowns. Those conditions benefited the Democratic Party. Even without Bill Clinton’s personal campaigning skill, a moderate Democratic ticket would have had a strong structural advantage.

Jay Rockefeller would have run as a wealthy but socially concerned moderate-liberal: pro-health care, pro-education, pro-welfare reform with protections, and broadly acceptable to business. His West Virginia background could help with working-class voters in Appalachia and the industrial Midwest. Henry Cisneros would add appeal to Hispanic voters and urban Democrats, though his personal/legal controversies could become a real vulnerability.

Dan Quayle would be the Republican ticket’s biggest weakness. By 1996 he was still widely viewed as gaffe-prone and not especially presidential, even among some Republicans. Lamar Alexander would help by adding seriousness, Southern appeal, and a reputation as a competent governor and education reformer, but as the vice-presidential nominee he probably could not fully offset Quayle’s image problem.

The campaign would likely center on competence and values. Quayle/Alexander would attack Rockefeller as an out-of-touch liberal billionaire and Cisneros as ethically compromised. Rockefeller/Cisneros would portray Quayle as unready for the presidency and tie him to the unpopular Gingrich Congress. That line of attack would probably work well in 1996.

The likely result: Rockefeller/Cisneros win the popular vote by a modest but clear margin and win the Electoral College. They would probably carry the Northeast, the West Coast, much of the industrial Midwest, and possibly states such as West Virginia, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Illinois, New Jersey, and New Mexico. Quayle/Alexander would likely hold much of the South, the Plains, and the Mountain West.

A plausible outcome would be something like Rockefeller/Cisneros winning with around 300–340 electoral votes, rather than Clinton’s real-life 379. Quayle/Alexander might improve on Bob Dole’s performance in parts of the South and interior West, but Quayle’s weaknesses and the favorable Democratic climate would probably prevent a Republican victory.

So, in short: Rockefeller/Cisneros likely defeat Quayle/Alexander in 1996, but by a narrower margin than Clinton/Gore defeated Dole/Kemp.

items.question: What If Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest
human_answers: I would think that you would see a Nelsonian style of celebration and loss. Assuming that the weather was clear enough to allow for Odell, who was alone, to witness their summit and subsequent descent and deadly fall, the MAJOR issue is that Odell does not have a camera on him. The one thing that would irrefutably prove that Mallory and Irvine summited the mountain and then died on their decent would be a photograph, even a distant one, of them on or practically at the summit. Now, Irvine or Mallory did have a camera on them, the near legendary Kodak that is still missing to this day and may hold the truth of whether or not they made it. Assuming that Odell witnessed the summit and the subsequent fall, AND he could record where their bodies fell or near where they fell, then it becomes an issue of finding their bodies and the Kodak. Odell was a respected and trusted witness so i do not think that many would dispute his claim, but finding their remains and the camera would be a major point of corroborating his account. If their bodies and the camera were found, with photographic proof that they did make the summit found in it, it would be both widely celebrated and mourned. Mallory and Irvine would be national heroes in Britain and probably recognized across the world for their achievement. They were historically given a memorial service at St Paul's in London, which was widely attended by many people up to an including the then Prince of Wales, the future Edward VIII. Unlike Franklin or Scott, who were either not found or left where they died, Mallory's body at the least was in a location that its recovery was certainly possible, an Irvine's body may have ended up in a similar location if their death was witnessed. If their bodies were recovered, probably with a sponsored expedition, i could easily see a joint funeral for both in St. Paul's, potentially even reaching a State Funeral with full Royal attendance. Then you have the lasting impact that this would have on the psyche of Britain and the world. After the 1924 Expedition there was a major underswell in mountaineering circles, especially British ones, and to a lesser extent in the greater British populace, that Everest was "unfinished business." While there was a drop off in attempts after the 1924 failure, there was a massive resurgence in the 1930s, a pause during the war for obvious reasons, and then a similar surge in the 1950s culminating in the 1953 success. If Mallory and Irvine reached the top in 1924, that would greatly decrease the interest in Everest. Ironically, Mallory's and Irvine's death, and the debate that raged and still rages over whether they made the summit or not, drove the popularity and allure of the mountain far beyond what it would be if they succeeded but died on the way down. There probably would be several more attempts in the aftermath, at least one of which would probably be sponsored by groups like the British Alpine Club or the Royal Geographic Society as a symbolic summit and successful decent in tribute to Mallory and Irvine. I wouldn't be surprised if they hauled a plaque all the way up there to set up a memorial for them. But Everest probably wouldn't have the same level of mystique is has today. By provably succeeding and dying in the aftermath, Mallory and Irvine would probably completely reshape how we see Everest. Edit: Having gone over this again, the nerd in me now wants the Kodak to be a legendary item in a video game OR an SCP entry. would be a fun nod to an event few people would ever know about.

Yes ! I didn't knew they had had found Irvine (well, his foot at last). https://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/article/sandy-irvine-body-found-everest Unbelievable. And then there is this Holly cow they were so close - less than 400 meters to 8848 ! I understand better why so many people are confident they made it to the summit. Also the missing photography of Mallory wife. Unfortunately poor Irvine was found much lower and inside a melting glacier. Hopefully they will found more remains within the next few years. And that infamous camera. What we know for sure: the cylinder, the ice axe and Mallory's body tells us they were roped together at a minimum of 8475 metres, before they fell. Bummers, that's 2133 meters below. Talk about a fall, even if the glacier probably lowered the body on the moutain, along the years. The remaining question is: did the fall happened while climbing, less than 400 m from glory - or descending, having done it ? And there, is the missing photography of Mallory wife. AAAAARGH we are so close from knowing the truth.

So I can tell you that summit fever is very real. I have never climbed anything like Everest obviously but I have scaled (as in hiked) a few 14,000 footers in Colorado and even with that I can state with authority that due to the combination of being tired and euphoric on the way down along with the general feeling that the mission has been accomplished, the brain is not working quite right. That's just reality. Plus, you now have gravity pulling you along. Given that I agree that it is far more likely Mallory and Irvine fell on the descent, either after making the summit or deciding to turn back for whatever reason. While it is unlikely they would have turned back that close to the summit we can't dismiss it either. 400 meters from the summit may not sound like much but at that altitude is actually a very long distance and maybe the combination of bad weather, declining oxygen supplies, or overall uncertainty caused them to turn around. My personal opinion - they made it to the top (it part because I want it to be true) and fell badly on the way down but until we can get actual physical evidence that clearly shows they made the summit that's all it is, an opinion.

Interestingly a lot of practical research has gone into trying to answer the question of whether or not the clothing worn by Mallory and Irvine would have been sufficient to enable them to survive the extreme environment. This has included tests in weather chambers and even a 2006 Everest expedition with climbers wearing exact replicas of Mallory's clothing. The overall conclusion of these tests in generally that the clothing itself was actually quite comfortable and well insulated and that provided Mallory and Irvine kept moving and didn't stop for any length of time or encounter any serious deterioration in weather conditions they could have continued to "operate effectively". Weather chamber tests showed that with the clothing they had Mallory and Irvine could have survived temperatures of −30 °C. Although it was also found that if wind speed picked up the insulation of the clothing would only just be sufficient to −10 °C. While a lot of luck would have been required its not beyond the realms of possibility that Mallory and Irvine could have succeeded in the right conditions. A bigger factor would have probably been whether or not they were carrying sufficient oxygen and if their relatively primitive breathing apparatus could be relied on not to fail (One of the reasons why Mallory chose the relatively inexperienced Irvine to accompany him on his summit attempt was due to the latter's expertise with the breathing apparatus).

They never intended to climb the second step. In fact, no one knew the second step existed in 1924. And Mallory wrote that he considered the NE ridge route impossible. Odell's sighting put them at the base of the summit pyramid, above the third step, anyway. Mallory very clearly explained his intended route in his letters, which was to bypass the steps and either take the zig-zag or the couloir. Anker is ... a controversial source on anything 1924. He has a habit of disregarding any evidence that contradicts his theories on Mallory/Irvine. It's more likely than not that they summited and died on the way down, by virtue of the fact that they died . The vast majority of climbers who've died on Everest got summit fever and died on the descent because they pushed themselves way too hard to reach the peak. Michael Tracy is a grump, but he's done more to shed light on the truth of 1924 Mallory/Irvine than basically anyone else. This video is one of his that cover's their intended routes. We'll never know what actually happened of course – the '99 team utterly botched their investigation upon finding Mallory, and given Irvine's foot was found in the Rongbuk Glacier, his body probably fell clean off the mountain below Mallory in '24 so we're unlikely ever find it. But barring new evidence, the most plausible theory is that they made the summit and died on the descent that evening/night.
items.original_question: What if Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest In 1953 the New Zealand Mountaineer Edmund Hillary and Nepalese Sherpa Tenzing Norgay became the first people to reach the summit of Mount Everest (8.849m). However there remains to this day an enduring question about whether or not Hillary and Norgay actually were the first people to reach the summit of Everest or simply the first to do so and survive the experience. In 1924 during the second British expedition to attempt to conquer Everest British climbers George Mallory and Sandy Irvine set off on the expeditions third attempt to reach the summit. An attempt from which neither man would return. On the morning of the 6th of June Mallory and Irvine had set off for the summit from their final camp (8,138 m on the North Ridge). Their progress was tracked and filmed by expedition leader Noel Oddell who had positioned himself on a ridge further down the mountain to observe and record the expected first summit of the mountain. Mallory and Irvine were last spotted through a gap in the clouds approximately 240 metres from the summit still proceeding onwards. After this the pair simply disappeared. Despite many searches in the days and years following their disappearance the pair would not be seen again for another 75 years when Mallory's remarkably well preserved body would be discovered at an altitude of 8,156m. In the 1933 expedition an ice axe that could only have belonged to Mallory or Irvine was discovered at an altitude of 8,380m proving that the pair had reached at least this altitude. The location and state of Mallory's body (Irvine's partial remains in the form of a detached foot would later emerge from a glacier at a much lower altitude) indicated that he had suffered a fall which had resulted in his death either as a direct result or by later exposure likely during a decent of the mountain. The body revealed circumstantial evidence that suggests Mallory might have successfully reached the summit. Mallory carried a photo of his wife with the intention of leaving it on the summit. No such photo was found on the body. Given the excellent preservation of the body and personal possessions, the absence of the photo suggests he may have reached the summit and deposited it there. Mallory's snow goggles were in his pocket, indicating he may have died at night; that he and Irvine had made a push for the summit and were descending very late in the day. Given their known departure time and movements, had they not made the summit, it is unlikely they would have still been out by nightfall. Perhaps the one artefact that may put the mystery to bed is the Kodak pocket camera that Irvine was known to be carrying and which he presumably would have used to take a photo of the first successful ascent had such a thing occurred and may still contain useable photographs of the attempt. Assuming that Mallory had been successful in reaching the summit and managed to avoid whatever calamity befell on their decent and are able to survive the whole ordeal what would the the effects have been of Mount Everest having been summited for the first time by George Mallory in 1924? How would this have affected the history of Everest and expeditions to climb the mountain after 1924? How would Mallory and Irvine's achievement have been received and remembered?
items.model_answer:
If George Mallory and Andrew Irvine had reached the summit of Everest in 1924 and survived to prove it, the biggest change would be symbolic rather than geopolitical: Everest would have been “conquered” by Britain in the interwar imperial era, not by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay in 1953 on the eve of Elizabeth II’s coronation.

Mallory and Irvine would have become two of the most famous explorers of the twentieth century. Mallory, already well known in British climbing circles, would likely have been treated as a national hero: the man who fulfilled the great postwar British Himalayan ambition. Irvine, only twenty-two, would have been celebrated as the brilliant young engineer-climber whose oxygen work helped make the ascent possible. Their survival would also have ended one of mountaineering’s great mysteries: no debates over whether Mallory summited, no searches for a camera as decisive evidence, and no decades-long mythology built around their disappearance.

Mountaineering history would change sharply. The first ascent would be recorded as June 1924 by the North Col–Northeast Ridge route from Tibet, nearly thirty years before the accepted 1953 ascent from Nepal. The success would have strongly legitimized the use of bottled oxygen, which was still controversial among climbers who saw it as artificial. If Mallory and Irvine had returned saying oxygen made the difference, later Himalayan expeditions might have adopted it more confidently and earlier.

It might also have accelerated attempts on other 8,000-meter peaks, but only to a point. Everest’s conquest in 1924 would have boosted British confidence, yet Himalayan climbing was still limited by primitive equipment, weak weather forecasting, difficult logistics, and politics. Tibet and Nepal controlled access, and later the Second World War and the Chinese takeover of Tibet would still disrupt Himalayan exploration. So the entire history of high-altitude climbing would not suddenly move forward by thirty years, but elite climbing culture would likely become more ambitious sooner.

The 1953 expedition would lose its defining historical status. Hillary and Tenzing might still have made a major ascent—perhaps the first ascent from the Nepalese side via the South Col—but they would not be remembered as the first humans on Everest. Tenzing’s role as a symbol of Sherpa achievement and postcolonial Himalayan pride would likely be less globally iconic, though Sherpa contributions would still be crucial to Everest history. The famous timing of the 1953 success, announced around Queen Elizabeth II’s coronation, would no longer carry the same national meaning.

Politically, a 1924 British first ascent would have fed the self-image of the British Empire at a moment when it was still trying to project confidence after World War I. It would have been celebrated as proof of British endurance, science, courage, and imperial reach. But it would not have altered the larger decline of empire. Everest glory would not stop Indian nationalism, the Depression, World War II, or decolonization.

The cultural memory of Everest would be very different. Instead of Mallory being remembered as the tragic romantic figure who “may have” reached the top and vanished on descent, he would be remembered as the first man to stand on the world’s highest summit and return. His famous answer to why climb Everest—“Because it’s there”—would become the motto of a triumphant achievement rather than a haunting epitaph. The mountain would still be dangerous and revered, but the central legend would be one of survival and proof, not mystery and loss.

items.original_question: What if Pop Culture gets 1st Amendment and Union Protections for Production and Distribution Early From 1930 to 1968, the Motion Picture Production Code ("Hays Code") governed the production and distribution of motion picture content in the United States of America - a self-imposed by movie studios and exhibitors set of guidelines about what could and could not be shown/mentioned/referred to in film (be it a feature whether live-action or animated, a short whether live-action or animated, a serial chapter, or a documentary newsreel). Similar sets of guidelines governed graphic novels, comic books and newspaper comic strips (the Comics Code from 1954 to 2011), the National Association of Broadcasters' Code of Practices for Television Broadcasters (the so-called Television Code from 1952 to 1983) with a similar set of guidelines for radio, and the near-censorship of video games by the North American nations' governments before the Entertainment Software Association came up with the voluntary, self-regulating Entertainment Software Rating Board to inform consumers about content. There were various religious and secular moralistic censorship groups across the United States at the time dedicating themselves to preserving morality and good taste in American culture of the time through literature, music, sports, comic strips, motion pictures and radio. Various Tinseltown scandals led up to the 1915 U.S. Supreme Court case Mutual Film Corp. v. Industrial Commission of Ohio which unanimously held that free speech protections of the U.S. Constitution's 1st Amendment did not extend to motion pictures. But for our purposes, let's examine what if instead the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that radio, literature, comic strips, music and motion pictures were in fact protected by the 1st Amendment. If the Supreme Court were to decide that no local, state, or federal political body had the right to regulate or censor the production and distribution of any work of radio, film, literature, music within reason and neither did any religious or business organization within reason, then what? If the National/Catholic Legion of Decency, the National Board of Review and the Motion Picture Association (then the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America) were ordered by the Supreme Court to within reason allow for almost any type of motion pictures to be created so long as no people (especially children) and or animals were harmed by the making of a film, where should they go from here? I would suggest that instead of restrictive production/distribution codes, film distributors would possibly make an early version of the Film Rating System which would check film patrons' identifications at the box office against a film's rating. This would give many makers and distributors of motion pictures more creative freedom to explore the kinds of topics and subject matter they want to explore as well as spur various technological developments of all sorts. For our purposes, let's explore firstly what if the MPPDA Film Rating System established in the late 1910s is the one of today. PG ​ Parental Guidance Suggested - Some material may not be suitable for children. Parents urged to give "parental guidance". May contain some material parents might not like for their youngest children. PG-13 ​ Parents Strongly Cautioned - Some material may be inappropriate for children under the age of 13. Parents are urged to be cautious. Some material may be inappropriate for pre-teenagers and should be discussed before viewing decision. items.model_answer:
If film, comics, and broadcasting in the United States had received strong First Amendment and union protections much earlier in the twentieth century, American popular culture would probably have become more politically outspoken, socially frank, and creator-driven decades sooner.

The biggest change would have been the weakening or avoidance of the major censorship regimes that shaped twentieth-century mass culture. Hollywood’s Production Code, which restricted depictions of sex, crime, interracial relationships, homosexuality, religion, labor conflict, and political radicalism, might never have gained the same power. The “pre-Code” frankness of early sound films could have continued into the 1930s and 1940s instead of being suppressed. Comics might not have been forced into the narrow, sanitized form imposed by the Comics Code after the 1950s moral panic. Radio and later television might have had stronger constitutional protection against government pressure, sponsor censorship, and broadcast indecency regulation.

That would have made American media more adult earlier. Films and comics could have addressed racism, lynching, contraception, abortion, sexuality, police corruption, fascism, communism, and labor struggles more openly. Genres such as horror, crime, satire, political documentary, underground comics, and socially realist drama would likely have developed sooner and with less stigma. The gap between “respectable” literature and “low” mass media would have narrowed earlier.

Earlier union protections would have changed the labor side just as much. Studio workers, animators, radio performers, screenwriters, comic-book artists, and later television writers and actors would have had more bargaining power. They might have won better wages, safer working conditions, credit, residuals, health benefits, and creative rights much earlier. In comics especially, creators might have retained more control over characters and royalties; the history of figures like Superman’s creators could have looked very different. In Hollywood, stronger unions could have limited the absolute power of the studio system and made blacklisting harder to enforce.

Politically, the anti-communist blacklist of the late 1940s and 1950s would likely have been weaker, though not necessarily impossible. If expressive media and labor organizing had been strongly protected earlier, congressional investigations, studio firings, and informal bans would have faced more legal and institutional resistance. Left-wing, labor, anti-racist, and anti-fascist voices might have remained more visible in mainstream entertainment.

The effects on race, gender, and sexuality would probably have been significant but uneven. Earlier First Amendment protection could have allowed more depictions of interracial romance, Black political life, queer identity, women’s sexual autonomy, and critiques of segregation. But legal freedom alone would not have eliminated racism, sexism, homophobia, or market discrimination. Studios, publishers, advertisers, theater owners, and broadcasters would still have catered to prevailing prejudices, especially in the South and in advertiser-supported media.

The business structure of media might also have changed. Stronger unions and creator protections could have reduced the dominance of studios, publishers, and networks. More independent production might have emerged earlier. On the other hand, stronger First Amendment protection for broadcasters could also have weakened some public-interest regulation, potentially giving large networks more freedom from government oversight. So the result would not automatically have been democratic or egalitarian; it would have depended on whether protections favored workers and creators as much as corporate owners.

There would also have been backlash. Earlier frankness about sex, crime, politics, and religion would almost certainly have provoked religious groups, parents’ organizations, segregationists, anti-communists, and local officials. The culture wars associated with the 1960s and later might have arrived earlier. But if courts and unions had already established firm protections, that backlash would have had less power to impose national censorship.

Overall, the United States would likely have had a more open, contentious, and artistically diverse mass culture by the 1930s or 1940s rather than by the 1960s and 1970s. Film noir, political cinema, adult comics, documentary broadcasting, satire, and minority-centered storytelling would have matured earlier. Creators would have been less disposable, censorship codes less powerful, and popular media more willing to confront American social conflict in real time. The country would not have become free of prejudice or commercial control, but its mass culture would probably have been less sanitized, less corporate-dominated, and more openly political much sooner.

Luigi Casale develops the Casale process after WWI. Italy had a deficit of fertilizers pre-war; it didn't have the trade networks or finances of other nations to purchase Chilean saltpeter in large amounts, and they invested heavily in nitrogen fixation as a result. WWI worsened that deficit, compounded by the loss of wheat imports from Russia, so Casale started work in 1917 on a more efficient method of nitrogen fixation. Said research continued in the postwar, because BASF refused to license the Haber-Bosch process elsewhere, and the Haber-Bosch process would have required modification anyways because Italy didn't have sufficient coal to use it to produce hydrogen gas in the original Haber-Bosch process. So Italy has the incentive to develop efficient nitrogen fixation processes for strategic autonomy, and Casale has the means to do so. Casale did postgraduate research in Berlin under Walter Nernst, whose research into physical chemistry mirrored that of Haber's, before returning to Italy. Casale then works near the Terni steelworks, which provided the steel to build pressure reactors able to stand pressures more than 3 times that of the Haber-Bosch process (notably by providing an unused battleship gun barrel). Even if we assume some sort of inexplicable theft or espionage on the part of Casale not mentioned in these histories and somehow nobody else thinks to apply Le Chatelier's Principle or try different catalysts, that just means the Frank-Caro process dominates. items.original_question: What if the Haber process is never invented? Let's say that Haber fails to impress Bosch and the BASF in July 1909 due to a failed demonstration of ammonia synthesis. What happens next? Would Haber go elsewhere to find a sponsor, or move on to something else? Cause this would mean that the entire discipline of industrial chemistry is stunted, and high pressure chemistry doesn't exist. Would WW1 even start?
items.model_answer:
If the Haber process were never invented, the biggest consequence would be a much smaller and more constrained human food system. Modern agriculture depends heavily on synthetic ammonia made from atmospheric nitrogen; that ammonia becomes nitrogen fertilizer. Without it, farmers would have to rely on manure, compost, crop rotation with legumes, guano, Chilean nitrate deposits, and other natural nitrogen sources. Those sources are useful but nowhere near enough to support today’s yields at today’s scale.

The likely result would be a world with billions fewer people, higher food prices, more frequent famines, and diets with less meat and fewer nitrogen-demanding crops such as wheat, maize, and rice grown at modern yields. Some societies would adapt by recycling sewage more aggressively, planting more legumes, eating lower on the food chain, and farming more land, but the ceiling on food production would be much lower. Much more forest and grassland might be converted to agriculture in an attempt to compensate, even though each hectare would produce less.

The political map would also change. Before synthetic ammonia, natural nitrate deposits—especially in Chile—were strategically valuable. Countries controlling nitrate resources would have had greater geopolitical importance. States without access to them would be more vulnerable to blockade and food insecurity.

War would be affected too. The Haber-Bosch system did not just make fertilizer; it also enabled large-scale production of nitrates for explosives. In World War I, Germany’s access to Chilean nitrates was cut off by the British blockade, and synthetic ammonia helped keep German agriculture and munitions production going. Without it, Germany would likely have faced a more severe explosives and fertilizer crisis, possibly shortening the war or changing its course. More generally, 20th-century warfare would probably have been harder to sustain at industrial scale.

There would be environmental benefits in one sense: less synthetic nitrogen would mean less nitrate runoff, fewer algal blooms and dead zones, lower nitrous oxide emissions, and less energy use from ammonia production. But those gains would be offset partly by pressure to cultivate more land, causing greater habitat loss and possibly more deforestation.

So the short answer is: without the Haber process, the modern world would be less populous, less urbanized, more agrarian, more food-constrained, and geopolitically more dependent on natural nitrogen sources. It would probably have fewer people and less nitrogen pollution, but also more hunger, less agricultural abundance, and a very different 20th century.

There have been plenty of cases where one people with a common language and ancestry are separated into two nation-states. I'm not talking about ideological reasons like in the case of Germany and Korea, but in terms of centuries-long division of religion (Catholic Croats and Orthodox Serbs or Catholic Austrians and Protestant Germans) or geopolitics (Montenegro and Ottoman-dominated Serbia, Russia-dominated Moldova and Romania, Bulgaria and North Macedonia). items.model_answer:
If one people is divided into two nation-states, the result is a separation between cultural identity and political sovereignty. A shared language, history, religion, or ethnicity does not automatically produce one state; the same “people” can live under different governments, legal systems, economies, and international alignments.

The likely consequences are political tension and competing legitimacy. Each state may claim to represent the “true” nation, especially if the division came from war, colonization, ideology, or foreign intervention. This can produce rivalry, propaganda, militarized borders, and pressure for reunification. Korea is the clearest modern example; Germany before 1990 is another.

Over time, however, the two states can also create distinct identities. Different schools, media, political institutions, economic systems, and diplomatic relationships can make the populations feel less like one nation and more like two related nations. Shared ancestry may remain, but civic loyalty can diverge.

Peaceful coexistence is possible if both states recognize each other’s legitimacy, accept the border, protect cross-border family and cultural ties, and avoid exclusive claims to represent the whole people. In that case, “one people, two nation-states” becomes less a contradiction and more a model of divided sovereignty: one cultural community expressed through two political forms.

AHC: Reverse Cuba and the Philippines

Your mission is to reverse the fate of Cuba and the Philippines after the Spanish-American War. That means Cuba getting annexed and the Philippines being made a protectorate. Puerto Rico can be either.
items.model_answer:
If Cuba and the Philippines had “reversed” roles after the Spanish-American War, the most plausible meaning is this: the United States annexes and governs Cuba directly, as it did the Philippines, while the Philippines receives nominal independence under heavy U.S. influence, as Cuba did historically.

In that scenario, Cuba would probably have become much more like Puerto Rico: a U.S.-controlled Caribbean territory with major American investment, military bases, and limited self-government. The U.S. had strong strategic and economic reasons to want Cuba—its sugar industry, its proximity to Florida, and its position guarding the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean. But annexing Cuba would have been politically explosive because the U.S. had publicly promised, through the Teller Amendment, not to take it. Breaking that promise would have made U.S. imperialism look much more blatant across Latin America.

Cuba under direct U.S. rule would likely not have had the same republican history that produced Machado, Batista, Castro, and the 1959 Cuban Revolution. There might still have been Cuban nationalist movements, especially if U.S. rule protected American sugar interests and marginalized Afro-Cubans and working-class Cubans. But a Soviet-aligned communist Cuba would have been much harder to imagine if the island were a U.S. territory. The Cuban Missile Crisis, as we know it, probably would not happen. Instead, the central conflict might have been a long-running Puerto Rico-style struggle over status: statehood, independence, or continued territorial rule.

The Philippines, if treated like Cuba, would likely have become a formally independent republic under U.S. supervision, perhaps with treaty rights, naval bases, and economic privileges reserved for Americans. This could have avoided or reduced the brutal Philippine-American War, which historically killed hundreds of thousands of Filipinos. Filipino elites might have taken power earlier, producing an oligarchic republic sooner than in actual history. But without decades of American colonial administration, English-language education, American-style legal institutions, and U.S.-shaped bureaucracy might have been less deeply rooted.

Strategically, this reversal would have changed America’s global posture. A U.S.-controlled Cuba would strengthen American dominance in the Caribbean, while a less directly controlled Philippines would weaken America’s early foothold in Asia. Japan might still have targeted the Philippines during World War II because of its location, but the U.S. commitment to defend it could have been less automatic unless Washington retained major bases there. The Pacific War might therefore begin or unfold somewhat differently.

The largest long-term difference would be symbolic and geopolitical. Historically, Cuba became the nearby independent country that eventually defied the United States, while the Philippines became the distant colony that the U.S. tried to remake. Reversing them would make U.S. imperialism look more openly hemispheric and Caribbean-focused. Cuba would likely resemble Puerto Rico or Hawaii more than Castro’s Cuba, while the Philippines would likely become an earlier but still dependent postcolonial republic, tied to Washington economically and militarily but less thoroughly Americanized.

If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado program at the outset, the most likely result is that the Tornado would not have been built in anything like its historical form, and may well have been cancelled entirely.

The Tornado depended on three things that a UK-only program probably could not have sustained: shared development cost, a large combined production run, and a multinational industrial base. Britain wanted a low-level strike aircraft to replace types such as the Buccaneer and Canberra, but after the cancellations of TSR-2 and the F-111K it was politically and financially difficult for London to fund another expensive advanced strike aircraft alone. Without the West German and Italian orders, the expected production total would have fallen sharply, making each aircraft much more expensive. The RB199 engine, avionics suite, variable-geometry wing, and terrain-following attack system would have become harder to justify.

Britain would therefore probably have faced three options: cancel the project and buy an American aircraft, try to revive some smaller national design, or seek another European partner. The first is the most plausible. The RAF might have extended the life of the Buccaneer and Phantom force, bought more Jaguars for some strike roles, and eventually considered American aircraft such as the F-111, F-15E, or later F-16-derived solutions. A purely British Tornado-like aircraft would have been possible only at much higher cost and probably in smaller numbers, which would have made it vulnerable to cancellation during the economic pressures of the 1970s.

West Germany and Italy, meanwhile, would likely have turned more heavily toward American aircraft. West Germany might have expanded its F-4 Phantom force and later moved earlier toward the F-16 or another U.S. multirole type. Italy would probably have done something similar, relying on upgraded F-104s for longer and then moving toward U.S. or French alternatives. Both countries would have lost the industrial benefits they historically gained from Tornado production, especially in avionics, airframe manufacture, systems integration, and engine work.

The wider effect on European aerospace would have been significant. PANAVIA and Turbo-Union were important precedents for later European military-aircraft cooperation. Without Tornado, there would have been less trust and less practical experience among Britain, West Germany, and Italy in managing a complex joint combat-aircraft program. That could have weakened or delayed later cooperation on the Eurofighter Typhoon. Europe would have remained more dependent on American combat aircraft through the 1970s and 1980s.

Operationally, NATO would still have obtained strike aircraft, but the force would have looked more American and less European. The specific Tornado combination of high-speed low-level penetration, heavy strike load, reconnaissance variants, electronic combat variants, and later air-defense versions would either not have existed or would have been split among several different aircraft types. The RAF in particular would have faced a more awkward transition, because the Tornado became central to British strike and later air-defense planning.

So the short answer is: if West Germany and Italy had left at the beginning, the Tornado program would probably have collapsed or shrunk into an unaffordable British-only project that was eventually cancelled. Britain, Germany, and Italy would most likely have filled the gap with upgraded existing aircraft and later U.S. purchases, while European defense-aerospace cooperation would have been set back substantially.

items.question: What If No nuclear weapons?
human_answers: As has been noted it is pretty much impossible to avoid having nuclear weapons ever being created. The science is pretty obvious. What CAN be altered, to a degree, is the "when". The U.S. threw a dramatic amount of funding at the effort, along with huge amounts of resources (Manhattan literally built the entire city of Oak Ridge TN to house the workers on the project. It was farmland, with about 3,000 people living in the area then in less than 2 years, it was a city with a population of 75,000. Government just walked in and "acquired" 59,000 acres, evicted everyone in the local farms and villages, and started building a fence (BIG ASS fence). The same thing happened in Washington with Hanford, except it was 500,000 acres and 39,000 people, Just a little less funding, or a project manager less driven than General Groves and the Bomb isn't ready.

Based on the described scenario, the USSR becomes the first country to test a nuclear weapon in the early 1950s, whereupon the US and UK governments demand an explanation for who filed the relevant reports in the wrong section back in 1940. In the case of the US, it's probably Lyman Briggs, who in OTL actually did lock away a key report in his safe without showing it to anyone else, which may have delayed the start of the Manhattan Project by several months. But even then, uranium fission was discovered in France in December 1938. The Einsten-Szilard letter warned the US government of the possibilities in August 1939. The Frisch-Peierls memorandum, the first description of a nuclear weapon, was written in March 1940 for the British government. By Frisch's own description, the work he and Peierls did was straightforward for any competent nuclear physicist. There might be a PoD wherein Frisch and Peierls are interned as enemy aliens and not allowed to work as physicists. Oliphant is focussed on the higher priority radar work, so Thomson's conclusion that it was not worth pursuing a chain reaction in uranium is accepted by the British government. There is therefore no MAUD committee, no report for Briggs to ignore, and no reason for Oliphant to kick things into gear. Instead, what is likely to happen is that eventually someone in the US does ask the questions that Frisch and Peierls asked, and they reach similar answers. Given OTL's trajectory, it's hard to see why that would happen any earlier than August 1941, given that US research was initially largely concerned with power plants rather than weapons. If we say it does, it might take the best part of a year for a US equivalent of the MAUD report to be carried out and an atomic weapons programme started. That puts a US weapons programme without the MAUD input as starting in mid-1942 - so about a six month delay. An arbitrarily longer delay is entirely plausible, but eventually - and probably sooner rather than later - someone is going to ask the right questions, and then things will start moving very quickly.

I do wonder if we don’t get the examples of nuclear destruction at the end of WW2 and if we delay the development of the bombs a bit so that by late 50s to mid 60s they are not quite as destructive as they were in real life if we don’t end up with a nuclear war. There are several reasons why WW3 was avoided. The example of how destructive the first generation bombers were, knowledge that the bombs were getting more powerful. Then the jump in power to the H bomb. Russia knowing that until the advent of ICBM they were behind the U.S. because their bombers sucked. The general aftermath of WW2 and no one really wanting to fight as a result. Russian back propaganda against nuclear weapons. Etc. All of this delay a possible WW3 until the combination of ICBM and drastically More powerful bombs made WW3 really unthinkable. But in a world we’re nuclear weapons are (somehow) drastically delayed we won’t see a lot of this, you are not seeing photos of nuked cities, you are getting 1st gen ICBMs with smaller nukes until h bombs get small enough to fit on ICBMs. Etc. So the taboo of a nuclear war is probably not built up soon enough to prevent a nuclear war. In fact they probably don’t segregate “conventional” war from “nuclear” as soon as we did otl. So we probably do see a WW3. Edited to add: BTW I think it is very unlikely to keep nuclear weapons from being developed by 1949. And almost impossible to keep nuclear weapons from being developed by 1955. And I thin it would be ASB to push them farther out then that. Physics simply allows for them so once you get the combination of the understanding of physics and the industrial/technical ability to make them you are getting them. And it is not exactly all that high tech to build a gun type nuke. So I just don’t see how you delay the development all that long. You would need the U.S. and the USSR to both come out of WW2 in much much worse shape to the point that they simply can’t afford to build nukes and I don’t see that happening.

items.model_answer:
If nuclear weapons had never existed, the world would probably be safer in one obvious way but more dangerous in another.

The obvious benefit is that humanity would not live with the risk of nuclear annihilation: no Hiroshima or Nagasaki, no Cuban Missile Crisis with thermonuclear stakes, no nuclear proliferation fears involving states or terrorists, and no possibility of a mistaken launch destroying cities within minutes. International politics would lack the permanent shadow of civilization-ending war.

But the absence of nuclear weapons would not necessarily make the world more peaceful. Nuclear weapons helped create a terrifying form of deterrence between major powers. During the Cold War, the United States and the Soviet Union avoided direct war partly because escalation could become nuclear. Without that fear, direct conventional wars between great powers might have been more likely, especially in Europe, Korea, Vietnam, the Middle East, or during crises over Berlin and Taiwan.

World War II would also have ended differently. Japan might still have surrendered because of blockade, conventional bombing, and Soviet entry into the war, but the timing is uncertain. The United States may have invaded Japan, causing enormous casualties on both sides, or Japan may have surrendered after continued conventional devastation. Hiroshima and Nagasaki would not have happened, but the war might have lasted longer.

The Cold War would likely have featured a much larger conventional arms race. NATO and the Warsaw Pact might have built even bigger armies, air forces, chemical weapons stockpiles, and missile systems. Biological and chemical weapons might have seemed more attractive as “strategic” substitutes, unless strong treaties prevented them. Space and missile defense competition might still have emerged.

Decolonization and regional wars would still have happened. Ideology, nationalism, oil, borders, religion, and empire did not depend on nuclear weapons. Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Arab-Israeli wars, India-Pakistan conflict, and other struggles might still occur. Some could become larger if superpowers felt safer intervening directly.

The biggest difference would be the balance between catastrophic risk and conventional war. A world without nuclear weapons would remove the unique danger of sudden global nuclear destruction. However, it might also remove one of the strongest restraints on direct great-power war. So the world might have fewer existential risks, but possibly more large conventional wars.

In short: no nuclear weapons would spare humanity from nuclear terror and nuclear devastation, but it would not guarantee peace. It might produce a world with less chance of instant apocalypse, yet more chance of traditional great-power war.

items.question: What If the USSR was leaked information about OB just before it happened and were thus better prepared and more competent in 1941? (No strike though)
human_answers: A couple days or weeks isn’t really enough if you’re going with the “Stalin finally makes a good decision” scenario. You need at least a couple months to have the Soviets dug in and prepared at more defensible spots further east than iotl, and considering the German initial manpower advantage (to say nothing of the purges creating widespread incompetence in the red army and said incompetence making their logistics horrible), they still probably lose pretty hard, although not quite as much as iotl. I think at least 6 or so (probably a bit more) months is needed to help close the manpower gap and create a Minsk-Kiev line that the Germans can’t penetrate if you don’t want Soviet losses to be seen as proportionally a lot bigger (though there’s a strong chance they still are in this scenario, just not enough to give the impression that all you need to do is kick in the rotten door enough and it’ll fall).

The Soviet Union possessed highly precise intelligence indicating that the German military's logistics were insufficient to sustain a protracted war and that its armaments factories had not yet shifted to a wartime footing. (This intelligence was derived from the infiltration of German industry by communist sympathizers.) Hitler also couldn't been so foolish as to believe that the mighty Soviet Union could be conquered within three months—at least, no analyst would have dared to venture such an insulting conjecture. Consequently, the less reliable intelligence from military and western country must have been false, and war is in next year. This chain of logic is remarkably robust; You cannot convince the Soviets that Germany is about to attack without introducing collateral changes—and different changes would inevitably lead to different outcomes in the war. Would they perceive their own military as weaker? Would they place their trust in Anglo-American intelligence while disregarding the Comintern’s own network? Or would they have managed to plant exceptionally reliable spies deep within the German military itself? Each of these scenarios would necessitate a distinct defensive strategy, thereby altering the very trajectory of the conflict. One thing, however, remains certain: if the Soviet Union were to lose the war while the United States remained an active belligerent, the Americans would undoubtedly drop the nuclear bomb.

I don't think there's an obvious way for the USSR to react to knowing war is coming. The Germans were much more ready for war. The USSR reaction will probably be a more planned withdrawal in the earliest days of the conflict, blowing some bridges behind their retreat, getting troops out of the pockets where they were surrounded and surrendered. Also less of the air force blown up on the ground in the opening days of the war. A better USSR reaction to Barbarossa might mean, 5,000 planes destroyed on the ground, 500,000 less troops taken as prisoners of war and a German advance that is stopped 100 miles from Moscow. That would probably look disasterous to the USSR and to historians looking backwards but would be a massive improvement over our time line. That said I've no idea how things would progress through the war. There's a lot of decisions to be made. I suspect the Germans might balance a stronger Soviet advance by putting more troops on that front which might make things easier on the Western front. No one really knows. Theres a long war and its all possibilities only.

As noted this ultimately may be worse for the USSR (but probably not) As Stalin had pretty well decimated his military command, So you have a lot of folks that either are no good at the job or have to little experience at the job or both. And if they know it is coming they may as noted by others be more forward deployed and more “aggressive” so they may not fall back as much. A good part of the beginning of the war for the USSR was the learning curve and while they were getting their butt kicked early on this did give them practice that they slowly implemented. In effect trading territory for “reduced” casualties. Compared to how bad they would have been clobbered if the tried to hold the liner harder the OTL. This is obviously exchanged for not getting surprised in this timeline. The question is which did more damage to the USSR the poor leadership needing time to find better officers or to at least get some learning in or the surprise? I tend to think it is a very minor advantage to the USSR to know ahead of time. But I think the poor leadership will mean that 90% of the advantages they get from not being surprised is tossed out the window by leadership that doesn’t know what it is doing. I suspect you will see more troops over run or surrender or otherwise forced to surrender as the order to not retreat will comedown and that there will be bigger battles sooner and closer to Germanies support system any anything that results in Germany have a shorter support line while still getting yo fight big battle vs the zuSSR is probably an improvement for Germany. Plus the war will be fought “faster” if the USSR is less inclined to pull back so the two don’t spend as much time traveling (retreating/advancing). So they are probably bigger battles sooner and more troops committed vs falling back so Germany by should able to kill more Russians faster. That being said it still ultimately sees Germany grind to a halt and it will see the USSR build enough troops and equipment and what have you to stop Germany so Germany will ultimately do better in terms of inflicting casualties on the USSR but they won’t get as far into the USSR. One thing I don’t know is if this fighting closer to the border will result in the German advance stoping before it gets so close that the USSR has to move its factories. Not moving a factory or two could make a big difference.

Again, as usual these scenarios entirely depend on one or both sides failing to react to changing circumstances. Firstly, USSR had information about possibility of German attack and was reacting. 'Stalin refused to believe the intelligence' is basically a myth. Soviet problem was not lack of the information or anyone's willingness or unwillingness 'to believe'. Soviet problem was lack of definitive information because everything that they had on Barbarossa was either utterly wrong, contaminated with enough false intelligence to make discerning what is true and what is not quite impossible or simply arrived too late for any sort of meaningful reaction. Secondly, USSR primary issue was that Germans at any point of preparation to Barbarossa were in position to speed these preparations up if they see an obvious Soviet reaction . And Germans were positioned to attack better than Soviets were positioned to defend. Let's say USSR starts mobilizing mid-April. Germany will not wait until June 22nd to attack because reality is not Hearts of Iron 4 game on a historical rails. Germans will simply attack in May before Soviet mobilization finishes. And yes, it could screw Mussolini by preventing Germany from bailing him out, but it was simple question of Germany already having mobilized army and having a better logistical infrastructure on their side of the border, so whatever obvious thing Soviets would do, Germans will have an opportunity to react. P.S. And no, Stalin will not give orders to pre-emptive attack against Germany for the very same reasons. Red Army was not in the position to attack anyone and everyone in Soviet leadership, including Stalin knew about that.
