items.original_question: What if Sea Beaufort and Sea Beaufighters used on Royal Navy aircraft carriers? What if the Royal Navy used a possible Bristol Sea variant of both Beauforts and Beaufighters on their carriers starting in 1940 replacing Fairy Swordfish aircraft in the torpedo attack role for example? Would this be possible design wise? Would they be better than the bomb and torpedo attack aircraft available at the time? Would the aircraft actually be able to be used like this or would they be too large? How effective would they be if used on aircraft carriers? Regards
items.model_answer:
If the Royal Navy had usable carrier-capable “Sea Beauforts” and “Sea Beaufighters” from 1940 onward, the Fleet Air Arm would have been substantially more dangerous in strike and fleet-defense roles, especially in the Mediterranean, but it probably would not have transformed the naval war by itself.

The biggest change would be that British carriers would no longer have been so dependent on very slow Swordfish and Albacore torpedo aircraft and mediocre Fulmar fighters during 1940–42. A naval Beaufort would have given the RN a faster, longer-ranged torpedo bomber and reconnaissance-strike aircraft. A naval Beaufighter would have given it a heavily armed long-range fighter, bomber-destroyer, night fighter, and anti-shipping aircraft years before comparable carrier strike fighters were common.

That would matter most in the Mediterranean. British carriers operating around Malta, Crete, Alexandria, and the central Mediterranean would have had a better chance of intercepting Italian and German bombers before they reached the fleet. Beaufighters, with cannon armament and later radar, would have been much better bomber-killers than Fulmars. They would not have been ideal dogfighters against Bf 109s or Macchi fighters, but against Ju 87s, Ju 88s, He 111s, SM.79s, and torpedo bombers they would have been formidable. Carrier losses and damage from Axis air attack might have been reduced, and convoy operations to Malta might have been somewhat less costly.

Sea Beauforts would also have improved British offensive pressure against Italian shipping. They could have attacked convoys to North Africa faster and from farther away than Swordfish or Albacores, and they would have been more survivable in daylight if not opposed by strong fighter cover. This could have worsened Axis supply problems in Libya and Tunisia. It would not automatically have strangled Rommel’s army, because intelligence, submarine operations, Malta-based aircraft, port capacity, and German air superiority all still mattered, but it could have tilted the attrition battle further in Britain’s favor.

The effect on famous actions would be mixed. At Taranto, Swordfish were actually well suited to the job: slow, stable, capable of night attack, and able to use modified shallow-running torpedoes. Sea Beauforts might not have improved the raid and could even have reduced the number of aircraft carried. Against Bismarck, faster carrier torpedo bombers might have made interception easier, but the historical Swordfish attack already succeeded. In the Norwegian and Arctic theaters, Sea Beaufighters would have been useful against German reconnaissance aircraft and bombers, and Sea Beauforts could have strengthened strikes against coastal shipping, but weather, range, and limited carrier availability would still have constrained operations.

In the Indian Ocean and early Pacific, the advantage would be real but not decisive. Sea Beaufighters would have been dangerous to Japanese bombers but poor substitutes for nimble single-seat fighters against Zeros. Sea Beauforts would have given British carriers a better modern torpedo-strike capability before large-scale availability of Avengers and Barracudas, but British armored carriers carried relatively small air groups. A few large twin-engined aircraft would consume a lot of hangar and deck space. That means a carrier might gain quality but lose aircraft numbers.

That is the central limitation. Carrier-capable Beauforts and Beaufighters would have been large, heavy aircraft for British carriers of the period. To operate them effectively, they would need folding wings, strengthened landing gear, arrestor hooks, good low-speed handling, and compatibility with British lifts and hangars. Even if all that were solved, each aircraft would take up much more space than a Swordfish, Martlet, Fulmar, or later Seafire. British armored-deck carriers already had restricted hangar capacity, so air groups would likely be smaller. A carrier full of Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters might hit harder, but it would launch fewer aircraft and maintain fewer combat air patrols.

There would also be industrial costs. Bristol engines, airframes, and development effort were already in demand for RAF Beauforts and Beaufighters. Navalizing both types from 1940 would likely reduce output elsewhere or delay other programs unless Britain somehow had extra production capacity. Training would also be harder: twin-engined carrier aircraft require more deck space, more maintenance, and more specialized pilots.

So the likely result is an RN that is noticeably stronger from 1941 to 1943, especially in the Mediterranean anti-shipping and fleet-defense campaigns. Malta convoys might suffer fewer losses, Axis convoys to North Africa might suffer more, and British carriers would be less vulnerable to bomber attack. The Fleet Air Arm’s embarrassing early-war capability gap would be narrowed earlier.

But it would not be a war-winning miracle. The aircraft would be too large to replace all carrier types, not agile enough to solve the fighter problem against modern single-seat fighters, and too few in number to give British carriers American-style striking mass. By 1944–45, when Corsairs, Hellcats, Avengers, Barracudas, and improved radar fighter direction became available, the unique advantage of Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters would diminish.

In short: carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 would probably have made the Royal Navy significantly more effective in the dangerous middle years of the war, especially in the Mediterranean, but they would have been a powerful supplement rather than a complete replacement for smaller carrier aircraft or for the later American types.

items.question: What If : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944
human_answers: The only Southerner who got any serious support at the DNC in 1944 was Alabama Senator John H. Bankhead II, who came in a distant third with 98 votes (8.33%) on the first ballot. The only other (non Alben W. Barkley) Southerners who got even one vote were: J. Melville Broughton (Governor of North Carolina), Prentice Cooper (Governor of Tennessee), Robert S. Kerr (Senator from Oklahoma), Herbert O'Conor (Governor of Maryland), Claude Pepper (Senator from Florida), Sam Rayburn (Speaker of the House), and Bascom N. Timmons (D.C. based newspaperman who grew up in Texas). Of these, only Bankhead II, Barkley, Broughton, Cooper, Kerr, and O’Conor got double digits. So your best case scenario is Roosevelt and/or the convention see a need to nominate a Southerner, and go with Bankhead II who IOTL died on June 12, 1946 following a stroke on May 24, 1946, which means you end up with three Presidents in little over a year. Based on the 1886 Succession Act, Bankhead II’s successor would be none other than… James F. Byrnes. IOTL, Truman appointed him in July of 1945, and it’s pretty likely Bankhead II does similarly, wanting to support a follow Southerner. (Prior to the Succession Act of 1947, neither the Speaker of the House nor the President pro tempore of the Senate were in the line of succession.) So in a roundabout way, you do end up with Byrnes as President…

Right. Byrnes thought he was Roosevelt's choice. Truman went to the DNC planning to make a nominating speech for Byrnes. If Byrnes does get the nod... FDR wins in 1944 anyway. But things diverge after that. IMO the Republicans sweep in 1946 as OTL. Byrnes was a very capable man and won't make any big missteps, so IMO he will be renominated in 1948. There may be a feeling that the 1948 nomination is a poisoned chalice, what with the 1946 GOP sweep and general public fatigue with 16 years of Democrat Presidents. The "Humphreyite" liberals may still try to push a civil rights plank at the DNC, but against Byrnes' at least tacit opposition will fail. They won't bolt to support Wallace overtly. Instead they may sit back to watch Byrnes crash and burn in November, while they regroup for 1952. Byrnes will lose a fair number of voters to Wallace outside the South. Also, AIUI, Dewey chose to soft-pedal civil rights OTL in the vain hope of winning some Upper South states with the Democrats divided. TTL that ignis fatuus isn't around, so Dewey probably emphasizes civil rights to draw the increasingly important black vote in the North and also some white liberals. This should be enough for Dewey to win. The next question is whether he has enough "coat tails" for Republicans to hold Congress. Another question is how the civil rights issue shapes across the next decade. OTL, leadership on the issue was taken by liberal non-Southern Democrats, with the low-key support of Republicans. The first cracks in the "Solid South" came in the 1950s, as a few white Southerners who could no longer rely on the national Democratic party to protect Jim Crow found they could vote Republican. If under Dewey, Republicans claim the leading role, that's not going to happen. The "Humphreyites" will gain control of the Democrats by 1952; there may be a Dixiecrat ticket that year. Dewey will be re-elected, barring some debacle in Korea or whatever. Warren won't be Chief Justice, but the Court will still be making rulings like Brown .
items.original_question: What if : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944 In 1944, after intense pressure, President Franklin Delano Roosevelt would drop Vice President Henry Asgard Wallace from the ticket but due to his initial choice of James F. Byrnes being rejected due to his conversion from Catholicism, he would ultimately be convinced to go with Missouri Senator Harry S. Truman. Truman, as President, proved to be a liberal on racial issues and on labor rights, seeing as his SCOTUS Appointments sealed the deal on Brown v Board of Education being unanimous. However, what if ultimately, FDR went with a strict segregationist who was in favor of the New Deal at least early in their career? What happens when he becomes President and any ideas who this could be (one idea is Russell and another is Connally but both might say no to the offer)? Who do they appoint to SCOTUS instead of Burton and Vinson in 1945 and 1946 and Clark and Minton if they won a full term in 1948? What would 1948 look like in this TL? I suspect the southern president would probably appoint segregationist justices or lawyers to the court who make it through thanks to the Conservative Coalition being aligned on this one issue, though I admit I am unsure how they would handle the post war time frame, especially with 1945-1949. Furthermore, I could see a case for Dewey not being nominated ittl as in 1948 iotl, his nomination wasn't guaranteed but his wing of the party was able to get things to align with him by the convention. Here, with a more conservative leaning court and administration, the Republicans may pick a Conservative who can bring stability to both the party and the nation as long as it isn't Taft Sr. Also, I imagine the effects this has on American politics, specifically the civil rights movement, especially if Brown v Board goes the other way, if this has happened with perhaps more radical actions being taken and maybe an earlier Black Panther Party if things get really bad, but that's up in the air for the first decade of this period in time.
items.model_answer:
If FDR had chosen a segregationist vice president in 1944, the biggest change would likely come after April 1945, when FDR died and that vice president became president. The war itself probably would not change dramatically, but postwar domestic politics, civil rights, and the Democratic Party’s future could change a great deal.

The most plausible “segregationist VP” would have been someone like James F. Byrnes of South Carolina, who was a serious 1944 contender and had major wartime administrative experience. If FDR had strongly backed him, the Democratic convention probably would have accepted him, though labor unions, Black voters, northern liberals, and some Catholic voters would have been much less enthusiastic than they were about Truman. FDR probably still wins in 1944 because of wartime incumbency and his personal popularity, but the margin could be narrower in key northern states.

Once FDR dies, a segregationist President Byrnes-type figure probably follows broadly similar military policy in 1945. Germany still surrenders in May. The atomic bomb is still likely used against Japan, perhaps even more readily, because Byrnes in real history was one of the strongest advocates of using it to end the war and strengthen the U.S. diplomatic position against the Soviet Union. Japan’s surrender probably still comes in August 1945 after the bombs and Soviet entry into the war.

Foreign policy would also be broadly recognizable. The U.S. would still face Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe, instability in Greece and Turkey, and the need to rebuild Western Europe. Containment, the Marshall Plan, and NATO might still emerge, though possibly under different names and with different timing. A Byrnes-like president might be more personally hard-line toward Moscow but less rhetorically idealistic than Truman. The Cold War probably still happens.

The major difference is civil rights. Truman, despite his own prejudices, became the first president since Reconstruction to make civil rights a serious national Democratic issue. He created the President’s Committee on Civil Rights, endorsed anti-lynching and anti-poll-tax measures, and desegregated the armed forces by executive order in 1948. A segregationist president almost certainly would not do those things. Federal civil-rights momentum would be delayed. The armed forces might remain segregated until the Korean War, a Republican administration, or military necessity forced change. The Justice Department would likely be less supportive of civil-rights litigation. The symbolic shift that made Black voters increasingly loyal Democrats would be weakened or postponed.

The 1948 election would be very different. In real history, Truman’s civil-rights turn caused the Dixiecrat revolt led by Strom Thurmond, while Henry Wallace ran on the left. A segregationist Democratic president would probably avoid the Dixiecrat split because the South would be satisfied. But he would alienate northern liberals, labor, and Black voters more deeply. The Democratic Party might hold the Solid South but lose more of the industrial North. That could make Republican Thomas Dewey more likely to win in 1948, especially if progressives bolted to Wallace or stayed home.

If a segregationist Democrat somehow won in 1948, the Democratic Party’s transformation into a civil-rights party would be delayed. The party would remain more openly dependent on its southern segregationist wing, and the eventual civil-rights realignment of the 1950s–60s might happen later or under different leadership. If Dewey won instead, the Republicans might claim more of the civil-rights mantle for a time, though Congress would still be a major obstacle because southern Democrats and conservative Republicans could block strong legislation.

So the short answer is: World War II’s ending probably remains similar, and the Cold War probably still begins. But Truman’s civil-rights turn likely disappears, the military remains segregated longer, Black voters may not consolidate as Democratic as quickly, and the 1948 election becomes much more favorable to the Republicans. The largest consequence would be a delayed or reshaped civil-rights realignment in American politics.

items.question: What If the Allies lose on the Salonica front?
human_answers: Alan Wakefield (IWM expert on Salonika, among other subjects) commented that most of the Bulgarian forces in September 1918 facing the British were well motivated, apart from the 1st Macedonian Bde that consisted of many men of Serbian origin. It was the collapse further west when the French & Serbian forces broke through three lines of defence, followed by the Greek breakthrough at Petit Couronne and Doiran Hill to the Bulgarian second line that unhinged the Bulgarian defences. Bulgarian C-in-C Todorov met with the German commanders von Steuben (German 11th Army) and von Reuter (Division Reuter) on 18 September, and agreed that Bulgarian 1st Army would be pulled back from positions east of the Vadar River, while the German 11th Army and Bulgarian 3rd Division would maintain contact. However the orders to 1st Army came as a severe blow to morale as the men were celebrating their stalling the British attacks, They started marching to Kosturino Pass but there was a serious shortage of draught animals, and of the survivors: " The majority of horses & oxen were absolutely unfit for work and they had need of at least six months rest in the interior, where they could be well nourished, Others had need of at least 45 days rest" - Major Nedeff, 9th Division, quoted in Under the Devil's Eye (Alan Wakefield & Simon Moody) from which much of the first three paragraphs are sourced. This was when the RAF caught the Bulgarian withdrawal through the passes, causing serious casualties & further delays. With foreign troops now on Bulgarian soil, political opposition to the war in the Sobranie was widespread. The PM, Malinov, was pro-western and had been appointed that June by Tsar Ferdinand with the purpose of proposing an armistice to the Allies, and on 26 September emissaries were sent through the lines to start discussions, although Franchet d'Esperey would only accept an unilateral unconditional armistice, which the Bugarian government then agreed to give, So it looks like the Bulgarian army was in generally good morale status until the final victories sparked by the French, Serbian & Greek forces, when the order of and losses taken on the retreat caused a final decline. But it looks like the home front collapsed first, if the Tsar was considering an armistice in June, so not sure what caused the domestic problems that drove the government to seek peace (I understand that a military rebelliion / mutiny at Radomir formulated by Bulgarian Agrarian National Union attempted to overthrow the government and establish a republic). Wiki suggests the following reasons: - Extreme war weariness, given Bulgaria had been at war since 1912 (short break 1914-15). Exhausted manpower (see #1 above) - I would add this resulted in dissatisfied minority groups supplying more troops, such as Macedonian Serbs & Greeks, diluting the Bulgar core. Both military & civilians suffering extreme food shortages (result of your point regarding harvests?). Troops poorly supplied - not only food but ammunition, clothing, boots, etc. Troops believing profiteers making hay at home at their expense. Feeling of betrayal by their allies, principally Germany, especialy regarding promised levels of supplies not being met, and lack of support for Bulgarian territorial ambitions at expense of Romania. Not sure how far the German troop levels had been reduced as you comment. The impact of the Russian Revolution. The impact of Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points (maybe a surrender would't be as bad as keep fighting) Recommended is 'The Enemy is Behind Us': The Morale Crisis in the Bulgarian Army during the Summer of 1918 - Richard C Hall, War in History Vol. 11 No. 4 which again refers to the collapse in morale starting by June 1918. Bulgarian C-in-C Nikola Zhekov reported to Tsar Ferdinand on 121 June that: "Today it is impossible ton have any illusions that the spirit of the soldiers is the same as at the beginning of the war, or even last year." I can't access as I don't have a school account! It does look like some units, such as the 9th (Pleven) Division, kept their high morale almost to the end. My main comment on demoralised forces would apply further north and primarily to the Austro-Hungarian troops who fell apart in October 1918, when I daresay no one suggests they were of high morale status. Earlier in the war that would not be the case, and I reckon me & a mountain goat could hold the Neretva Valley!

When you mentioned the Allies, I almost thought it was World War II. In reality, due to the division of Greece, neither the Entente nor the Central Powers could make any progress on the Thessaloniki front. Launching a large-scale offensive meant turning Greece into a battlefield, alienating more Greeks, and pushing more Greeks to the other side. The Entente was able to launch its offensive on the Macedonian front in 1917-1918 because the Entente countries had a large surplus of French reserves, willing to do everything except attack the Germans, such as conducting political work with the Greeks (Germany's reserves were smaller but more elite, and needed to do more important things; Bulgaria and the Ottomans were absolutely unacceptable to the Greeks). Ultimately, the deployment of hundreds of thousands of soldiers from the core countries of the Triple Entente only resulted in the defeat of one vassal state. The Central Powers could not accept this waste of reserves (unless Italy joined the Central Powers, providing some low ability soldiers). Even so, the problem of resource shortages must be taken into account.

It's my impression that it's something of a convention on this post 1900 forum to use "Entente" instead of "Allies", presumably to avoid confusion with the Allies of WW2. IMVHO I do prefer "Allies" for the WW1 military coalition because "Entente" is a derivation of the "Triple Entente" which applies to France/Russia/Britain, but by the end of WW1 the key great powers were Britain/France/Italy/America (and Russia was out) and there were multiple smaller allied powers. Why couldn't the Central Powers advance? Like, I thought Gallipoli ultimately failed because it was a trench-warfare stalemate; the Allies couldn't overcome a German client state. IIRC the proximal reason for the Gallipoli evacuation was that Bulgaria had joined the Central Powers, providing a route for German war material (not merely advisor personnel) like heavy siege artillery to be delivered to Turkey, which the Allies thought would be decisive. Was that assessment correct? Are you saying the Ottomans (with German support) could do something (push an Allied army into the sea) the Bulgarians (with their German support) could not? Or do you think that if the Allies had dug in on the Gallipoli peninsula in 1916, they might have obtained a stalemate which lasted until 1917/1918 when further offensives could be launched? I read that because of the potential futility of the front, Britain (and France) contemplated withdrawing their troops from mainland Greece before lines were solidified. Surely the Central Powers could have conquered Greece under those circumstances, no? I suppose in a grand strategy sense I recognize Germany was trying to fight a multi-front conflict against [the entire rest of the world] and was ultimately all but certain to lose the war. But in the narrower sense of "could the Balkan theater have played out differently", isn't it possible that the Central Powers could have achieved more success? Like, what if some resources from a different offensive (which surely would see less success than in OTL) devoted towards breaking through on the Macedonian front?

The allies couldn't overcome a German ally with more than 50 divisions and more than a million men on the field you mean, which in 1915 were about as well armed as their own troops. This is not 1942 in the Eastern front. But to get to the actual question in the fall of 1915 Greece was fully mobilized with 16 divisions and 325,000 troops in Macedonia and the Germans were doing their level best to keep Constantine in control and Greece out of the war. If they invade Greek territory you can kiss that neutrality goodbye and these 16 divisions just come into play added to the British and French divisions already landed in Salonica. And you'd better time it after the Serbs have been pushed into retreating into Albania, if your invasion comes before you just saved the lives of a couple hundred thousand Serbs. No. You essentially suggest Berlin says "to hell with the shenanigans to keep the Greeks neutral, let's invade them too. " So you just about gave numerical parity to the defenders... who don't have to move everything but food and fodder for the Macedonian and Turkish fronts though a single track railway going all the way back to Vienna. Before Dobro Polie and Desperate Frankie advancing all the way to Hungary and Austria putting the final nail in the Austro-Hungarian empire's coffin the actual front looked a pretty good deal to Berlin. Over 400,000 allied troops before the Greeks joined, that could be fighting elsewhere contained through mostly Bulgarian manpower... which could not be used elsewhere. Biggest POW camp in the world jokes and all that.

Well, Alternate History Challenge: An equivalent of Dobro Polie and subsequent desperate Frankie advances happen six months to a year earlier than OTL, *before* the Germans start getting pushed back on the western front, not after, and perhaps as a consequence, we get to see see the desperate Frankie international force *keep advancing* through the territory of capitulated Austria-Hungary, and over onto German territory from its southern and eastern borders (to Munich, Passau, Dresden, Gorlitz, Liegnitz or further to Cottbus or Berlin) before the Germans actually capitulate. Could this have ever happened in the right combination of circumstances? Could an earlier resolution of the Greek political divide in favor of the Venizelist side, committing the full Greek Army to the Entente side earlier, have helped with this? What might it take, faster French seduction? Or, going the opposite direction, more in line with what the OP wants, is there any way the Venizelist side could have been so marginalized that the Royalist side in Greece became willing to openly side with the Central Powers and openly welcomed/sought CP support in expelling Allied forces from Salonica and any other parts of Greece at any point during the war?
items.original_question: What if the Allies lose on the Salonica front? As I loosely understand it, the Salonica front was established after the Serbian army was routed. What if the Central Powers were able to continue advancing into Greece and expelled the Allies from the mainland Balkans? The Salonica front in some ways seems to resemble Gallipoli (an Allied lodgment supplied by sea) and the Central powers were able to prevail at Gallipoli, so it seems possible. The Allies also had to deal with the fact that the Greek government was divided - if the Central powers were more successful it seems possible Greece would have “switched sides”, or at least had a compliant government installed.
items.model_answer:
If the Allies lost on the Salonica front, the main result would probably be a longer and less sudden collapse of the Central Powers in 1918, not a decisive Central Powers victory by itself.

The Salonica, or Macedonian, front mattered because the Allied breakthrough there in September 1918 knocked Bulgaria out of the war. Bulgaria’s surrender opened the Balkans, threatened Austria-Hungary from the south, cut the land connection between Germany/Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire, and helped create the chain reaction that ended World War I within weeks.

If instead the Allies were defeated there—meaning their army at Salonica was forced onto the defensive, evacuated, or destroyed—Bulgaria would likely remain in the war longer. Serbia would not be liberated in 1918, the Central Powers would keep control of the Balkan corridor, and Austria-Hungary would not face an immediate Allied advance from the south. The Ottoman Empire would also benefit because the overland connection through the Balkans would remain more secure, though by late 1918 the Ottomans were already under severe pressure in Palestine, Syria, Mesopotamia, and from internal exhaustion.

Politically, an Allied defeat would also damage Allied prestige in Greece. Greece might become unstable again, and the pro-Allied Venizelist government could be weakened. A serious defeat might even revive royalist or neutralist forces. Bulgaria, by contrast, would gain breathing space and possibly a stronger bargaining position at the end of the war.

But this would not automatically save Germany. By autumn 1918 Germany was losing on the Western Front, suffering from blockade, manpower shortages, collapsing morale, and the arrival of large numbers of American troops. Even if the Salonica front held for the Central Powers, Germany still faced defeat in France and Belgium. Austria-Hungary was also disintegrating internally because of nationalist tensions, food shortages, and war exhaustion. Those problems would remain.

So the most likely outcome is that the war lasts longer—perhaps into late 1918 or 1919—and ends less dramatically in the Balkans. Bulgaria might surrender later, Austria-Hungary might collapse more slowly, and the Allies would have less leverage in southeastern Europe. Serbia’s recovery would be delayed, Greece’s postwar position would be weaker, and the Balkan settlement after the war might look different.

In short: an Allied defeat at Salonica would remove one of the triggers of the Central Powers’ rapid collapse, but it probably would not reverse the overall result of World War I unless combined with major German success on the Western Front.

items.question: What If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin engine?
human_answers: 1 - as noted by the fellow member, the P-40F and L used the Merlin 2 - it was a pretty simple upgrade 3 - engine itself does not require a laminar flow wing; a laminar flow wing will cut some drag, however, and thus allow for some speed increase 4 - historically, it offered some 30 mph over the P-40E at 18000 ft and above, IOW it was an improvement the P-40 badly needed 5 - P-51s used the better Merlins, these with 2-stage supercharger; a P-40 with such an engine would've probably be as fast as the Spitfire IX, but not as fast as the Merlin Mustang, nor as rangy - and thus the answer is 'no' 6 - as-is, the performance was better on the P-40F than on the ubiquitous P-40E; with 2-stage Merlin, it would've probably been good for 400+ mph, and much better rate of climb (the XP-40Q did 420+ mph with a 2-stage supercharged V-1710)

I'll have to take your word for it as I'm forbidden from your links but that sounds about right. A more advanced Merlin won't really help the P-40 though. There are availability issues with the Merlin, as ever, which historically forced Curtiss to revert to the V-1710-81 for the P-40M, despite more than half the production run going to the RAF. Not even every P-40F/L received a Merlin as some were completed as V-1710-81 engined P-40Rs. More though, there is the tale of the XP-60, which was a P-40D fuselage with a new laminar-flow wing. It was an improvement, with 387mph at 22,000ft. Modified as the XP-60D with an enlarged tail, it may or may not have received the V-1650-3 slated for it by the time of it's destruction in a crash on 6th May 1943. It certainly didn't perform any substantive testing with it. By that time the Merlin Mustang was established as superior in performance and was already entering production. The XP-60A with 1425hp V-1710-75, good for 420mph at 29,000ft, was part-cancelled in January 1942 (with the remainder following in June 1943) in favour of P-40Ks, Ls and P-47Gs. I think that is going to be the fate of any advanced or improved P-40 variant. Cancelled in favour of sustained production of known quantities.
items.original_question: What if Curtiss P-40 used Merlins? What instead of using Allison V-12's the Curtiss P-40 used the Merlin V-12 instead ? Would this be possible or would it need major airframe development? Would it need a redesigned laminar flow wing to really utilise the engine? How successful would this instillation be? Would it allow the P-40 to be more successful than the later P-51? What boost in combat performance would this instillation allow? Regards
items.model_answer:
If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed from the start around the Rolls-Royce Merlin, it probably would have been a better fighter, especially above medium altitude, but it would not have become another P-51 Mustang.

The main historical weakness of the P-40 was not that the Allison V-1710 was a bad engine; it was that most early Allisons lacked an effective two-stage supercharger. The P-40 was strong, rugged, well armed, and good at low to medium altitude, but its performance fell off badly at higher altitude. A Merlin-powered P-40, especially one designed from the beginning with proper cooling, cowling, weight distribution, and supercharger installation, would have had better climb, ceiling, and high-altitude speed. It would have been more useful in Europe, where combat often occurred higher up, and it would have been less outclassed by Bf 109s and Fw 190s.

But the improvement would have had limits. The P-40 airframe came from the P-36 lineage and was not as aerodynamically efficient as the later P-51. Its wing, cooling layout, fuselage drag, and general design philosophy were older. The Mustang did not become exceptional merely because it received a Merlin; it became exceptional because the Merlin was combined with a very clean airframe, excellent radiator ducting, low drag, good range, and later high-altitude optimization. A Merlin P-40 would likely have been faster and better-climbing than the standard Allison P-40, but it still would not have matched a Spitfire IX, Bf 109G, Fw 190A, or Merlin Mustang at altitude.

Historically, Curtiss did build Merlin-powered P-40s: the P-40F and P-40L used Packard-built Merlins. They were improvements in some respects, particularly at altitude, but they were not transformative. They were somewhat heavier, not dramatically faster, and still limited by the basic P-40 airframe. A P-40 designed around the Merlin from the beginning would probably have been better than those conversions, because the installation could have been cleaner and better balanced, but the gains would likely have been evolutionary rather than revolutionary.

The biggest counterfactual effect would depend on timing. If a Merlin P-40 had appeared in 1940–41 in large numbers, it could have given the RAF, USAAF, and Allied export customers a more capable interim fighter. In North Africa, China, Burma, and the Southwest Pacific, it would have been highly useful. In the European theater it might have performed respectably as a second-line or fighter-bomber aircraft rather than being largely unsuitable for high-altitude air superiority.

However, there is also the production problem. Merlin engines were scarce and strategically valuable. Britain needed them for Spitfires, Hurricanes, Lancasters, and Mosquitoes; later the United States needed Packard Merlins for P-51s. Giving large numbers of Merlins to the P-40 would have meant fewer engines for aircraft that used them more effectively. Once the P-51 existed, it made far more sense to put Merlins into Mustangs than into P-40s.

So the likely result is this: a Merlin-designed P-40 would have been a noticeably better P-40, with improved high-altitude performance and a longer useful front-line life. It might have narrowed the gap with contemporary German and Japanese fighters and made the type more attractive to the RAF and USAAF. But it would not have changed the balance of the air war by itself, and it would probably have been overtaken anyway by cleaner, more modern designs such as the P-51, Spitfire IX, P-47, and later Fw 190 and Bf 109 variants.

items.question: PT-109: What If JFK Died on 7/2/43?
human_answers: It seems plausible to me that if Jack were to die in the Pacific, Sr would use connections to ensure that Jr would come home in one piece so that grooming for public office could begin. That said, I've read several accounts that suggest/indicate Jr was not as approachable/astute/able to think on his feet as well as Jack. That might make a political career more challenging: still feasible, but more challenging and quite possibly more costly (Sr might have had to write more and/or larger checks to make things happen?). I could see Jr with a House, and later a Senate seat. Then the question becomes: could he work his way into such a position that Adlai Stevenson might consider him as a running mate in 1956? Arguably, that propelled Jack into the limelight enough to become a presidential contender in 1960. My sense is that Jr would not get the same consideration ITTL that Jack did IOTL. Rather, he would plausibly have tried a presidential run having something like 8-10 years of Senate experience under his belt in 1960. We're talking a crowded field for the Dems in 1960: Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Jr, and the usual cast of favorite sons. Johnson might be the favorite, but not a prohibitive favorite: coming from Texas would assure that. Too manybut Lodge won northerners would be skeptical. On the other hand, Humphrey would definitely not play well in the south. Could Jr emerge as a compromise candidate? Maybe, but he'd be a tough sell in the south given his Catholic faith. My sense is that a protracted, multiple ballot convention would ultimately result in a Johnson nomination, with a middle of the road midwesterner (I'll yield to someone else here) as a VP candidate. Nixon will still be the GOP nominee, but Lodge won't be his running mate: don't need to counter a Kennedy. I suggest it would be MD governor Theodore McKeldin, a man who knew how to work with both sides (he was the last GOP mayor of Baltimore). McKeldin would bring a great deal more to the ticket than Lodge, but that's a pretty low bar. While we're at it, look for the 1960 campaign to be nasty. Lyndon Johnson had few scruples if any as far as that went, so I wouldn't be surprised if he started it. Then all Nixon has to do is take the high road and point out how well things have gone during Ike's tenure, and pump up his role (maybe this time Ike wouldn't make his famous "...if you give me a week..." remark?). And I don't see Richard Daley doing much to help Lyndon Johnson in Chicago, so IL might well flip to the GOP. Long story short: Nixon wins in '60. That leaves 1968 as Jr's next shot at the White House: he wouldn't try to unseat Nixon unless something totally unforeseen happened.

I once posted on another thread about a different pathway that Joe Jr's career would look like. IOTL JFK had the choice of running for Congress or for Lt. Governor of Massachusetts, and he chose to run for Congress in 1946. My alternate path for Joe Jr. had him running for Lt. Governor in 1946 and getting Statewide exposure, IOTL the Democratic ticket lost, but with Joe Sr's money the Democrats win. Joe Jr. runs for US Senate against Republican incumbent Leverett Saltonstall in 1948 and wins in a Democratic year. The main character flaw of Joe Jr. was his fierce loyalty to his father. There is a story about how Joe Sr. was on the Harvard baseball team and by playing on the Harvard-Yale game he would get a letter, but due to anti-Catholic bigotry, he was left on the bench and didn't get a letter. When Joe Jr. as a senior on the team, he was the first baseman and made the final put out of the Harvard-Yale game, and by tradition the ball is given to the team captain and Joe Jr. kept it himself and gave the ball to his father. How this would play out is uncertain, how far would he go in defending Joe Sr.'s isolation? JFK was able use his service to separate himself against any criticism against his father, but could Joe Jr. do that?

Both are possible, but I do think that Jor Sr trying to pull some strings would be more plausible (at least to me). But if Joe Jr still does his mission (maybe the dates between Jack's death and Joe's mission are too close), it could be that Robert gets chosen as the next. That being said... This was something I didn't think about, but from what I read it would make sense. Robert was always known as the black sheep of the family. If Ted was chosen by Joe Sr, he may very well have been thrown into Korea. The only question would be where Ted's future would go: He would have been far too young to run for President in 1960, but he could have won a seat as Senator in Massachusetts (although it would have been difficult). Maybe eight years later (say 1968), Ted might try to make his move, although 1972 might be more plausible.
items.original_question: PT-109: What if JFK Died on 7/2/43? In 1943, John F Kennedy's patrol boat PT-109 was rammed by the battleship Amagiri. After PT-109 exploded, JFK was able to survive, swimming from the wreck to a nearby island to stay alive while also saving his fellow soldiers. The moment cemented Jack as a war hero, and after his brother Joe died in a special mission, Jack was seen as next in line to join the Senate, before finally becoming President (which we all know how it ended). But what if things went slightly differently? Maybe Jack is closer to the blast and dies in the initial explosion. What next? What would happen to Joe Jr, and by extension, the Kennedy family? In our timeline, Joe Jr was killed in a special mission, but could the death of JFK stopped Joe Jr from going on the mission, and continue to stay alive to be the frontrunner of the family? Joe Jr had approved of Hitler, but his ideals could have easily morphed over time. Could Joe have done what Jack did and become President, and how would his presidency have looked? And if Joe Jr did in fact die anyway, who would replace him? Robert would have been far too young, along with Ted. Would the Kennedy family fade out of the limelight? What would become of the 1960 elections? The more obvious question, with Jack dead, who would be the man to lead the Democrats against Nixon? The most likely options are Hubert Humphrey, Lyndon Baines Johnson, and (although less likely), Adali Stevenson. Who would have been able to win the primaries, and could they have dealt with Nixon? With whoever becomes President, how would their Presidency look, and what could happen to them if they were also assassinated? For me personally, the most likely ticket would have been Johnson, causing him to be President.
items.model_answer:
If JFK had died in the PT-109 episode in 1943, the largest consequence is simple: there is almost certainly no President John F. Kennedy, no Kennedy–Nixon race in 1960 as we know it, no JFK assassination in 1963, and no “Camelot” mythology shaping later American politics. Strictly speaking, PT-109 was rammed on August 2, 1943, not July 2, but assuming the counterfactual is that Kennedy dies in that wartime incident, the political effects would be profound.

Kennedy would likely have been remembered, if at all nationally, as a young Navy officer and son of Joseph P. Kennedy who died heroically in the Pacific. Since his older brother Joseph Kennedy Jr. died in 1944, the Kennedy family might have lost both intended political heirs within a year. Joseph Kennedy Sr. might then have pushed Robert Kennedy or, later, Ted Kennedy into politics, but neither would have been positioned to become president in 1960. RFK was too young and lacked the independent political base JFK built through the House, Senate, and 1960 campaign.

In Massachusetts politics, JFK’s absence matters immediately. He would not win a House seat in 1946, would not become senator in 1952, and would not defeat Henry Cabot Lodge Jr. That likely leaves Lodge stronger and changes the Republican Party’s bench. More importantly, the Democrats lose their most telegenic, moderate, Catholic, Cold War liberal candidate in 1960.

The 1960 Democratic nomination probably goes to Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Stuart Symington, or possibly Adlai Stevenson. Johnson is the most plausible if he campaigns aggressively, but he lacked JFK’s national glamour and Northern appeal. Against Richard Nixon, the election would likely be very close, but Nixon’s chances improve substantially without JFK. A Nixon victory in 1960 is probably the most likely single outcome, though a Johnson victory is still plausible.

If Nixon becomes president in 1961, Cuba, civil rights, Vietnam, and space policy all change. The Bay of Pigs plan might still happen, since it originated under Eisenhower, but Nixon may have used more direct American air support or handled Cuba more aggressively. That could either make the invasion more successful or produce an earlier and more dangerous confrontation with Castro and the Soviet Union. The Cuban Missile Crisis as we know it likely does not occur in the same form.

Civil rights probably advances more slowly without JFK’s assassination and without Lyndon Johnson using JFK’s martyrdom and his own congressional skill to pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The civil rights movement would still force national action, but the timing and strength of federal legislation might differ. Vietnam might still escalate, because Cold War pressures pushed both parties in that direction, but the exact path would not be LBJ’s 1964–65 escalation. The Moon program might also be less dramatic or slower without JFK’s 1961 commitment to landing a man on the Moon before the decade’s end.

So the direct answer is: if JFK died in 1943, American politics loses a future president, the Kennedy dynasty is greatly weakened or delayed, Nixon is more likely to win in 1960, the Civil Rights Act and Vietnam escalation unfold differently, and the iconic sequence of JFK’s presidency, assassination, LBJ’s Great Society, and the 1960s as we remember them is fundamentally altered.

items.question: What If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981?
human_answers: The core problem with these discussions is that you wind up with a lot of people who had personal experience with home computers imagining their home computer was a long-term viable platform particularly killed by the IBM PC. The inherent market dynamic was, instead, that all the home computers were doomed to extinction at the hands of the standard business personal computer platform. It is businesses that care about backward compatibility with their internal installed base, while the home computer user market has an observable willingness to abandon old platforms and adopt new ones. This means home-targeted versions of the business platform can easily be adopted by the home market, while business-targeted versions of home platforms can only get adopted by businesses if they have a specific compelling business advantage. And then, as soon as the business platform clones the advantage, the home platform is again on the defensive. Home platforms are thus in an inherently weak position, and will be smashed flat by the standard business platform. And, well, there was already a standard business personal computer platform in 1980-1981 -- the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. You could buy that platform as an Osborne 1, or as a Xerox 820, or from any of dozens of other of other makers. You even had the Microsoft Softcard (originally, "Z-80 Softcard", but Zilog complained) which used an Apple II as a host for a 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The major problem that the CP/M-80 platform had going forward was that it had run up against the 64k RAM addressing limit of the 8080/8085/Z80, at a time when RAM prices had dropped enough that it was entirely practical to buy more. And since none of the chipmakers had had the sense to make a 8080-compatible processor with wider addressing, the only real way forward was the 8086/8088, since 8080 assembly code could be easily machine-translated into 8086 code. Everybody was just waiting on Digital Research to get CP/M-86 out. The IBM PC then arrived, with an OS that was arguably even more compatible in its system calls with CP/M-80, and the ability to use all the RAM anybody could practically afford. (Even if Gates never said 640K was enough for anybody, in 1981 that was true. Indeed, the first version of the PC's BIOS had a 544K limit.) It was the perfectly natural successor to the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The IBM endorsement made the transition smoother, and did have some secondary consequences (killing the S-100 bus, for example), but the true key to the IBM PC's success is that it was the natural successor-host for a software ecosystem that had grown up on top of the Altair 8800. What happens in the absence of the IBM PC is simple enough. Digital Research will release CP/M-86. At which point the CP/M-86 systems take over the business market, and eventually all the home computer platforms are killed by the multi-manufacturer business standard, just as in the original timeline.

As I understand it, the IBM machine was intended as an 'intelligent terminal' for their mainframes .. Businesses already had mainframes & dumb terminals but because the terminals were dumb the mainframe had to do everything - which led to limits on the numbers - and whilst IBM would be happy to sell (rent) you another mainframe they then run into the problem of getting the mainframes to talk 'seamlessly' to each other ... so IBM work on evermore powerful / more expensive mainframes as the number of users go up .. If, however, you can off-load some of the 'housekeeping' (things like deciding how to repaint the screen as the user edits a file, without the entire screen contents having to be resent from the mainframe, for example) onto the terminal, you can roll out cheap low end mainframes (at the same cost as the high end ones, naturally) able to cope with 100's more users .. Other companies wanted to 'get in on' IBM's business but had difficulties building mainframes as powerful as the IBM ones = thus, sooner or later, some-one else is going to come up with the concept of 'intelligent terminals' .. after which the PC becomes more or less inevitable ..
items.original_question: What if no IBM PC (2026 ed.) In short - the IBM PC (model 5150) was not an inevitable thing, the IBM leadership was highly skeptical of the project and it would not have seen the light of the day had things gone just slightly differently. So, what if that computer had never been created? My take - the personal computer market would look a lot like mobile or console market - a walled garden of 2-3 incompatible standards, probably Apple and Commodore (which, would do better financially without the competition from PC clones). It's interesting what would happen in Japan and (later) China.
items.model_answer:
If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981, the personal computer industry would probably still have grown, but it would have grown more slowly, less uniformly, and with a very different balance of power.

The IBM PC mattered less because it was technically revolutionary and more because it gave the microcomputer business corporate legitimacy. Before 1981, personal computers already existed: Apple II, Commodore PET/VIC, TRS-80, Atari machines, CP/M business systems, and others. But many large companies still saw them as hobbyist or departmental tools. IBM’s entry signaled to conservative businesses that personal computers were safe to buy. Without that endorsement, business adoption would likely have been slower and more fragmented.

The biggest difference would be the absence, or at least delay, of the “IBM-compatible PC” standard. The original IBM PC used off-the-shelf parts and had a relatively open architecture, which allowed companies such as Compaq, Dell, AST, and many others to build compatible machines. That created a massive clone market and eventually made “PC” mean a DOS/Intel-compatible computer. Without the 1981 IBM PC, there may have been no single dominant hardware standard in the early 1980s. Instead, the market might have remained divided among Apple, CP/M machines, Commodore, Tandy, Atari, and various business systems.

Microsoft’s rise would also have been much less certain. MS-DOS became important because IBM chose it for the PC, and then the clone industry spread it everywhere. Without that deal, Microsoft might still have been a successful software company through BASIC, applications, and later operating systems, but it probably would not have become dominant so quickly. Digital Research’s CP/M-86 might have had a better chance, Unix variants might have gained more ground in business, or Apple’s operating systems might have become more influential.

The processor landscape could also have changed. The IBM PC helped cement Intel’s x86 architecture as the center of the personal computer world. Without it, Motorola 68000-based systems, used in machines like the Apple Macintosh, Amiga, Atari ST, and some workstations, might have had a stronger position. The eventual dominance of x86 was not guaranteed before the IBM PC clone ecosystem formed.

Apple might have benefited significantly. The Apple II was already strong in education and small business, and the Macintosh might have faced a less entrenched DOS-compatible world when it arrived in 1984. However, Apple’s more closed and higher-priced strategy could still have limited its market share. A world without the IBM PC does not automatically mean Apple dominates; it more likely means a longer period of competing incompatible platforms.

Business software would have developed differently too. Programs such as Lotus 1-2-3, dBASE, WordPerfect, and later Excel and Windows benefited from the large standardized PC market. Without that standard, software companies would have had to support more platforms, raising costs and slowing the creation of mass-market business software. Corporate computing might have stayed tied longer to minicomputers, terminals, and proprietary office systems.

Eventually, some standard probably would have emerged, because businesses strongly prefer compatibility and software developers prefer large markets. But it might have emerged later, from a different company, with a different operating system and processor architecture. The modern computer world could have been less Microsoft-centered, less x86-centered, and possibly more influenced by Apple, Unix, Motorola-based systems, or a different corporate-backed platform.

So the most likely outcome is not that personal computers fail to take off. They almost certainly still do. But without the IBM PC in 1981, the PC revolution would probably have been delayed, more fragmented, and less dominated by the Microsoft-Intel “Wintel” standard that shaped computing for the next several decades.

items.question: What If No P51 Bomber Escort?
human_answers: The P-51B/C/D was clearly a better dogfighter at medium and low altitude, but at 25-30,000ft the R-2800 engine in the P-47 maintained power even better than the Packard Merlin and the DB-605 engine in the Bf-109G. The P-47 was made to rule at 30,000ft. The P-47 shootdown almost the same number of fighters as the P-51, and the highest scoring USAAF groups in the ETO were P-47 units. Yes, the P-51 was shooting down more German fighters from mid-1944 on but that was because the P-51 was given the high-altitude job where they would encounter more enemy fighters while the P-47 was given most of the low altitude work like CAS, and interdiction missions. This is not to take away any credit from the P-51 but in most histories the Mustang gets the glory, and the Thunderbolt is relegated to being a ground support aircraft. The Mustang was clearly given the right name. She was fast and graceful and could dance with the best of them. The Thunderbolt had the right name as well. She was a warhorse that could absorb more punishment and bring her pilot home while raining thunder on the enemy. The P-38 Lightning is another also run for more complicated reasons, but she has her admirers for many reasons. And in 4th place the P-40 Warhawk held the line from 1940-43. Strangely it's the Mustang and the Flying Tigers Warhawk that are remembered best.

Hence my post about Big Week, P-47 provided 80% of the escort fighters during that effort. I doubt very many people realize that. P-38 is an interesting plane, read an interview with a high scoring German ace who said that provided it was being flown by a pilot who knew how to handle it he thought the P-38 was the toughest Allied fighter he faced. It also presented the Japanese with a difficult tactical problem in that it flew higher and faster than both the Zero and the Oscar. General Kenney liked it best because of the two engines. His pilots flew a lot of missions over water and he appreciated what two engines provided in that sense. General Chennault did not like for the same reason. He was at the ass end of a long logistics chain in a lower priority theater. To him two engines just meant twice the engine maintenance. The P-40 deserves much more credit that it gets. Only the P-51 and P-47 were produced in greater numbers (for US fighters), it was used extensively in the MTO, PTO, and CBI theaters well into 1944 and it was used by more Allied air forces than any other fighter. It was not a thoroughbred by it was definitely a work horse and sometimes that is what you need.

Cost to buy and operate the P-47 was not a factor - USA have had the money, material and fuel. They were after all buying and using the P-38, that offered no savings in any category. P-47 was made in more than 15000 copies. The P-47 was turned into a ground attack aircraft after the fact, and fact being that Merlin Mustang was rangier, a bit faster and a better climber. A combination of the P-51 getting the drop tanks earlier, and the better mileage on internal fuel made it the premier LR fighter of the war. Two very common 75 gal drop tanks make the P-51 going much further than if two 75 gal drop tanks are carried by the P-47 or the P-38. Some mix-up happened there. As-is, it could not do the job. With a bit of foresight, it might've come close. People at USAAF will need to request that P-47 is outfitted with wing racks from day one (ie. already in 1942, so it is debugged and ready for 1943), and there should be the drive to increase the internal fuel tankage. In OTL, the 1st increase was achieved by removing the stuff between the main tank and the top of fuselage so the main tank can get bigger, now with 270 instead of 205 US gals. That change upped the internal fuel tankage to 370 gals, that, together with 2x 150 gal drop tanks, enabled the theoretical 600 mile combat radius under the demanding ETO rules (that included cruising at more than 300 mph TAS at 25000 ft). There is also the need for the actual drop tanks to be available in the UK, with clear contracts with the suppliers. The know 'bubbletop' P-47Ds were the 1st with the main tank being at 270 gals. If there was the earlier go with adding some fuel tanks in the wings - even if it is not a 'surgery' as what was done with the P-47N, but perhaps 2x 50 gals? - together with a drop tank under the fuselage, the radius would've been increased even more, equaling the best P-51D values.

The P 47 was an incredible fighter and despite it's sheer size was fairly good in a dogfight. The P-51 Mustang was until the Rolls Royce Merlin was used a low level fighter at best. The V-1710 engine was fine but needed the two stage supercharger and the like which did happen it just took time. Drop Tanks and education on how to achieve maximum range needed to happen in order to make the Mustand what it became. The P-51 B was the start of the Merlin engines and gave it excellent high altitude performance. The P-47 on the other hand did not need an engine swap to be effective. Instead doctrine and production numbers made the difference. The most important use of the daylight bomber offensive, was the decimation of the Luftwaffe and this occurred in measurable ways. The P-38 was suffering from poor pilot training and tactics. THe presence of 3 high performance fighters whose abilities compliment each other is very desirable.
items.original_question: What if No P51 Bomber Escort? From Jan 1944 the Merlin engined P51 could escort the Bombers all the way to Berlin and beyond and destroyed the Luftwaffe in doing so. However, I would argue the P47 could have done the same job but The P47 did not get the escort gig because it was twice the cost and it was a superb ground attack aircraft. twice the cost in construction and fuel consumption. Really the game changer was the drop tank although the P51 was the best host for them by far I think of the P51 as the sleek technical European sports car sipping fuel, with the P47 as a brute, "cubes is everything", American muscle car guzzling gas like there was no tomorrow. The POD would be North American builds P40s instead of creating the new P51 design for the British. items.model_answer:
If there had been no P-51 Mustang long-range escort for Allied bombers over Europe, the daylight bombing campaign against Germany would probably have been much less effective and far more costly, but it likely would not have changed the ultimate outcome of the war.

The key point is that the P-51 did not merely protect bombers; it helped destroy the Luftwaffe. Before long-range escorts were available, deep raids such as Schweinfurt in 1943 suffered unsustainable losses. B-17s and B-24s could defend themselves to a point, but unescorted formations deep over Germany were vulnerable to coordinated fighter attacks. Without the P-51’s range, speed, and high-altitude performance, the U.S. Eighth Air Force would have faced a choice: keep sending bombers deep into Germany and lose crews at crippling rates, or restrict daylight raids to targets within range of shorter-legged fighters like the Spitfire, P-47, or P-38.

That would have had several major effects. Deep daylight bombing of German aircraft factories, oil plants, transportation hubs, and industrial centers would have been delayed or reduced. The Luftwaffe would have suffered fewer losses in early 1944, especially among experienced fighter pilots. “Big Week” in February 1944, which helped break German fighter strength before D-Day, would have been far less decisive. German air defenses would have remained stronger for longer.

The Normandy invasion could still have happened, because Allied tactical air power over France did not depend solely on the P-51; shorter-range fighters could operate from Britain and later from forward airfields in France. But the invasion would likely have been riskier and more costly. A less-damaged Luftwaffe might have mounted more attacks against shipping, beachheads, and supply lines, though it still would have faced overwhelming Allied numbers, radar control, fuel shortages, and tactical air forces.

The air war would probably have shifted more heavily toward RAF night bombing, medium bombers, tactical strikes, and attacks on targets closer to Allied bases. The Allies might also have accelerated development or deployment of longer-range versions of the P-47 or P-38, but those aircraft did not combine range, efficiency, and performance over Germany as well as the P-51 did in 1944.

So the most likely result is not a German victory, but a longer and bloodier war in Europe. Germany was already being crushed by the Soviet Union in the east, blockaded at sea, outproduced by the Allies, and increasingly short of fuel. But without P-51 escorts, Allied strategic bombing would have been less successful, German fighter forces would have survived longer, D-Day might have been delayed or costlier, and the collapse of Nazi Germany could plausibly have been pushed back by months, perhaps into later 1945.

items.original_question: How would the population of the Falklands have been treated if Argentina had won in 1982? Let’s suppose that HMS Hermes and HMS Invincible had been sunk, forcing the British to make peace and accept the loss of the Falklands. Let’s also suppose that this victory gave the Argentine junta a reprieve of 2-3 additional years, but that it still eventually collapsed so that Argentina followed a political path similar as IOTL. What would the Falklands population have faced? It's almost certain that Buenos Aires would have sent thousands of Argentine settlers to Puerto Argentino/Port Stanley in order to, at least, make the Anglo population a numerical minority and to extinguish any secessionist aspirations. But would this Anglo population have been allowed to remain and then obtain full Argentine citizenship, perhaps even some degree of cultural autonomy, or would it have faced a complete ethnic cleansing in order to permanently erase the Anglo identity of the Falklands? There are fewer than 2,000 people, so if Argentina decided to do it, it wouldn’t have any problem doing so.
items.model_answer:
If Argentina had won the 1982 Falklands War, the islanders would probably not have been massacred or immediately expelled en masse, but they would very likely have been placed under Argentine military administration and pressured over time to accept Argentine sovereignty, law, language, and citizenship.

During the actual occupation, Argentina removed the British governor and garrison, imposed military rule, censored communications, restricted movement, renamed places in Spanish, and treated the islands as the “Malvinas.” The civilian population was generally handled with some restraint, partly because Argentina wanted international legitimacy, but the occupation was still coercive and the islanders had no political say. Given the Argentine junta’s wider record of repression, any open pro-British resistance would likely have been tightly controlled or punished.

In the longer term, Argentina would probably have tried to integrate the islands into Argentina: replacing British institutions, introducing Spanish-language administration and schooling, encouraging or requiring Argentine citizenship, and possibly settling Argentines there. Islanders might have been allowed to remain if they accepted Argentine rule, but many would likely have emigrated to Britain or elsewhere rather than live under a government they overwhelmingly rejected.

So the most plausible answer is: they would have been treated as residents of Argentine territory, not as a people with a right to self-determination. They might have been given formal protections and some guarantees for property and local customs, especially under international pressure, but their British political identity and institutions would likely have been dismantled. The result would probably have been coercive assimilation, surveillance, and substantial emigration rather than immediate mass deportation or extermination.

items.original_question: If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank? If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank in the twentieth century? In other words, it takes all the modernization and technological upgrade steps it can to protect its sovereignty in the late 19th century world, but either is deterred or self-deters from annexing Chinese or Russian territory, or territory possibly in their sphere, like Korea, or if attempting to do so, because such attempts were rather fashionable among *many* (but not all) modern industrial states, they fail, would the same things constraining Japanese aggression or success *also* doom Japan's ability to increase its economic productive capacity and standard of living over most of the decades of the 20th century? Or not? Could Japan do as well, or better, in absolute GDP growth, per capital GDP growth, PPP measured GDP growth, and GDP global rank, by, for instance, 1920, 1940, or 1960 or 1980, without having any expansionary success beyond consolidating control over the Ryukyu Kingdom and diplomatically clarifying its ownership of the Kurile and Bonin Islands and never having won a territory in a foreign war? I think I can illustrate it best using this graphic. This helpfully long term chart of real GDP growth of Japan, Britain and the US shows Japan's growth curve in * red *. Would Japan's line be higher, lower, or about the same, without Japan's early successful wars with China and Russia, annexation of Korea, WWI absorption of Micronesia, 1930s exploitation of Manchuria and then occupied China, followed by the ultimately futile and highly destructive Pacific War, and the Cold War alliance arrangement the US and Japan set up to deal with the Soviet Union and avoid the recurrence of mutual war? Maybe the red line in the alternate history of an alternate Japan would have lower at some points and higher at others, but if so, please specify roughly when, and where do you think things would be stabilizing by the 1960 through present-day era. It may be tempting to call a Meiji (and beyond) Japan, with this type of foreign policy record that lacks success at military-naval territorial expansion as a Japan "pulling a Thailand" or analogous to a Thailand. But I would urge caution in making such an analogy. Sure, Thailand protected its sovereignty uniquely within its Southeast Asian neighborhood, while not being able to clash with colonial powers head on. But that's as far as the analogy would apply. Thailand's technological advancement and industrialization was for long, until the 1960s, pretty weak, and a Japan on Thailand's *economic* trajectory would be *categorically* poorer and less technologically, industrially, scientifically, and financially sophisticated than OTL's Japan. Thailand also only *began* experiments with constitutional government about fifty years later than Japan, even though Japan in the mid-20th century had some spectacular democratic and especially liberal failures and has some democratic deficits to this day. But their internal political cultures and societies are quite different.
items.model_answer:
Yes, it plausibly could have grown to something like G7 rank, especially if “no expansion” means a modernizing Meiji Japan that remains politically stable, trades freely, and avoids the costs of empire and major war. It might have grown more slowly at first, but lack of colonies would not by itself prevent Japan from becoming a major industrial economy.

Japan’s later rise to G7 status was not fundamentally based on keeping Taiwan, Korea, Manchuria, or Chinese concessions. In fact, Japan became a G7-level economy after 1945, after losing its empire completely and after suffering enormous wartime destruction. Its strongest advantages were domestic: high literacy, effective state institutions, a large and disciplined labor force, strong savings, industrial policy, technology importation, and an export-oriented manufacturing base. Those advantages existed largely in the home islands.

Imperial expansion did help Meiji and prewar Japan in some ways. The indemnity from Qing China after 1895 helped finance the gold standard and military-industrial expansion. Korea and Taiwan provided food, markets, land, and strategic depth. Manchuria later mattered for coal, iron, railways, and military planning. But these were accelerants, not the core engine of Japanese development. Japan’s home population was large enough, and its human-capital base strong enough, to support great-power industrialization even without colonies. Resource poverty was a constraint, but not a fatal one: postwar Japan proved that a resource-poor island state could import raw materials and export high-value manufactured goods.

A non-expansionist Japan might even have had advantages. It would have avoided the huge fiscal burden of militarism, the international isolation caused by aggression in China, and the catastrophic destruction of the Pacific War. More capital and administrative talent could have gone into civilian industry, infrastructure, education, finance, shipping, and consumer manufacturing. If it remained integrated into world trade, it could have resembled a larger version of Britain, the Netherlands, or later South Korea: resource-poor but commercially and industrially sophisticated.

The harder version is if Japan “fails to expand” because it loses badly to China or Russia. A limited defeat would probably delay development and damage prestige, but not necessarily prevent eventual great-power economic status. A catastrophic defeat, occupation, crippling indemnities, or domestic collapse could have derailed the Meiji project. So the answer depends on the severity of failure. Losing the Russo-Japanese War narrowly, for example, would be painful but probably survivable. Being broken financially or politically by repeated failed wars would be much more serious.

So the careful answer is: yes, a Meiji Japan that modernized but did not build an empire could very plausibly have reached G7-level wealth and industrial power, perhaps later but also perhaps more peacefully and sustainably. The empire helped Japan’s rise in some respects, but it was not necessary for Japan to become a first-rank industrial economy. Its decisive assets were not colonies; they were institutions, education, industrial capacity, social mobilization, and access to global trade.

items.question: What If the attack on Pearl Harbor completely failed?
human_answers: Define failed - do you just mean the fighter planes are sitting armed in their revetments, the AA guns (both fleet and land based) are manned, the ships are at condition ZED, the radar stations are manned, and the Air Information Center has been set up (probably not fully manned but at least some minimal level of staffing). Damage to the Pacific Fleet is a lot less because the ships are buttoned up and a lot less planes are destroyed on the ground because they are either in the air or in protected revetments or at least dispersed. Losses to fighter pilots are higher because of more guys getting shot down but they also take their measure of the Japanese. That constitutes failure for the Japanese, particularly given the losses in trained air crews. What it means going forward I'm not sure but it sure is an ugly start. Or, do you mean by failure the US does all of the above but also has knowledge a Japanese carrier task force is going to attack Oahu during the morning of 7 December from a position between 200-250 miles north of Oahu. This means every available attack aircraft on Oahu is bombed up and ready to go (6 B-17s, 21 B-18s, 5 A-20s, 23 SBDs, 8 SB2Us) and Kimmel is able to position Enterprise and Lexington 150 miles to the southwest of where the KB is expected to be operating as well as sending the small number of submarines he has in port to the north as well. By the way, Kimmel also has a moment of profound insight and realizes the safest place for his fat slow battleships is sitting in port at Condition ZED. Scenario Two is a lot less realistic but if you squint hard enough you can probably come up with some PODs that still make it work. Scenario One the attacking aircraft get butchered but the KB likely gets away clean. Scenario Two the attacking aircraft get butchered and Nagumo loses at least two carrier maybe as many as four depending on the breaks.

items.model_answer:
If the attack on Pearl Harbor completely failed but Japan still attempted it, the United States would almost certainly still have entered World War II. The political effect of a Japanese surprise attack on American territory would have been enormous even if the bombs missed, the ships survived, or the attackers were shot down. Congress would likely still have declared war on Japan, and Germany probably still would have declared war on the United States shortly afterward, as it did historically.

The biggest difference would be military, not political. With the U.S. Pacific Fleet intact, Japan’s early-war position would have been much more dangerous. Japan’s strategy depended on quickly crippling American naval power long enough to seize Southeast Asia, the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore, the Dutch East Indies, and defensive island positions. If Pearl Harbor failed, the United States would have had more battleships, aircraft, repair capacity, and morale available immediately.

That said, an intact Pacific Fleet would not automatically have stopped Japan in December 1941. The U.S. Navy was still not fully prepared for a trans-Pacific offensive, and many of its battleships were older, slower, and vulnerable to carrier air power. Japan still had a highly trained carrier force and strong momentum across Asia. The Philippines would probably still have been in grave danger because Japanese air and naval forces were already positioned nearby, and American forces there were isolated. Singapore and the Dutch East Indies might still have fallen.

But the Japanese timetable would likely have been disrupted. The U.S. could have mounted stronger raids, reinforced key bases sooner, and forced Japan to divert ships and aircraft from its southern offensives. If the failed attack also meant Japan lost many aircraft, pilots, or even carriers, the consequences would have been severe. Japan’s elite naval air arm was hard to replace. Heavy Japanese losses at Pearl Harbor would have weakened Japan before later battles such as Coral Sea and Midway, possibly causing Japan to lose the strategic initiative much earlier.

The Pacific War would probably have been shorter. The United States would have begun the war with more naval strength, Japan would have gained less breathing room, and American industrial superiority would have become overwhelming even faster. Some campaigns might have been avoided or shortened, especially if Japan’s carrier fleet had been badly damaged during the failed attack.

However, Japan probably would not have surrendered immediately. Its leaders were committed to seizing the resource-rich territories of Southeast Asia, especially oil from the Dutch East Indies. Even with Pearl Harbor a failure, Japan would likely have continued fighting, hoping to create a defensive perimeter and force a negotiated peace.

So the most likely outcome is: the United States still enters the war, Japan still makes major gains in the first months, but its strategic position is much worse. The U.S. counteroffensive begins earlier and with greater strength, Japan loses the initiative sooner, and the Pacific War likely ends earlier than it did historically—especially if the failed attack cost Japan many of its best pilots or carriers.
