If the Holy Roman Empire had never existed, Europe would probably have become less “imperial” and less constitutionally fragmented in the center, but not necessarily more peaceful or more unified. The biggest changes would have been in Germany, northern Italy, the papacy, and the long-term balance between France, Austria, and the rest of Europe.

The first point is that something would still have filled the space. Even without the Holy Roman Empire, the lands that became Germany, Burgundy, Austria, Bohemia, and northern Italy would not have been empty of political structure. The Carolingian world would still have broken into regional kingdoms and duchies. Local nobles, bishops, cities, and dynasties would still have competed for power. So the likely alternative is not “no central Europe,” but a different kind of central Europe.

The most likely major difference is that Germany might have developed into a more ordinary kingdom. Historically, German kings who became emperors spent enormous effort trying to control Italy, manage relations with the pope, and defend the idea of universal Christian empire. That weakened royal authority north of the Alps. Emperors often had to bargain with princes, bishops, and cities, granting privileges in exchange for support. Over centuries this helped produce the famously fragmented German political landscape: duchies, bishoprics, free cities, knightly territories, and semi-independent principalities.

Without the imperial title and the duty to intervene in Italy, an East Frankish or German monarchy might have focused more on consolidating power inside Germany itself. It might have become more like France or England: still feudal, still contested, but eventually more centralized. If that happened, Europe might have seen a unified German kingdom centuries before the nineteenth century. Such a state would have been a major rival to France and Poland-Lithuania and might have prevented France from expanding toward the Rhine.

But the opposite is also possible. The Holy Roman Empire, weak though it often was, provided a legal and symbolic framework that held many central European territories together. Without it, Bavaria, Saxony, Swabia, Austria, Bohemia, Burgundy, and the Rhineland might have drifted into separate kingdoms or fallen under French, Danish, Polish, Hungarian, or papal influence. So the central question is whether the absence of the Empire would have allowed German monarchy to centralize, or whether it would have removed the only institution holding the region together. On balance, a somewhat more centralized German kingdom is plausible, but not guaranteed.

Italy would also have changed greatly. The medieval emperors repeatedly claimed authority over northern and central Italy. Their involvement helped shape the conflict between imperial and papal factions, later remembered as Ghibellines and Guelphs. Without the Empire, northern Italy’s city-states—Milan, Venice, Florence, Genoa, Pisa, and others—would still likely have become wealthy and competitive, because that was driven by trade, banking, urbanization, and geography. But their politics would have been less organized around loyalty or opposition to the emperor. The papacy, France, the Normans of southern Italy, Byzantium, and later Spain might have intervened earlier or more directly.

The papacy would have been one of the biggest winners and losers at the same time. It would not have faced the same imperial rival in Rome and northern Italy, so the Investiture Controversy—the great medieval struggle between pope and emperor over appointing bishops—would either not occur in the same way or would be much less central. But the pope also relied on emperors, at least in theory, as protectors and enforcers. Without a western emperor, the papacy would have had to depend more on France, the Normans, local Italian powers, or its own military resources. That could have made the pope more independent in doctrine but more vulnerable politically.

France would probably have gained room to expand. Historically, the Empire formed a loose but real barrier along France’s eastern frontier. Burgundy, Lorraine, Alsace, the Low Countries, and parts of northern Italy were often contested zones between French kings and imperial authority. Without the Empire, French expansion eastward might have happened earlier, unless a strong German kingdom emerged in its place. A Europe without the Holy Roman Empire could therefore have become either more French-dominated or more sharply divided between France and a consolidated Germany.

The Habsburgs would likely have been less powerful. Their rise was deeply connected to the imperial crown, Austrian lands, dynastic marriages, and the prestige of being emperors. They might still have become important rulers in Austria and Central Europe, especially because of the Ottoman threat, but without the imperial office they would have lacked a major source of legitimacy and influence. The later “Habsburg encirclement” of France—Spain, Austria, the Low Countries, and imperial politics—would probably have been weaker or differently shaped.

The Protestant Reformation would have looked very different. In real history, the fragmented structure of the Holy Roman Empire allowed Lutheranism and other Protestant movements to survive. Princes could protect reformers; imperial law was slow and negotiated; Charles V could not simply impose religious uniformity. Without the Empire, if Germany had become a centralized monarchy, the Reformation might have either been suppressed more effectively or adopted more uniformly by the crown. There might have been no Peace of Augsburg, no Thirty Years’ War in its familiar form, and no Westphalian settlement as we know it. Religious conflict would still have occurred, but its geography and political logic would have changed.

The modern map of Europe would probably be less filled with small German-speaking states. The Holy Roman Empire preserved a tradition of local autonomy that delayed German unification until the nineteenth century. Without it, Germany might have unified earlier, or its regions might have been absorbed into neighboring powers. Switzerland and the Netherlands might also have developed differently, since both emerged partly from the imperial borderlands. They could still have become independent because of geography, commerce, and local resistance, but not in the same way.

So the short answer is: Europe would probably have had a less fragmented central region, a different relationship between pope and secular rulers, less Habsburg dominance, and a very different Reformation. The absence of the Holy Roman Empire would not automatically create a peaceful or rationally organized Europe. It would more likely replace the Empire’s loose, legalistic, multi-princely order with sharper competition among dynastic kingdoms—especially France, a possible German kingdom, Poland-Hungary, the papacy, and later Spain. The Europe that emerged would probably be more centralized in some areas, but also more prone to direct great-power rivalry in the heart of the continent.

items.question: What If the Roman Empire never fell and lived to the year 2020?
human_answers: Note: Parts of this answer will be copied from this one . However, this is a different scenario than that one. Note: I do not claim that this answer is realistic, nor that everything would happen the way I say it would. This is, of course, impossible to predict. Anyway, the point of divergence here is 378 AD, with the battle of Adrianople. Battle of Adrianople You see, Rome could have won this battle quite decisively. They had numerical parity, if not superiority, to the Gothic forces. They had great heavy cavalry. Valens had a large amount of additional reinforcements marching in from the west as well. They likely would have arrived within the next few days. Had the two forces linked up, they would have likely beaten the Goths. Why did I have the Romans win at Adrianople? The Roman defeat at Adrianople and the resulting Gothic invasions devastated the Balkans, to the point where they were somewhat depopulated. This is avoided in this timeline. This also avoids the Goths rising up in revolt within the Empire later on. With the Balkans in a much better position, the Romans are able to largely keep the Huns at bay, forcing them west. The Huns were defeated in battle by the Western Romans and their allies in 451 AD, so I could see the Eastern Romans doing the same here. Next, Theodosius the Great recognizes Eunegius as Emperor in 394, rather than killing and deposing him. This avoids the problem of Honorius becoming Emperor and also doesn’t kill over a third of the western army. Eunegius agrees to let Flavius Stilicho become Magister Militum of the west in exchange for being recognized as Emperor. Stilicho would survive longer in this timeline due to Honorius not rising to power, allowing him to better contain the barbarians invading the Empire. He would represent a bridge between the barbarians living within the Empire, allowing them to be more easily assimalated and showing that the two could coexist. Flavius Aetius would also survive longer, giving Rome a strong military leader to hold the Empire together. Next, Majorian is not betrayed in 460 AD, and his fleet is not destroyed. This allows him to retake North Africa, giving Western Rome fresh sources of manpower, taxes, food, and resources. Majorian finds out about Ricimier’s plots and has him executed. His replacement would be loyal and competent. Majorian would stabalize Italy and North Africa, and implement his reforms to the imperial administration. This would make the Empire more stable. Majorian would implement laws to whip the decedant and lazy upper class back into shape, reinvigorate pride in the Roman state, and reintroduce native Italians into the army. Majorian’s successor, likely Julius Nepos, would continue his reforms, enforcing and expanding upon them. Roman Empire in 460 AD. In this timeline, Carthage is under Roman rule as well. Under Majorian’s successors, Gaul and most of Hispania would still be lost, but the Empire would survive. Julius Nepos comes to power in the mid-late 470s, continuing the reforms of Majorian and strengthening the Empire. He would fortify the borders and choose a competent successor, who would continue the reforms of Majorian and Nepos. Majorian, Nepos, and their successors would recognize that the Empire could not rely on slavery, and that it needed to bolster its population in order to survive. Therefore, they would implement more efficient farming practices and the use of technology such as water wheels and mills in order to make the production of flour more efficient. They would also update architectural codes and improve living standards in order to increase stability and keep more people alive and healthy. They would massively revamp sanitation systems to reduce the risk of disease and improve healthcare for pregnant mothers in order to bolster the population further. They would also choose a competent successor, who would likely free most remaining slaves to increase the conscriptable, taxable population. Barbagel water mill complex During this time monuments and architecture would be restored. Propaganda would hearken back to the old days and the resilience of the Roman people, reinvigorating pride in the Empire. Leo I in the East would die a few years later than in our timeline, helping out the West. The West largely goes on as a regional power until Justinian comes along. He would officially reunify the East and West, although there would still be two emperors. Without Italy being devastated by the Gothic wars, its population thrives, and the Roman spirit is reignited in the East as well. Justinian implements the reforms of the West all across the Empire, and Rome reaches a new technological golden age. Hispania and southern Gaul are retaken for the Empire, and the whole of North Africa up to the Atlantic is under Roman control as well. The Justinian Plague is still devastating, but with the improved sanitation and without the devastation of the Gothic wars, Rome is still going strong. The Plague would drive demand for labor up as the population declines, allowing the middle class to grow and seeing the further implementation of technology into the everyday lives of Romans. Women would be allowed to hold more jobs and to work in factories, and would slowly gain more power and rights in society from there. In this timeline, with the Balkans secured and giving Rome much greater manpower than it had in our world, Germanus would be able to destroy the Persians at Antioch, making Persia rethink Rome’s weakness. The Persians would sue for peace, restoring the “Eternal Peace” they had signed with Rome not long before. They would have to make several concessions, allowing Rome to fortify the border. In this timeline, Germanus would not have to fight the Ostrogoths in Italy, and would thus not fall ill. He would become Emperor after Justinian, and after him would be Justin Germanus, who would be another competent ruler. These two would further expand on the reforms of their predecessors, upholding them and giving them time to stick. IRL Rome under Justinian With large sources of manpower from North Africa, the Balkans, and Italy, Rome is not percieved as weak by Persia. In this timeline, Phokas would not rise to power and severely weaken the Empire, as Justin Germanus would not order him to camp north of the Danube for the winter. Maurice would still rise to power after Justin, and would be a fairly competent Emperor as he was in our timeline. After Maurice, Heraclius would not want to see the Empire split between Maurice’s sons and would rise to power. Heraclius was also fairly competent. Without Phokas, and with Persia having been stopped by Germanus decades earlier, the Persians wouldn’t attack the Romans. When the Arabs explode out of the Arabian peninsula, Rome would abandon Gaul and lose Hispania and parts of North Africa. However, they would still hold Carthage, Egypt, and the Levant. They’d also lose bits of the northern Balkans to the Slavs and Avars. However, they’d still hold much of the Balkans. Persia, due to not being exhausted by fighting Rome, would be in a stronger position, and would survive the Arab invasions, though with a loss of territory. In the same way Rome was Europe’s shield during the middle ages, Persia would be Rome’s shield, taking blow after blow and lessening the effects of these invasions on the Roman Empire. The balance of power within the Empire would still shift east, with Constantinople being the capital. The Empire would closely resemble the Eastern Roman/Byzantine Empire of our timeline, but with more Latin influence. During this time, northern Europe still largely develops as it did in our timeline, with the Kingdom of the Franks still emerging and splitting. Hispania is still slowly reconquered by the Europeans, but this time the Romans would participate. Eventually they’d end up with what would be Aragon in our timeline. Much of the middle ages in Europe would be Roman tributary states paying the Romans in exchange for protection. The Pope, chafing under Roman rule, would flee and set up a new branch of Christianity, namely Catholicism. The Romans are able to hold back the Turks as well, keeping them out of the Empire. They win at Manzikert. Rome has entered a period of slow but steady decline, as it did in our timeline. It’s still surviving and prospering, but beginning to rot from the inside. The Great Schism never happens, and neither do the Crusades. Rome is one of the most technologically advanced nations on the planet, being near a state of industrialization. They would have rudimentary air conditioning, sanitation, advanded plumbing and running water, all in every apartment building. They would have hospitals and universities. Their military would be formidable. Factory-like complexes would be common, using water power to produce flour and goods. Slavery would come to be regarded as the mark of a less advanced civilization. Basil II would reinvigorate the Empire, bringing back Roman pride and defeating the Bulgars. He would reform the Empire, and leave it in a much stronger position than it was before his reign. In this timeline, he would choose a competent successor, similarly to Germanus and Justinian. Europe and the Middle East in 1025 AD In 1190, the Romans beat the Bulgarians at the battle of Trinova. This leads to Isaac II not being deposed and the Roman army not being demoralized like in our timeline. Alexios III does not rise to power, and the 4th Crusade never happens, as Alexios IV never needs to contact the crusaders to depose Alexios III. The Romans would have good relations with Hungary to the north. In the 1200s, the Mongol invasions would happen. Whatever Persion/Turkish state that would exists east of Rome would take the brunt of the blow, but Rome would still be hit fairly hard. They wouldn’t be devastated, but they wouldn’t be able to brush it off either. The Black Death would also be devastating, but experience with plagues and sanitation would somewhat mitigate the effects. Like the Justinian Plague before, the Black Death would again grow the middle class, increasing their power within society. The Romans would recover. Mongol expansion The world in 1250 The Turks would still carve out an Empire like they did in our timeline, leading to several wars with the Romans. They would very nearly succeed in taking Constantinople in 1453, but Rome would be able to drive them back. Roman propaganda would once again hearken back to the determination of the Roman people and the strength and culture of classical Rome. There would be a resurgance in classical ideas, innovation, and technology and philosophy, as well as the arts. This would spread throughout Europe, sparking the Renaissance. Rome would reconquer what territory it lost to the Turks, and even expand in some places. Constantine XI and his successor would implement broad reforms to protect from invasions and to make it so that the internal rot that had weakened Rome would not happen again. The 100 Years War ends the way it did in our timeline, and Poland-Lithuania still emerges, as does something like the Tutonic Order. In this timeline, they would fight in the Reconquista before eventually getting evicted and moving up to the Baltic region to stamp out paganism there. Europe in 1450 Rome for centuries would dominate East-West trade, leading the Iberian kingdoms impoverished. They would search for new trade routes, and would travel around Africa and eventually find the Americas. Now the race is on to colonize the New World. In the early 16th century, Rome would conquer down to the Horn of Africa and set up client kingdoms. This would give them access to the lucrative Indian Ocean trade routes. Rome at this point would be incredibly advanced, rich, and prosperous. Huge factory complexes and industrial scale agricultural and mining operations would exist. Roman towns and cities would be among the cleanest in the world. By now almost every building would have a flush toilet and sink. Plumbing would be common in towns as well as cities. Gunpowder weapons would be appearing. Analog computers would be used. The printing press would allow ideas to spread rapidly, spreading technology. The world in 1550 Protestantism would be spreading throughout the northern lands of Europe, and in the early 1610s Germany would be ripped apart by religous war. The Hapsburgs would control Austria, Germany, and Spain, and in a bid to exploit the Hapsburg’s weakness, the French, Romans, and Russians would fight them. The Romans and Russians in particular would support the Protestants against the Catholics, who were enemies of Roman Orthodoxy. The war would end with Germany and Spain crippled, the former of which would be reduced to a messy confederation of states. The Romans would annex Hungary. Brandenburg, Bavaria, and Prussia would come to dominate Germany. Meanwhile, for the past few centuries England, Spain, Portugal, Rome, France, and Holland have been setting up colonies in the Americas. The Romans would not partake in the Atlantic Slave Trade, viewing slavery as the mark of a less advanced civilization. The Portugese would colonize Brazil. The French and British colonies would grow fast in the Americas. Meanwhile, Brandenburg would become a dominant power in Germany alongside Bavaria and Prussia. The three would become close allies, hoping to unite Germany. They would attempt to annex Transnistria, leading to the Seven Years War. The world at the start of the Seven Years War The British side of the war would be: Prussia Brandenburg Bavaria Britain Portugal Rome Russia The French side of the war would be: Austria France Spain Persia Poland Holland The war would be even larger here than in our timeline. Russia would move into Poland-Lithuania, gaining territory until the Polish stop them with a defensive trench line. The Romans would move against the Persians/Turks, pushing them back and taking Armenia. They would advance into Arabia. The British and French would fight in the Americas, and the Romans would advance against the Spanish in both the New World and Old World. The British would seize Spanish islands in the Carribean. The armies of Prussia, Bavaria, and Brandenburg initially push the Austrians back, but get bogged down. After the first winter in Europe, spring offensives begin. However, inspired by Poland, the other powers have built trench lines and fortresses, bogging down any advance. The British and French would fight in India. The Dutch would fight the British, hoping to protect their interests in India. After years of brutal war, Poland is carved up by Prussia and Russia. The Americas largely shake out the way they did in our timeline. Austria is weakened. Rome annexes Persia and Arabia entirely. The Romans would industrialize fairly easily, soon after the British. They had the technology, and the Romans were historically nothing if not adaptable, and during the Medieval era were able to change their institutions to fit the changing world around them. The American colonies still become independent following the Great War. Following a trade dispute in the Indian Ocean due to British control of India, relations between Rome and Britain sour. Rome starts to ally with France and supports the Americans in response. They would also support the native tribes, hoping to stop America from threatening Roman interests in the Americas. The Romans would sell Corsica to France just in time for Napoleon to be born, and the Napoleonic wars still happen. Rome allies with France due to soured relations with Britain. When France invades Russia, however, the Romans turn on Napoleon and deal his empire the death blow. However, the other European powers are mad at the Romans, and force territorial concessions. The Romans lose land both at home and overseas, notably in Iberia and Africa. During their time as a Napoleonic ally, the Roman senate would gain much more power, and the Emperor’s power would be reduced. The Emperor would still be powerful, but they would have to share power with the Senate. The world after the Napoleonic Wars The Romans are embittered by this loss of land. Brandenburg and Prussia would rise in power immensely following this war, becoming the dominant forces in Germany. They would become the de-facto leader of the German Confederation, and would eventually unify Germany in the 1860s and 70s during and after the Franco-German war. During the 1850s, a dispute between ethnic Romans and Slavs in the Crimean Peninsula leads to the Crimean War. Russia and Rome would had been traditional allies for centuries by this point, but Russian expansionism would sour relations between the two. The British and French would intervene on Rome’s side, and the war would ultimately not accomplish anything. In the 1870s, France is devastated by the Franco-Prussian war. The Romans take the opportunity to invade and occupy France, a hugely controversial move. They also annex Spain and Portugal, and move deeper into North Africa. Without the French, the British take the Congo and French West Africa and Indochina. France, Spain, and Portugal are all very rebellious, and fight for independence for decades. However, the Romans are determined to hold on to them. The world in 1914 Then comes the 20th century, the graveyard of empires. While many would say that nationalism would rip the Empire apart, I disagree. In our timeline, even after the Roman Empire died in 1453, the people living in the lands it occupied considered themselves Roman up until well into the 19th century. With a much stronger Roman state and culture, Rome would not succumb to nationalism like so many other Empires would. In 1914, a rogue nationalist assasinates Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Everyone in Europe has been itching to beat each other up, and this is a conventient excuse. Austria blames the Romans and declares war. Russia joins Austria. Britain joins the Romans, and Germany joins Russia and Austria. The war is long and unthinkably bloody. Eventually, the United States would get involved. Russia would collapse into revolution and leave the war. Germany and Austria surrender. Austria is carved up. Britain gets Germany’s colonies. Germany is forced to pay heavy reparations. Russia becomes communist. Austria-Hungary is carved up, with the Romans gaining new lands. The world after World War I I fail to see why the Great Depression would not happen in this timeline, and Germany, already suffering after the war, is utterly devastated, like in our timeline. Hitler or someone like him still takes power and institutes the same policies, stirring German nationalists with anti-Semitic and anti-Slavic propaganda. Japan and Germany still ally. If the Roman Empire never fell and survived as a continuous state until 2020, it would almost certainly not look like the ancient empire of Augustus, Nero, or Constantine. It would have had to transform repeatedly—politically, religiously, militarily, economically, and culturally—much as China, Japan, or the Byzantine Empire changed over centuries while preserving a sense of institutional continuity.

By 2020, a surviving Roman Empire would probably be a vast modern federal or constitutional empire centered on the Mediterranean and Europe, not a world of togas, gladiators, and legions. It would likely have parliaments or provincial assemblies, a professional bureaucracy, modern courts based on Roman law, a powerful military, and either a symbolic emperor or an emperor with powers limited by constitutional institutions. Its identity would be “Roman” in the same way modern citizens can be “Chinese,” “Indian,” or “European”: not ethnically uniform, but tied to citizenship, law, language, history, and state institutions.

The biggest change would be that Europe would probably never develop in the same fragmented way. There might be no medieval Western Europe as we know it, no Holy Roman Empire, no France, Spain, England, or Germany in their familiar forms, and perhaps no European Union because a Roman imperial union would already exist. Local cultures would still survive—Gaulish, Iberian, Greek, Germanic, Egyptian, Syrian, North African, and others—but they would exist as provincial identities inside a larger Roman political order.

Christianity would probably remain central, since the late Roman Empire had already become Christian. But the relationship between church and state would be very different. The pope might never become an independent medieval political figure in the same way, because a strong emperor would likely keep the church more tightly tied to imperial authority. The split between Catholic and Orthodox Christianity might not happen, or it might take a different form. Islam’s rise would also be affected: if Rome retained North Africa, Egypt, Syria, and the eastern Mediterranean, the Arab conquests of the 600s might be slowed, contained, or redirected. That would drastically change the religious and political map of the Middle East and North Africa.

Languages would also be different. Latin might remain a major administrative or scholarly language, perhaps evolving into a standardized modern “Imperial Latin,” while Greek would remain extremely important in the eastern provinces. The Romance languages—Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Romanian—might not develop in the same way, or they might exist as regional dialects under a common imperial standard. English, German, and Slavic languages would still exist if those regions remained culturally distinct, but their political histories would be very different.

Colonial history would be transformed. Instead of Spain, Portugal, France, Britain, and the Netherlands competing overseas, a surviving Roman Empire might sponsor exploration and colonization as a single imperial project. The Americas could have become Roman colonial provinces, or later independent states with Roman legal, linguistic, and political traditions. There might be no British Empire, no United States in its familiar form, and no Spanish-speaking Latin America exactly as we know it. A “New Rome” across the Atlantic is plausible, but its culture would depend on whether the empire colonized aggressively, traded cautiously, or focused inward.

Technological development could go either way. A stable Roman Empire might create large unified markets, roads, universities, legal standards, and engineering traditions that encourage growth. On the other hand, Europe’s real-world scientific and industrial revolutions were partly fueled by competition among rival states. If one giant empire dominated Europe and the Mediterranean, innovation might be more centralized and possibly slower unless the empire encouraged universities, merchants, and technical experimentation. By 2020, however, any Roman state that had survived would almost certainly be industrialized and technologically modern; otherwise it would have been conquered or broken apart.

Politically, the empire would face the same pressures as every large multiethnic state: succession crises, regional separatism, religious conflict, economic inequality, border defense, and debates over citizenship. To survive to 2020, it would have needed to solve the problems that damaged the real Roman Empire: unstable leadership, military overreach, fiscal weakness, elite corruption, and difficulty integrating new peoples. The most realistic surviving Rome would therefore be highly adaptive—perhaps more like a Roman version of the European Union combined with a constitutional monarchy and a powerful federal army.

So the direct answer is: if the Roman Empire had never fallen and still existed in 2020, the modern world would be far less shaped by nation-states like France, Britain, Spain, Germany, and Italy, and far more shaped by one continuous Mediterranean-European imperial civilization. Law, language, religion, colonialism, and global power would all be radically different. But it would not be “ancient Rome still alive.” It would be a modern state claiming Roman continuity—Christian or post-Christian, bureaucratic, multilingual, technologically advanced, and probably federal—whose citizens might still proudly call themselves Romans.

items.question: What If the Roman Empire never fell? How would this change most of our history today?
human_answers: The problem with the previous answer is that it is ahistorical. The Roman Empire did not fall until 1453, when the Ottoman Turks conquered Constantinople. Emperor Constantine had moved the capitol to the Greek city of Byzantium because of its excellent geographic, strategic, and central location, calling it New Rome, although at that point the empire was then split between eastern and western halves until the west collapsed in the fifth century. Subsequently renamed Constantinople, it then became the center of the world and continued long after the city of Rome itself declined sharply as the locus of empire shifted. Attempts, sometimes successful, were made to reclaim parts of the west. Indeed the name of the city itself continued until the cataclysm of World War I. In addition, Justinian was the last Emperor to use Latin rather than Greek, which prevailed for another eight centuries, or far longer than Rome itself. There was never a “Byzantine Empire.” That was a far later German concoction in order to legitimate their own “Holy Roman Empire, which, as Voltaire once said, was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire, What actually existed, as I have suggested elsewhere, was not something “Byzantine,” but rather a Greco-Roman Empire that lasted for a millennium. This is still confused and not well known due to the ignorance and prejudice of northwestern Europeans towards the south. Thus, the Roman Empire did not fall or disappear the way you have been led to believe. In fact, if the empire began with Augustus, the Rome-based portion only lasted for a bit more than four centuries, while the Eastern Roman Empire continued for another thousand years, and all the people in the empire, including the Greeks, referred to and considered themselves Romans until the very end. The empire itself was polyglot as it always was, but the dominant language was Greek. Thus, while the “Middle Ages” or medieval period happened in the west, which was still backward, that was not the case in the east, in what in fact was the bulk of the empire, which continued a thriving, but heavily Christianized civilization. Thus, in the year 1000 Constantinople had a population of over a million people. The original Roman Empire was far better at practical things, particularly organization, administration, functional engineering, etc. than the quarrelsome Greeks, who otherwise brilliantly developed and dominated culture, art, science, philosophy, etc. Romans provided the critical stability, legal and social infrastructure that was previously lacking in an otherwise largely Greek world that had been established by Alexander and his successors. As a result, Roman law, justice and organization provided the framework which sustained an otherwise largely Greek cultural entity. The empire would not have fallen had it not been for the Fourth Crusade (1202–1204) which, instead of going to Jerusalem to fight Muslims attacked other Christians via Venetian ships and encouragement. The barbarian Knights/Crusaders literally destroyed the city of Constantinople, pillaging and worse, burning down much of the city while the Venetians, at least having some artistic sense, carted off a lot of treasures that you still see in St. Marks to this day. The crusaders took over what was left of the city setting up their own “empire” for a few decades until the Romans finally reclaimed it, but in a much-weakened state. Thus, by the time the Turks finally conquered the city in 1453 with new long-range cannons, there were only about 50,000 people left there. That is when the Roman Empire finally fell, in its Greco-Roman-Christian incarnation. Given true history then, if the empire hadn’t fallen it is quite possible that Greek would still be the common language, you might be speaking it, and the European world would be very different. The “old” nations of Europe after all, have only existed for around five centuries. They really ascended after the fall of the City and the “renaissance” that followed, (another retroactively coined term), instilled to a considerable extent by Greek refugee scholars who fled to the Italian city-states, which welcomed then as teachers, given their thirst for knowledge and ancient manuscripts. Many other things would be different, starting with religion. In the empire the church was subordinate to the Emperor, and less powerful than in the west, where given the power vacuum, the Bishop of Rome, or Pope, was able to claim supremacy. Consequently, if the empire had continued the church would not have had so much power, and it is likely there would never have been a Protestant Reformation. Regions would have had their own Patriarchs. There is no way to know how geography would have taken shape, given uncertainty as to how far the empire might have reached, or how competent it would have been, but at its maximum it could have stretched over all of Europe. Alternatively, it could have been smaller, as it continued to fend of endless barbarian invasions from the east, allowing other powers to emerge in the west anyway, but possibly without the virulent nationalism that eventually developed and led to catastrophic wars and mass murder in the last century. Much would depend on whether the empire could regain Italy, which was essential to the emergence of modern Europe. (In 1500 Italy was richer than all of western Europe combined and more culturally advanced). Since it was then divided into competing city-states in the fashion of ancient Greece, that might have transpired if the empire was relatively free from barbarian invasions. Slavs, at least in the south were already being absorbed before the fall of the empire and thus would likely still be integrated. Unknowns are how the Russians, or more importantly the Germans might have emerged. But generally, the empire had always done a great job of absorbing and integrating other peoples, until the rise of Islam. If the empire had remained strong it is unlikely that the Arabs would have conquered what was then European Christian north Africa and Egypt, or even much of what is now called the “middle east,” which would have remained Christian and Roman, linked to the west via Constantinople. The empire took the brunt of Muslim invasion, thus protecting the west for centuries, and if not for the Fourth Crusade could have grown stronger and more powerful and Europe would not have been threatened or invaded. In addition, Persian culture might still exist, possibly as yet another empire. Greek rationalism did not disappear as the church in the east largely reconciled itself with it and focused on spiritual matters. Consequently, the church would not have been able to significantly thwart scientific progress. Europe, including a good portion of the east would still dominate the world. and remain centered in Constantinople. They would likely still have found the Americas, but development might have been different, possibly without African slavery, among other things. The culture would be more advanced and sophisticated, but economic growth might not be as robust, given a different emphasis and outlook, and without a “Protestant ethic” but rather a sort of merchant mentality. Higher education might not have been found in universities as we know them, but rather closer to the academic format of the ancient world, more focused on the development of the mind and learning. Ultimately we cannot know because of vicissitudes of one-man rule. There can be a great ruler and then a terrible ruler. You can have a Marcus Aurelius or a Caligula. So given different personalities there is no way to know, and that can be precarious and lead to instability or conflict until someone else consolidates power. What we can learn clearly from history is the less power we surrender to others over us the better off we are. Finally, the Fourth Crusade was clearly the worst disaster in western history even beyond World War I if only because the latter might never have happened if the empire hadn’t fallen. Such a general and vague question can lead to endless possibilities and alternatives, but in the end all that is left is what actually happened.

If the Roman Empire “never fell,” the biggest change would be that Europe would probably not have developed into the fragmented medieval world that produced modern European nations. But the empire could not simply have stayed frozen as it was in the 2nd century. To survive, it would have had to transform: decentralize some authority, absorb Germanic peoples more successfully, maintain tax revenues, preserve its army, and avoid the political breakdown that destroyed the Western Empire in the 5th century.

The most immediate difference would be in Western Europe. There would likely be no Frankish kingdom in the same form, no Charlemagne as we know him, no Holy Roman Empire, and probably no France, Spain, Germany, or Italy developing along their actual historical paths. Latin or evolved Romance dialects might have remained more unified under imperial administration, so modern European languages could be very different. English, for example, might not exist in its current form if Anglo-Saxon migration into Britain had been prevented or absorbed by a still-powerful Roman state.

Christianity would still likely be central, since the empire had already become Christian before the Western collapse. But the relationship between church and state would be different. The pope became especially powerful partly because imperial authority disappeared in the West. If Rome or a western imperial government remained strong, the papacy might have been more subordinate to the emperor, as the patriarch of Constantinople often was in the Eastern Roman Empire. This could mean no medieval papacy in the same form, no Investiture Controversy, and possibly no Protestant Reformation as it actually happened.

The Islamic conquests might also have unfolded differently. In real history, the Eastern Roman and Persian empires were exhausted by war, which helped early Muslim armies expand rapidly. If a unified or stronger Roman Empire still controlled the Mediterranean, North Africa, Syria, and Egypt might have been harder to conquer. Islam would still likely arise, but its political expansion could have been slower, more limited, or directed differently. This would profoundly change the religious and cultural history of the Middle East, North Africa, and Europe.

Economically, a surviving empire might have preserved Mediterranean trade, cities, roads, coinage, and bureaucratic administration more continuously. Western Europe may not have experienced the same degree of ruralization and political fragmentation associated with the early Middle Ages. Roman law and institutions would likely have remained dominant, perhaps producing a more centralized, legalistic, bureaucratic civilization.

But this does not necessarily mean modern technology would have arrived earlier. Rome was impressive administratively and militarily, but it was not on a clear path toward industrialization. Slavery, aristocratic landholding, and limited mechanical experimentation may still have slowed technological change. A stable empire could encourage trade and infrastructure, but it could also suppress political competition and innovation. The Scientific Revolution might happen earlier, later, or in a very different form.

The Age of Exploration would also change. Spain, Portugal, France, the Netherlands, and England were products of post-Roman Europe. If a Roman imperial state still dominated the West, voyages to the Americas might have been sponsored by imperial authorities rather than competing nation-states. Colonization might have been more centralized, perhaps slower or more systematic. The Americas would still eventually be contacted by Afro-Eurasian powers, but by whom, when, and with what consequences could be very different.

In the modern world, we might see a large Mediterranean-centered superstate instead of many European countries. Nationalism might be weaker or take a different form, because people might identify more with imperial citizenship than with nation-states. Modern law, language, religion, borders, and global power structures would all be altered.

So the short answer is: if Rome never fell, most of world history would be dramatically different. Medieval Europe, the papacy, Islam’s expansion, modern European nations, colonialism, and even the languages we speak could all change. But the surviving “Roman Empire” would not look like ancient Rome forever. It would become a new kind of long-lived imperial civilization, and our world would likely be more Roman in law, administration, religion, and political identity, but not necessarily more advanced or more peaceful.

If Rome had remained intact, there might be no France, Germany, Italy, Spain, or perhaps even England in their current forms. Latin, or a descendant of Latin, might be the main administrative and prestige language across much of Europe. Local languages would still exist, but their development would be different. Modern French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, and Romanian might not exist in their current forms, or they might be regional dialects inside a broader Latin-speaking civilization. items.question: What If the Roman Empire survived into the 21st century?
human_answers: A surviving Roman Empire in the 21st century would reshape politics, culture, technology diffusion, religion, law, and global power structures. Below is a compact, structured scenario sketching plausible continuities, ruptures, and systemic consequences while anchoring changes in realistic mechanisms (institutional inertia, technological adoption, conquest limits, cultural assimilation). Core-continuities and institutions Imperial continuity: The Empire preserves imperial institutions—an emperor (or imperial council), provincial administration, legions as core armed forces, and a bureaucratic elite—adapted over centuries into flexible, meritocratic civil service and imperial parliament/assemblies to manage scale. Roman law as global lingua franca: Codified law (an evolved Corpus Juris) becomes the legal foundation across the Empire and, by prestige and trade, a dominant model beyond it; concepts like property rights, contracts, corporate forms, and administrative law are widespread. Urbanism and infrastructure: Roman urban planning, roads, aqueduct successors, ports, and integrated logistics persist and modernize. Dense metropolitan networks across the Mediterranean, Western and parts of Central Europe, North Africa, Anatolia and the Levant remain economic cores. Multilingual administration: Latin remains the imperial legal-administrative language but coexists with vernaculars (Greek, Punic, Syriac, Germanic, Celtic, Berber dialects). A strong tradition of bilingual or trilingual elites exists. Geopolitics and territorial shape Core territories: The Empire holds the Mediterranean rim (Iberia to Levant), much of North Africa, Italy, the Balkans, Anatolia, parts of Central Europe and possibly Britain as a client or integrated province—boundaries adjusted by later contingencies. Successor or extra-European states: Outside the imperial ambit, consolidated polities (a unified Frankish realm, Slavic federations, Islamic caliphates expanded differently, and later colonial states in the Americas, sub-Saharan Africa, and East Asia) create a multipolar world. The Empire competes with and sometimes partners with maritime powers. Imperial fragmentation avoided or mitigated: Rather than a single uninterrupted polity by 2025, the Empire is likely a federated imperial system—suffragan kingdoms, semi-autonomous provinces, and imperial dynasties alternating with elective mechanisms—preventing collapse while allowing regional autonomy. Religion and ideology Religion pluralism anchored in Roman legalism: Early Christianity, or a pluralized Roman state religion that incorporated Christianity, remains influential but subject to imperial regulation. Religious plurality (Judaism, localized pagan survivals, later Islam and Eastern religions) exists with legal frameworks for toleration and civic participation. Secularization pathways: Enlightenment-like movements and commercial modernization produce robust secular administrative norms by the 19th–20th centuries; an imperial secular public sphere coexists with powerful religious institutions. Economy and technology Industrialization: The Empire experiences industrial revolutions driven by integrated markets, stable property law, and urban demand. State investment in infrastructure and military spurs rail, steam, later electric and digital technologies. Industrial centers cluster where Roman urban networks were densest. Trade networks: The Empire’s Mediterranean-centered trade orientation evolves into global commerce via long-distance maritime routes; imperial ports become hubs connecting to Atlantic and Indian Ocean circuits. Maritime technology advances compete with and eventually match Atlantic powers. Banking and corporate forms: Advanced Roman legal corporations (sodalitates, societates) evolve into joint-stock companies, central banking, and imperial-chartered trading companies. Rome-centric financial systems influence global credit norms. Military and diplomacy Professionalized legions: Legions transform into modern, well-funded standing forces with combined-arms doctrine, naval fleets, and expeditionary capabilities; conscription and recruitment adapt to demographic realities. Gunpowder, industrial warfare, nuclear age: The Empire participates fully in the technological military revolution. Its strategic choices (naval investments, alliances, nuclear development) shape 20th-century geopolitics. Balance with other great powers prevents unlimited expansion. Diplomacy: Roman legal diplomacy—treaties, client states, and provincial autonomy—produces layered influence: direct rule where feasible, client kingdoms and protectorates elsewhere, and trade-dominant zones beyond. Culture, identity, and languages Roman identity as civic, not ethnic: Imperial civic identity (civis Romana) emphasizes legal status, obligations, and urban participation rather than ethnicity. Cultural assimilation is patchy; local identities persist under Roman civic frameworks. Latin’s evolution: Vulgar Latin branches into multiple Romance languages with imperial Latin retained for law, liturgy, and academia. Greek remains influential in eastern provinces; multilingualism is common in elites. Arts and sciences: Patronage systems shift from emperors and aristocrats to universities, public institutions, and corporate sponsors. A continuous tradition of Roman engineering and medicine blends with global scientific developments. Colonialism and global expansion Atlantic exploration: Roman maritime institutions and entrepreneurial elites engage in Atlantic exploration. Depending on timing and internal politics, Rome might participate in early colonial ventures or be competed against by independent maritime republics and emergent Atlantic states. Americas and Asia: If Rome delays Atlantic expansion, independent colonial empires arise (Portuguese/Spanish-analogs, Dutch/English-analogs), producing a patchwork of territories. Alternatively, Roman-chartered companies acquire colonies, producing a Roman-speaking settler/merchant presence in the Americas or parts of Africa. Non-European contacts: Sustained contact with Chinese, Indian, and later Pacific polities leads to trade, technology transfer, and complex diplomacy rather than simple conquest. Science, education, and bureaucracy State-sponsored technical education: Roman practicality produces strong engineering schools and imperial academies; public health and civil engineering remain priorities. Literacy rates among urban populations are higher than in many historical analogs. Administrative continuity fosters record-keeping, statistics, and early modern state capacities (census, taxation, public works), accelerating institutional modernization. Possible alternative 20th–21st century dynamics Different alignments in world wars or great-power wars: If imperial fragmentation is limited, large-scale continental wars might occur between the Empire and other consolidated powers. The Empire’s size and resources could prevent dominance by any single non-imperial power, producing a multipolar 20th century with competing blocs. Cold-war analogues: Ideological divides (imperial corporatism vs. revolutionary republics, religious empires vs. secular federations) could create bipolar tensions that include spheres of influence, proxy conflicts, intelligence competition, and arms races including nuclear weapons. European integration replaced by imperial federalization: Instead of EU-style nation-states, regional federal assemblies and an imperial senate coordinate economic policy, standards, and internal mobility at an imperial scale. Society and daily life in 21st-century Roman Empire Urban-rural divide: Highly urbanized imperial cores with advanced services contrast with peripheral provinces with varying development. Provincial capitals are modern metros with Roman street plans, monumental continuity, and modern skyscrapers intermingled with ancient fabric. Civic rituals and symbolism: Imperial ceremonies, legal oaths, and municipal collegia persist as public rituals; imperial monuments and restored ancient sites are central to civic pride and tourism. Social mobility: Legal pathways (citizenship-by-service, trade-based citizenship, imperial grants) enable mobility. Aristocratic families persist but compete with bureaucratic meritocrats and industrial capitalists. Long-term cultural impact beyond the Empire Legal and bureaucratic export: Roman-derived legal codes and administrative practices diffuse globally through trade, education, and colonialism, shaping modern governance worldwide. Architectural and engineering legacy: Roman building methods evolve into modern construction norms in the imperial sphere; global architecture shows stronger classical continuity. Intellectual tradition: A continuous stream of classical scholarship, merged with scientific revolutions, produces different emphases in philosophy, law, and humanistic studies—less romantic nationalism, more civic-universalist discourse. Summary — plausible consequences The 21st-century world would be multipolar but strongly influenced by a Rome-centered legal, administrative, and infrastructural complex. Technological and industrial modernity develops within Roman institutional forms rather than in nation-state molds. Colonial and global expansions produce complex interactions with Americas, Asia, and Africa; outcomes depend crucially on early maritime strategy and whether Rome embraced or ceded Atlantic exploration. Socially and culturally, a Roman civic identity coexists with strong local cultures and multilingualism; legal-civic institutions and urban infrastructure are the Empire’s durable strengths. Global politics would differ in alignments, ideologies, and the balance of maritime vs. continental power, but modern technologies (industrialization, nuclear weapons, digital networks) and economic forces remain drivers—shaping a recognizable but distinct modern world. Examples and analogues Byzantine survival gives a model: An eastern Roman continuity (Byzantium) demonstrates how Roman law, bureaucracy, and urbanism can endure, adapt to new religions and languages, and project power for centuries. Ottoman adaptation shows how a premodern empire modernizes militarily and administratively under internal reform pressures. British imperial experience illustrates how an empire with maritime orientation, legal export, and industrial base shapes world systems—transpose British mechanisms onto Roman institutions for multiple plausible outcomes. This scenario emphasizes institutional adaptability, legal continuity, and urban infrastructure as the key mechanisms enabling a Roman Empire’s survival and modernization, producing a 21st century both recognizably Roman and reshaped by global technological and political currents.
items.model_answer:
If the Roman Empire survived into the 21st century, it would almost certainly not look like the ancient empire of Augustus or Constantine. It would have had to transform repeatedly—politically, militarily, religiously, economically, and culturally—to survive. A “21st-century Roman Empire” would likely be a modern state or federation claiming continuous Roman institutional legitimacy, much as modern states preserve old names while changing their systems completely.

The most plausible version is not a pagan, Latin-speaking empire ruling the whole Mediterranean by legions. It would more likely resemble a large, bureaucratic, multiethnic Mediterranean superstate descended from the late Roman or Byzantine Empire. Its capital might be Rome, Constantinople, or possibly both in some dual arrangement. It would probably be Christian in origin, though by the 21st century it might be secular or constitutionally pluralist. Its languages could include Latin, Greek, Italian, Arabic, Turkish, or regional Romance languages depending on which territories it retained.

Politically, survival would require the empire to solve the problems that destroyed or weakened historical Rome: succession crises, overreliance on military strongmen, fiscal strain, frontier defense, elite fragmentation, and provincial separatism. By the modern era, it would probably have evolved into either a constitutional monarchy, a centralized republic using Roman titles, or a federal imperial commonwealth. The emperor, if still present, might be ceremonial, comparable to the British monarch or Japanese emperor, while real power would rest with elected institutions and a professional civil service.

Geographically, it is unlikely that Rome would still control all the lands it held at its height. A surviving empire might retain Italy, Greece, parts of the Balkans, Anatolia, the Levant, North Africa, or some combination of these. If it successfully held the eastern Mediterranean, there might be no Ottoman Empire in the form we know, or Islam’s expansion into former Roman provinces might have taken a very different path. If it retained the western Mediterranean, the later histories of France, Spain, Italy, and North Africa would be profoundly altered.

European history would change dramatically. The idea of a “fall of Rome” shaped the Middle Ages, the papacy, feudalism, the Holy Roman Empire, the Renaissance, and later European nationalism. If Rome remained a powerful state, there might be no Holy Roman Empire, no independent papal monarchy in the same form, and perhaps no Italy as a late-unifying nation-state. Western Europe might develop under the shadow of a continuing Roman superpower, either as its provinces, rivals, or breakaway successor states.

Religion would also be transformed. If the empire remained Christian, the relationship between emperor and church would be central. The pope might be subordinate to, allied with, or in rivalry with the imperial government. The split between Catholic and Orthodox Christianity might not occur in the same way, especially if Rome and Constantinople remained politically connected. Alternatively, a surviving empire could intensify church-state conflict and produce different religious reforms from those of the historical Protestant Reformation.

The modern geopolitical map would be very different. A strong Roman state spanning the Mediterranean would be a major world power, comparable to the European Union, Russia, China, India, or the United States, depending on its size and industrial development. It could control key sea routes, energy corridors, and cultural centers. Its existence would reshape colonialism: Spain, France, Britain, and Portugal might never rise in the same way if the western Mediterranean remained Roman, or they might emerge as anti-Roman maritime powers.

Culturally, Roman identity would likely be broader than ethnicity. Just as “Roman” in late antiquity became a political and legal identity, a modern Roman citizen might be Italian, Greek, Arab, Berber, Balkan Slavic, Armenian, Turkish, Jewish, or something else. Roman law, civic administration, engineering traditions, and imperial symbolism would remain central to national identity. The fasces, eagle, Senate, consul, prefect, province, and legion might survive as ceremonial or institutional terms, though with modern meanings.

Technologically and economically, Rome would not remain ancient. It would industrialize if it survived competition with modern states. It would have railways, universities, corporations, a central bank, intelligence agencies, air forces, and digital infrastructure. Its famous roads and aqueducts might be remembered as the ancestors of a long tradition of state infrastructure. Roman law might have an even deeper influence on global legal systems than it already does.

The biggest uncertainty is whether such an empire could remain authoritarian. A long-surviving Rome might preserve a strong bureaucratic and military state, producing something like a modern centralized imperial republic. But the pressures of literacy, commerce, nationalism, mass politics, and industrial society would likely force constitutional reform. If it failed to adapt, it would face revolutions, civil wars, and nationalist secessions.

So the short answer is: if the Roman Empire survived into the 21st century, it would be a transformed, modernized successor to ancient Rome, not a frozen ancient empire. It would probably be a major Mediterranean power with Roman law, imperial symbolism, a multiethnic population, and a complex relationship with Christianity and European identity. Its survival would radically alter the development of Europe, Islam, nationalism, colonialism, and the modern international order.

items.question: What If the war between the Byzantine empire and Persia never happened?
human_answers: Counterfactual premise: the long series of Byzantine–Sasanian wars that culminated in the devastating 602–628 conflict (and the immediate prelude wars of the 6th century) never occurred—either because the two powers reached durable accommodation, Persia collapsed earlier to internal factors, or both empires diverted energies elsewhere. Below is a compact roadmap of plausible political, military, economic, and cultural consequences from the early 7th century through the following two centuries. Big-picture consequence The eastern Mediterranean and the Near East remain dominated by two strong, economically healthy, and militarily competent imperial states into the mid–7th century instead of being exhausted and depopulated. That retention of resources, infrastructure, and institutional capacity substantially alters the environment encountered by the early Islamic caliphates. Political and military effects Byzantine fiscal and military capacity preserved: Without the catastrophic drain of men and treasure (including the loss of major provinces, siege costs, and troop attrition), Byzantium retains stronger field armies, garrisons in Anatolia and the Levant, intact fortifications, and greater naval strength in the Mediterranean. Persian state stability and resources preserved: Sasanian administrative structures, tax revenue, and veteran forces remain intact; fewer internal revolts or usurpations are provoked by wartime exhaustion. Frontier security improved: With garrisons and infrastructure intact, both empires can better repel nomadic incursions, control caravan routes, and project power into buffer zones (Armenia, Caucasus, northern Mesopotamia). Reduced political turmoil: The domestic crises that often follow sustained warfare—court coups, revolts, and rapid changes of leadership—are less frequent, so both polities experience longer periods of bureaucratic continuity. Economic and demographic consequences Population retention in Syria, Palestine, Mesopotamia, and Anatolia: Cities and countryside ravaged in our timeline would have higher populations, more agricultural production, and intact tax bases. Trade continuity: Silk routes, Red Sea–Indian Ocean commerce, and Mediterranean maritime trade continue with fewer disruptions. Constantinople and Ctesiphon remain major commercial hubs. Urban resilience: Major cities (Alexandria, Antioch, Edessa, Nisibis, Ctesiphon) keep elites, artisans, and institutions that in reality were severely weakened, supporting more rapid technological and craft continuity. Religious and cultural consequences Christianity and Zoroastrianism remain robust: Strong imperial patronage and intact communities slow religious conversion dynamics. Christian church hierarchies in the Levant and Egypt remain less disrupted; Zoroastrian clergy and institutions in Persia retain state support. Jewish communities: Less displacement and fewer communal fractures in Palestine and Mesopotamia; the demographic balance across communities differs. Intellectual life preserved: Scholarship in Greek, Syriac, and Middle Persian continues with less interruption; key centers of learning retain teachers and manuscripts. Consequence for the early Islamic expansion A stronger, intact Byzantine and Sasanian world makes early rapid Arab-Muslim conquests far less automatic: Military resistance likely stiffer. Well-supplied, experienced garrisons and a functioning cavalry-based Persian army and disciplined Byzantine field forces raise the cost and uncertainty of conquest. Local populations less prone to collaborate. In the historical timeline, some local elites and populations welcomed Muslim rule or made pragmatic arrangements because they preferred taxation stability to Byzantine/Persian warfare or oppressive policies; with stronger, less-rapacious imperial rule, fewer defections occur. Slower or limited territorial gains. Initial Muslim incursions might be contained, repulsed, or confined to frontier zones for decades, producing a patchwork frontier rather than wholesale collapse of two empires. Possible new equilibrium outcomes: Stalled expansion: The early Caliphate converts into a coastal and steppe power whose expansion is checked, resulting in long-term coexistence and negotiated frontiers. Hybrid frontier states: Protracted warfare and demographic intermixing could still produce autonomous Arab principalities under nominal imperial suzerainty; integration proceeds more slowly. Different conversion patterns: Islam spreads more gradually by trade, Sufi missionaries, and elites adopting Islam over generations, instead of rapid state conversion tied to conquest. Geopolitical ripple effects in Europe, Africa, and Central Asia Byzantine-Avar-Slavic dynamics: A stronger Byzantium can better defend the Balkans; Slavic settlement patterns might be moderated by more robust imperial responses, slowing Slavic consolidation in certain regions. Italy and the West: Resources available for Byzantine reconquest or defense in Italy could increase; the Lombard problem is still complex, but a less-weakened Byzantium could retain more Italian holdings longer. North Africa and Egypt: If Byzantine control in Egypt and Byzantine North Africa remains strong, Arab conquests of those regions become harder; Mediterranean grain flows to Constantinople and Europe remain more stable. Central Asia: A functioning Sasanian state sustains Iranian cultural and political influence in Transoxiana and the Caucasus; Turkic and steppe pressures continue but face a stronger buffer. Long-run cultural and institutional consequences Stronger continuity of Late Antique institutions: Roman law, Byzantine bureaucracy, classical learning, and urban civic life have stronger survivals into the medieval period. Persian cultural continuities: Court poetry, Zoroastrian institutions, and Sasanian administrative models continue to shape Iranian civilization and neighboring polities. Different religious map: Christianity and Zoroastrianism remain dominant for longer in many regions; Islam still expands but on a more complex, regionally varied timeline, yielding a richer pluralism into the high Middle Ages. Possible alternative high-level outcomes (three scenario sketches) Containment scenario (most plausible): Byzantium and Persia jointly resist Arab advances; frontier stalemate produces centuries of competition, trade, occasional war, and cultural exchange. Islam grows chiefly through trade and conversion rather than rapid conquest. Delayed conquest scenario: The caliphates achieve limited early gains but conquest of Levant, Egypt, and Persia is slower, fragmented, and occurs over generations, competing with resurgent Byzantine and Persian counteroffensives. The map of medieval Eurasia becomes polycentric. Divergent collapse scenario (less likely under premise but possible): One empire collapses for internal reasons unrelated to war (plague, dynasty failure), producing a more complex set of outcomes—Arab expansion may still succeed into the vacuum, but with different timelines and successor states. Key caveats and constraints Contingencies remain: Epidemics (e.g., plague), climate events, internal political crises, or changing tribal dynamics could still produce instability that alters these outcomes. Agency of the Arabs: The religious zeal, political organization, and military innovation of the early Muslim polities were significant independent variables; even with stronger empires opposing them, expansionary impulses might find alternate routes or exploit future weaknesses. Gradation not absolutes: “Never happened” should be read as “did not happen at the scale and timing of our history”; many other local conflicts and friction would still shape results. Bottom line If the Byzantine–Sasanian wars of the 6th–7th centuries had not devastated both empires, the Near East would likely have remained dominated by two powerful states into the mid–7th century. That would have made the early Arab-Muslim expansions harder, slower, and more contingent, producing a medieval Eurasia that was more polycentric, with stronger continuities of Roman-Byzantine and Sasanian institutions, different trade and demographic patterns, and a more gradual, regionally varied diffusion of Islam. The precise map depends on subsequent contingencies—epidemics, leadership, and steppe pressures—but the central effect is clear: less imperial exhaustion means a very different political and cultural trajectory across the eastern Mediterranean and Iran.
items.model_answer:
If the major Byzantine–Persian war of 602–628 had never happened, the history of the Middle East and Mediterranean would likely have been dramatically different.

That war exhausted both empires. Byzantium technically won, but it was financially ruined, militarily depleted, and had lost years of stability. Persia was even worse off: the Sasanian Empire fell into political chaos after the war, with rapid changes of rulers and weakened central authority. This exhaustion made the early Muslim Arab conquests in the 630s and 640s much easier.

If the war never happened, the Byzantine Empire would probably have remained much stronger in Syria, Palestine, and Egypt. Those provinces were wealthy and strategically vital. A stronger Byzantium might have been able to resist Arab expansion more effectively, or at least slow it greatly. Egypt, in particular, might have stayed Byzantine for much longer, preserving Byzantine control over a major source of grain and tax revenue.

Persia would also likely have survived longer. Without the devastation and internal collapse caused by the war, the Sasanian state would have been better able to defend Iraq and Iran. The Arab conquest of Persia might have failed, been delayed, or resulted in only limited border gains rather than the complete destruction of the empire.

Islam would still likely have emerged in Arabia, but its expansion beyond Arabia might have been much slower and more limited. Instead of rapidly creating a vast caliphate stretching from Spain to Persia, the early Muslim community may have had to negotiate, raid, trade, or fight gradually against two still-powerful imperial neighbors. The religious and cultural transformation of the Middle East might therefore have taken centuries rather than decades, or followed a very different path.

A stronger Byzantium could also have affected Europe. With more money and troops, it might have held its Balkan and Italian territories more effectively and remained a dominant Mediterranean power for longer. The later medieval balance between Byzantium, the Islamic world, and Western Europe would have looked very different.

In short, without the Byzantine–Persian war, neither empire would have been so badly weakened at the exact moment Islam began expanding. The most likely result is that Byzantium and Persia survive as major powers for longer, the Arab conquests are delayed or reduced, and the religious, linguistic, and political map of the Middle East develops much more slowly and differently.

items.question: What If A Danish-Speaking Country with at least 40 million people
human_answers: As other people have said the low hanging fruit would be a Danish settler colony in the America. The next easiest one would be a Danish colony, where Danish end up Lingua Franca and becomes widespread adopted. Next one would be a united Scandinavia under Danish rule but with significant population growth (as there are only roughly 22-23 million Scandinavian speakers) The second hardest is a continued Danish-Norwegian union with massive population growth (as there are only 11 million Danish and Norwegian speakers). The hardest one would be Denmark with roughly OTL borders just with insane population growth, it at first look impossible but Denmark is somewhat bigger than Netherlands, and Netherlands have three times the population. But such a Denmark would demand centuries of different policies to enable it to have such a large population. Some would say that Norwegians and Swedes do not speak Danish as such including them in a Danish speaking state would not increase the number of Danish speakers. People are wrong, the three languages are simply written standards of the same language or for several related languages[1], if OTL Kalmar Union had lasted until after the Reformation had been implemented and the Bible had been translated, the Swedes would have used a Danish translation of the Bible for a long time and that would have become the core of what we think of as Swedish. Norwegian as most people think about it as a modern language only truly split from Danish in 1917. [1] if you split East Scandinavian into different languages based on the old dialects, it would not follow the existing language borders. Jutland would be split into three languages (Anglish in the south, Jutish in the west and Danish in the east), Gotlandic would be its own language. Norwegian would only be spoken in the West and North. Viken would speak Danish and so would coastal Southern Sweden, the rest of Sweden would be split between Swedish around Stockholm and in the north and Geatish in the inland south.

items.model_answer:
A Danish-speaking country with at least 40 million people would be a major cultural and political power compared with present-day Denmark, whose population is under 6 million. For that to happen, history would have had to be very different: Denmark might have retained and absorbed much larger territories, built a much larger colonial-settler state, or formed a durable Scandinavian/North Sea union in which Danish became the dominant common language.

The biggest effect would be linguistic. Danish would no longer be a small Nordic language; it would be comparable in speaker numbers to Polish, Ukrainian, or Spanish within a large single country. Danish-language media, literature, universities, software, film, and music would have a much larger market. International companies would localize more heavily into Danish, and Danish might have more diplomatic importance, especially in Europe and the North Atlantic.

Politically, such a country would likely be a significant middle or great power, depending on its economy and territory. If it had Denmark’s present social-democratic traditions, it could be one of the world’s largest welfare states, with major influence on labor policy, education, healthcare, green energy, and social equality. It would probably play a much larger role in the EU, NATO, Arctic policy, Baltic Sea politics, and global climate diplomacy.

Culturally, “Danishness” would probably be less homogeneous than in real life. A 40-million-person Danish-speaking country would almost certainly include regional identities, dialects, immigrant communities, and possibly formerly non-Danish populations that had become Danish-speaking over time. The national culture would be broader and more internally diverse, less like a small Nordic society and more like a large European nation with multiple regions and social divisions.

If the country occupied only modern Denmark’s land area, it would be extremely densely populated, far more urbanized, and under heavy pressure for housing, transportation, energy, water, and farmland. Copenhagen and other cities would become massive metropolitan areas. If the country instead had a much larger territory, the outcome would depend on geography: a larger North Atlantic, Scandinavian, or colonial-derived state could support 40 million people more plausibly.

In short, a Danish-speaking country of 40 million people would transform Danish from a small national language into a major world language, make the country a serious geopolitical actor, and produce a much more diverse and urban society than modern Denmark. Its exact character would depend on whether it grew through union, conquest, colonization, migration, or demographic expansion.

items.question: What If You Hit a Baseball at 90% of the Speed of Light?
human_answers: Let’s set aside the question of how we got the baseball moving that fast. We'll suppose it's a normal pitch, except in the instant the pitcher releases the ball, it magically accelerates to 0.9c. From that point onward, everything proceeds according to normal physics.: [Image: image] The answer turns out to be “a lot of things”, and they all happen very quickly, and it doesn’t end well for the batter (or the pitcher). I sat down with some physics books, a Nolan Ryan action figure, and a bunch of videotapes of nuclear tests and tried to sort it all out. What follows is my best guess at a nanosecond-by-nanosecond portrait: The ball is going so fast that everything else is practically stationary. Even the molecules in the air are stationary. Air molecules vibrate back and forth at a few hundred miles per hour, but the ball is moving through them at 600 million miles per hour. This means that as far as the ball is concerned, they’re just hanging there, frozen. The ideas of aerodynamics don’t apply here. Normally, air would flow around anything moving through it. But the air molecules in front of this ball don’t have time to be jostled out of the way. The ball smacks into them so hard that the atoms in the air molecules actually fuse with the atoms in the ball’s surface. Each collision releases a burst of gamma rays and scattered particles. [Image: image] [Image: image] These gamma rays and debris expand outward in a bubble centered on the pitcher’s mound. They start to tear apart the molecules in the air, ripping the electrons from the nuclei and turning the air in the stadium into an expanding bubble of incandescent plasma. The wall of this bubble approaches the batter at about the speed of light—only slightly ahead of the ball itself. [Image: image] The constant fusion at the front of the ball pushes back on it, slowing it down, as if the ball were a rocket flying tail-first while firing its engines. Unfortunately, the ball is going so fast that even the tremendous force from this ongoing thermonuclear explosion barely slows it down at all. It does, however, start to eat away at the surface, blasting tiny particulate fragments of the ball in all directions.
