items.model_answer:
If modern China had fully replaced Chinese characters with a phonetic script—most likely a Pinyin-like alphabet based on Mandarin—the biggest effects would have been faster standardization, some gains in basic literacy, and a major cultural rupture.

The reform would probably have strengthened Mandarin dramatically. A phonetic national script would need to choose one pronunciation as the standard, and in modern China that would almost certainly be Putonghua/Mandarin. Once schools, newspapers, laws, and books were written phonetically in Mandarin, speakers of Cantonese, Shanghainese, Hokkien, Hakka, and other Sinitic languages would face stronger pressure to read and think in Mandarin rather than in a shared character-based written form. Chinese characters allow people with different pronunciations to read the same text more easily than a purely phonetic Mandarin script would. Replacing them would therefore have accelerated linguistic centralization and weakened regional Chinese languages.

Literacy might have improved somewhat, especially in the early decades of mass education. Learning thousands of characters is harder than learning a phonetic alphabet, so children and adult learners could probably have reached basic reading and writing proficiency faster. This would have mattered in the mid-20th century, when China was trying to expand education rapidly. But it would not have been a magic solution. Literacy also depends on schools, teachers, poverty, access to books, and state capacity. Countries using alphabets can still have low literacy, and China achieved very high literacy with characters once schooling expanded. So the gain would likely be real but not revolutionary.

The cost would have been enormous disruption to China’s literary and historical continuity. Classical Chinese, premodern poetry, calligraphy, historical documents, inscriptions, and much of the cultural prestige attached to writing would become less immediately accessible. They could still be studied in transliteration or translation, just as ancient Greek or Latin are studied through specialized education, but ordinary educated readers would be cut off from the visual continuity of the older written tradition. Calligraphy would likely survive as an art form, but more like a classical or antiquarian practice than a normal part of literacy.

A phonetic script would also create practical problems because Chinese has many homophones, especially in Mandarin. This problem is sometimes overstated: context would resolve many ambiguities, as it does in spoken Chinese. Modern Chinese can be spoken and understood, so it can also be written phonetically. But written Mandarin would probably need clearer word spacing, stricter grammar, more disambiguating vocabulary, and possibly tone marks. Without tones, many words would be ambiguous; with tones, the writing system would be more accurate but slightly less simple. Over time, written Chinese might evolve toward longer compound words and more explicit phrasing to compensate.

Politically, such a reform would have been extremely difficult. The early PRC did consider more radical script reform, and Pinyin was introduced, but abolishing characters would have faced resistance from scholars, officials, teachers, publishers, and ordinary people attached to the inherited script. It would also have required reprinting textbooks, retraining teachers, changing signage, converting archives, and standardizing orthography across the country. A forced transition might have succeeded only under intense state pressure and would likely have produced decades of mixed-script usage.

Technologically, China might have benefited earlier from easier typing, telegraphy, indexing, and printing. Before modern computers, alphabetic scripts had advantages in mechanical typewriters and data processing. However, this advantage would have mattered less after digital input systems improved. In the real world, Pinyin-based input methods already allow people to type characters efficiently. So a phonetic script would have made early modern information handling easier, but it would not necessarily give China a large long-term technological edge.

Internationally, China would look more linguistically similar to alphabet-using countries. Foreign learners might find basic reading easier, and Chinese names and terms would be more consistently written. But the cultural distinctiveness of Chinese writing would be reduced. The character-based connections among China, Japan, Korea’s historical writing, and Vietnam’s older written culture would weaken further. Japanese would not abandon kanji simply because China did, but the symbolic status of Chinese characters across East Asia would decline.

The likely result is that China would become more uniformly Mandarin-speaking, somewhat easier to educate at the basic level, and better adapted to some modern bureaucratic and technological systems earlier. But it would also lose a major source of cultural continuity and would place much greater pressure on non-Mandarin Chinese languages. In short, replacing characters with a phonetic script would probably have made modern China more linguistically centralized and administratively efficient, but also less connected to its classical past and less tolerant of internal linguistic diversity.

items.question: What If Japan Had Attacked the Panama Canal Instead of Pearl Harbor?
human_answers: > So I want to know, did the Japanese Navy have the ability to destroy it in a surprise attack, let's say on 1941 Dec 7? I'm asking if the Japanese Navy had the ability.

The Canal is 8400 miles from Tokyo, compared to 4000 miles for Pearl Harbour. The Japanese carriers are stated of having a range of 10,000 miles at a cruising speed of about 16 knots, but remember that drag varies as the square of speed.

Destroying those locks is going to be harder than you think. They are very large, at 110 feet x 1,050 feet, and the lock gates have to have been built to stand up to accidental collisions with large ships (at low speed, admittedly).

items.model_answer:
If Japan had attacked the Panama Canal instead of Pearl Harbor in December 1941, it would probably have gained a dramatic but temporary disruption while putting itself in a worse strategic position.

The Panama Canal was an important target because it allowed the United States to shift warships between the Atlantic and Pacific quickly. If Japan had seriously damaged the locks, especially at Gatun or Miraflores, the canal might have been closed for weeks or months. That would have forced ships to go around Cape Horn, adding thousands of miles and perhaps two to three weeks to major transfers between oceans. In the opening phase of the Pacific War, that delay would have been inconvenient and embarrassing for the United States.

But it would not have been as strategically useful to Japan as Pearl Harbor was intended to be.

Japan’s immediate problem in late 1941 was the U.S. Pacific Fleet based at Pearl Harbor. Japan wanted time to seize the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore, the Dutch East Indies, and their oil resources without major American naval interference. An attack on the Panama Canal would not neutralize the battleships, cruisers, destroyers, submarines, aircraft, repair facilities, and fuel infrastructure in Hawaii. The U.S. Pacific Fleet would remain intact and much closer to Japan’s intended conquests than any force moving through Panama.

So the likely result is: the United States still enters the war, but its Pacific Fleet is not crippled.

That is a bad trade for Japan. Historically, the attack on Pearl Harbor temporarily reduced American battleship strength and gave Japan several months of freedom of action in the western Pacific. If Japan had hit Panama instead, American anger would have been just as intense, but the U.S. Navy would have retained more immediate fighting power in the Pacific. Even if the canal were blocked, the ships already in the Pacific would still be available.

There is also the question of feasibility. A carrier strike on Panama would have been vastly harder than the strike on Pearl Harbor. Panama was much farther from Japanese bases, required a longer and more exposed approach, and would have demanded major refueling and navigation risks. Japanese carriers were optimized for a fast surprise blow across the central Pacific, not for an enormous raid deep into the eastern Pacific or Caribbean approaches. Submarine-carried aircraft or sabotage might have been possible, but such attacks would likely have caused limited damage unless they hit the locks with great precision.

Even a successful raid probably would not have closed the canal permanently. The United States heavily defended the Canal Zone and would have made reopening it an urgent national priority. Destroyed lock gates or machinery could be repaired or replaced; catastrophic destruction of the dams would have been much harder to achieve from an air raid. Japan could damage the canal, but it could not occupy it or keep attacking it repeatedly.

In the broader war, the effect would likely be modest. American ship movements between oceans would slow, but U.S. industrial capacity, naval construction, and Pacific bases would remain decisive. The United States could still reinforce Hawaii and the Pacific from the West Coast. Meanwhile, Japan would have sacrificed the one operation that actually bought it time in the real war: the crippling of the Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor.

So the most likely outcome is that Japan’s early offensives become riskier, American naval resistance in the Pacific is stronger sooner, and the United States still mobilizes overwhelmingly against Japan. A Panama Canal attack might have been spectacular, but it would not have changed the fundamental balance of the war. If anything, replacing Pearl Harbor with Panama probably makes Japan’s strategic position worse, not better.

items.model_answer:
If eighteenth-century European armies had replaced their flintlock muskets with crossbows, the result would almost certainly have been military regression, not an improvement. Crossbows had some attractive qualities—better individual accuracy in some circumstances, no smoke, less noise, and less dependence on gunpowder—but they were poorly suited to the kind of mass warfare European states were fighting by the 1700s.

The decisive problem would have been rate of fire and battlefield volume. A trained eighteenth-century infantryman with a flintlock musket could fire roughly two to four shots per minute in formation. A powerful military crossbow, especially one strong enough to match musket lethality, would usually be much slower to reload unless it sacrificed power. Even if individual shots were more carefully aimed, crossbow units would throw far fewer projectiles downrange. Eighteenth-century battles relied heavily on massed volleys, not precision marksmanship. A crossbow army would be outshot before it could exploit any accuracy advantage.

The musket also had a tactical feature the crossbow lacked: the socket bayonet. By the early eighteenth century, the bayonet had effectively combined firearm and pike into one weapon. Infantry could fire volleys and then resist cavalry or charge enemy infantry without changing equipment. Crossbowmen would need separate polearms, shields, or supporting pikemen to survive cavalry and close assault. That would make armies more cumbersome and would reverse a century of tactical simplification.

Logistics and production would not necessarily favor the crossbow either. Gunpowder required specialized supply, but muskets and ammunition were highly standardized and suited to state arsenals. Lead balls were simple to cast in enormous quantities. Crossbow bolts were more complex projectiles, and powerful crossbows required strong prods, mechanisms, strings, and maintenance. A musket was not a simple weapon, but by the eighteenth century European states were very good at making and supplying them.

If one country alone returned to the crossbow while its rivals kept muskets, it would probably suffer severe defeats. Its infantry would have less shock effect, lower sustained fire, and poorer ability to defend itself in the open. It might perform tolerably in ambushes, sieges, forests, night actions, or irregular warfare, where silence and lack of smoke mattered. But on the open battlefield against disciplined musket infantry and artillery, it would be at a major disadvantage.

If all European armies somehow returned to crossbows at once, warfare would change more broadly. Battlefields would be less smoky and quieter, and commanders might place more emphasis on skirmishing, cover, and aimed fire. Armor might make a limited comeback, since crossbow lethality would be more dependent on draw weight and range than musket fire. Cavalry might become more important again because infantry without bayoneted firearms would be more vulnerable. Armies might also reintroduce mixed formations of missile troops and polearm troops, resembling late medieval or early Renaissance warfare more than the linear warfare of Frederick the Great.

But artillery would remain a major issue. If cannon still existed, then armies using crossbows would be even more exposed to artillery dominance. Muskets and bayonets allowed infantry to deliver firepower and hold ground despite cannon and cavalry. Crossbow infantry would struggle to close with or withstand artillery-supported musket-style formations if firearms survived anywhere on the battlefield.

So the short answer is: a return to the crossbow would have made eighteenth-century armies less effective in conventional war. Crossbows might have found niche use among scouts, raiders, or special troops, but as a general replacement for muskets they would have reduced firepower, complicated tactics, weakened infantry against cavalry, and likely made armies that adopted them vulnerable to any opponent that kept firearms.

items.model_answer:
If the Black Death had devastated Poland as severely as it did much of Western and Central Europe, medieval Polish history would probably have become more unstable, less prosperous, and less capable of supporting the later rise of the Polish-Lithuanian state.

Historically, Poland appears to have suffered less from the mid-14th-century plague than many regions to its west. That relative escape helped preserve population, agricultural production, royal revenue, town growth, and internal colonization under Casimir III the Great. If Poland had instead lost perhaps a third to a half of its population, the immediate result would have been abandoned villages, labor shortages, falling tax income, disrupted trade, and weaker towns such as Kraków, Poznań, and other commercial centers. Casimir’s program of legal reform, castle-building, urban development, and royal consolidation would have been harder to sustain.

The monarchy would likely have been weakened at a crucial moment. Poland in the 14th century was still recovering from earlier fragmentation, and royal authority depended on restoring order, collecting revenue, and balancing nobles, towns, clergy, and foreign rivals. A severe demographic collapse would have reduced the crown’s resources and increased its dependence on the nobility. To secure military service and taxation, kings might have granted privileges earlier or more extensively, accelerating the political power of the szlachta. Poland’s later “noble republic” tendencies could therefore have emerged sooner, but from a position of weakness rather than confidence.

The social effects would have been mixed. In the short term, surviving peasants and artisans would have had more bargaining power because labor was scarce. Wages could have risen, and some peasants might have moved to better land or demanded lighter obligations. But in the longer term, Polish nobles would probably have tried to restrict mobility and tie labor more tightly to estates. The later development of serfdom and grain-export manorial agriculture might still have occurred, but under harsher conditions and perhaps with earlier legal efforts to control peasants.

A devastated Poland would also have been less attractive as a refuge for Jews and other migrants. Historically, Poland became one of the major centers of European Jewish life, partly because royal protection and relative stability made it safer than many western lands where plague-era scapegoating led to massacres. If plague panic had struck Poland heavily, anti-Jewish violence might have been more likely, or Jewish migration eastward might have been smaller. That would have changed Poland’s urban, financial, and commercial development significantly.

The biggest geopolitical consequence concerns the union with Lithuania. The Polish-Lithuanian partnership depended on Poland being a valuable Christian kingdom with institutions, prestige, and resources. If plague had badly weakened Poland, Lithuania might have found union with it less attractive, or the union might have taken a different form. Jadwiga’s marriage to Jogaila in 1386 could still have happened, since dynastic politics were powerful, but a depopulated and poorer Poland would have been a weaker partner. The later defeat of the Teutonic Order at Grunwald/Tannenberg in 1410 might have been harder to achieve, and the rise of a major Polish-Lithuanian power in Eastern Europe might have been delayed or reduced.

In short, a Poland devastated by the Black Death would probably have remained a kingdom, but a poorer, more politically dependent, and more demographically fragile one. Its towns would have grown more slowly, royal power would have been weaker, noble privileges stronger, Jewish settlement likely smaller or less secure, and the Polish-Lithuanian union less formidable. The long-term result might have been a Central-Eastern Europe in which the Teutonic Order, Hungary, Bohemia, or Lithuania had relatively more influence, while Poland’s later golden age was diminished or postponed.

items.original_question: 为什么中国能够统一而欧洲却不能？如果你看一下中国历代地图，你通常会发现（大约从汉朝开始）代表中国的巨大物体。另一方面，如果你看一下欧洲地图，你通常会看到大量的国家。为什么中国能够统一，而欧洲却不能？
items.model_answer:
If Europe had unified early and durably in the way China did under the Qin-Han model, world history would probably have been less shaped by European interstate rivalry and more by a single large imperial civilization centered on the Mediterranean or the old Roman core.

The most likely starting point would be a Roman Empire that did not permanently fragment in the West, or a post-Roman successor that reunified Europe and built lasting institutions: a common legal system, unified taxation, imperial bureaucracy, standardized weights and measures, state roads, common currency, and a shared elite language, probably Latin or a Latin-Greek administrative culture. Europe would have looked less like medieval France, England, Spain, Venice, the Holy Roman Empire, and Poland competing with one another, and more like a vast imperial state containing many regions and languages but governed through a common administrative framework.

The immediate effect would likely have been greater internal stability. Medieval Europe’s constant warfare, feudal fragmentation, dynastic conflicts, border raids, and church-state struggles would have been reduced or channeled into court politics and provincial administration. Trade across Europe would have been easier. Roads, ports, taxation, and law could have been more standardized. A unified empire might have preserved more of Roman urban life, engineering knowledge, and long-distance commerce, avoiding some of the sharp disruptions associated with the fall of the western Roman Empire.

Christianity would probably have become even more tightly bound to the state. Instead of a medieval Europe divided between popes, kings, emperors, bishops, and city-states, a unified Europe might have had something closer to a state church under imperial supervision, as in Byzantium or in imperial China’s relationship to Confucian orthodoxy. That could have reduced religious wars, but it might also have made dissent more difficult. Movements like the Protestant Reformation might either never occur in the same form or be crushed, absorbed, or bureaucratized much earlier.

The biggest difference would concern competition. Fragmented Europe produced intense rivalry among states. That rivalry was destructive, but it also encouraged military innovation, shipbuilding, finance, cartography, universities, printing, and overseas exploration. If one ruler rejected an idea, an inventor, banker, dissident, or navigator could often move to another court. Columbus could be rejected by Portugal and still find support in Spain. Protestants, Jews, scientists, merchants, and political exiles could relocate across borders. A unified Europe would have had fewer alternative patrons and fewer safe havens.

Because of that, early European unification might have slowed some of the forces that later made Europe globally dominant. The age of exploration may have happened later or in a more centralized form. There might have been no Portuguese-Spanish-Dutch-English-French competition for sea routes, colonies, and trade monopolies. A single European empire might still have explored the Atlantic and Indian Oceans, especially if it wanted access to spices, gold, or trade with Asia, but the urgency would have been lower. Overseas expansion might have resembled large state expeditions rather than competitive private and national ventures.

Colonialism would therefore have looked different. A unified Europe could have been powerful enough to colonize abroad on an enormous scale, but it might also have been less motivated to do so quickly. Fragmented Europe’s colonial expansion was fueled by rival states seeking wealth, converts, naval bases, and prestige. Without that rivalry, the Americas might have been contacted later, colonized more slowly, or dominated by a single imperial administration rather than several competing colonial empires. Indigenous societies might have had more time before European conquest, though disease transmission would still have been catastrophic once contact occurred.

Science and technology would also be ambiguous. A unified Europe could have funded large observatories, universities, canals, libraries, and engineering projects. It might have preserved classical knowledge better and produced impressive state-sponsored scholarship. But intellectual life might have become more orthodox. China’s imperial system generated major inventions and sophisticated administration, but its unity sometimes reduced institutional competition and made it easier for the state to suppress disruptive ideas or redirect priorities. A unified Europe might have had fewer independent universities, fewer competing printing markets, fewer military laboratories, and less pressure to innovate rapidly.

The Industrial Revolution might have happened later, differently, or possibly outside Europe. Britain’s industrialization depended on coal, wages, commercial law, empire, finance, naval competition, and political institutions. In a unified Europe, Britain might not exist as an independent maritime power. Coal-rich regions could still industrialize, but whether the imperial center encouraged mechanized capitalism would matter greatly. If the empire was bureaucratic, land-tax-based, and conservative, it might prefer stability over disruptive industrial growth. If it was commercially minded and invested in infrastructure, it could industrialize on a continental scale.

Politically, Europe might have avoided many devastating wars: the Hundred Years’ War, the Thirty Years’ War, the Napoleonic Wars, perhaps even the world wars in their familiar form. But unity would not mean peace. Conflict would shift from interstate war to civil war, succession crises, frontier rebellions, separatist movements, palace coups, and provincial uprisings. A single Europe could also produce larger internal catastrophes if the central state made bad decisions, because there would be fewer rival systems to offer alternatives.

Culturally, Europe would probably be more standardized. Local languages and identities would survive, as they did in China with regional languages and cultures, but elite culture would be more uniform. Latin, imperial law, official examinations, and bureaucratic service might dominate. National identities such as French, English, Spanish, German, and Italian might be weaker or emerge mainly as regional identities within the empire. Europe might think of itself less as a continent of nations and more as one civilization-state.

The global balance of power would likely be very different. A unified Europe might have resembled China: rich, populous, administratively sophisticated, culturally confident, and sometimes inward-looking. It might not have developed the same aggressive maritime capitalism that fragmented Europe produced. As a result, Asia might have remained more economically and politically central for longer. The Ottoman Empire, Persia, India, and China would have faced either a single powerful western empire or a less expansionist Europe, depending on that empire’s priorities.

So the short answer is: early European unification would probably have produced a richer, more stable, more bureaucratic, and more culturally unified Europe, but possibly a less competitive and less outward-expansionist one. It might have avoided some of Europe’s worst wars, but it also might have slowed the exploration, capitalism, scientific pluralism, and industrial acceleration that came from Europe’s fragmentation. The modern world would likely be less dominated by competing European nation-states and perhaps less shaped by rapid European colonial expansion.

items.original_question: 第二次世界大战期间日本帝国为何不进攻苏联？日本和苏联在满洲有共同边界，德国对苏联的入侵极大地削弱了苏联。鉴于日本击败苏联的优势（更不用说西伯利亚的资源了），而且日本驻有大量关东军基本上无所事事，为什么日本不进攻呢？
items.model_answer:
If Japan had attacked the Soviet Far East in World War II, the most likely result would have been a costly diversion that helped Germany somewhat in 1941 but did not by itself guarantee Soviet defeat. For Japan, it would probably have been a strategic mistake unless the Soviet Union was already collapsing.

The key moment would have been summer or autumn 1941, after Germany invaded the USSR. Japan did consider a northern attack plan, often associated with the Kwantung Army in Manchuria, but chose the “southern strategy” instead: striking toward Southeast Asia for oil, rubber, and other resources. That choice was driven by necessity. Japan’s war in China and the U.S.-led oil embargo meant Japan needed fuel. Siberia offered territory and prestige, but not the oil Japan urgently required.

A Japanese attack on the Soviet Far East would have created serious problems for Moscow. The Soviet Union relied on troops stationed in Siberia and the Far East as a strategic reserve. Once Stalin became confident Japan would not attack, some of those forces were transferred west and helped defend Moscow in late 1941. If Japan had attacked, Stalin would likely have kept more divisions in the east. That could have made the Battle of Moscow more dangerous for the USSR and improved Germany’s chances of taking the city or forcing a deeper Soviet crisis.

However, “Japan attacks Siberia” does not automatically mean “Germany wins.” The Soviet Far East was huge, difficult terrain with poor roads, long distances, brutal weather, and limited infrastructure. Japan’s army was experienced, but it had already been badly checked by Soviet forces at Khalkhin Gol in 1939. The Red Army in the Far East was not helpless, and the Soviets had armor, artillery, and air power that Japan could not easily match in a continental mechanized war.

Japan’s likely objectives would have been Vladivostok, the Maritime Province, parts of the Amur region, and perhaps the Trans-Siberian Railway. Taking and holding those areas would have been extremely difficult. The Trans-Siberian Railway was vital, but it ran across vast territory. Japan could disrupt it locally, but conquering enough of Siberia to knock the USSR out of the war was beyond Japan’s realistic capacity.

The biggest effect would have been indirect: tying down Soviet troops and reducing Soviet confidence in shifting forces west. That might have weakened the Soviet winter counteroffensive before Moscow. In the most favorable Axis scenario, Moscow might have fallen or the Soviet position in 1941–42 might have become much more precarious. But even if Moscow fell, the Soviet government could have continued the war from farther east, as it had prepared to do. The USSR’s industrial heart had already been partly evacuated beyond the Urals, and Germany still faced immense logistical and manpower problems.

For Japan, the consequences would have been severe. If Japan attacked the USSR instead of attacking the United States, Britain, and the Dutch East Indies, it would still face the oil embargo and would gradually run out of fuel. Siberia would not solve that problem. Japan could win some border battles and still lose the larger strategic war through economic exhaustion.

If Japan attacked both the Soviet Union and the Western colonies in Southeast Asia, the situation would be even worse for Japan. It would be fighting China, the USSR, the United States, Britain, the Netherlands, and eventually probably others at the same time. That would stretch Japanese shipping, air power, fuel, and manpower beyond sustainability. The Japanese Army and Navy already had competing priorities; adding a major Siberian land war would intensify those weaknesses.

There is also the question of American involvement. If Japan attacked only the USSR and avoided Pearl Harbor, the United States might not have entered the war immediately. That could have been advantageous for the Axis in the short term. But Japan would still lack oil, and U.S. aid to the USSR and China would likely continue or increase. If Japan also moved south to seize oil, war with the United States and Britain would still be highly likely.

So the most plausible outcome is this: Japan might have captured some Soviet Far Eastern territory and forced Stalin to keep more troops in the east. This could have made 1941 more dangerous for the Soviet Union and possibly improved Germany’s chances around Moscow. But Japan probably could not have conquered Siberia or knocked the USSR out of the war. Over time, the campaign would drain Japan, worsen its fuel crisis, and expose it to a broader coalition.

In short, a Japanese attack on the Soviet Far East would have been a serious blow to the USSR at a critical moment, but probably not a war-winning move for the Axis. It would have helped Germany tactically and operationally, while harming Japan strategically.

These outcroppings are called Bastions and they became common when muskets and cannons became common in European warfare. The problem with a square or circle forts is that when the enemy has reached the wall, they are in your dead zone.
items.original_question: 为什么古老的防御工事形状像星星而不是圆形？哥本哈根、腓特烈西亚和阿卡的防御工事呈星形。 （哥本哈根防御工事如下图所示。）为什么不把防御工事或防御工事做成纯粹的正方形或圆形呢？
items.model_answer:
If gunpowder-era fortresses had remained simple circles or squares instead of becoming star forts, they would generally have been much easier to besiege and storm.

The star shape was not aesthetic; it was a solution to artillery warfare. Cannon made tall medieval walls vulnerable, so fortifications became lower, thicker, and earth-backed. But the key geometric problem was not just resisting cannon fire. It was making sure every part of the wall, ditch, and approach could be covered by defensive fire. Star forts used projecting bastions so defenders could fire along the faces of neighboring walls and sweep the ditch with flanking fire. This eliminated “dead ground” where attackers could shelter close to the walls.

A simple square fortress would have serious weaknesses. Its flat walls could be battered by siege artillery, and the areas near the base of the walls and at the corners would be hard to defend unless towers or bastions projected outward. But once you add projecting corner works designed for flanking fire, the square begins turning into a bastioned or star-shaped fort anyway.

A circular fortress would solve some problems but create others. A circle has no sharp corners and can distribute impact well, but it is poor at providing straight, controlled flanking fire along the ditch. Defenders on a curved wall cannot as easily sweep the base of adjacent sections. Attackers could get close to the wall in sectors that were not well covered, dig trenches, place mines, or establish batteries. Circular forts could work for small redoubts, towers, or isolated strongpoints, but they were not ideal for defending large towns against systematic siege warfare.

So in practice, if major gunpowder-era fortresses had been built as simple circles or squares, sieges would likely have become shorter and more successful for attackers. Defenders would have needed larger garrisons, more external works, more artillery, or reliance on natural obstacles to compensate. Military engineers would probably have rediscovered projecting bastions quickly, because battlefield experience would show that circular and square plans left too many blind spots.

In short: circular or square gunpowder fortresses could exist, especially on a small scale, but against serious artillery siegecraft they would be inferior. The star fort became dominant because it combined artillery resistance with interlocking fields of fire, especially in the ditch and along the approaches. Without that geometry, early modern fortresses would have been more vulnerable and less strategically effective.

items.model_answer:
If Germany had successfully blockaded the Strait of Gibraltar in World War II, the biggest immediate effect would have been to make the western Mediterranean far more dangerous or effectively closed to British and Allied shipping. It would have been a serious strategic setback for Britain, especially for operations around Malta, North Africa, and later the Allied invasion routes into French North Africa, Sicily, and Italy. But by itself it probably would not have won the war for Germany.

The key issue is feasibility. Germany could not simply “blockade” Gibraltar from the sea with its own navy. The Royal Navy was too strong, and Germany’s surface fleet was too limited. A real blockade would have required control of the land around the strait: Gibraltar itself, Spanish territory nearby, or Spanish Morocco. That meant either Spain joining the Axis or allowing German forces to operate from Spanish soil. Hitler did consider taking Gibraltar through Spain in Operation Felix, but Franco resisted because Spain was exhausted after its civil war, short of food and fuel, and vulnerable to British naval pressure. If Spain openly joined Germany, Britain could retaliate against Spanish shipping, colonies, the Canary Islands, and possibly Spanish Morocco. Germany would also have had to supply forces across Spain over poor infrastructure while fighting elsewhere.

Assuming Germany somehow did close the strait, Britain’s Mediterranean position would become much harder. Gibraltar was the western gate into the Mediterranean and the base for Force H, the British naval force that operated from there. A German-controlled or German-neutralized Gibraltar would have cut off easy movement between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Malta would have been harder to supply from the west. British convoys to Egypt and the Middle East would have relied even more heavily on the long route around the Cape of Good Hope and through the Red Sea. This would have increased shipping times, strained escorts, and made British logistics more expensive.

The North African campaign might have shifted in Germany’s favor, but not automatically. Rommel’s problem was not only British interference through Gibraltar; it was also the limited capacity of Italian and Libyan ports, Axis fuel shortages, Allied attacks on supply convoys, and the enormous distance from Tripoli to the Egyptian front. Even if Gibraltar were closed, Axis supplies still had to cross the central Mediterranean and then move hundreds of miles overland. Malta’s survival was more directly important than Gibraltar. If closing Gibraltar helped the Axis capture or neutralize Malta, then Rommel’s supply situation could have improved substantially. That might have made the 1941–42 desert war much more dangerous for Britain and perhaps delayed or altered the British victory at El Alamein.

The Allied invasion of North Africa in 1942, Operation Torch, would have been the most visibly affected. Torch relied heavily on access through the Strait of Gibraltar and on Gibraltar as a staging and command base. If the strait were blocked, the landings in Morocco and Algeria would have been much harder, perhaps impossible in their historical form. The Allies might have had to land farther west on the Atlantic coast of Morocco, seize the Canaries or other bases first, or delay the whole Mediterranean strategy. That could have postponed the invasions of Sicily and Italy, keeping Italy in the war longer and delaying the diversion of German forces to the Italian front.

However, Britain would not have been strangled. The British Empire had already adapted to the Mediterranean being highly contested. Supplies to Egypt, India, and the Middle East could move around Africa. This was slower and costly, but possible. The Suez Canal mattered greatly, but Gibraltar’s loss did not automatically mean Suez would fall. Germany still lacked the naval and logistical reach to exploit the closure decisively unless it also won major victories in North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean.

The broader war would probably still have turned against Germany. The decisive factors remained Germany’s failure to defeat the Soviet Union, the growing industrial power of the United States, Allied control of the Atlantic, and Germany’s chronic fuel and production shortages. A blocked Gibraltar would have made the Mediterranean war longer and more costly for the Allies. It might have delayed Torch, Sicily, and Italy by months, possibly a year or more under favorable Axis conditions. It might also have increased the chances of Malta falling and Egypt being seriously threatened.

But unless the blockade was part of a much larger Axis success—Spain joining the war, Gibraltar captured, Malta neutralized, Egypt and Suez taken, and the Axis supply crisis solved—it would not have been decisive. The most likely result is a harder, longer Mediterranean campaign and delayed Allied offensives, not a German victory in World War II.

Cooool. Just how far away is this portal? If we put it near the Earth, the ocean would just fall back down into the atmosphere. So let's put the ocean-dumping portal far away—say, on Mars. [Image: image] New Zealand grows dramatically. The Arctic Ocean is cut off and its the water level stops falling. The Netherlands cross the new land bridge into North America. [Image: image] The sea has dropped by two kilometers. New islands are popping up left and right. The Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico are losing their connections with the Atlantic. I don't even know what New Zealand is doing. [Image: image] At three kilometers, many of the peaks of the mid-ocean ridge—the world's longest mountain range—break the surface. Vast swaths of rugged new land emerge. [Image: image] By this point, most of the major oceans have become disconnected and stopped draining. The exact locations and sizes of the various inland seas are hard to predict; this is only a rough estimate. [Image: image] This is what the map looks like when the drain finally empties. There's a surprising amount of water left, although much of it consists of very shallow seas, with a few trenches where the water is as deep as four or five kilometers. Vacuuming up half the oceans would massively alter the climate and ecosystems in ways that are hard to predict. At the very least, it would almost certainly involve a collapse of the biosphere and mass extinctions at every level. But it's possible—if unlikely—that humans could manage to survive. If we did, we'd have this to look forward to: [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果在挑战者深渊底部创建一个半径 10 米通向太空的圆形入口，海洋的排空速度有多快？
items.model_answer:
Assuming a “10-meter drain” means a 10-meter-diameter magical opening at the bottom of Challenger Deep connected to vacuum, the ocean would not suddenly vanish. It would produce an extremely violent local outflow, but globally it would drain very slowly.

At Challenger Deep the pressure is about 110 MPa, roughly 1,100 atmospheres. Water forced into a vacuum through a 10 m diameter hole would initially accelerate to roughly

\[
v \approx \sqrt{2gh} \approx 460 \text{ m/s}
\]

in the ideal case, where \(h \approx 11{,}000\) m. Real turbulence, cavitation, and contraction at the opening would reduce that somewhat, but the flow would still be hundreds of meters per second.

The hole area would be about 78.5 m², so the initial flow rate would be on the order of

\[
20{,}000\text{–}40{,}000 \text{ m}^3/\text{s}
\]

or tens of millions of kilograms of water per second. That sounds enormous, but it is only a fraction of the Amazon River’s discharge. Spread over the whole ocean surface, it would lower sea level by only a few millimeters per year at first.

Near the drain, though, it would be catastrophic. Water, sediment, rocks, and anything nearby would be dragged into a high-speed, cavitating flow. There would not be a giant bathtub whirlpool visible at the ocean surface 11 km above; the flow would be intense only relatively close to the opening.

At the space end, the water would erupt into vacuum as a high-speed plume. It would flash-boil, cool, partly freeze into ice crystals, and expand into a cloud of vapor and snow-like ice. If the outlet were merely in low Earth orbit or near Earth, much of that material would not have escape velocity and could eventually fall back. To truly remove the water from Earth, the drain would need to send it far away or give it enough energy to escape.

The drain probably would not simply “freeze shut.” The pressure-driven flow is too energetic, and any ice forming in the vacuum plume would mostly be carried away. But an ordinary physical pipe or tunnel could not realistically survive the pressure, erosion, collapse, and geological stresses; this requires a magic or indestructible drain.

If it stayed open, the oceans would lower slowly on human timescales: about meters per millennium initially. Draining a large fraction of the oceans would take millions of years, and the rate would decrease as sea level fell because the pressure head would drop. Also, real ocean basins would eventually become isolated by ridges and continents, so not every last sea would necessarily drain through one hole in the Mariana Trench.

So the short answer is: a 10-meter drain to space would create a terrifying deep-sea jet and an ice-vapor geyser into space, but it would not empty the oceans quickly. It would be a local disaster and a planet-changing process only over geological time.

items.question: What If Earth Expanded by 1 Centimeter per Second?
human_answers: The Earth is not, currently, expanding.[1]Yes, I have a citation for this. "In conclusion, no statistically significant present expansion rate is detected by our study within the current measurement uncertainty of 0.2 mm yr−1." People have long suggested that it might be. Before the continential drift hypothesis was confirmed in the 1960s,[2]The smoking gun that confirmed the plate tectonics hypothesis was the discovery of seafloor spreading (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seafloor_spreading). The way seafloor spreading and magnetic pole reversal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geomagnetic_reversal) neatly confirmed each other is one of my favorite examples of scientific discovery at work. people had noticed that the continents fit together. Various ideas were put forward to explain this, including the idea that the ocean basins were rifts that opened in the surface of a previously-smooth Earth as it expanded. This theory was never very widespread,[3]It turns out it's kind of dumb. although it still periodically makes the rounds on YouTube. To avoid the problem of rifts in the ground, let's imagine all the matter in the Earth, from the crust to the core, starts expanding uniformly. To avoid another Drain the Oceans (http://what-if.xkcd.com/53/) scenario, we'll assume the ocean expands, too.[4]As it turns out, the ocean is expanding, since it's getting warmer. This is (currently) the main way global warming is raising the sea level. All human structures will stay. t = 1 second: [Image: image] As the Earth started expanding, you'd feel a slight jolt, and might even lose your balance for a moment. This would be very brief. Since you're moving steadily upward at 1 cm/s, you woudn't feel any kind of ongoing acceleration. For the rest of the day, you wouldn't notice much of anything. t = 1 day: After the first day, the Earth would have expanded by 864 meters. [Image: image] Gravity would take a long time to increase. If you weighed 70 kilograms when the expansion started, you'd weigh 70.01 at the end of the day. What about our roads and bridges? Eventually, they would have to break up, right? Not as quickly as you might think. Here's a puzzle I once heard: Imagine you tied a rope tightly around the Earth, so it was hugging the surface all the way around. [Image: image] Now imagine you wanted to raise the rope one meter off the ground. [Image: image] How much extra length will you need to add to the rope? Though it may seem like you'd need miles of rope, the answer is 6.28 meters. Circumference is proportional to radius, so if you increase radius by 1 unit, you increase circumference by 2π units. Stretching a 40,000-kilometer line an extra 6.28 meters is pretty negligible. Even after a day, the extra 5.4 kilometers would be handled easily by virtually all structures. Concrete expands and contracts by more than that every day.[5]Lawrence Grybosky, Thermal Expansion and Contraction (http://www.engr.psu.edu/ce/courses/ce584/concrete/library/cracking/thermalexpansioncontraction/thermalexpcontr.htm) After the initial jolt, one of the first effects you'd notice would be that your GPS would stop working. The satellites would stay in roughly the same orbits, but the delicate timing that the GPS system is based on would be completely ruined within hours. GPS timing is incredibly precise; of all the problems in engineering, it's one of the only ones in which engineers have been forced to include both special and general relativity in their calculations. Most other clocks would keep working fine. However, if you have a very precise pendulum clock, you might notice something odd—by the end of the day, it would be three seconds ahead of where it should be. t = 1 month: After a month, the Earth would have expanded by 26 kilometers—an increase of 0.4%—and its mass would have increased by 1.2%. Surface gravity would only have gone up by 0.4%, rather than 1.2%, since surface gravity is proportional to radius.[6]Mass is proportional to radius cubed, and gravity is proportional to mass times inverse square of radius, so radius3 / radius2 = radius. You might notice the difference in weight on a scale, but it's not a big deal. Gravity varies by this much between different cities already. This is a good thing to keep in mind if you buy a digital scale. If your scale has a precision of more than two decimal places, you need to calibrate it with a test weight—the force of gravity at the scale factory isn't necessarily the same as the force of gravity at your house. While you might not notice the increased gravity just yet, you'd notice the expansion. After a month, you'd see a lot of cracks opening up in long concrete structures and the failure of elevated roads and old bridges. Most buildings would probably be ok, although those anchored firmly into bedrock might start to behave unpredictably.[7]Just what you want in a skyscraper. At this point, astronauts on the ISS would start getting worried. Not only would the ground (and atmosphere) be rising toward them, but the increased gravity would also cause their orbit to slowly shrink. They'd need to evacuate quickly; they'd have at most a few months before the station reentered the atmosphere and deorbited. t = 1 year: After a year, gravity would be 5% stronger. You'd probably notice the weight gain, and you'd definitely notice the failure of roads, bridges, power lines, satellites, and undersea cables. Your pendulum clock would now be ahead by five days. What about the atmosphere? If the atmosphere isn't growing like the land and water are, air pressure would start dropping. This is due to a combination of factors. As gravity increases, then air gets heavier. But since that air is spread out over a larger area, the overall effect would be decreasing air pressure. On the other hand, if the atmosphere is also expanding, surface air pressure would rise. After years had passed, the top of Mt. Everest would no longer be in the "death zone".[8]See What-If #64 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/64/). On the other hand, since you'd be heavier—and the mountain would be taller—climbing would be more work. t = 5 years: After five years, gravity would be 25% stronger. If you weighed 70 kg when the expansion started, you'd weigh 88 kg now. Most of our infrastructure would have collapsed. The cause of the collapse would be the expanding ground below them, not the increased gravity. Surprisingly, most skyscrapers would hold up fine under much higher gravity.[9]Although I wouldn't trust the elevators. For most of them, the limiting factor isn't weight, but wind. t = 10 years: After 10 years, gravity would be 50% stronger. In the scenario where the atmosphere isn't expanding, the air would become thin enough to be difficult to breathe even at sea level. In the other scenario, we'd be ok for a little while longer. t = 40 years: After 40 years, Earth's surface gravity would have tripled.[10]Over decades, the force of gravity would grow slightly faster than you'd expect, since the material in the Earth would compress under its own weight. The pressure inside planets is roughly proportional to the square of their surface area (http://cseligman.com/text/planets/internalpressure.htm), so the Earth's core would be squeezed tightly. At this point, even the strongest humans would only be able to walk with great difficulty. Breathing would be difficult. Trees would collapse. Crops wouldn't stand up under their own weight. Virtually every mountainside would see massive landslides as material sought out a shallower angle of repose (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle_of_repose). Geologic activity would also accelerate. Most of the Earth's heat is provided by radioactive decay of minerals in the crust and mantle,[12]Although some radioactive elements, like uranium, are heavy, they get squeezed out of the lower layers because their atoms don't mesh well with the rock lattices at those depths. For more, see this chapter (http://igppweb.ucsd.edu/~guy/sio103/chap3.pdf) and this article (http://world-nuclear.org/info/Nuclear-Fuel-Cycle/Uranium-Resources/The-Cosmic-Origins-of-Uranium/#.UlxuGmRDJf4). and more Earth means more heat. Since the volume expands faster than the surface area, the overall heat flowing out per square meter will increase. It's not actually enough to substantially warm the planet—Earth's surface temperature is dominated by the atmosphere and the Sun—but it would lead to more volcanoes, more earthquakes, and faster tectonic movement. This would be similar to the situation on Earth billions of years ago, when we had more radioactive material and thus a hotter mantle. More active plate tectonics might be good for life. Plate tectonics play a key role in stabilizing the Earth's climate, and planets smaller than Earth (like Mars) don't have enough internal heat to sustain long-term geologic activity. A larger planet would allow for more geologic activity, which is why some scientists think that exoplanets slightly larger than Earth ("super-Earths") could be more friendly to life than Earth-sized ones.[11]Sasselov, Dimitar D.. The life of super-Earths: how the hunt for alien worlds and artificial cells will revolutionize life on our planet. New York: Basic Books, 2012. t = 100 years: After 100 years, we'd be experiencing over six gees of gravity. Not only would we be unable to move around to find food, but our hearts would be unable to pump blood to our brains. Only small insects (and sea animals) would be physically able to move around. Perhaps humans could survive in specially-built controlled-pressure domes, moving around by keeping most of our bodies submerged in water. [Image: image] Breathing in this situation would be difficult. It's hard to suck in air against the weight of the water, which is why snorkels can only work when your lungs are near the surface. Outside of low-pressure domes, the air would become unbreathable for a different reason. At somewhere around 6 atmospheres, even ordinary air becomes toxic.[13]R.M. Franz and P.C. Schutte, Barometric hazards within the context of deep-level mining (http://www.saimm.co.za/Journal/v105n06p387.pdf), The Journal of The South African Institute of Mining and Metallurgy Even if we'd managed to survive all the other problems, by 100 years, we'd be dead from oxygen toxicity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_toxicity). Toxicity aside, breathing dense air is difficult simply because it's heavy. Black hole? When would the Earth eventually become a black hole? It's hard to answer that, because the premise of the question is that the radius is steadily expanding while the density stays the same—whereas a black hole, the density increases. The dynamics of really huge rocky planets aren't often analyzed, since there's no obvious way that they could form; anything that large will have enough gravity to gather hydrogen and helium during planet formation and become a gas giant. At some point, our growing Earth would reach the point where adding more mass causes it to contract, rather than expand. After this point, it would collapse into something like a sputtering white dwarf or neutron star, and then—if its mass kept increasing—eventually become a black hole. But before it gets that far ... t = 300 years: It's a shame humans wouldn't live this long, because at this point, something really neat would happen. As the Earth grows, the Moon would, like all our satellites, gradually spiral inward.[14]Plummer, H. C., Note on the motion about an attracting centre of slowly increasing mass (http://adsabs.harvard.edu/full/1906MNRAS..66...83P), Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, Vol. 66, p.83 After several centuries, it would be close enough to the swollen Earth that the tidal forces between Earth and the Moon would be stronger than the gravitational forces holding the Moon together. When the Moon passed this boundary—called the Roche limit (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roche_limit)—it would gradually break apart ... [Image: image] ... and Earth would, for a short time, have rings.
items.original_question: 如果世界平均半径每秒扩大 1 厘米，人们需要多长时间才能注意到自己的体重增加？
items.model_answer:
If Earth’s radius expanded by 1 centimeter per second, it would be a slow-looking but globally catastrophic change. That is about 864 meters per day, 315 kilometers per year, and about 5% of Earth’s radius per year. Earth would double in radius in only about 20 years.

Assuming Earth’s mass stayed the same and only its radius increased, surface gravity would gradually weaken because

\[
g=\frac{GM}{R^2}.
\]

After one year, Earth’s radius would be about 1.05 times larger, so surface gravity would fall to about 91% of today’s value. After 20 years, when Earth’s radius had roughly doubled, gravity would be only one-quarter as strong as it is now.

The immediate disaster would not be lower gravity, though. It would be the stretching of the crust. Earth’s circumference would increase by about

\[
2\pi(1\text{ cm/s}) \approx 6.3\text{ cm/s},
\]

which is about 5.4 kilometers per day. Every 100-kilometer-long stretch of ground would need to become roughly 14 meters longer each day. Rock cannot deform smoothly that fast on a planetary scale, so the lithosphere would fracture violently. There would be global earthquakes, massive rifting, continent-scale tearing, and likely extreme volcanism as the crust and mantle adjusted.

Infrastructure would fail quickly. Roads, pipelines, railways, bridges, tunnels, power lines, and buildings would be torn apart as the ground stretched beneath them. Modern civilization would probably collapse within days to weeks, depending on how uniformly the expansion occurred.

The oceans would also be severely affected. As Earth’s surface area increased, the same amount of ocean water would be spread over a larger area. Sea levels would tend to fall relative to the expanding surface, exposing continental shelves in some places, while earthquakes and crustal collapse could produce huge regional floods and tsunamis elsewhere.

The atmosphere would thin. With a larger surface area and weaker gravity, air pressure at sea level would decrease over time. After a year, under simple assumptions, surface pressure could be noticeably lower; after decades, the atmosphere would be much more diffuse and less able to support present-day life.

Earth’s rotation would also change. If angular momentum were conserved, the planet’s spin would slow as its radius increased. The length of the day scales roughly with \(R^2\), so after one year the day would be about 10% longer, around 26 hours. After Earth doubled in radius, a day would be roughly four times longer, about 96 hours.

Satellites would have a problem too. Low Earth orbit is only a few hundred kilometers above the surface. Since the surface would rise by about 315 kilometers per year, many low-orbit satellites would be overtaken by the expanding atmosphere and eventually the expanding Earth itself within a year or two.

So the short answer is: Earth expanding by 1 cm/s would not feel explosive moment by moment, but it would be geologically and biologically disastrous. The planet’s crust would rip apart, gravity and air pressure would change substantially, the oceans and atmosphere would be redistributed, days would lengthen, and human civilization would likely be destroyed long before the planet had expanded by even a small fraction of its radius.

items.question: What If the Romans Had Built a Working Steam Engine?
human_answers: If a civilization finds an example of advanced technology, can they learn to duplicate the technology? You have two variables: The current technological state of the civilization. Call this "A." The technological difference between the civilization and the example. Call this "B." Therefore... The earlier "A" is, the more likely the answer is "No." The greater "B" is, the more likely the answer is "No." (This is a necessary axiom of Clarkian Magic .) As "A" advances, "B" can grow wider and the answer can still be a "Yes." What is our year point of reference? The Romans were technological marvels, but most of their advancement was in structural engineering. Had your example technology been anything involving electricity my instant answer would have been "absolutely not." However, the Roman empire encompassed a large amount of time and a large amount of technological innovation. Just as my grandmother during her lifetime saw the horse-and-buggy and steam ships as the pinnacle of transportation technology give way to walking on the moon and air flight so common people don't dress up for it any more, the Romans shifted from their early years ("absolutely not") to 300ish AD when the answer becomes "possibly, maybe even probably." An important date is 1 AD. That's when Hero of Alexandria created the Aeolipile . The Aeolipile was, basically, the first steam turbine. At this point they may not have had the other technological know-how to build a fully functioning 1800s steam engine... but they would have played with it for a while and, maybe, would have concluded, "you know, that looks an awful lot like a really complicated Aeolipile." So far, I'm convinced that Romans from at least, say, 50 A.D. would have understood what they were looking at (after enough examination & experimentation) just as we have the ability to understand string theory without having the slightest idea how to prove it. That leaves the question, could they duplicate it? The components of a steam engine are improved with milling, but do not require milling. They can all be cast. The Romans knew how to do this, so they could build the shape of everything they need. That leaves metallurgical strength. And that's where the last point I can make comes into play. The Romans knew how to think The ancient Romans knew how to figure things out. It would take time, because they're basically stuck with empirical research, but they could do it. Now the answer is "Yes, given enough time." How much time do you need between when they found the engine and when you need them to duplicate the engine? The following are all gut instinct and open to vociferous argument, but... If the answer is found in 50 A.D., needed by 300 A.D., I'm willing to go out on a limb and say "Yes." If the answer is found in 50 A.D., needed by 100 A.D., it's "very unlikely." If the answer is found in 50 B.C., needed by anything less than 200 A.D., it's "probably no." If the answer is found before 50 B.C., the answer is "impossible." There's not enough technological understanding in the Roman Empire to be capable of comprehending what they're looking at and by the time the Aeliopile came into being the example would be deteriorated or lost. Some of the comments are wondering why the Romans would care to pursue steam engine technology. The OP hasn't told us the context of the future technology appearing in the past. If all that appeared was the engine, then it might be a hard sell unless someone was bright enough to think, "what if we hook this sucker up to a cart?" On the other hand, if what appeared was a working car... the Romans would be all over this technology considering the difficulties of their wide-spread empire. The real question is, what if it was a train engine? Something that needed tracks to be valuable? That's a whomping maybe because suddenly the infrastructure investment (laying rail) is enormous. However, none of that is relevant as the OP didn't ask about it. It's the OP's problem to solve. If he hasn't, it's another question and not a valid answer to this one. A number of commenters have expressed disbelief that reverse engineering can bring substantial value to the technological innovation process. Their premise is that the technologies didn't develop for a millennia or more on their own, which assumes they couldn't have developed in 200-300 years with a working example to experiment with or to motivate them. Such commenters have no experience with reverse engineering. I do. Knowing that something is possible and you only need to duplicate it is much, much, much more powerful than not knowing something is possible and waiting around for the combination of imagination and scientific development to merge. The simple truth is if the Romans were shown with irrefutable proof the value of a working steam engine, they wouldn't have one or two guys out there tinkering around with a vague idea (which is why it took millennia naturally). They'd have thousands and more people dedicated to realizing the military advantage. (Unless as previously indicated you want to choose that they don't see the value, in which case this is all a moot conversation. You won't invent what you don't care about.) Some people like to think that innovation is somehow a fixed process, that it can't happen any faster than it did, but our own recent history in computer development has proven that wrong time and time again. You need not understand why something works to duplicate it. To conclude with an example, I wonder if some believe the specifications of an antique steam engine are as difficult to achieve as a 2017 combustion engine. Obviously, the metals and precision needed for a 2017 engine could not be duplicated by the romans during their time. But that isn't what was asked for. When I once read The Grapes of Wrath I noted a moment in the story when the family had to repair their engine. They'd lost compression, so they wrapped copper wire around the piston, shoved it back into the chamber, and off they went. I wondered about that and so asked my grandmother, who said things like that did, indeed, happen. That's an awful lot of imprecision to still have a working and useful engine. If you still want to believe the Romans couldn't reverse engineer something as simple as a steam engine (with operating documents!) under the conditions I've specified, by all means, downvote my answer. I won't feel bad.

What's a "steam engine"? A steam engine is an external combustion engine which uses steam as the working fluid. So we have: Newcomen's original atmospheric engine ? The Romans (or rather the Greek engineers on which the empire depended) could have copied it, most likely; using it is another question -- it's a very very inefficient engine, which was useful only to pump water out of coal mines, eating lots of locally extracted coal in the process. The Romans did not have coal mines... An early separate-condenser Watt engine ? Copying it would have been either impossible or very very difficult; using it may have been possible. This type of engine is much more efficient than Newcomen's contraption, but it uses axles and bearings which may or may not be possible to make with late Greco-Roman technology. Anyway, this is the only type of engine which is both useful and not light-years beyond late Greco-Roman technology. At least they could understand what they couldn't make and work to find a solution. One of the most perfect mid-19th century Corliss engines , some of which are still operational in the early 21st century? No way could the late Antiquity copy it. They wouldn't even have had the ability to express the dimensions of the pieces accurately enough, much less to make the spherical valves. Not to mention that Corliss engines operate at pressures high enough to blow up any kind of sealed vessels that an artisan could dream of in Roman times. A middle-to-late 19th century locomotive engine? I hope they don't even try. Locomotive engines operate under tight space constraints, so that in order to achieve acceptable efficiency "ordinary" locomotive engines worked with pressures starting at 12 atm up to about 20 atm, while "high-pressure" locomotive engines reached about 100 atm . A late 19th century nautical triple-expansion engine, as used, for example, on Nansen's Fram ? No way unless by magic. The physics and engineering in a late 19th century nautical steam engine are way beyond what was understandable by late Antiquity engineers. An early 20th century naval steam turbine engine? Not even with magic.

Necessity is the mother of invention. Most of the innovation related points have been well covered in other answers. This includes the Aeolipyle. Other mechanical concepts of converting circular motion into linear (screw) also existed. Could the Romans have copied the steam engine? Yes! Would the Romans have copied the steam engine? Maybe! Could/Would the Romans have used the steam engine? NO! Technology isn't developed because it can be, it is developed because it must be. There are several forces at work here. Someone needs to fund the research and development. Someone needs to invest a lot of money and resources towards the critical initial growth of the technology. There needs to be sufficient scope for returns on investment. If the new technology is disruptive, then there will also be opposition from stakeholders in the existing technology that will be affected. If the new technology is extremely prolific and could affect the balance of political power, then politics will play a part as well. The OP has not specified a date/period so lets assume the Roman empire is already established. The Romans are spread thin and find it difficult to simultaneously control their entire empire with insurgency issues everywhere. Can the steam engine aid them in consolidating their empire? Or will the emergence of a steam engine ruin existing economy and consequently their grip on the empire? Even worse, the steam engine could well fall in the hands of rebellious entities in the empire and serve as force multiplier, which once again leads to the fall of the Roman empire. In view of potentially counter productive influence of steam engine technology, the Romans may choose not to build it. In the modern era, we have a similar situation with regards to alternative energy sources. The powerful transportation and energy lobby supporting conventional sources like gas and coal are opposing alternatives. Could we develop energy efficient solar cells, wind turbines, etc? Sure! But are we? Well, kinda, to the extent that it is being allowed to and not more. What will happen to the livelihoods of millions of workers directly and indirectly affected by the gas and coal industry? What will happen to their votes? Will availability of cheap energy alter the balance of geo-political power? -- An entirely different point is that of technology innovation date. Damascus steel existed centuries ago, but last I checked, we can still not replicate it. This brings to light the point of challenge in fabrication and know-how about the fabrication process. Will it may not apply specifically to steam engine (too simple), it is conceptually possible that humans couple of thousand years from now (working with nano-tubes, micro-robots and quantum computers), may not be able to copy a steam engine! and even if they somehow managed to do so, will not use it for sure!

Knowing that something is possible is a huge headstart It's extremely common in the modern market for someone to come up with a new exciting product that opens up a whole new field (iPod, iPhone, Ford's Model T, IBM PCs, and so on) to be copied in short order. Competitors will quickly acquire copies of the invention then tweak it to make it their own. This process of copying is so widespread that patents exist to give the inventor a little breathing room to make some money before facing strong competition. A significant portion of the time spent in the process of invention is finding all the things that don't work. Handing the inventive, industrious and power hungry Romans a working example of a small steam engine that can do real work would light off a firestorm of investment. I trust that they're smart enough to realize that a machine that can do real work without muscle, whip or feed is a huge improvement. I think most people assume that the Romans would immediately jump straight to the enormous steam engines of mid-1800s Europe involving cast steel parts with highly precise machined faces and surfaces. I disagee. Given that the example they have is small, they will likely build small, low precision examples at first. Due to the imprecision, these machines won't be efficient. They won't have the theory to drive the math to get higher efficiency, at least not to start. Materials & Precision Limitations A major limitation they will have is in materials, specifically their metals. While the Romans did work in iron, the ability required to achieve high quality steel at high speed, minimal cost and in large quantity wouldn't happen till the invention of the Bessemer Process in 1855 . (High quality was available before Bessemer but not cheaply or quickly. ) The Romans would have to use copper or bronze for their pressure vessels, limiting the pressures achievable. While not ideal, it just means their steam engines won't be as efficient as machines made from steel. Higher pressures might be achievable with thicker pressure vessel walls with the added cost in materials and increased difficulty in manufacture. They'll need to invent new means of measuring distance and diameter in order to get high precision. Math A classic failing of the Roman numeric representation is the difficulty in doing multiplication. Inventing a new numerical system capable of zero and multiplication may be a bit much to ask. Evolution Just like in the 1800s, steam engines will start with large static installations. As precision and materials improves, the steam engines can be made lighter and more mobile. Fitting them to ships, who naturally have huge capacity already, will be a natural choice. Smaller engines fitted to carts might be the early tractors. Not only will this steam engine give them a leg-up on the development of steam power but also screws, bolts and nuts. The invention of these fasteners will go on to revolutionize many other areas of Roman life.

Answer is, as most often is the case with "what if" questions, complicated. But in short it can be said: no problem understanding the theory, Replicating the machinery is a different matter. Simple steam engine was known in 1st Century AD - look up aeolipyle - and Romans had excellent understanding of parts of hydrodynamics - dams, pipes, aqueducts, pumps. So they would have no problems grasping the concept. But building a working engine requires more than just knowledge. I would say that it's possible to build very simple steam engine using Roman tech, but it would be very heavy and unreliable. As sphennings points out it requires high quality of metal alloy and a degree of precision manufacture not available to Roman tech base. I believe they would quickly found out that and after maybe several decades (on the fast end) to maybe a century at least (on the slow end) to be able to produce stable output. But the issue is not the tech, but the culture. Romans were uninterested in such things simply because they had enormous excess of power (slavery). Steam engine gained in popularity after it became light and small enough to build locomotive, for example, thus Romans would not have any use for their version. You would have to put this "discovery" in proper context (warship, i.e. ironclad maybe?). Industrial revolution in England began as a attempt to address the labor shortage that plagued (no pun intended) the Europe since.. well, the plague. Add wars (most notably the 100-years war, 30 Years War and 1000 Years Muslim Invasion) and the labor shortages are a fact of life until end of 19th century. In fact, the wars were mainly why the Europe was so poor for so long, as they sucked away lives needed to improve livelihood across the continent. What Roman need would a steam engine address? Most of the Roman trade is water-borne. Mediterranean is rather small sea, there is no economic nor political reason to invest huge capital to shorten the travel times by half - it sounds impressive until you realize that it means 3 days from Alexandria to rome instead of 7 or so (admit, I'm guessing here), and there are huge grain ships plying this route already. Sail ships, cheapest possible type. Rome-Londinium route? Again - current tech is enough and speed is not economically explainable. Raw materials needed to equip Roman legions and address needs of the population are there in sufficient numbers... The only way to improve average roman life is to increase supply of raw materials, but there is no way to do it. Last thing - for widespread use of steam engine supply of coal is needed. Wood is not good source of fuel.
items.original_question: 如果罗马人发现一台可以工作的蒸汽机，他们是否能够复制和使用它？
items.model_answer:
If the Romans had built a working steam engine, the result would probably not have been an immediate ancient Industrial Revolution. It would have depended heavily on what kind of steam engine they built and whether Roman society found it economically useful enough to improve and spread.

The Romans already knew some steam principles through devices like Hero of Alexandria’s aeolipile, a small steam-powered spinning sphere. The missing step was not simply “knowing steam can move things,” but building a durable, efficient engine that could do useful work: pumping water, grinding grain, driving bellows, or powering machinery. That required good metallurgy, precision manufacturing, reliable seals, pressure vessels, and an economic reason to invest in replacing human, animal, or water power.

If Rome had developed a practical low-pressure steam engine, its first major use would likely have been in mining. Roman mines often struggled with flooding, and they already used water wheels, screws, and human labor to drain them. A steam pump could have allowed deeper mining for silver, gold, copper, tin, and iron. That might have increased state revenue, coinage, weapons production, and construction capacity. It could also have strengthened imperial logistics by improving metal supply and perhaps expanding large-scale manufacturing.

Steam power might also have helped in agriculture and urban industry. Steam-driven mills could supplement water mills where rivers were unsuitable. Workshops could use mechanical power for sawing stone, crushing ore, grinding grain, fulling cloth, or operating bellows for furnaces. In cities, steam pumps might improve water management, baths, drainage, and firefighting. The Roman army might benefit indirectly through better roads, weapons, armor, and supply production, though steam-powered vehicles or war machines would be far less likely at first.

However, several factors would limit the transformation. Roman industry was not organized around continuous technological reinvestment in the modern capitalist sense. Labor, including slave labor, was often cheaper and more socially embedded than machinery. Water power was already available in many places. Fuel would also be a constraint: large-scale steam power requires huge amounts of wood or coal. Rome used charcoal and wood heavily, but widespread steam use could have caused serious deforestation unless coal mining and transport developed alongside it. Without cheap fuel and a culture of iterative mechanical improvement, the engine might remain a specialized tool rather than a civilization-changing force.

The biggest historical change would come if the steam engine became part of a broader Roman engineering tradition: better ironworking, standardized parts, technical manuals, skilled machinists, and state or private investment in mechanical power. In that stronger scenario, Rome could experience an early form of mechanization. Its mines, mills, and arsenals might become far more productive. The empire might be wealthier and more militarily resilient, possibly delaying or changing the Western Empire’s decline. A richer technological base could also alter trade patterns, urban growth, and social organization.

But even then, a full Industrial Revolution in antiquity is unlikely without several additional developments: abundant coal use, precision machine tools, stronger scientific theory, financial institutions that reward industrial investment, and markets that favor productivity gains over labor control. Steam engines alone do not create industrialization; they become revolutionary only when embedded in the right economic and technical system.
