So rather than trying to take things away from the story, let's see what strange new pieces science can add. If there really were a superdense asteroid with enough surface gravity to walk around on, it would have some pretty surprising properties. If the asteroid has a radius of 1.75 meters, then in order to have Earth-like gravity at the surface, it would need to have a mass of about 500 million tons. This is roughly equal to the combined mass of every human on Earth. If you stood on the surface, you'd experience tidal forces. Your feet would feel heavier than your head, which you'd feel as a gentle stretching sensation. It would feel like you were stretched out on a curved rubber ball, or were lying on a merry-go-round with your head near the center. [Image: image] The escape velocity at the surface would be about 5 meters per second. That's slower than a sprint, but still pretty fast. As a rule of thumb, if you can't dunk a basketball, you wouldn't be able to escape by jumping straight up. [Image: image] However, the weird thing about escape velocity is that it doesn't matter which direction you're going.[5]... which is why it should really be called "escape speed"—the fact that it has no direction (which is the distinction between "speed" and "velocity") is actually very significant here. If you go faster than the escape speed, as long as you don't actually go toward the planet, you'll escape. That means you might be able to leave our asteroid by running horizontally and jumping off the end of a ramp. [Image: image] If you didn't go fast enough to escape the planet, you'd go into orbit around it. Your orbital speed would be roughly 3 meters per second, which is a typical jogging speed. [Image: image] But this would be a weird orbit. Tidal forces would act on you in several ways. If you reach your arm down toward the planet, it would be pulled much harder than the rest of you. And if you reach down with one arm, the rest of you gets pushed upward, which means other parts of your body feel even less gravity. Effectively, every part of your body would be trying to go in a different orbit. A large orbiting object under these kinds of tidal forces—say, a moon—will generally break apart into rings. This wouldn't happen to you. However, your orbit would become chaotic and unstable. These types of orbits were investigated in an interesting paper by Radu D. Rugescu and Daniele Mortari.[6]Rugescu, Radu D., Mortari, Daniele, "Ultra Long Orbital Tethers Behave Highly Non-Keplerian and Unstable (http://www.academia.edu/3453325/Ultra_Long_Orbital_Tethers_Behave_Highly_Non-Keplerian_and_Unstable)", WSEAS Transactions on Mathematics, Vol. 7, No. 3, March 2008, pp. 87-94. Their simulations showed that large, elongated objects follow strange patterns around their central bodies. Even their centers of mass don't move in the traditional ellipses; some adopt pentagonal orbits, while others spin chaotically and crash into the planet. [Image: image] This type of analysis could actually have practical applications. There have been various proposals over the years to use long, whirling tethers to move cargo in and out of gravity wells—a sort of free-floating space elevator (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_elevator). Such tethers could transport cargo to and from the surface of the Moon, or to pick up spacecraft from the edge of the Earth's atmosphere. The inherent instability of many tether orbits poses an interesting challenge for this kind of project. As for the residents of our superdense asteroid, they'd have to be careful; if they ran too fast, they'd be in serious danger of going into a tumble and losing their lunch. Fortunately, vertical jumps would be fine. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果一颗小行星很小但质量却很大，你真的能像小王子一样住在上面吗？
items.model_answer:
You could not live on a tiny but ultra-massive asteroid in any ordinary sense. If an asteroid were physically small but had enormous mass, it would behave less like an asteroid and more like an exotic compact object: a miniature planet, neutron-star-like body, or, if dense enough, a black hole.

Suppose the asteroid were only about 1 kilometer in radius but had Earth’s mass. Its surface gravity would be

\[
g=\frac{GM}{R^2}
\]

which would be roughly 40 million times Earth gravity. You would be flattened instantly. Even before “standing” became meaningful, the tidal forces across your body would be lethal: your feet would be pulled much more strongly than your head, tearing you apart. The escape velocity would be nearly 900 km/s, so rockets, thrown objects, and even gases would have great difficulty leaving.

Such an object also could not be made of normal rock. An Earth-mass object squeezed into a 1-km radius would have a density far beyond ordinary matter. Normal minerals would collapse under their own gravity. The body would have to be made of exotic ultra-dense matter, or it would continue collapsing.

If the asteroid were made still more massive while remaining tiny, it would eventually become a black hole. The condition is that its radius falls inside its Schwarzschild radius:

\[
R_s=\frac{2GM}{c^2}
\]

For a 1-km-radius object, anything above about one-third the mass of the Sun would be inside its own event horizon. Then there would be no solid surface to live on at all; “the asteroid” would simply be a black hole.

Even in a less extreme case where the object was not a black hole, life would be impossible. The gravity would crush you, the tidal forces would rip you apart, the surface would likely be intensely hot or unstable, and any atmosphere would be compressed into an extremely dense, crushing layer or lost depending on conditions. Time would also run slightly or strongly slower near the surface if the object were compact enough.

So the careful answer is: if it is merely somewhat massive, it becomes a tiny high-gravity world where humans could not survive; if it is ultra-massive while remaining tiny, it stops being an asteroid and becomes a compact object or black hole. Either way, you would not be able to live on it.

items.question: Could You Boil Water by Stirring It?
human_answers: No. The basic idea makes sense. Temperature is just kinetic energy. When you stir tea, you're adding kinetic energy to it, and that energy goes somewhere. Since the tea doesn't do anything dramatic like rise into the air or emit light, the energy must be turning to heat. [Image: image] The reason you don't notice the heat is that you're not adding very much of it. It takes a huge amount of energy to heat water; by volume, it has a greater heat capacity than any other common substance.[1]Hydrogen and helium have a higher heat capacity by mass, but they're diffuse gasses. The only other common substance with a higher heat capacity by mass is ammonia. All three of these lose to water when measured by volume. If you want to heat water from room temperature to nearly boiling in two minutes, you'll need a lot of power: \[1\text{ cup}\times\text{Water heat capacity}\times\tfrac{100^\circ\rm{C}-20^\circ\rm{C}}{2\text{ minutes}}=700\text{ watts}\] (Note: Pushing almost-boiling water to boiling takes a large burst of extra energy on top of what's required to heat it to the boiling point—this is called the enthalpy of vaporization (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enthalpy_of_vaporization).) Our formula tells us that if we want to make a cup of hot water in two minutes, we'll need a 700-watt power source. A typical microwave uses 700 to 1100 watts, and it takes about two minutes to heat a mug of water to make tea. It's nice when things work out![2]If they didn't, we'd just blame "inefficiency" or "vortices". 700 watts for two minutes is an awful lot of energy. When water falls from the top of Niagara Falls, it gains kinetic energy, which is converted to heat at the bottom. But even after falling that great distance, the water only heats up by a fraction of a degree.[3]\(\text{Height of Niagra Falls}\times\frac{\text{Acceleration of gravity}}{\text{Specific heat of water}}=0.12^\circ\text{C}\) To boil a cup of water, you'd have to drop it from higher than the top of the atmosphere. [Image: image] How does stirring compare to microwaving? Based on figures from industrial mixer engineering reports,[4]Brawn Mixer, Inc., Principles of Fluid Mixing (http://www.craneengineering.net/products/mixers/documents/craneEngineeringPrinciplesOfFluidMixing.pdf) (2003) I estimate that vigorously stirring a cup of tea adds heat at a rate of about a ten-millionth of a watt. That's completely negligible.[5]Tea loses heat a much higher rate than this. See: Ben Harden, Tea temperature vs. Time graph (http://www.whoi.edu/vanishingarctic/page.do?pid=48597&tid=441&cid=120786&ct=61&article=82910) The physical effect of stirring is actually a little complicated.[6]In some situations, mixing liquids can actually help keep them warm. Hot water rises, and when a body of water is large and still enough (like the ocean) a warm layer forms on the surface. This warm layer radiates heat much more quickly than a cold layer would. If you disrupt this hot layer by mixing the water, the rate of heat loss decreases. This is why hurricanes tend to lose strength if they stop moving forward—their waves churn up cold water from the depths, cutting them off from the thin layer of hot surface water that was their main source of energy. Most of the heat is carried away from teacups by the air convecting over them, and so they cool from the top down. Stirring brings fresh hot water from the depths, so it can help this process. But there are other things going on—stirring disturbs the air, and it heats the walls of the mug. It's hard to be sure what's really going on without data. Fortunately, we have the internet. StackExchange user drhodes measured the rate of teacup cooling (http://physics.stackexchange.com/a/5510) from stirring vs. not stirring vs. repeatedly dipping a spoon into the cup vs. lifting it. Helpfully, drhodes posted both high-resolution graphs and the raw data itself, which is more than you can say for a lot of journal articles. The conclusion: It doesn't really matter whether you stir, dip, or do nothing; the tea cools at about the same rate (although dipping the spoon in and out of the tea cooled it slightly faster). Which brings us back to the original question: Could you boil tea if you just stirred it hard enough? No. The first problem is power. 700 watts is about a horsepower, so if you want to boil tea in two minutes, you'll need at least one horse to stir it hard enough. [Image: image] You can reduce the power requirement by heating the tea over a longer period of time, but if you reduce it too far the tea will be cooling as fast as you're heating it. Even if you could churn the spoon hard enough—tens of thousands of stirs per second—fluid dynamics would get in the way. At those high speeds, the tea would cavitate; a vacuum would form along the path of the spoon and stirring would become ineffective. And if you stir hard enough that your tea cavitates, its surface area will increase very rapidly, and it will cool to room temperature in seconds: [Image: image] No matter how hard you stir your tea, it's not going to get any warmer.
items.original_question: 我心不在焉地搅拌着一杯热茶，心里想：我这不是给杯子里加了动能吗？我知道搅拌确实有助于冷却茶，但如果我搅拌得更快怎么办？我可以通过搅拌来煮一杯水吗？
items.model_answer:
Yes, in principle you can boil water by stirring it, because stirring does mechanical work on the water, and that work is ultimately dissipated as heat through viscosity and turbulence. This is the same basic idea as Joule’s paddle-wheel experiment: mechanical energy can be converted into thermal energy.

But in practice, with ordinary hand stirring, it is extremely hard. To heat 1 liter of water from room temperature to boiling requires roughly

\[
4.2\,\text{kJ/kg°C} \times 1\,\text{kg} \times 80°C \approx 330\,\text{kJ}
\]

of energy, not counting heat losses. A person stirring with a spoon might deliver only a few watts to tens of watts into the water, so it would take hours under ideal insulation, and in a real open container heat loss and evaporation would likely prevent it from reaching boiling.

With a powerful motorized stirrer or blender, however, it is quite possible. For example, if 500 W of mechanical power were converted into heat in the water, 1 liter could be brought from room temperature to 100°C in about 10–15 minutes, allowing for losses. Some high-power blenders can noticeably heat liquids this way.

So the careful answer is: yes, water can be boiled by stirring if enough mechanical power is supplied and heat losses are controlled; no, ordinary hand stirring in an open cup will not realistically boil it.

items.question: What If a Nearby Supernova Hit Earth with Lethal Neutrino Radiation?
human_answers: The phrase "lethal dose of neutrino radiation" is a weird one. I had to turn it over in my head a few times after I heard it. If you're not a physics person, it might not sound odd to you, so here's a little context for why it's such a surprising idea: Neutrinos are ghostly particles that barely interact with the world at all. Look at your hand—there are about a trillion neutrinos from the Sun passing through it every second. [Image: image] The reason you don't notice the neutrino flood is that neutrinos hardly interact with ordinary matter at all. On average, out of that massive flood, only one neutrino will "hit" an atom in your body every few years.[1]Less often if you're a child, since you have fewer atoms to be hit. Statistically, my first neutrino interaction probably happened somewhere around age 10. In fact, neutrinos are so shadowy that the entire Earth is transparent to them; nearly all of the Sun's neutrino flood goes straight through it unaffected. To detect neutrinos, people build giant tanks filled with hundreds of tons of material in the hopes that they'll register the impact of a single solar neutrino. This means that when a particle accelerator (which produces neutrinos) wants to send a neutrino beam to a detector somewhere else in the world, all it has to do is point the beam at the detector—even if it's on the other side of the Earth! [Image: image] That's why the phrase "lethal dose of neutrino radiation" sounds weird—it mixes scales in an incongruous way. It's like the idiom "knock me over with a feather" or the phrase "football stadium filled to the brim with ants".[2]Which would still be less than 1% of the ants in the world. If you have a math background, it's sort of like seeing the expression "ln(x)e"—it's not that, taken literally, it doesn't make sense, but it's hard to imagine a situation where it would apply.[3]If you want to be mean to first-year calculus students, you can ask them to take the derivative of ln(x)e dx. It looks like it should be "1" or something, but it's not. Similarly, it's so hard to get enough neutrinos to compel even a single one of them to interact with matter, making it hard to picture a scenario in which there'd be enough of them to affect you. Supernovae[4]"Supernovas" is also fine. "Supernovii" is discouraged. provide that scenario. The physicist who mentioned this problem to me told me his rule of thumb for estimating supernova-related numbers: However big you think supernovae are, they're bigger than that. Here's a question to give you a sense of scale: Which of the following would be brighter, in terms of the amount of energy delivered to your retina: A supernova, seen from as far away as the Sun is from the Earth, or The detonation of a hydrogen bomb pressed against your eyeball? [Image: image] Applying the physicist rule of thumb suggests that the supernova is brighter. And indeed, it is ... by nine orders of magnitude. That's why this is a neat question; supernovae are unimaginably huge and neutrinos are unimaginably insubstantial. At what point do these two unimaginable things cancel out to produce an effect on a human scale? A paper by radiation expert Andrew Karam provides an answer.[5]Karam, P. Andrew. "Gamma And Neutrino Radiation Dose From Gamma Ray Bursts And Nearby Supernovae. (http://wayback.archive.org/web/20120313045458/http://www.andrewkaram.com/andy/pdf/HPJ.pdf)" Health Physics 82, no. 4 (2002): 491-499. It explains that during certain supernovae, the collapse of a stellar core into a neutron star, 1057 neutrinos can be released (one for every proton in the star that collapses to become a neutron). Karam calculates that the neutrino radiation dose at a distance of one parsec[6]3.262 light-years, or a little less than the distance from here to Alpha Centauri. would be around half a nanosievert, or 1/500th the dose from eating a banana.[7]xkcd.com/radiation (http://xkcd.com/radiation/) A fatal radiation dose is about 4 sieverts. Using the inverse-square law, we can calculate the radiation dose: \[ 0.5\text{ nanosieverts} \times\left ( \frac{1\text{ parsec}}{x}\right )^2 = 5\text{ sieverts} \] \[ x=0.00001118\text{ parsecs}=2.3\text{ AU} \] 2.3 AU is a little more than the distance between the Sun and Mars. Core collapse supernovae happen to giant stars, so if you observed a supernova from that distance, you'd probably be inside the outer layers of the star that created it. [Image: image] The idea of neutrino radiation damage reinforces just how big supernovae are. If you observed a supernova from 1 AU away—and you somehow avoided being being incinerated, vaporized, and converted to some type of exotic plasma—even the flood of ghostly neutrinos would be dense enough to kill you. If it's going fast enough, a feather can absolutely knock you over. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 距离超新星有多近才能获得致命剂量的中微子辐射？
items.model_answer:
A supernova close enough to give Earth a lethal dose from neutrinos would be an extreme, essentially solar-system-scale event, not an ordinary “nearby star” event.

In a core-collapse supernova, roughly 99% of the released energy comes out as neutrinos in a burst lasting about 10 seconds. Normally neutrinos pass through matter almost unhindered; a supernova in our galaxy would send trillions through each person with essentially no biological effect. But if the supernova were close enough—on the order of a few to perhaps tens of astronomical units, depending on the supernova and neutrino spectrum—the flux would be so enormous that even rare neutrino interactions would deposit a lethal ionizing-radiation dose throughout the Earth.

The immediate effect would be unusual compared with ordinary radiation disasters: there would be almost no shielding. The neutrinos would pass through the atmosphere, oceans, rock, bunkers, and the far side of Earth. People underground or underwater would receive nearly the same dose as people on the surface. The burst would irradiate bodies internally and uniformly over seconds. At merely “lethal” levels, humans and many animals would suffer acute radiation sickness and die over hours to weeks; at much higher doses, death could be rapid from nervous-system and organ failure. Many microbes and hardy organisms might survive a human-lethal dose, but a sufficiently larger neutrino dose could sterilize much of the biosphere.

The Earth itself would not be blown apart by the neutrinos. Even a biologically catastrophic neutrino dose corresponds to a tiny temperature rise in rock and ocean. The planet would remain physically intact.

However, a supernova close enough for lethal neutrino radiation would bring much worse follow-up effects. The neutrinos would arrive first, escaping the collapsing core before the main light and shock. Soon afterward, intense X-rays, ultraviolet radiation, visible light, and later the supernova ejecta would strike. At AU-scale distances, that radiation and blast would likely scorch or vaporize the surface, strip atmosphere, boil oceans, and make the planet utterly uninhabitable. In that scenario, neutrinos would be the first killer, not the final one.

For real Earth, this is not a plausible natural threat. There is no massive star close enough to do this; even famous candidates like Betelgeuse are hundreds of light-years away. A supernova at those distances could be spectacular and scientifically valuable, and a very close one within tens of parsecs could damage the ozone layer via cosmic rays and gamma rays, but its neutrino radiation would be harmless to life.

human_answers: Tall. [Image: image] From this initial height of 0.5 meters, they grow to about 1.5 or 2.0 meters: [Image: image] Babies grow fastest right after they're born. During their first month, infants grow about 4.4 centimeters, ten times their growth rate during their early teenage years. [Image: image] In Maria's scenario, this growth rate continues until about age 20: [Image: image] Let's follow that child's growth over the years. By its first birthday, the baby would be a meter long: [Image: image] At 2 years and 3 months, the kid would reach 169 centimeters (5'7"), the average adult height in the US. [Image: image] By age 3, we'd have a 2.08 meter (6'10") toddler, taller than Darth Vader ... [Image: image] ... and much taller than Yoda: [Image: image] By age 4, the child would be nearly nine feet tall, able to dunk a basketball without jumping.[2]A 7'8" Harlem Globetrotters player can almost dunk without jumping (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HTnC0RBXwws), so the threshold for a clear no-jump dunk is probably around 8 feet. Even breathing would be difficult; we might be able to position ourselves to keep our airways opened, but to breathe in a lungful of air would require very high airflow rates; we'd experience tornado winds all the way down our airways. Our giant would reach a final height of between 10 and 12 meters, assuming growth tapered off around age 20. At that height, they'd be able to comfortably dunk a basketball while keeping one hand on the court outside the three-point line.[3]A creative NBA 2K3 mod shows us what that player might look like (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vGt10eu4XB8). [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果我们在整个发育期（即直到十几岁/二十岁出头）都以与第一个月相同的速度生长，人类会达到什么高度？
items.model_answer:
If humans kept growing at the absolute growth rate of a one-month-old baby, they would become giants very quickly.

A one-month-old baby typically gains about 3–4 cm in length per month and about 0.8–1 kg in mass per month. If that height growth never slowed, a person who was about 50 cm long at birth would be roughly 4–5 meters tall by age 12 and around 7–9 meters tall by age 20. By old age, they could be tens of meters tall if growth continued indefinitely.

But the body could not simply scale up safely. Weight does not scale the same way height does. If a human became, say, 8 meters tall while keeping normal proportions, their mass would likely be several tonnes, not merely a few hundred kilograms. This runs into the square-cube law: as height increases, body mass grows roughly with volume, while bone and muscle strength grow only with cross-sectional area. In simpler terms, the person would get heavy faster than their skeleton and muscles got strong.

So biologically, such a human would need radically thicker bones, stronger muscles, a much more powerful heart, huge lungs, and an enormous food supply. Heat removal would also become a problem, because large bodies have less surface area relative to volume. Without major anatomical changes, they would likely suffer bone failure, heart failure, breathing problems, and mobility collapse long before reaching giant size.

If “rate” means percentage growth rather than absolute centimeters per month, the result is even more impossible. Babies grow by a large fraction of their body size in early infancy; compounding that monthly would produce absurdly huge sizes in only a few years.

So the direct answer is: if humans kept growing like one-month-old babies, they would become enormous, potentially many meters tall by adulthood, but ordinary human biology could not support it. They would either need a completely redesigned body or they would not survive.

items.original_question: 如果霸王龙被释放到纽约市，它每天需要消耗多少人才能获得所需的卡路里摄入量？
items.model_answer:
If a Tyrannosaurus rex were suddenly released in New York City, the most likely outcome would be a short-lived but extremely dangerous emergency, not a city-destroying disaster.

At first, there would be panic. A T. rex was roughly 12 meters long, stood several meters high at the hips, and weighed perhaps 6–9 tons. In a dense area like Manhattan, it could flip cars, smash through storefronts, crush pedestrians, and cause stampedes or traffic crashes. The biggest immediate danger might not even be the dinosaur deliberately hunting people, but the chaos it would create.

The T. rex would probably be confused and stressed. New York is full of loud vehicles, lights, hard pavement, narrow streets, glass, steel, and unfamiliar smells. It would not understand roads, traffic, subway grates, bridges, or crowds. It might lash out defensively, bite at moving objects, or pursue people or animals that trigger predatory instincts. Its bite would be catastrophic to any person or vehicle part it grabbed, but it would not be an unstoppable monster. It would have trouble maneuvering in tight streets, could slip on pavement, injure its feet or legs, and might be boxed in by buildings and traffic barriers.

Emergency services would quickly mobilize. Police would establish a perimeter, shut down streets, evacuate nearby buildings, and use helicopters or drones to track it. Animal control tranquilizers would be difficult: an animal that large would require a very large dose, and sedatives might take too long to work. If the T. rex were actively killing people or moving toward dense crowds, authorities would likely use lethal force. Heavy firearms would be effective against it, especially from protected positions or helicopters. The military or specialized police units could probably stop it within hours if necessary.

If officials tried to capture it alive, the safest approach would be containment: lure or drive it into a large open area such as a park, stadium, industrial yard, or fenced zone, then immobilize it with carefully dosed drugs and physical barriers. Central Park would be especially dangerous because it provides open space and crowds, but it would also be easier to cordon off than dense streets.

Ecologically, one T. rex would not establish a population. It could eat zoo animals, horses, dogs, livestock in transport, or people if it encountered them, but it would need huge amounts of meat and would not be well adapted to the modern urban environment. It might also be vulnerable to modern pathogens, pollution, stress, overheating, or injuries from concrete and metal structures.

So the realistic answer is: there would be severe local destruction, injuries, likely deaths, massive media attention, and an enormous emergency response. But New York City would not “fall.” A single T. rex would probably be contained, tranquilized, or killed fairly quickly—most likely within the same day.

items.question: What If You Dumped All the World's Tea into the Great Lakes?
human_answers: Weak, bordering on homeopathic. The standard cup of tea, as described by the International Organization for Standardization in ISO 3103 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=8250), contains two grams of tea per 100 mL of water.[1]Further ISO standards concerning tea include ISO 3720 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=51541) (black tea), ISO 11287 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=51540) (green tea), and ISO 14502-2 (http://www.iso.org/iso/iso_catalogue/catalogue_tc/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=31357) (the difference between black tea and green tea). The Great Lakes have a volume of about 22,600 cubic kilometers, which means we would need about 450 billion tons of tea to reach proper strength. According to the Tea Board of India, one year's global tea harvest totals only about 4.8 million tons,[2]Using figures from this report (http://www.teaboard.gov.in/pdf/Tea%20Statistics%20Global%20Scenario.pdf) extrapolated forward to 2014. only 1/100,000th of what we'd require to make Great Lake Tea. If we dumped those 4.8 million tons into the lakes, the resulting tea would be about as strong as if we'd dripped two drops of tea in a bathtub.[3]Technically, calling this kind of tea "homeopathic" is an exaggeration, since substances in homeopathy are diluted way more than this. Proper bathtub tea, of course, requires one 3-kg bag. [Image: image] For better lake tea, we should find a lake with a volume of 240 million cubic meters (0.24 cubic kilometers). Wular Lake in Kashmir is one candidate. Its volume varies with the seasons, but during the winter it's just about exactly the right size.[4]Unfortunately, it's shrinking (http://www.ramsar.org/pdf/wurc/wurc_mgtplan_india_wular.pdf). (For winter volume, see the chart on page 18 of that report.) India is the world's second-largest tea producer, so it's also conveniently located. Ullswater, in the UK's Lake District, is another great candidate. With a relatively stable year-round volume of about 0.23 cubic kilometers, it would be an excellent site for brewing a global cup of tea. Of course, while neither Wular Lake or Ullswater has ever been used as a giant teakettle, something like this was—famously—attempted in my own backyard in Boston. In 1773, a group of colonists disguised as American Indians[5]They dressed up as American Indians to align themselves politically with the Americas—against Britain—invoking the popular European stereotype of the free and noble savage. The Mohawk people, the actual Indians who the protesters were mimicking, mistrusted the settlers encroaching on their land, sided with the British during the subsequent war, and afterward were driven from their homes by the Americans and fled to Canada. boarded three British ships and threw the cargo of tea—around 44 tons of it—into Boston Harbor to protest British-run tax policy. Boston Harbor has a volume of about 0.44 cubic kilometers, which means that the "tea" brewed in 1773 would have been even more dilute than our Great Lakes tea. The harbor is also somewhat larger[6]The tidal range in Boston is so large (over three meters) that the harbor's volume at high tide is nearly double what it is at low. than Wular Lake or Ullswater, so all the tea in the world would still make Boston Harbor slightly too weak. [Image: image] There's another problem: Heat. If you wanted to make tea from a lake, such as Ullswater or Wular Lake, you'd have to heat the water up. Is that even possible? There's clearly enough stored energy in the world to do it. After all, we presumably heat that amount of water for tea every year already; we just do it in small batches around the world. To heat up Ullswater to 80°C[7]Lots of people have very strong opinions on what this temperature should be. Please direct any corrections on this matter to What-If Tea-Related Complaints Dep't, c/o Her Majesty The Queen, Buckingham Palace, London SW1A 1AA. would take \(6.6 \times 10^{16}\) joules of energy—about 20 days worth of British electricity consumption. which is roughly what would be released if you dropped a water bottle full of antimatter in the lake. [Image: image] Asking Britain to go without electricity for 20 days just to fill one of their lakes with tea seems like it might be a hard sell. Fortunately, there's an easier solution. Boiling Lake in Dominica is a volcanic lake about 60 meters across. Its temperature varies, but it's often near boiling at the edges and vigorously boiling in the center. Measuring the depth of the lake is difficult, so it's hard to get an estimate of the total volume. [Image: image] Frying Pan Lake in New Zealand, on the other hand, is the largest hot lake in the world. It has a volume of about 200,000 m3, and an average temperature of around 50°C—not quite hot enough for tea, but much closer than Ullswater or Wular Lake. New Zealanders consume about 600 grams of tea per person,[8]Kerryn Pollock. 'Tea, coffee and soft drinks (http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/tea-coffee-and-soft-drinks)', Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand, updated 15-Jul-13 for a total of 2,700 tons of tea. If they waited until Frying Pan Lake got particularly hot, then dunked it all in at once ... [Image: image] ... they could brew a year's worth of tea in minutes.
items.original_question: 如果我们把世界上所有的茶叶都倒进五大湖怎么办？与普通的茶相比，湖茶的浓度如何？
items.model_answer:
Assuming “all the world’s tea” means roughly one year of global dry tea production, about 6–7 million tonnes, dumping it into the Great Lakes would not turn them into drinkable tea.

The Great Lakes contain about 22,700 cubic kilometers of water, or 2.27 × 10¹⁶ liters. Spreading 6.5 million tonnes of dry tea evenly through that gives a concentration of only about 0.3 milligrams of tea per liter. Normal brewed tea is roughly 8 grams per liter, so the lakes would be about 25,000–30,000 times too dilute to taste like tea. It would be more like putting one cup of tea into several thousand liters of water.

If instead you brewed all that tea first and dumped the liquid in, it still would not matter much physically. All the brewed tea from a year’s global production would be less than 1 cubic kilometer, compared with 22,700 cubic kilometers in the Great Lakes. Lake levels would rise only a few millimeters, and even if the tea were hot, the temperature change would be only a few thousandths of a degree.

Environmentally, though, it would be bad, especially near wherever the dumping occurred. Millions of tonnes of wet tea leaves would form mats, clog intakes, wash onto shores, and sink into sediments. As the leaves decomposed, microbes would consume oxygen, causing local anoxic zones and possible fish kills. The tea would also add caffeine, tannins, nitrogen, phosphorus, and other organic compounds; if perfectly mixed, the caffeine concentration might be on the order of several micrograms per liter, not instantly lethal lake-wide but definitely a major pollution event.

So the direct answer is: the Great Lakes would not become giant cups of tea. They are far too large. But the dumping site and nearby ecosystems would suffer a serious organic-waste pollution disaster.

items.question: What If All the World's Viruses Were Gathered in One Place?
human_answers: It would be a huge pile, but human viruses would make up only a tiny fraction of it. HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, has killed tens of millions of people worldwide, and over 30 million people are currently living with HIV. The number of copies of the virus carried in someone's blood can vary dramatically,[1]Data on viral load—the number of copies of the virus per mL of blood—can be found in this paper (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23196933). but across all the people in the world, there probably exists about a spoonful worth of HIV. [Image: image] The typical healthy human body contains about \(3 \times 10^{12}\) viruses. This is actually not as many as you might expect; by volume, humans are apparently a less friendly environment for viruses than, say, soil.[2]An area of wetlands in Delaware (http://www.rcn.montana.edu/pubs/pdf/2008/Srinivasiah%20Res%20%20Micro%202008.pdf) contains something like four billion viruses per mL of soil, in case you were looking for a fun vacation destination. If you gathered together all the viruses in all the humans in the world, they would fill about ten oil drums: [Image: image] These 10 barrels only represent a tiny portion of the global virus community. Most of the world's viruses aren't found in humans. They're found in the sea. Seawater is full of microorganisms, and we've recently learned that those microorganisms are preyed on by viruses in a big way. Every day, about one in five living cells in the ocean is killed by a virus.[3]Marine viruses—major players in the global ecosystem (https://www.uni-due.de/imperia/md/content/water-science/ws0910/2031b_02z_ws0910_suttle_marine_viruses.pdf) These viruses are found from the surface of the ocean down to the depths.[4]Oddly, as you go further offshore and further down, the concentration of viruses doesn't decrease as much as the concentration of bacteria, so the virus-to-bacteria ratio is higher in the deep oceans than near the shore. Because the sea is so big,[5]Citation: Go and look at the sea. It's big. it contains a staggering number of viruses. If you piled up all these viruses—more than 1030 of them—in one place, they would be the size of a small mountain. [Image: image] It's hard to say exactly what the virus mountain would look like, but it would probably resemble something in between pus and meat slurry.[6]Blame Dave—he's the one who asked. Regardless of its exact appearance, it would almost certainly be disgusting. [Image: image] The pile wouldn't stay mountain-shaped for long, any more than a mountain of any organic secretion would.[7]If you don't believe me, try building a mountain of earwax or snot. You'll find you can't make it higher than a few inches before your friends and family show up and sit you down for a talk. To avoid a gigantic flood, it might be better to collect them into some kind of container. MetLife Stadium, host of Super Bowl XLVIII, has a volume of about 1.5 million cubic meters. Earth's viruses could fill the stadium about 150 times over. So if you watch the Super Bowl, take a moment to picture all the players floating, suspended, in a sea of yellowish-white secretions. [Image: image] Enjoy the game!
items.original_question: 如果世界上的所有病毒都集中到一个区域会怎样？它们会占据多少体积以及它们会是什么样子？
items.model_answer:
If all the world’s viruses were gathered into one place, they would not make a planet-sized mass or a continent-sized heap. They would probably form something on the order of a kilometer-scale pile or reservoir.

Earth contains roughly \(10^{31}\) virus particles, most of them bacteriophages that infect bacteria and archaea, especially in the oceans. Individual viruses are tiny, typically tens to hundreds of nanometers across. If compressed together as particles, their total volume would be roughly \(10^8\) to \(10^{10}\) cubic meters, depending on the assumed average virus size. That corresponds to a cube perhaps several hundred meters to a couple of kilometers on a side, or a mound comparable in scale to a small mountain or large lake basin. Their total mass might be around hundreds of millions to several billion tonnes, very uncertain but not astronomically large.

It would not behave like a giant living organism. Viruses have no metabolism of their own; they do not eat, move, or reproduce unless they enter suitable host cells. A huge pile of viruses would mostly be an inert biological powder, sludge, or aerosol hazard. Many would quickly degrade from heat, drying, ultraviolet light, oxidation, or chemical damage unless preserved.

It would also not be uniformly deadly to humans. The overwhelming majority of viruses on Earth cannot infect humans at all. Most infect bacteria, archaea, algae, plants, insects, fungi, or other organisms. However, a concentrated collection containing every human pathogen—smallpox-like viruses if any existed, influenza viruses, coronaviruses, Ebola-like viruses, HIV, rabies, measles, and many others—would be an extreme biohazard. If aerosolized or spread into water, food, or wounds, it could expose people to enormous infectious doses of many diseases at once.

The larger consequence would be ecological. Viruses are deeply involved in regulating microbial populations, especially in the oceans. They kill vast numbers of bacteria and plankton daily, recycle nutrients, shape evolution, and influence carbon cycling. Removing all viruses from everywhere else and putting them in one place would abruptly disrupt ecosystems, microbial food webs, ocean chemistry, soil biology, and many host–parasite balances. Some disease burdens would temporarily vanish, but the biosphere would be thrown into a major and probably dangerous imbalance.

So the short answer is: all the world’s viruses would make a surprisingly modest, kilometer-scale mass of mostly inert microscopic particles, but it would be one of the most hazardous biological materials imaginable, and removing those viruses from the rest of Earth would seriously destabilize global ecosystems.

items.question: What If You Tried to Catch a Bullet after It Slowed Down?
human_answers: Yes. The "bullet catch" is a common magic trick in which a magician appears to catch a fired bullet in mid-flight—often between their teeth. This an illusion, of course; it's not possible to catch a bullet like that.[1]This was confirmed (http://www.discovery.com/tv-shows/mythbusters/mythbusters-database/catch-bullet-teeth.htm) by Mythbusters in episode 4 of Season 4. But under the right conditions, you could catch a bullet. It would just take a lot of patience.[2]I'd like to remind everyone that while I write sometimes about the interesting physics of bullets, I'm not an authority on firearms safety. I was raised Quaker (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers); I've never held a gun, much less fired one. A bullet fired straight up would eventually reach a maximum height.[3]Don't do this. In neighborhoods where people fire guns upward in celebration, bystanders are routinely killed (http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/PDF/wk/mm5350.pdf) by falling bullets. It probably wouldn't stop completely; more likely, it would be drifting sideways at a couple meters per second. At that speed, as long as you were in the right place at the right time, you could snatch it out of the air. If someone fired a bullet upward ... [Image: image] ... and you were hanging out in a hot-air balloon directly above the firing range ... [Image: image] ... it's possible that you could reach out and snag the bullet at the apex of its flight. If you succeeded, you might notice something odd: In addition to being hot, the bullet would be spinning. It would have lost its upward momentum, but not its rotational momentum; it would still have the spin given to it by the barrel of the gun. [Image: image] This effect can be seen, dramatically, when a bullet is fired at ice.[4]Floor water. As confirmed by dozens of YouTube videos (https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=bullet%20spinning%20ice) (and Mythbusters), bullets fired into ice are often found still spinning rapidly. You'd have to grab the bullet firmly; otherwise, it might jump out of your hand. If you don't have a balloon, you could potentially make this work from a mountain peak. Mount Thor, which you may remember from question #51 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/51/), features a vertical drop of 1,250 meters. According to ballistics lab Close Focus Research, this is almost exactly how high a .22 Long Rifle bullet will fly if fired directly upward.[5]Close Focus Research, Maximum Altitude For Bullets Fired Vertically (http://www.closefocusresearch.com/maximum-altitude-bullets-fired-vertically) [Image: image] If you want to use larger bullets, you'll need a much larger drop; an AK-47's bullet can go over two kilometers upward. There are no purely vertical cliffs that are that tall, so you'd need to fire the bullet at an angle, and it would have significant sideways speed at the top of its arc. However, a suitably tough baseball glove might be able to snag it.[6]In fact, according to Rifle Magazine, a gun writer once claimed (https://www.riflemagazine.com/magazine/article.cfm?magid=78&tocid=1094) that at a thousand yards, he could catch ordinary rifle bullets with a baseball glove. Of course, he was being figurative—you wouldn't see the bullet coming, so you'd be just as likely to catch it with your face as with your glove. In any of these scenarios, you'd have to get extraordinarily lucky. Given the uncertainty in the bullet's exact arc, you'd probably have to fire thousands of shots before catching one at exactly the right spot. And by that point, you may find you've attracted some attention. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 有没有什么方法可以让枪射击后子弹飞到空中，然后可以安全地用手接住？例如射手位于海平面，捕手位于山上，位于枪的最远射程处。
items.model_answer:
If the bullet has only “slowed down” from muzzle speed, you should not try to catch it. A typical handgun bullet might leave the barrel at around 300–400 m/s with hundreds of joules of energy. Even after slowing to, say, 100 m/s, an 8-gram bullet still has about 40 joules of kinetic energy. That is much less than at the muzzle, but it is delivered by a small, hard piece of metal over a tiny area, so it can still penetrate skin or seriously injure your hand.

A falling bullet that was fired straight up may reach terminal velocity rather than returning at muzzle speed. Depending on its shape and whether it is tumbling, that might be on the order of tens to over 100 m/s. That is often not as deadly as a normally fired bullet, but it is still dangerous and not something you can safely catch barehanded. Bullets fired at an angle are worse: they can stay stabilized and retain much more horizontal speed, remaining lethal at long distances.

In principle, if a bullet were slowed enough — to the speed of a tossed pebble, perhaps only a few meters per second — you could catch it, especially with a glove or soft padding. But at ordinary “spent bullet” speeds, the problem is not just momentum; it is the concentrated impact. So the direct answer is: only if it has been slowed to a harmless thrown-object speed. A merely “slowed” bullet is still very unsafe to catch.

items.question: What If Astronauts Tried to Reach the Moon by Hitting Golf Balls in Orbit?
human_answers: It depends how good your swing is. That sounds glib, but it's sort of true. The answer to this question hinges on exactly how fast you can hit a golf ball. Sometimes, exact numbers don't matter that much. If my baseball, car, dog, or Zamboni goes a little faster than yours,[1]$20 says they will! it will go a little farther. But that's not how it works in rocket golf. The design of our spaceship turns out to involve an equation where the speed of the golf ball is in the exponent. That means a small change in speed can make a big difference. The equation in question—which might be my favorite in all of physics—the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation: \[ \Delta v = v_\text{exhaust} \ln \frac{m_\text{initial}}{m_\text{final}} \] This equation comes up a lot in What If calculations. I like it both because it says something fundamental about our ability to explore the universe, and because you can use it to get really good at Kerbal Space Program. With some rearranging, the equation can help us figure out how much of our ship's weight has to be golf balls: \[ \frac{\text{Mass of ship plus golf balls}}{\text{Mass of ship alone}} = e ^ \left ( \frac{\text{Ship's change in speed}}{\text{Speed of golf ball}} \right ) \] Someone who, like me, has never been golfing before, might—after swinging and missing a few times—manage to hit the ball at 120 mph (50 m/s).[2]See Trackman's page on ball speed (http://mytrackman.com/explore/trackman-data/trackman-ball-data/ball-speed) To get to the Moon from low Earth orbit, you would need enough fuel to add 5,300 m/s to your ship's speed. By putting those numbers into the rocket equation, we can find out how large a sack of golf balls would have to be for the average golfer to reach the Moon. If we plug it in to Wolfram|Alpha (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=please+calculate+2*%28%283%2F%284*pi%29%29*%28%28e%5E%285300+m%2Fs+%2F+120mph%29%29*200+kg%29+%2F+%2865%25*1.15+kg%2FL%29%29%5E%281%2F3%29+thank+you) ... [Image: image] ... we find that the bag of golf balls will have to be just about exactly 100 billion miles in diameter. That's much, much bigger than our Solar System.[3]As a Fermi rule of thumb, planets in the inner Solar System are 100 million kilometers away and planets in the outer Solar System are a billion kilometers away. Or miles; either one works. [Image: image] It would also promptly and violently collapse into a black hole. Fortunately, we should be able to avert that disaster by making relatively small changes to the "120" in that equation. If we increase the golf ball's speed from 120 mph to 150, it shrinks the answer dramatically, and the required number of golf balls would fit snugly between the Sun and Mars. Still too big to avoid a catastrophic collapse, but we're getting somewhere. [Image: image] Tiger Woods can hit a golf ball at about 180 mph, which means that if he were powering our spaceship, the bag of golf balls would be only twice the diameter of the Sun! [Image: image] According (http://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/records-10000/fastest-golf-drive/) to the Guinness Book of World Records, the record for fastest golf drive is 211 mph, set by Maurice Allen in 2012. This corresponds to a bag of golf balls only 100,000 kilometers across—smaller than Jupiter, but still (obviously) not practical. However, golfer Ryan Winther claims (http://www.ryanwinther.com/about_records.htm) to have beaten this record, though without Guinness observers there.[4]And, obviously, it doesn't count unless it's overseen by people from a beer company. If you want to set a world record, hit a golf ball at a radar gun and get it certified by the Mike's Hard Lemonade people. His ball speed was measured by something called the "Titleist Performance Institute" to be 226.7 mph, and he claims a personal best of 237 mph. If he could consistently hit 237 mph, we could shrink our fuel container down to the size of Earth[5]Although it would still be large enough to partially collapse under its own gravity, similar to what happened to the mole of moles (http://what-if.xkcd.com/4/). [Image: image] This still wouldn't work; even in a high orbit, the massive tides from your ship—which is much more massive than the Moon—would be highly disruptive. We could probably shrink the fuel tank further by using "illegal" equipment. There are Superball-style balls and "trampoline face" clubs which can hit much farther, and which would not be permitted in tournament play.[6]On the other hand, we're talking about a sport that brought whites-only clubs with it into the 21st century (http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/06/01/AR2010060103918.html), and Agusta, host of the Masters, admitted its first woman in 2012 (http://www.reuters.com/article/2012/08/20/us-golf-augusta-idUSBRE87J0IE20120820). So maybe we shouldn't worry too much about their traditional rules. A hypothetical 270 mph drive would allow a fuel tank the size of the Moon. At this point, why are we even using a club? According (http://arxiv.org/abs/1305.0966) to research from the US Air Force Academy and BTG Research,[7]Oddly, both researchers have the name "Courtney". There are probably about 200,000 people in the US named Courtney (first or last); maybe we should recruit them to all build potato cannons. a potato cannon fueled by acetylene can launch a potato at 140 m/s (310 mph). If it were capable of launching golf balls at that speed,[8]We're not factoring in the weight of the acetylene—but then again, we also weren't factoring in the weight of the hamburgers the golfer would need to eat to keep hitting those drives. our ship would have a diameter of only 150 miles! [Image: image] There's the small problem that manufacturing that many golf balls would cost quintillions of dollars. You could bring the size down further by making the potato cannon more and more powerful and efficient, but at that point you're simply building a rocket. And the potato cannon scenario has an extra perk. If you somehow made the balls durable enough to survive atmospheric entry, and you set up your maneuver so the ejected golf balls covered the middle latitudes evenly, then over the course of this maneuver you would be statistically likely to hit a hole-in-one ... at every golf course in the world. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 假设你有一艘绕地球轨道运行的宇宙飞船，你能通过向另一个方向击打高尔夫球来推动你的飞船达到超过逃逸速度的速度吗？如果是这样，需要多少个高尔夫球才能到达月球？
items.model_answer:
No, not from any normal Earth orbit.

From a low Earth orbit like the ISS, an astronaut and a golf ball are already moving around Earth at about 7.7 km/s. To send the ball onto a Moon-reaching trajectory, you would need to add roughly 3.1 km/s in the forward orbital direction. A very hard golf shot gives a ball only about 50–80 m/s of extra speed. That is less than 3% of what is needed.

If the astronaut hit the ball perfectly prograde from ISS altitude, it would not head to the Moon. It would enter a slightly higher Earth orbit, perhaps raising its apogee by a few hundred kilometers. If hit backward, it would lower its orbit and likely reenter sooner. In either case, it becomes dangerous space debris, not a lunar projectile.

If the idea is that astronauts propel themselves toward the Moon by hitting golf balls backward, momentum conservation makes that hopeless too. A 46-gram golf ball struck at 70 m/s gives a 150-kg suited astronaut only about 0.02 m/s of recoil. Reaching the Moon from low Earth orbit requires thousands of meters per second, so you would need an absurd number of balls, and if you had to carry them, the mass requirement becomes effectively impossible.

So the careful answer is: a golf ball hit in orbit could slightly change orbit, but it cannot reach the Moon unless it is already on an almost lunar-reaching trajectory. To get from low Earth orbit to the Moon, you need rocket-scale delta-v, not golf-swing-scale delta-v.

items.question: How Powerful Would Radar Have to Be to Stop a Speeding Car?
human_answers: Radio waves exert force on things. Not a lot of force. The average cell phone transmitter exerts about a billionth of a newton of pressure on its surroundings. That means that it would take several trillion cell phones to collectively levitate a snowflake; the pressure from one phone wouldn't even measurably slow it down. [Image: image] If the phone did put out enough energy to levitate a snowflake by radiation pressure, the power flowing through the snowflake (a few kilowatts) would quickly cause the snowflake to become a raindrop, which would quickly become water vapor, which would quickly become the least of your problems. [Image: image] The fate of the snowflake hints at what kinds of problems our car will encounter. If you want to slow down a one-ton car by radiation pressure, your radar gun would need to deliver about two trillion joules worth of radiation—the energy of a small nuclear weapon.[1]The formula for figuring out that amount out is simple: The energy required is equal to the desired change in speed (say, 20 mph) times the mass of the car times the speed of light. The radar gun would need to emit even more energy than that, since not all of the radiation will be absorbed (or reflected) by the car.[2]The fact that some of it is reflected makes things easier, since that doubles the momentum delivered by the radiation. This is why simple solar sails are white and not black. For more on radar reflectivity of materials, you can check out one of the worst scanned PDFs I've ever seen (http://www.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/601365.pdf). Your radar gun would also vaporize the car. This is a problem, in one sense, but it's also a solution. Even if most of the energy is reflected, the portion that was absorbed would convert the materials in the car into gas or plasma. The expanding cloud would exert a lot more pressure on the car than the radiation itself.[3]This process, called ablation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_ablation), is also what got rid of the Moon in the What If #13 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/13/). This is convenient—it means that we wouldn't need nearly as much energy to stop the car as we would using radiation pressure alone. There are even simpler ways to slow down a car with radiation. For example, you could aim a radiation beam at the tires and melt them, or use the electromagnetic radiation to knock out the car's electrical systems. Or just use a laser pointer to blind the driver and hope they reflexively slow down. Of course, you don't need any of those things. If your goal is to slow down the car—rather than to catch speeders—your radar gun doesn't need any power. You can just stand by the side of the road next to a police car holding a fake radar gun. [Image: image] In the end, a radar gun capable of slowing cars through radiation pressure would be roughly equivalent to a nuclear weapon, and using nuclear strikes in response to traffic violations is probably overkill. It would work, in the literal sense, but it would also destroy the offender, car, police officer, road, and all other traffic for miles around.[4]It would also cause fragments of the driver to violate the speed limit in all directions at once. Of course, maybe using the apocalyptic radar gun wouldn't be necessary; just the threat of a nuclear strike against drivers would probably deter speeding. Come to think of it, maybe that's what those other signs you sometimes see are hinting at. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 我偶尔会在限速标志上看到“雷达强制执行”，我不禁要问：无线电波必须有多强才能阻止汽车超速，如果尝试这样做会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If you mean “stop it by pushing on it with the radar beam,” the radar would need to be absurdly powerful: on the order of terawatts at the car.

Radiation carries momentum. A beam of power \(P\) produces a force of roughly

\[
F=\frac{P}{c}
\]

if absorbed, or at best

\[
F=\frac{2P}{c}
\]

if perfectly reflected, where \(c\) is the speed of light.

Take a typical car:

\[
m \approx 1500\ \text{kg}
\]

moving at highway speed:

\[
v \approx 30\ \text{m/s}
\]

To stop it in about 3 seconds, the needed force is

\[
F=\frac{mv}{t} \approx \frac{1500 \times 30}{3} \approx 15{,}000\ \text{N}
\]

So the radar power would have to be

\[
P \approx Fc \approx 15{,}000 \times 3\times10^8
\approx 4.5\times10^{12}\ \text{W}
\]

for absorption, or about half that for perfect reflection:

\[
P \sim 2\text{–}5\ \text{terawatts}
\]

That is trillions of watts delivered onto the car. The total beam energy required would be about

\[
E \approx mvc \approx 1.4\times10^{13}\ \text{J}
\]

which is a few kilotons of TNT equivalent. Long before it “gently stopped” the car, it would likely fry, melt, ignite, or explosively damage it and its surroundings.

For comparison, an ordinary police radar gun emits milliwatts to tens of milliwatts. Its radiation pressure on a car is so tiny that it would take millions of years to noticeably slow the car.

So the direct answer is: to stop a speeding car using radar radiation pressure, you would need roughly terawatt-class power focused on the car, far beyond ordinary radar and catastrophically destructive.

items.question: What If All the CO2 in Bottled Soda Were Released into the Atmosphere?
human_answers: For most of the history of civilization, there were about 270 parts per million of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. In the last hundred years, industrial activity has pushed that number up (http://www.skepticalscience.com/print.php?r=45) to 400 parts per million. One "part per million" of CO2 weighs about 7.8 billion tons. A can of soda contains in the neighborhood of 2.2 grams of CO2, so you would need about 450 quadrillion cans of soda. That's enough to cover the Earth's land with ten layers of cans. [Image: image] There's clearly not enough room to do this. Even if we stacked the cans up to the edge of space,[1]I don't have any hard numbers, but my guess would be that you could probably stack supermarket soda six-pack crates a few hundred meters high before the bottom layer ruptures. they'd still take up an area the size of Rhode Island.[2]We shouldn't actually try it, given what happened last time (http://what-if.xkcd.com/8/). We'd need to add even more cans to keep up with ongoing emissions. We're currently increasing the atmosphere's CO2 concentration by an average of 2 parts per million each year: [Image: image] At that rate, we'd need to add one can of soda per person every 30 seconds, which is about 10,000 times the current consumption rate.[3]The global average (http://what-if.xkcd.com/74/) is one can per person every 5 days. In the US, the average is one every 18 hours. That would add a new layer of cans to the ground every 6[4]I originally had the wrong number here; thank you to Paulina for catching it! years or so. This layer of cans would get pretty annoying. [Image: image] Are there any ways out of this predicament? In some areas, you can turn in soda cans for recycling and receive a small amount of money; in Massachusetts, where I live, it's 5 cents. If you collected one year's worth of soda cans—instead of layering them across the Earth's surface—and emptied them out, you could redeem them for $372 trillion. With that much money, you could simply buy the world's current reserves[5]Source: xkcd.com/980 (http://xkcd.com/980), bottom right. of coal, oil, and natural gas—the source of the whole problem. Then, you put it all back in the ground and leave it there. [Image: image] Problem solved.
items.original_question: 全球瓶装碳酸饮料库存中含有多少 CO 2？需要多少苏打水才能使大气中的CO 2 恢复到工业化前的水平？
items.model_answer:
If all the CO₂ dissolved in bottled soda were released into the atmosphere, the global effect would be essentially negligible.

A typical liter of soda contains roughly 5–8 grams of CO₂, depending on carbonation level. Global carbonated soft-drink production is on the order of a few hundred billion liters per year, so even if an entire year’s worth of bottled soda released its CO₂ at once, that would be roughly 1–2 million metric tons of CO₂.

For comparison, the atmosphere contains about 7.8 billion metric tons of CO₂ per 1 ppm increase in concentration. So releasing all the CO₂ from a year’s worth of soda would raise atmospheric CO₂ by only about:

\[
\frac{1.5\text{ million tons}}{7.8\text{ billion tons/ppm}} \approx 0.0002\text{ ppm}
\]

That is far too small to matter for climate, weather, or global air composition. Human activity currently emits around 37 billion metric tons of CO₂ per year, so the CO₂ in all annual bottled soda is comparable to only minutes to perhaps half an hour of global fossil-fuel emissions.

Locally, if a huge amount were released in an enclosed warehouse or factory, CO₂ could build up and create an asphyxiation hazard. But in the open atmosphere, it would disperse quickly and have no meaningful global effect. Also, most soda CO₂ is released eventually anyway when bottles are opened and the drink goes flat or is consumed.

items.question: What If I Threw a Tungsten Countertop into the Sun?
human_answers: Not very far. With its high melting point, tungsten is a good[1]Except that the word "good" implies that you have some kind of goal you're working toward, which—given how strange the thing you're doing is—I'm not sure about. choice for a sundiving countertop. The first problem would be sunlight. As the countertop approached the Sun, it would heat up. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any element, but the Sun is one of the meltiest things in the Solar System. When the countertop got within a couple of solar radii, it would liquify. [Image: image] If you protected it with a heat shield of some kind, or dropped it from a sundiving spaceship, it could enter the Sun's atmosphere relatively intact. In this case, some interesting physical effects would destroy it.[2]"Some interesting physical effects would destroy it" summarizes the answers to a large percentage of the questions submitted to this blog. Because the Sun is so heavy, anything that falls to its surface will be accelerated to a tremendous speed by its gravity. A falling countertop would reach speeds of over 600 km/s—0.2% of the speed of light. (Our rockets can only accelerate spacecraft to 10-20 km/s.) From the countertop's point of view, particles from the Sun's atmosphere would be slamming into it at 600 km/s. These particles would pack quite a punch.[3]From a particle physics point of view, the individual protons would have energy of about 2 keV. When the countertop got within about a few thousand kilometers[4]I don't want another unit-related word to mentally keep track of, but it's always seemed a little weird that we don't call thousands of kilometers "megameters". of the Sun's surface, these collisions would start delivering more energy to the countertop than the sunlight. The collisions would fling individual tungsten atoms away from the surface—a process called sputtering (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputtering). Between the sputtering and ordinary heating from the impacts, the countertop would start to absorb a lot of energy very quickly. If the countertop were larger, it could penetrate into the Sun's photosphere—the first layer beneath the "surface"—and potentially trigger a solar flare.[5]For a scientific discussion of this, see the article Impacts of comets onto the Sun and coronal mass ejections (http://meetings.copernicus.org/www.cosis.net/abstracts/EGU05/04384/EGU05-J-04384.pdf). For a science fiction discussion of this, see Stephen Baxter and Arthur C. Clarke's 2005 novel Sunstorm. But as it is, it wouldn't even make it through the Sun's atmosphere—it would be vaporized somewhere in the Sun's chromosphere. [Image: image] This brings us around to a key question: Who the hell has tungsten countertops? Sure, it has good heat tolerance. But I'd be nervous about using tungsten as a food-preparation surface. In September of 1994 (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8874460), a French soldier drank wine from a rifle barrel. Fifteen minutes later, he started having seizures. He was rushed to the hospital and treated for "acute tungsten intoxication"—the first known case in medical history. He reportedly made a full recovery, although concentrations of tungsten were present in all his body tissues for weeks. The lesson here is to use normal materials. Michael, just make your countertops out of granite and don't drop them in the Sun. And if you're a French soldier, please just drink wine like a normal person. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果我把钨制台面扔进太阳里，它会下降多远？
items.model_answer:
If you somehow got a tungsten countertop onto a Sun-grazing trajectory, it would not remain a countertop for long.

Tungsten is extremely heat-resistant: it melts at about 3422°C and boils at about 5555°C. But near the Sun, even before reaching the visible “surface,” solar radiation would heat it to thousands of degrees. It would glow white-hot and melt. Once it entered the solar atmosphere, it would be moving at hundreds of kilometers per second, and the ram pressure and frictional heating from plowing through solar plasma would rapidly tear it apart and vaporize it.

The Sun has no solid surface for it to “land” on. The countertop would become a cloud of tungsten vapor, then ionized tungsten plasma, mixing into the outer solar layers. Some of the material might be carried around by convection; over very long times, heavy atoms tend to diffuse downward, but for practical purposes it just becomes an utterly negligible impurity in the Sun.

The energy released could be locally dramatic. A roughly kitchen-sized tungsten slab might have a mass of hundreds of kilograms to over a ton, and falling into the Sun at solar escape speed would release energy comparable to tens of kilotons of TNT. But compared with the Sun, that is nothing: the Sun emits that much energy in far less than a trillionth of a second. There would be no meaningful effect on the Sun.

So the short answer is: it melts, vaporizes, ionizes, and disappears into the solar plasma, producing at most a tiny, brief flash by solar standards.

items.question: What If Earth Spun Fast Enough for a Day to Last One Second?
human_answers: If this is going to happen, I hope it doesn't happen late in the afternoon next Friday. The Earth rotates,[citation needed (https://web.archive.org/web/20151210155028/http://www.timecube.com/)] which means its midsection is being flung outward by centrifugal force.[1]Which is still a real thing (http://xkcd.com/123/). This centrifugal force isn't strong enough to overcome gravity and tear the Earth apart, but it's enough to flatten the Earth slightly and make it so you weigh almost a pound less at the Equator than you do at the poles.[2]This is due to several effects, including centrifugal force, the flattened shape of the Earth, and the fact that if you go far enough toward the pole in North America people start offering you poutine. If the Earth (and everything on it) were suddenly sped up so that a day only lasted one second, the Earth wouldn't even last a single day.[3]Either kind. The Equator would be moving at over 10% of the speed of light. Centrifugal force would become much stronger than gravity, and the material that makes up the Earth would be flung outward. [Image: image] You wouldn't die instantly—you might survive for a few milliseconds or even seconds. That might not seem like much, but compared to the speed at which you'd die in other What If articles (http://what-if.xkcd.com/1/) involving relativistic speeds, it's pretty long. The Earth's crust and mantle would break apart into building-sized chunks. By the time a second[4]I mean, a day. had passed, the atmosphere would have spread out too thin to breathe—although even at the relatively stationary poles, you probably wouldn't survive long enough to asphyxiate. [Image: image] In the first few seconds, the expansion would shatter the crust into spinning fragments and kill just about everyone on the planet, but that's relatively peaceful compared to what would happen next. Everything would be moving at relativistic speeds, but each piece of the crust would be moving at close to the same speed at its neighbors. This means things would be relatively calm ... until the disk hit something. The first obstacle would be the belt of satellites around the Earth. After 40 milliseconds, the ISS would be struck by the edge of the expanding atmosphere and would be vaporized instantly. More satellites would follow. After a second and a half, the disc would reach the belt of geostationary satellites orbiting above the Equator. Each one would release a violent burst of gamma rays as the Earth consumed it. [Image: image] The debris from the Earth would slice outward like an expanding buzzsaw. The disk would take about ten seconds to pass the Moon, another hour to spread past the Sun, and would span the Solar System within a day or two. Each time the disc engulfed an asteroid, it would spray a flood of energy in all directions, eventually sterilizing every surface in the Solar System. Since the Earth is tilted, the Sun and the planets aren't usually lined up with the plane of the Earth's equator. They'd have a good chance of avoiding the buzzsaw[5]I keep reading this as "Buzzfeed". directly. However, Next Friday, April 25th, the Moon will cross the plane of the Earth's equator (as it does every two weeks). If Dylan sped up the Earth at this moment, the Moon would be right in the path of the resulting planetary buzzsaw. The impact would turn the moon into a comet, sending it rocketing from the Solar System in a spray of debris. The flash of light and heat would be so bright that if you were standing at the surface of the Sun, it would be brighter above you than below. Every surface in the Solar System—Europa's ice, Saturn's rings, and Mercury's rocky crust—would be scoured clean ... [Image: image] ... by moonlight.
items.original_question: 如果地球自转加速到一天只持续一秒钟会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If Earth spun once every second, it would not be a faster version of today’s Earth with rapid sunrises and sunsets. It would be destroyed almost instantly.

A one-second rotation period means the equator would move at about:

\[
v = \frac{40{,}000\ \text{km}}{1\ \text{s}} \approx 40{,}000\ \text{km/s}
\]

That is about 13% the speed of light. The outward centrifugal acceleration at the equator would be roughly:

\[
a = \omega^2 R \approx 2.5 \times 10^8\ \text{m/s}^2
\]

That is about 25 million times stronger than Earth’s gravity.

So instead of feeling slightly lighter at the equator, everything would be flung outward with absurd violence. The oceans, atmosphere, crust, mantle, and eventually the whole planet would be torn apart. Earth’s gravity is far too weak to hold material moving that fast; the equatorial surface speed would be thousands of times greater than orbital or escape velocity.

The rotational kinetic energy would also be enormous: around

\[
10^{39}\ \text{joules}
\]

which is millions of times larger than Earth’s gravitational binding energy. In other words, the energy associated with spinning Earth that fast would be vastly more than enough to rip the planet apart and vaporize or disperse much of it.

Relativistic effects would exist, since the equator would be moving at about 0.13c, but they would not be the main issue. The main issue is that Earth cannot remain a planet under those conditions.

So the direct answer is: if Earth spun fast enough for a day to last one second, Earth would catastrophically disintegrate into an expanding cloud or disk of rock, metal, gas, and plasma. There would be no survivable surface, no normal gravity, no stable atmosphere, and no meaningful “day” as we understand it.

items.question: What If Rain Broke a Windshield before Speed Did?
human_answers: Fast. [Image: image] Raindrops are tiny. Even in the heaviest rainstorms, the water in the air weighs less than the air itself (which is one of several reasons you can't swim upward in a rainstorm). Even at very high speeds, they can't break a windshield via their momentum alone. Under ordinary circumstances, raindrops don't damage car windshields at all. However, they can destroy the windows of supersonic aircraft. Here's what happens when a raindrop hits a glass surface at high speed: When the droplet makes contact with the surface, a shockwave travels back up through the droplet. [Image: image] Normally, this shockwave would move at the speed of sound within the liquid—about 1300 m/s, four times faster than in air. However, at high impact speeds, this shockwave actually moves substantially faster than the speed of sound in water. The water is squeezed between the incoming drop and the glass surface, which makes it squirt sideways in all directions. These jets of water can move even faster than the original (already supersonic) droplet, and even faster than the shockwaves we mentioned. [Image: image] One paper (http://e-collection.library.ethz.ch/eserv/eth:26251/eth-26251-02.pdf) ran a simulation of water droplets hitting a surface at 500 m/s (about Mach 1.5), and found that the water sprayed out from the point of contact at over 6000 m/s—Mach 18.[1]That's a pretty simple way to expel material at 6 km/s. I wonder if anyone's ever tried to come up with a spacecraft propulsion system using it ... The sharp pulse from the shockwave can crack glass. The highest pressures are found in the ring around the edge of the droplet, and only exist for a tiny fraction of the impact. [Image: image] In addition to the direct downward pressure, the water jetting sideways can cause damage, too. If the material has any microscopic holes, cracks, or bumps, those jets can strike them and create new cracks or widen existing ones. Even at high speeds, a raindrop won't create a bullet hole on its own—but a long series of supersonic droplets would start to eat away at the glass, cracking and pitting it like sand.[2]This type of "erosion" can also cause damage to steam turbine blades (http://www.technicaljournalsonline.com/ijeat/VOL%20II/IJAET%20VOL%20II%20ISSUE%20II%20APRIL%20JUNE%202011/ARTICLE%2014%20IJAET%20VOLII%20ISSUE%20II%20APRIL-%20JUNE%202011.pdf). Eventually, the windshield could fail catastrophically. Luckily, cars can't drive at Mach 1 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/61/) without lifting off, so your windshield is safe from ordinary rain. On the other hand, if you're driving under a thunderstorm with strong updrafts ... [Image: image] ... the precipitation can smash your windshield at any speed.
items.original_question: 如果下雨的话，挡风玻璃会被雨打碎，你需要以多快的速度行驶？
items.model_answer:
At normal road speeds, rain would not break a windshield before speed-related forces did. A raindrop is too light and too deformable: it splashes and spreads its energy over time and area, unlike a stone, which stays rigid and concentrates the impact.

A large 5 mm raindrop has a mass of only about 0.06 grams. At 70 mph, its kinetic energy is only around 0.03 joules. Even at 200 mph, it is still far less damaging than a small pebble at highway speed. Heavy rain also does not add much average force to the windshield; the momentum load from even torrential rain is tiny compared with the aerodynamic pressure from the air itself.

At very high speeds, though, the story changes. Around aircraft speeds — hundreds of miles per hour — raindrops can behave like tiny high-speed liquid projectiles. They can erode paint, damage coatings, pit surfaces, and eventually crack weaker transparent materials. Aircraft and missiles have to account for “rain erosion” for this reason.

For an ordinary car windshield, the likely sequence would be: wipers fail, visibility disappears, seals and bodywork suffer, aerodynamic loads become extreme, and only at very high subsonic speeds might raindrop impacts begin seriously pitting or cracking the glass. By then the car itself would be in far more trouble from speed, drag, lift, vibration, and loss of control.

So if the question is whether rain alone could shatter a windshield before sheer speed and airflow became destructive: practically, no. Rain could become damaging at aircraft-like speeds, but for a car the speed-related forces and overall vehicle failure would almost certainly arrive first.

items.question: What If You Drank the Blood of a Drunk Person?
human_answers: You would have to drink a lot of blood. A person contains about 5 liters of blood, or 14 glasses. [Image: image] If your blood is more than about half a percent alcohol, you stand a pretty good chance of dying. There have been a handful of cases of people surviving with a blood alcohol level of above 1%, but the LD50—the level at which 50% of people will die—is 0.40 (http://www.nellis.af.mil/shared/media/document/AFD-110211-015.pdf) (0.4%). If someone had a BAC of 0.40, and you drank all 14 glasses of their blood in a short amount of time,[1]Hey, there's a 50% chance they were going to die anyway. you would throw up: [Image: image] You wouldn't throw up because because of the alcohol; you'd just throw up because you're drinking blood. If you somehow avoided vomiting, you would have ingested a total of 20[2]Thank you to Conor Braman, among others, for correcting a missing zero in the original version of this calculation. grams of ethanol, which is the amount you'd get from a pint of beer. [Image: image] Depending on your weight, drinking that much blood could raise your own blood alcohol level to about 0.05. This is low enough that you could legally drive in many jurisdictions, but high enough to double your risk of an accident if you did. If your BAC is 0.05, it means only 1/8th of the alcohol from the other person's blood made it into yours. Supposing that after you drank all this blood, someone killed you and drank your blood,[3]It's only fair. they would then have a BAC of 0.006. If this process were repeated about 25 times, there would be fewer than 8 molecules of ethanol left in the last person's blood. After a few more cycles, there would likely be none;[4]By homeopathic standards, this is still quite concentrated. they'd just be drinking regular blood.[5]Like a loser. Whether there's any alcohol in it or not, drinking 14 glasses of blood wouldn't be fun.
