items.model_answer:
Strictly speaking, “the speed of light is 100 times faster” is not fully meaningful by itself, because \(c\) is a dimensional constant. Physics only changes if dimensionless ratios change, such as particle speeds compared with \(c\), the fine-structure constant, or gravitational compactness \(GM/(Rc^2)\). If all dimensionless constants stayed the same, then saying \(c\) is 100 times larger would mostly amount to using different units, with no observable change.

But if we mean that the universe is otherwise like ours while the limiting speed for light, gravity, and causality is \(100c\), then the effects would be large.

Light-travel times would shrink by a factor of 100. Sunlight would reach Earth in about 5 seconds instead of 8 minutes 20 seconds. A radio message to the Moon would take about 0.013 seconds one way instead of 1.3 seconds. Interstellar communication would still not be instant, but Alpha Centauri would be about 16 days away by light signal rather than 4.3 years.

Relativity would become much harder to notice at ordinary speeds. Since relativistic effects depend on \(v/c\), objects moving at today’s high speeds would be far less relativistic. GPS corrections, particle accelerator behavior, time dilation, and length contraction would all be much smaller unless particles were accelerated to much higher speeds. The new rest energy would be

\[
E = mc^2
\]

with \(c\) 100 times larger, so rest energy per unit mass would be 10,000 times larger. If mass defects in nuclear reactions remained comparable, nuclear reactions would release vastly more energy. However, in a fully consistent universe, nuclear binding itself would probably also change.

Gravity would also look less relativistic. Black holes would be much harder to form, because the Schwarzschild radius

\[
r_s = \frac{2GM}{c^2}
\]

would be 10,000 times smaller for the same mass. Many objects that are black holes in our universe would no longer be black holes under the same mass and size. General-relativistic effects such as gravitational time dilation, light bending, and orbital precession would be much weaker. Gravitational waves would also travel 100 times faster.

Electromagnetism and atomic physics could change drastically depending on what else is held fixed. The speed of light is tied to electric and magnetic constants, and changing it can change the fine-structure constant, which controls the strength of electromagnetic interactions in atoms. If the change made electromagnetism effectively weaker, chemistry, atomic spectra, stellar fusion, and material properties could be very different. If instead the dimensionless electromagnetic constants were somehow preserved, ordinary chemistry might look more familiar, but relativistic fine-structure effects would be reduced.

Cosmologically, the observable universe could be much larger in causal contact, because light and gravitational influence would cross space 100 times faster. The horizon problem would be less severe. Signals from distant galaxies would arrive sooner, and causal processes in the early universe could smooth regions over larger distances.

For everyday life, the most obvious effects would be faster communication and weaker relativistic limitations. Electronics and computers would not automatically become 100 times faster, because they are also limited by material properties, heat, quantum effects, and circuit design, but signal propagation delays would be much smaller. Astronomy would be less delayed: we would see solar-system events almost in real time, though distant stars and galaxies would still be viewed in the past.

So, in short: if the causal speed of the universe were truly 100 times higher while other familiar quantities stayed similar, the universe would be less relativistic, communication would be much faster, black holes would be rarer and smaller, rest-mass energy would be 10,000 times larger, and many details of atoms, stars, and cosmology could change profoundly.

items.model_answer:
Humans could survive on an oxygen-bearing planet only if the atmosphere had the right oxygen partial pressure and lacked harmful gases. The mere presence of oxygen would not make the planet breathable.

The key factor is not the percentage of oxygen, but its partial pressure: how much oxygen pressure is available to the lungs. On Earth at sea level, oxygen is about 21% of a 1-atmosphere atmosphere, giving an oxygen partial pressure of about 21 kPa. Humans can tolerate some variation, but if the oxygen partial pressure is too low, they become hypoxic; if it is too high for long periods, oxygen becomes toxic.

For example, an atmosphere with 10% oxygen at twice Earth’s pressure could feel roughly as oxygen-rich as Earth’s air. But an atmosphere with 21% oxygen at only half Earth’s pressure would be like being at high altitude and could cause altitude sickness or suffocation. Conversely, a very oxygen-rich or high-pressure atmosphere could cause lung and nervous-system damage over time and would make fires extremely easy to start and spread.

The rest of the atmosphere matters just as much. Nitrogen is not biologically required; humans could breathe oxygen mixed with argon, helium, neon, or other mostly inert gases if the pressure were suitable. But some gases would be dangerous even in small amounts. High carbon dioxide would cause headaches, panic, acidosis, unconsciousness, or death. Carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, chlorine, ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, or many volcanic and industrial-type gases could make the atmosphere lethal despite the presence of oxygen.

Total atmospheric pressure would also matter. If pressure were too low, humans could not breathe effectively and exposed body fluids could begin to boil at extremely low pressures. If pressure were too high, breathing could become physically difficult, inert gases could cause narcosis, and decompression sickness could become a risk when returning to lower pressure.

So the short answer is: if the planet had an oxygen partial pressure near Earth’s, tolerable total pressure, low carbon dioxide, no toxic contaminants, and acceptable temperature and humidity, humans could breathe and survive there, at least in the short term. If any of those conditions were far outside human limits, they would need breathing equipment, pressure suits, or sealed habitats—or they would quickly become ill or die.

items.model_answer:
You couldn’t reliably guarantee a false archaeological interpretation 4,000 years later, but the most plausible way—at a high level—would be to create an ambiguous disaster signature rather than a distinctive one.

Archaeologists infer causes from patterns: burn layers, collapsed walls, weapon trauma, mass graves, tsunami deposits, volcanic ash, impact glass, unusual isotopes, rebuilding gaps, written records, and regional comparisons. The easiest causes to misread are those that produce similar remains. A city destroyed by collapse followed by fire, abandonment, erosion, looting, and later rebuilding could be mistaken for an earthquake, siege, accidental conflagration, or social collapse depending on what survives.

The most misleading scenario would therefore be something like: widespread structural collapse, intense but ordinary-looking fires, loss of records, rapid abandonment, and centuries of natural disturbance afterward. That kind of layered destruction can leave archaeologists arguing between “earthquake,” “war,” “urban fire,” “famine-driven abandonment,” or “political collapse.”

By contrast, exotic methods are harder to hide. A volcanic eruption leaves tephra and chemical fingerprints. A tsunami leaves marine sediments and distinctive debris patterns. A meteor impact leaves shocked minerals and impact glass. Nuclear destruction would likely leave abnormal isotopic and material signatures, even if many short-lived radionuclides decayed.

So the direct answer is: the best way to make future archaeologists misread the cause would not be to obliterate everything with a unique signature, but to produce a common-looking destruction layer—rubble, ash, abandonment, and post-disaster disturbance—that resembles several ordinary ancient catastrophes at once. The ambiguity, not the completeness of destruction, is what would fool them.

items.model_answer:
A birdlike species that almost never touched the ground would likely resemble an extreme version of swifts, frigatebirds, albatrosses, and some seabirds: an animal whose entire body plan, life cycle, and behavior were organized around continuous flight.

The most important point is that “almost never” is biologically plausible, while “literally never” is much harder. Flight can handle feeding, travel, mating, sleeping, and escape, but reproduction usually requires some place to put eggs or young. So such a species would probably still use cliffs, tree cavities, floating vegetation, hanging nests, or isolated rock ledges for breeding, even if it almost never landed on flat ground.

Its anatomy would be highly specialized for efficient flight. It would probably have long, narrow wings for soaring or very high-aspect wings for gliding on thermals and wind currents. If it lived over oceans, it might exploit dynamic soaring like albatrosses, using wind gradients over waves to travel huge distances with little flapping. If it lived inland, it might follow rising warm air, storms, insect swarms, or seasonal winds. Its legs would be reduced, weak, or awkward on land, because walking would no longer matter much. Its feet might be adapted for clinging to vertical surfaces rather than standing, like swifts that cling to cliffs or walls.

Feeding would have to occur in the air or at the surface of water. It might catch insects, small flying animals, airborne seeds, spores, or pollen. A marine version could snatch fish, squid, or planktonic organisms from the water surface without landing. A scavenging form might take floating carrion or steal food from other flying animals. If it fed on insects, it could become a major aerial predator, shaping insect populations much like swallows, bats, and swifts do today.

Sleeping in flight is also possible in principle. Some modern birds can sleep with one brain hemisphere at a time, and frigatebirds have been observed sleeping during long flights. An extreme aerial species could take brief microsleeps while gliding, especially if it had stable wings and lived in predictable wind systems. It might spend days, weeks, or even months aloft, only returning to breeding sites seasonally.

Drinking would require special behavior. It could skim water from lakes or oceans, drink rain in flight, collect dew from leaves while hovering or brushing past vegetation, or obtain most of its water from food. If marine, it might have salt glands to remove excess salt, as many seabirds do.

Reproduction would be the main limiting factor. Eggs are heavy, fragile, and need incubation. A species that rarely touched the ground would likely nest on vertical cliffs, in caves, on high branches, on floating mats, or in colonies on predator-free islands. The young might be born or hatched highly developed, with strong wings relatively early. Chicks would need to launch successfully from a height, because landing on the ground could be fatal if their legs were poor and takeoff required dropping into air. This is similar to how some cliff-nesting birds rely on gravity and open space for their first flight.

A more extreme evolutionary path could involve fewer, larger offspring and intense parental care. The parents might feed the young entirely in midair once they fledge, transferring food during flight. Courtship and mating could also happen in the air, with elaborate aerial displays, synchronized gliding, and brief contact during flight.

Such a species would be very safe from most ground predators, but it would have other vulnerabilities. It would depend heavily on wind, weather, and open airspace. Storms, smoke, volcanic ash, or prolonged calm could be dangerous. Destruction of nesting cliffs or aerial feeding zones could be catastrophic. Because it could not forage easily on land, ecological disruptions affecting flying insects, ocean surfaces, or wind patterns would hit it hard.

Evolutionarily, this species would probably become less and less “land-capable” over time. Its legs would shrink, its feet would specialize, its bones and muscles would optimize for endurance flight, and its behavior would avoid landing except at nesting sites. On the ground it might be clumsy, vulnerable, and unable to take off without a drop or strong headwind.

So the result would be an animal that lives in the sky the way fish live in water: feeding, sleeping, migrating, courting, and escaping almost entirely in the air. It would not be impossible, because Earth already has partial examples. But its life would still be anchored—literally and evolutionarily—by reproduction, because even the most aerial birdlike species would need some safe place for the next generation to begin.

items.model_answer:
A human pig cavalry would be a bad idea in almost every practical sense.

The main problem is size and load. A cavalry mount has to carry a rider, saddle, weapons, armor, and supplies while still being fast and controllable. A typical adult soldier with gear might weigh 90–120 kg. Pack and riding animals usually should not carry much more than about 15–25% of their body weight for sustained work. That means you would want a pig weighing perhaps 400–600 kg, and not just weighing that much, but being athletic at that size. Some domestic pigs can reach enormous weights, but the really huge ones are usually not fast, durable, or structurally suited for riding. They are livestock, not mounts.

Pigs also have the wrong body plan. They have short legs, low ground clearance, and backs not well shaped for supporting a seated rider over distance. A horse’s long legs, shoulder structure, spine, and gait make it efficient as a riding animal. A pig could maybe carry a small child briefly, but an adult rider would be uncomfortable for both pig and rider and likely injure the animal if done seriously.

Speed and endurance are also poor compared with cavalry animals. Pigs and wild boars can sprint surprisingly fast over short distances, but cavalry needs controlled movement, formation, long marches, charges, retreats, and repeated action. Pigs overheat easily, do not sweat like horses, and are not built for sustained high-speed travel.

Training would be another problem. Pigs are intelligent and trainable, but cavalry mounts need to tolerate noise, weapons, blood, crowds, other animals, and confusing commands under stress. Pigs can be stubborn, panicky, aggressive, and extremely food-motivated. A frightened formation of battle pigs would probably scatter, bite, crash into things, or run toward whatever smells interesting.

There is one historical exception: pigs were supposedly used in war to frighten elephants, especially by setting them on fire or using their squeals to panic enemy animals. That is not cavalry, though; that is battlefield chaos using pigs as terror weapons. It says more about elephants disliking screaming pigs than about pigs being good mounts.

If you tried to build pig cavalry anyway, the closest workable version would be very small riders on very large, selectively bred pigs, used only for short-distance novelty or intimidation. They would be slower, less controllable, less durable, and less useful than horse, camel, mule, or even dog-based transport systems. As a military arm, pig cavalry would be expensive comic disaster: terrifying at close range, but mostly to its own side.

items.model_answer:
If everyone on Earth vanished except 35 people, the main question would be whether those 35 are scattered randomly or placed together.

If they were random people in random locations, humanity would almost certainly die out. Most survivors would be alone or separated by oceans and continents, with no functioning communication, transport networks, or supply chains. Even if some survived for years by scavenging, they probably would not find enough other survivors to rebuild a breeding population.

If the 35 people were together, healthy, and included enough young fertile men and women, survival would be possible but extremely difficult.

Modern civilization would collapse almost immediately. Power grids would fail within hours to days. Water treatment, fuel distribution, hospitals, the internet, shipping, and food logistics would stop. Nuclear reactors would mostly shut down automatically, though some industrial sites, chemical plants, oil refineries, and unattended fires could create local disasters. Satellites would keep orbiting for a while but become useless as ground systems failed.

For the first few years, the survivors would have access to enormous abandoned resources: canned food, tools, vehicles, medicines, books, seeds, clothing, weapons, and shelter. Their best strategy would be to move to a mild, fertile region with fresh water, arable land, livestock, and existing infrastructure. They would need to focus on farming, sanitation, childbirth, basic medicine, tool repair, and defense against accidents and wild animals.

But 35 people could not maintain industrial society. They could not run factories, mines, global supply chains, semiconductor plants, hospitals, universities, and power systems. Within decades, most advanced technology would become unusable. The survivors would likely fall back to a small agrarian or preindustrial community, using scavenged modern materials for as long as they lasted.

The biggest long-term problem would be genetics. Thirty-five people is a very small founder population. If they were unrelated, young, healthy, and reproduction were carefully managed, humanity might survive, but inbreeding would become a serious danger. Genetic diseases, low fertility, and vulnerability to epidemics could threaten the group. If the 35 included many elderly people, children, close relatives, or too few women of reproductive age, extinction would be likely. A viable long-term human population is usually safer with hundreds or thousands of unrelated individuals, not dozens.

The natural world would change dramatically. Greenhouse gas emissions would stop, though climate change would continue for some time due to existing carbon dioxide. Cities would decay, roads would crack, buildings would collapse over decades to centuries, and forests and animals would reclaim much of the planet. Many domestic animals would die, while some—dogs, cats, pigs, goats, cattle, chickens—might survive feral in certain regions.

So the short answer is: 35 random survivors probably means the end of humanity. Thirty-five carefully chosen, colocated, cooperative survivors might preserve the species, but they would not preserve modern civilization. Earth would mostly rewild, and the future of humans would depend on whether that tiny group could farm, reproduce, avoid disease, and manage inbreeding for many generations.

After 50 years on the seafloor, a Cold War submarine would usually still be recognizable as a submarine, but it would look like a dark, corroded, partly collapsed industrial wreck rather than a clean “sunken vessel.”

If it lay in deep, cold water, the outline could remain surprisingly intact: a long cylindrical pressure hull, a sail/conning tower, broken masts, and pieces of casing or deck structure. Paint would be mostly gone or patchy. Steel surfaces would be covered with rust, corrosion nodules, and “rusticle”-like deposits. The thinner outer casing, deck plating, railings, sonar fairings, and exposed equipment would be far more degraded than the thick pressure hull. Rubber coatings, anechoic tiles, gaskets, and sonar domes would likely be peeling, missing, or reduced to fragments.

If the submarine sank in shallow, oxygen-rich water, it would look much more decayed. It could be heavily encrusted with marine life: barnacles, corals, sponges, tube worms, algae, and shells depending on location. Sediment might bury the lower hull. Fishing nets or cables could be snagged on the sail and bow. Corrosion would be faster, and large sections of thin metal could be gone or collapsed.

The biggest factor is whether the pressure hull imploded. If the submarine was intact and flooded before reaching the bottom, it might sit fairly whole, like a corroded cigar-shaped wreck. But if it sank into deep water with compartments still sealed, pressure could crush it violently. In that case, after 50 years it would look torn open: the pressure hull ruptured, bow or stern sections separated, machinery exposed, and a debris field spread around it. Many real deep-ocean submarine wrecks show this kind of damage.

Inside, compartments would be dark, silted, and heavily corroded. Bulkheads, pipes, valves, bunks, control panels, and machinery might survive in recognizable form, but delicate items would be gone or buried. Batteries would be degraded; acid would long since have mixed and neutralized, though lead and other materials would remain. Torpedoes, if present, could still be hazardous. A nuclear-powered submarine’s reactor compartment would likely remain a distinct, heavily built section; it would not “glow,” but it could pose contamination and corrosion concerns depending on damage and conditions.

So, in visual terms: a Cold War submarine after 50 years would probably be a rusted, sediment-dusted, marine-encrusted hull with a battered sail, missing fittings, torn or collapsed thin structures, and possibly a debris field if it imploded—still identifiable, but clearly transformed by pressure, corrosion, biology, and time.
